FAIRY

Pages 5-6

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> traditions and romances, signifies a sort of deity, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> imaginary genius, conversant on the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and distinguished by a variety of fantastical actions either good or bad. They were most usually imagined to be women of an order superior to <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, yet subject to wants, passions, accidents, and even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; sprightly and benevolent while young and handsome; morose, peevish, and malignant, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ugly, or in the decline of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>; fond of appearance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, whence they are often called the white ladies. Concerning these imaginary beings, no less a person than Jervaise de Tilleberry, marshal of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARLES">Arles</a>, who lived in the beginning of the 13th century, writes thus in a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Otho IV. "It has been asserted by persons of unexceptionable <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREDIT">credit</a>, that fairies used to choose themselves gallants from among men, and rewarded their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> with an affluence of worldly goods; but if they married, or boasted of a fairy's favours, they as severely smarted for such indiscretion." The like tales still go current in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUEDOC">Languedoc</a>; and throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a>, there is not a village without some ancient seat or cavern which had the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of being a fairy's residence, or at least some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> where a fairy used to bathe. This idea of fairies has a near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFINITY">affinity</a> with that of the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, concerning the nymphs of the woods, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>; and an ancient scholiast on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEOCRITUS">Theocritus</a> says, "The nymphs are demons which appear on the mountains in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of women;" and what is more surprising, the Arabs and other orientals have their ginn and peri, of whom they entertain the like notions. But fairies have been likewise described as of either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a>, and generally as of minute stature, though capable of assuming various forms and dimensions. The most charming representation imaginable of these children of romantic fancy, is in the Midsummer Night's Dream of Shakespeare; in referring to which, we no doubt have been anticipated by the recollection of almost every reader. Spenser's Faery Queene is an epic poem, under the persons and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> of fairies. This sort of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a> raises a pleasing kind of horror in the mind of the reader, and amuses his imagination with the strangeness and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOVELTY">novelty</a> of the persons who are represented in it; but, as a vehicle of instruction, the judicious object to it, as not having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> enough to make any moral <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-IMPRESSION">impression</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELIEF">belief</a> of fairies still subsists in many parts of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. The "Swart fairy of the mine" (of German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>), has scarce yet quitted our subterraneous works; (vid. next article.) Puck, or Robin Good-Fellow, still haunts many of our villages. And in many parts of Scotland, new born children are watched till the christening is over, lest they should be stolen or changed by some of these fantastical existences. FAIRY of the Mine; an imaginary being, an inhabitant of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINES">mines</a>. The Germans believed in two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>; one fierce and malevolent: the other a gentle <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, appearing like little old men dressed like the miners, and not much above two feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. These wander about the drifts and chambers of the works; seem perpetually employed, FAIRY Circle or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">Ring</a>, a phenomenon pretty frequent in the fields, &c., supposed by the vulgar to be traced by the fairies in their dances. There are two kinds of it; one of about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> yards in diameter, containing a round bare path, a foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, with green grass in the middle of it. The other is of different bigness, encompassed with a circumference of grass. Messrs. Jessop and Walker, in the Philosophical Transactions, ascribe them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a>; which is thought to be confirmed by their being most frequently produced after storms of that kind, as well as by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and brilliancy of the grass roots when first observed. Lightning, like all other fires, moves round, and burns more in the extremity than in the middle: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> circle arises from the first, the grass burnt up growing very plentifully afterwards. Others maintain that these circles are made by ants, which are frequently found in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers therein.—Mr. Cavallo, in his treatise on <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELECTRICITY">electricity</a>, does not think that lightning is at all concerned in the formation of them: "They are not (says he) always of a circular figure; and, as I am informed, they seem to be rather beds of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSHROOMS">mushrooms</a> than the effects of lightning." We have frequently observed beds of mushrooms arranged in a circular form like what are called fairy rings; but it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be difficult to account for the mushroom feed being disposed in this manner. It is probable that the feed is dispersed over the whole field, and remains dormant till it is acted on by some stimulus to excite its vegetating powers. Perhaps this stimulus is atmospheric electricity, which acting on particular spots only, produces on them an abundant crop of mushrooms, while none appear in other places.

FAITH

Pages 6-6

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">Theology</a>, that assent which we give to a proposition advanced by another, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of which we do not immediately perceive from our own reason <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>; or it is a judgment or assent of the mind, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTIVE">motive</a> whereof is not any intrinsic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>, but the authority or testimony of some other who reveals or relates it. Hence, as there are two kinds of authorities and testimonies, the one of God, and the other of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, faith becomes distinguished into divine and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>. Divine Faith, is that founded on the authority of God; or it is that assent we give to what is revealed by God. The objects of this faith, therefore, are matters of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a>. See Revelation and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">Religion</a>. Human Faith, is that whereby we believe what is told us by men. The object hereof is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of human testimony and evidence. See <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-METAPHYSICS">Metaphysics</a>. Faith, in practical theology, makes the first of the theological virtues or graces. Faith in God, in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, denotes such a conviction of his being, perfections, character, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, as produces <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a>, trust, worship, obedience, and resignation. Faith in Christ, as it has been defined by some, is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> assent to the gospel as true; according to others, it signifies such a persuasion that he is the Messiah, and such a desire and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPECTATION">expectation</a> of the blessings which he has promised in his gospel to his sincere disciples, as engage the mind to fix its dependence upon him, and subject itself to him in all the ways of holy obedience. See Theology. Faith, likewise, in respect to futurity, is a moral principle, implying faith a conviction of the reality and importance of a future state, as is sufficient to regulate the temper and conduct. Fides, or Fidelity (Fides), was deified by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, and had a temple in the Capitol consecrated to her by Attilius Catalinus. Her priests wore <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> veils: unbloody sacrifices were offered to her, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> were taken in her name. Horace clothes her in white, places her in the retinue of Fortune, and makes her the filter of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">Justice</a>, Od. 24, 35. l. i. Public Faith is represented in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of medals; sometimes with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a> of fruit in one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and some ears of corn in the other; and sometimes holding a turtle-dove. But the most usual symbol is two <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> joined together. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> are generally, Fides Augufis, Fides Exercitus, or Fides Militum, &c.

FAITHORN

Pages 6-6

WILLIAM, an ingenious English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTIST">artist</a>, a native of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLE">disciple</a> of Peak the painter, and worked with him three <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four years. At the breaking out of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, Peak espoused the cause of his sovereign: and Faithorn, who accompanied his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>, was taken prisoner by the rebels at Baringhouse, from whence he was sent to London, and confined in Aldergate. In this uncomfortable situation he exercised his graver; and a small head of the first Villars <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCKINGHAM">Buckingham</a>, in the style of Melan, is reckoned among his performances at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. The solicitations of his friends in his favour at last prevailed; and he was released from prison, with permission to retire to the continent. In France he found protection and encouragement from the Abbé de Marolles; and it was at this time that he formed an acquaintance with Nanteuil, from whose instructions he derived very considerable advantages. About the year 1650 he returned to England, and soon after married the filter of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Croun. By her he had two sons; Henry, who was a bookeller, and William an engraver in mezzotinto. Faithorn opened a shop near Temple-<a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">Bar</a>, where he sold not only his own engravings, but those of other English artists, and imported a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, France, and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. About the year 1680, he retired from his shop, and resided in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">Printing</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">House</a> Yard; but he still <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> for the bookellers, especially Royton, Martin, and Peak the younger, his former master's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a>. He painted portraits from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in crayons; which art he learned of Nanteuil during his abode in France. He also painted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINIATURE">miniature</a>; and his performances in both these styles were much esteemed. His spirits were broken by the indifferency and dilapidation of his son William; and a lingering consumption put an end to his life in 1691. He wrote a book Upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">Drawing</a>, Graving, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETCHING">Etching</a>, for which he was celebrated by his friend Thomas Flatman the poet.

FAKIRS

Pages 6-7
Indian monks or friars. They outdo the fervency and mortification of the ancient Ancho- rets or Solitaries. Some of them make a vow of con- tinuing all their lifetime in one posture, and keep it effectually. Others never lie down; but continue in a standing posture all their lives, supported only by a stick, or rope under their arm pits. Some mangle their bodies with scourges and knives. They look upon themselves to have conquered every passion, and triumphed over the world; and accordingly scruple not, as if in a state of innocence, to appear entirely naked in public. The common people of East India are thoroughly persuaded of the virtue and innocence of the fakirs; notwithstanding which, they are accused of commit- ting the most enormous crimes in private. They have also another kind of fakirs, who do not practice such severities: these flock together in com- panies, and go from village to village; prophesying, and telling fortunes. They are wicked villains, and it is dangerous for a man to meet them in a lone place: nevertheless, the Indian idolaters have them in the ut- most veneration. They make use of drums, trumpets, and other musical instruments, to rouse their souls, and work themselves up to an artificial ecstacy, the better to publish their pretended prophecies. Some of the votaries of these fakirs most devoutly kiss their privy parts; and they receive this monstrous declaration of respect with a kind of ecstatic pleasure. The most sober and discreet Indians consult them in this preposterous attitude; and their female votaries converse with them a considerable time with the most indecent freedom. The fire they burn is made of cows dung, dried in the sun. When they are disposed to sleep, they repose themselves on cows dung, and sometimes on ordure itself. They are so indulgent towards every living creature, that they suffer themselves to be overrun with vermin, or stung by insects, without the least re- luctancy or complaint. It is more than probable, those Indian friars have some secret art to kill their senses asleep, in order to render themselves in a great measure insensible of the excessive torments they voluntarily undergo. Oving- ton affirms us, that "as he was one day in an assem- bly of fakirs, he observed, that they drank opiates in- fused in water; the intoxicating virtue thereof was enough to turn their brain." The garment of the chief fakirs consists of three or four yards of orange-colored linen, which they tie round them, and a tiger's skin, which hangs over their shoulders. Their hair is woven in tresses, and forms a kind of turban. The superior of the fakirs is distin- guished from the rest by having a greater number of pieces in his garment, and by a chain of iron, two yards long, tied to his leg. When he deigns to rest in any place, a garment is spread upon the ground; on which he sits and gives audience, whilst his disciples publish his virtues. Some persons of quality in India have become fa- kirs: among others, five great lords belonging to the court of Shah Gahan, Mogul of the Indies. It is said, there are about two millions of fakirs in the East In- dies.

FALASHA

Pages 7-8

a people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>, of Jewish ori- gin, described by Mr Bruce, who was at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> pains to acquaint himself with their <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> by cultivating the friendship of the most learned persons among them he could meet with. According to the accounts received from them, the Falasha are the descendants of those Jews who came from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALESTINE">Palestine</a> into Ethiopia, as attendants of Menilek the son of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Sheba <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Saba by <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLOMON">Solomon</a>. They agree in the relations given by the Abyssinians of that princess, but deny that the posterity of those who came with Menilek ever embraced the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, as the Abyssinians say they did. They say, that at the decline of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, when the ports of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a> fell into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of other na- tions, and no intercourse took <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> between them and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>, the Jewish inhabitants quitted the sea coasts and retired into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEMBEA">Dembea</a>. While they remained in the cities on the Red Sea, they exercised the trade of brick and tile making, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POTTERY">pottery</a>, thatching houses, &c., and after leaving the sea coasts, they chose the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of Dembea on account of the plenty of materials afforded for exercising the trades they pro- fessed. Here they carried the art of pottery to a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, multiplied exceedingly, and became very numerous and powerful about the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that the Abyssinians were converted to Chris- tianity. As this event was accounted by them an apo- tasy from the true religion, they now separated them- selves from the Abyssinians, and declared one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHINEAS">Phineas</a>, of the line of Solomon, their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>. Thus they say, they have still a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of Judah for their sovereign, though their affection is treated with con- tempt, and a nickname bestowed on the Falashan fam- ily by the other Abyssinians. About the year 960, the queen of this people, after extirpating the Abyssi- nian princes on the rock Damo, assumed the sover- eignty of the whole empire, which they retained for some time; but their power being by degrees reduced, they were obliged to take up their residence among the rugged <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> of Samen; one of which they chose for their <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a>, and which has ever since been called the Jew's Rock. About the year 1600, they were al- most entirely ruined by an overthrow from the Abyssi- nians, in which both their king and queen were slain; since which time they have been in subjection to the emperors of that country, but are still governed by their own princes. When Mr Bruce was in Abyssinia they were supposed to amount to about 100,000 effective men. Gideon and Judith were the names of the king and queen at that time; and these, according to our author, seem to be preferred to others for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> family. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of this people is very different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a>, Samaritan, or any other which the Jews ever spoke in their own country. On being interro- gated concerning it by Mr Bruce, they said, that it was probably one of those spoken by the nations on the Red Sea, among whom they had settled at their first coming. They arrived in Abyssinia speaking Hebrew, and with the advantage of having books in that lan- guage; but had now forgot it, which indeed is not to be wondered at, as they had lost their Hebrew books, and were entirely ignorant of the art of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. At the time of their leaving Jerusalem, they were in pos- session both of the Hebrew and Samaritan copies of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; but when their fleet was destroyed in the time of Rehoboam, and no farther <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMUNICATION">communication</a> with Jerusalem took place, they were obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> translations of the Scriptures, or those copies which were in possession of the shepherds, who, they say, were all Jews before the time of Solomon. On being asked, however, where the shepherds got their copy, and being told, that notwithstanding the invasion of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a> by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEBUCHADNEZZAR">Nebuchadnezzar</a>, there was still a communication with Jerusalem by means of the Ishmaelite Arabs through <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARABIA">Arabia</a>, they frankly acknowledged that they could not tell; neither had they any memorials of the history either of their own or any other country; all that they believed in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> being derived from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, their histories, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any existed, having been destroyed by the famous Moorish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> Gragné. They say that the first book of Scripture they received was that of Enoch; and they place that of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> immediately after it, supposing that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRIARCH">patriarch</a> to have lived soon after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>. They have no copy of the Old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TESTAMENT">Testament</a> in the Falasha language, what they make use of being in that of Geez. This is sold to them by the Abyssinian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a>, who are the only scribes in that country. No <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> takes place about corruptions of the text; nor do the Falasha know anything of the Jewish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALMUD">Talmud</a>, Targum, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABALA">Cabala</a>. See Abyssinia.

FALCADE

Pages 8-8

in the manege, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> when he throws himself upon his haunches two <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> three times, as in very quick curves; which is done in forming a stop and half stop. See Stop.

FALCATED

Pages 8-8

something in the form of a sickle; thus the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> is said to be falcated when she appears horned.

FALCO

Pages 8-8

the eagle, and hawk, a genus of birds belonging to the order of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCIPITRES">accipitres</a>. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALCON

Pages 8-8
or Falcon, a bird of prey of the hawk kind, superior to all others for courage, docility, gentleness, and nobleness of nature*. Several authors take the name falcon to have been occasioned by its crooked talons or pounces, which resemble a falx or sickle. Giraldus derives it à falcando, because it flies in a curve. The falcon, or falcon gentle, is both for the fist and for the lure. In the choice, take one that has wide nostrils, high and large eyelids, a large black eye; a round head, somewhat full on the top; barb feathers on the clap of the beaks, which should be short, thick, and of an azure colour; the breast large, round, and fleshy; and the thighs, legs, and feet, large and strong, with the fear of the foot soft and bluish: the pounces should be black, with wings long and crofling the train, which should be short and very pliable. The name falcon is refrained to the female: for the male is much smaller, weaker, and less courageous, than the female; and therefore is denominated taffel, or tirelet. The falcon is excellent at the river, brook, and even field; and flies chiefly at the larger game, as wild bole, kite, crow, heron, crane, pye, shoveler, &c. For further particulars, see Falconry and Hawking. The custom of carrying a falcon extended to many countries, and was esteemed a distinction of a man of rank. The Welsh had a saying, That you may know a gentleman by his hawk, horse, and greyhound. In fact, a person of rank seldom went without one on his hand. Harold, afterwards king of England, is painted going on a most important embassy, with a hawk on his hand and a dog under his arm. Henry VI. is represented at his nuptials, attended by a nobleman and his falcon. Even the ladies were not without them in earlier times; for in an ancient sculpture in the church of Milton Abbas, in Dorsetshire, appears the comfort of King Athelstan with a falcon on her royal fist tearing a bird.

FALCONER

Pages 8-8

William, an ingenious Scots sailor, who, about the year 1762, came up to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> with a pretty pathetic poem, called the Shipwreck, founded on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>. The publication of this piece recommended him to the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>; and he would in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> have been suitably preferred, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> shipwreck, as may be supposed, had not proved fatal to him, and to many gentlemen of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fortune with whom he failed. In 1770, he went out a volunteer in the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AURORA">Aurora</a> frigate, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to carry Messrs Vanfittart, Scrafton, and Ford, the supervisors appointed to regulate our East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> settlements; which vessel, after it had touched at the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope, was never more heard of. Before his departure, he published a very useful Marine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">Dictionary</a>, in one volume 4to.

FALCONRY

Pages 9-10

the art of training all manner of hawks, but more especially the larger ones called falcons, to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAWKING">hawking</a>. See Hawking. When a falcon is taken, the must be fed in such a manner, that, as the feeling slackens, she may see what provision lies before her; but care ought to be taken, not to feed her too hard. A falcon <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hawk newly taken should have all new furniture, as new jesses of good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, mailed leashes with buttons at the end, and new bewets. There should also be provided a small round stick, to stroke the hawk; because, the oftener this is done, the sooner and better <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> she be mannered. She must also have two good bells, that she may be found when she scattereth. Her hood should be well fashioned, raised, and embossed against her eyes, deep, and yet tight enough beneath, that it may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> about her head without hurting her; and her beak and talons must be a little coped, but not so near as to make them bleed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> it be a foar-falcon, which had already passed the seas, she will indeed be harder to reclaim, but will prove the best of falcons. Her food must be good and warm, and given her twice or thrice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, till she be full gorged: the best for this purpose is pigeons, larks, or other live birds; because she must be broken off by degrees from her accustomed feeding. When she is fed, you must hoop and lure, as you do when you call a hawk, that she may know when you intend to give her meat. On this occasion the must be unhooded gently; and after giving her two or three bits, her hood must be put on again, when she is to get two or three bits more. Care must be taken that she be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> fed; and after three or four days, her diet may be lessened: the falconer setting her every night to perch by him, that he may awaken her often in the night. In this manner he must proceed, till he find her to grow tame and gentle; and when she begins to feed eagerly, he may give her a sheep's heart. He may now begin to unhood her in the daytime; but it must be far from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, first giving her a bit or two, then hooding her gently, and giving her as much more. When she is sharp fed, he may now unhood her, and give her some meat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> against his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> and eyes, which will make her less afraid of the countenance of others. She must be borne continually on the silt, till she is properly mannered, causing her to feed in company, giving her in the morning, about sunrise, the wing of a pullet; and in the evening, the foot of a hare or coney, cut off above the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a>, flayed and laid in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, which being squeezed, is to be given her with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">pinion</a> of a hen's wing. For two or three days give her washed meat, and then plumage in more or less <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> as she is thought to be more or less foul within. After this, being hooded again, she Falcons, (Servius). Here they made an excellent sauce, Falernus called Ventus Faliscus (Martial). When the Falisci were besieged by Camillus, a schoolmaster went out of the gates of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> with his pupils, and proposed to betray them into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Roman enemy, that by such a possession he might easily oblige the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> to surrender. Camillus heard the proposal with indignation, and ordered the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to be stripped naked, and whipped back to the town by those whom his perfidy wished to betray. This instance of generosity operated upon the people so powerfully that they surrendered to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>.

FALERIUS

Pages 10-10

Mons Malicus (so called, Martial); Falernus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGER">ager</a>, a district at the foot of Mount Malicus in Campania; famous for its generous wines, (Horace, Pliny). Now called Monte Maffeo. FALISCI. See FALERII.

FALKIA

Pages 10-10

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the hexandria clas. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALKIRK

Pages 10-10

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STIRLINGSHIRE">Stirlingshire</a> in Scotland, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3° 48'. N. Lat. 56° 20'. It is a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> ill-built <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and is supported by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> cattle from the Highlands, it being computed that 24,000 head are annually sold there. A great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> is also got here by the carriage of goods landed at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARRON">Carron</a> wharf to Glasgow. This town is remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought in its neighbourhood between Edward I. of England, and the Scots commanded by the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEWARD">steward</a> of Scotland, Cummin of Bardenoch, and Sir William Wallace. The latter had been invested with the supreme command; but perceiving that this gave umbrage to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, he resigned his power into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the noblemen above mentioned, referring to himself only the command of a small body who refused to follow another leader. The Scots generals placed their pikemen along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a>, and lined the intervals between the three bodies of which their <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> was composed, with archers; and dreading the great superiority of the English cavalry, endeavoured to secure their front by palliadoes tied together with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>. The battle was fought on the 22nd of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1298. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of England divided his army likewise into three bodies; and by the superiority of his archers, defeated the Scots with great slaughter. Wallace alone preferred entire the troops he commanded; and retiring behind the Carron, marched leisurely along the banks of that river, which protected him from the enemy. In this battle fell John de Graham, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> much celebrated for his valour, and styled the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> of the gallant Wallace. His epitaph is still to be seen on a plain <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCHYARD">churchyard</a> of Falkirk. On the 18th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1746, a battle was fought here between the king's forces commanded by General Hawley, and the Highlanders headed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> Stuart. The former was seized with a panic, and fled; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> Halk with two regiments, who kept their ground, prevented the Highlanders from pursuing their victory. Extensive ruins are perceived in the neighbourhood of this town, supposed by some antiquarians to have been the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the Pictish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>; but others believe them to be the remains of some Roman stations.

FALKLAND

Pages 10-12

a small town of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIFESHIRE">Fifeshire</a> in Scotland, made a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> burgh by James II. in 1458. Here stood one of the seats of the Macduffs earls of Fife. On the attainer of Munro Stewart, the 17th <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a>, it became forfeited to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> in 1424. James V, who grew very fond of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, enlarged and improved it. The remains evince its former magnificence and elegance, and the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> of the princely <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. The gateway is placed between two fine round towers; on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> joins the chapel, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> is of wood, handsomely gilt and painted, but in a most ruinous condition. Beneath are several apartments. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> next to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> was beautifully adorned with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a>, heads in bas relief, and elegant columns not reducible to any order, but of fine proportion, with capitals approaching the Ionic scroll. Beneath some of these pillars was <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSCRIBED">inscribed</a> I. R. M. G. 1537, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Jacobus Rex, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARIA">Maria</a> de Guise.—This place was also a favourite residence of James VI, on account of the fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a> and plenty of deer. The east side was accidentally burnt in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II, and the park ruined during Cromwell's usurpation, when the fine oaks were cut <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in order to build the fort at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERTH">Perth</a>.—This place gives <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of viscount to the English family of Carey; Sir Henry Carey being so created by James VI. 1620. His son was the celebrated Lucius, who sacrificed his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in a fit of royal delirium at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEWBURY">Newbury</a>, and from whom the present family is lineally descended. Falkland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>. See Carey. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">Fall</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> of a heavy body towards the centre of the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>. It is also the name of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of length used in Scotland, containing five ells. Fall of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">Man</a>, in sacred <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, that terrible event by which sin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> were introduced into the world. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTEDILUVIANS">Antediluvians</a>, and Original Sin. The account which Moses gives of this transaction is extremely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> and concise. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENT">serpent</a>, he informs us, being more subtle than any beast of the field, asked the woman, whether it was true that God had not granted her and her husband leave to eat of every tree in the garden? She answered, That God had allowed them to eat of all, except only the fruit of the tree in the midst of the garden; which he commanded they should not taste, nor so much as touch, lest they should die. The serpent replied, That they should not die; for God knew the virtue of the tree; and that, so soon as they ate of it, their eyes would be opened, and they would become like gods, knowing good and evil. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVE">Eve</a>, seeing the fruit tempting to the view, took of the fruit and ate; and gave also to her husband of it, and he did eat. Immediately the eyes of both were opened; when perceiving they were naked, they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves aprons. Adam and Eve, hearing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of God walking in the garden in the cool of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, hid themselves among the trees; but, on God's calling for Adam, he excused himself for not appearing, because he was naked. God demanded of him, who it was that told him he was naked; and whether he had disobeyed his command, in eating the forbidden fruit? Adam confessed that the woman had offered him the fruit, and he had tasted it. She, being examined likewise, acknowledged what she had done; but said, the serpent had seduced and deceived her. God then proceeded to judgment; he first cursed the serpent above all beasts, and condemned him to go on his belly, and eat the dust; adding, that he would put enmity between him and the woman, and their offspring; that the seed of the woman should bruise the serpent's head, who should bruise the other's heel. The woman was subjected to the pains of childbirth, as well as to the dominion of her husband; and as to the man, God cursed the ground for his sake, declaring, that it should bring forth thorns and thistles, and he should earn his <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> by the sweat of his brow, till he returned to the dust, from whence he was taken. At last, having clothed them both with skins, he turned them out of the garden, lest they should take of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever; then, to prevent any attempt to return to their former habitation, he placed cherubims at the east of the garden, and a flaming <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a> which turned every way, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the passage to the tree of life. This concise account being, at first view, encumbered with some difficulties, several learned and pious men have been inclined to believe the whole ought to be taken in an allegorical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, and not according to the strictness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a>: they allege, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and particularly the eastern nations, had two different ways of delivering their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, one popular, and the other mysterious; that the Scripture uses both occasionally; sometimes accommodating itself to the capacities of the people, and at other times to the real but more veiled <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>; and that, to obviate the many difficulties which occur in the literal history of this sad catastrophe, the safest way is to understand it as a parabolical story, under which the real circumstances are disguised and concealed, as a mystery not fit to be more explicitly declared. Though it cannot be denied that some of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> philosophers affected such an allegorical way of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, to conceal their notions from the vulgar, and keep their learning within the bounds of their own school; yet it is apparent Moses had no such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>; and as he pretends only to relate matters of fact, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they happened, without art or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, it cannot be supposed that this history of the fall is to be taken in a literal sense, as well as the rest of his writings. It is generally agreed, that the serpent which tempted Eve was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">devil</a>, who envying the privileges of man in innocence, tempted him, and was the cause of his forfeiting all those advantages which he had received from God at his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>; and that to this end he assumed the form of a serpent. These interpretations are supported by many <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> of Scripture, where the devil is called the serpent, and the old serpent. (See John viii. 44. 2 Cor. xi. 3. and Rev. xii. 9.) Some believe that the serpent had then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of speech, and conversed familiarly with the woman, without her conceiving any distrust of him; and that God, to punish the malice with which he had abused Eve, deprived him of the use of speech. Others maintain, that a real serpent having eaten of the forbidden fruit, Eve from thence concluded, that she too might eat of it without danger; that in effect she did eat of it, and incurred the displeasure of God by her disobedience. This, say these last authors, is the plain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of fact which Moses would relate under the allegorical representation of the serpent conversing with Eve. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of such as believe this was not a real serpent, but only the devil under that name, is no less liable liable to exception than any of the rest. For though the devil is frequently styled in Scripture the serpent, and the old serpent, yet why he should be called the most subtle beast of the field, we cannot conceive; neither <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> inflicted on the serpent suffer us to doubt, but that a serpent's body at least was employed in the transaction. The <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the forbidden fruit is another circumstance in this relation that has occasioned no less variety of conjectures. The Rabbins believe it was the vine; others that it was wheat; and others, from the circumstance of Adam and Eve's covering themselves with fig leaves immediately after their transgression, tell us, that this fruit must have been the fig; some think it was the cherry; and the generality of the Latins will have it to be the apple. Those who admire allegorical interpretations, will have the forbidden fruit to have been no other than the sensual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, for which the punishment inflicted on the woman was the pain of childbirth. But this opinion has not the least foundation in the words of Moses, especially <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> we consider that Adam knew not his wife till after their expulsion out of Paradise. Many have been the suppositions and conjectures upon this subject in general; and some have so far indulged their fancy in the circumstances of the fall, that they have perverted the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NARRATION">narration</a> of Moses into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">fable</a> full of the most shameful extravagancies.

FALLACY

Pages 12-12

a deception, fraud, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> false appearance. The Epicureans deny that there is any such thing as a fallacy of the senses: for, according to them, all our sensations and perceptions, both of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> and phantasy, are true; whence they make sense the primary criterion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>. The Cartesians, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, maintain, that we should suspect as false, or at most as dubious, everything that presents itself to us by means only of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> senses, because they frequently deceive us. They add, that our senses, as being fallacious, were never given us by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> for the discovery of truth, or the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPLATION">contemplation</a> of the principles of things; but only for pointing out to us what things are convenient or hurtful to our bodies. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIPATETICS">Peripatetics</a> keep a middle course. They say, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a sensible object be taken in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> or general view, the sense cannot be deceived about it; but that if the object be taken under its specific view, the sense may be mistaken about it, from the want of the dispositions necessary to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, as a disorder in the organ, or anything uncommon in the medium: thus, in some disorders of the eye, all objects appear <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>; a stick in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> appears broken or crooked, &c.

FALLOPIAN TUBES

Pages 12-12

in Anatomy, two ducts arising from the womb, one on each side of the fundus, and thence extended to the ovaries, having a considerable share in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCEPTION">conception</a>. They are called tubæ, from their form, which bears some resemblance to a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">trumpet</a>; and their denomination Fallopian, they take from Gabriel Fallopius, mentioned in the next article. Fallopius See ANATOMY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALLOPIUS

Pages 12-12

GABRIEL, a most celebrated physician and anatomist, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODENA">Modena</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the year 1523, and descended of a noble family. He made several discoveries in anatomy, one of which was that of the tubes, called from him the Fallopian tubes. He travelled through the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and obtained the character of being one of the ablest physicians of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. He was made professor of anatomy at <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a> in the year 1548, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PADUA">Padua</a> in the year 1551: here he died in 1562, aged 39. His writings, which are numerous, were first printed separately, and afterwards collected under the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "<a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">Opera</a> genuina omnia, tam practica quam theoretica, in tres tomos distributa." They were printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1585 and in 1606, at Frankfort in 1600, cum operum appendice; and in 1606, in folio.

FALLOW

Pages 12-12

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, like that of brick half burnt; such is that of a fallow deer. FALLOW Field, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fallow ground; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> laid up, or that has been untilled for a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. FALLOWING of Land, a particular method of improving land. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">AGRICULTURE</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FALMOUTH

Pages 12-12

a port town of Cornwall in England, situated in W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 5° 30' N. Lat. 50° 15' on a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> on the English Channel. It is the richest and most trading town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>, and larger than any three of its boroughs that send members to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>. It is so commodious a harbour, that ships of the greatest burden come up to its quay. It is guarded by the castle of St Mawes and Pendennis, on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> rock at the entrance; and there is such shelter in the many creeks belonging to it, that the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a> may ride safe here in any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, it being next to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLYMOUTH">Plymouth</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILFORD">Milford</a>-Haven, the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> for shipping in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. It is well-built; and its trade is considerably increased since the establishment of the packet-boats here for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>, and the West Indies, which not only bring vast quantities of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> in specie and in bars, on account of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but the Falmouth merchants trade with the Portuguese in ships of their own, and they have a great share also in the gainful pilchard trade. The <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CUSTOM_HOUSE"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> for most of the Cornish <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a>, as well as the head collector, is settled here, where the duties, including those of the other ports, are very considerable. It is a corporation, governed by a mayor and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALDERMAN">alderman</a>. Here is a market on Thursday, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 27, and October 30.

FALSE

Pages 12-12

in general, something contrary to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> not what it ought to be: thus we say a false <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>, false weights, false claim, &c.

FALSE ACTION

Pages 12-12
if brought against one whereby he is cast into prison, and dies pending the suit, the law gives no remedy in this case, because the truth or falsehood of the matter cannot appear before it is tried: and if the plaintiff is barred, or non-suited at common law, regularly all the punishment is amercement.

FALSE IMPRISONMENT

Pages 12-13

is a trespass committed against a person, by arresting and imprisoning him without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> cause, contrary to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is unlawfully detained without legal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>: and it is al- so used for a writ which is brought for this trefpals. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a person be any way unlawfully detained, it is false imprisonment; and considerable damages are recoverable in those actions. False News, spreading of, in order to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCORD">discord</a> between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, or concerning any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> man of the realm, is punishable by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> law with fine and imprisonment; which is confirmed by statutes Welfm. i. 3 Edw. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 34. 2 Ric. II. stat. i. cap. 5. and 12 Ric. II. cap. ii. False Oath. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERJURY">Perjury</a>. False Prophecy. See Prophecy. False <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">Quarter</a>, in Farriery. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">Quarters</a>, Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. False <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">Bay</a>, a bay lying to the eastward of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> of Good Hope; frequented by vessels during the prevalence of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>-westerly winds, which begin to exert their influence in May, and render it dangerous to remain in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a> bay. It is terminated to the eastward by False Cape, and to the westward by the Cape of Good Hope. It is .8 miles wide at its entrance, and the two capes bear due east and west from each other.

FALSI CRIMEN

Pages 13-13

in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is fraudulent fabrication <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> concealment, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> to darken or hide the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, and make things appear otherwise than they are. The crimen falsi is committed, 1. By words, as when a witness swears falsely. 2. By <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, as when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> antedates a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a>, or the like. 3. By <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEED">deed</a>, as when he sells by false <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WEIGHTS_AND_MEASURES">weights and <a class</a>="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>.

FALSIFY

Pages 13-13

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is used for proving anything to be false. Hence we find, Falsifying a record, for showing it to be erroneous. Thus lawyers teach, that a person purchasing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of another, who is afterwards outlawed of felony, &c. may falsify the record, not only as to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wherein the felony is supposed to have been committed, but also as to the point of the offence. But where a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> is found guilty by verdict, a purchaser cannot falsify as to the offence; though he may for the time, where the party is found guilty generally in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, because the time is not material upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a>. FALSTAFF. See FASTOLFF.

FALX

Pages 13-13

in Anatomy, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the dura mater, descending between the two hemispheres of the brain, and separating the fore part from the hinder. It is called falx, i.e. "fickle," because of its curvature, occasioned by the convexity of the brain. It divides the brain as low as the corpus callosum.

FAMA CLAMOSA

Pages 13-13

in the judicial procedure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Scotland, a ground of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> before a presbytery against one of its members, independent of any regular complaint by a particular accuser. See PRESBYTERY. Any person who is of a good character, may give to the presbytery a complaint against one of their members; but the presbytery is not to proceed to the citation of the person accused, until the accuser under his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> gives in the complaint, with some account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a>, and undertakes to make out the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LIBEL">libel</a>, under the pain of being considered as a flanderer. When such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCUSATION">accusation</a> is brought before them, they are obliged candidly to examine the affair. But, besides this, the presbytery considers itself obliged to proceed against any of its members, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a fama clamosa of the scandal is so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> that they cannot be vindicated unless they begin the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a>. This they can do without any particular accuser, after they have inquired into the rise, occasion, and authors, of this report. It is a maxim in the kirk of Scotland, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> must suffer if the scandalous <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> immoral actions of a minister are not corrected. And wherever a minister is reputed guilty of any immorality (although before the most popular preacher in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>), none almost <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> attend upon his ministry. Therefore the presbytery, for the sake of religion, is obliged to proceed against a minister in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of a fama clamosa. This, however, is generally done with great tenderness. After they have considered the report raised against him, then they order him to be cited, draw out a full copy of what is reported, with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of the witnesses' names to be led for proving this allegation. He is now to be formally summoned to appear before them; and he has warning given him, at least 10 days before the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his appearance, to give in his answers to what is termed the libel; and the names of the witnesses ought also to be sent him. If at the time appointed the minister appear, the libel is to be read to him, and his answers are also to be read. If the libel be found relevant, then the presbytery is to endeavour to bring him to a confession. If the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> confessed be of a scandalous <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, such as uncleanness, the presbytery generally depose him from his office, and appoint him in due time to appear before the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONGREGATION">congregation</a> where the scandal was given, and to make public confession of his crime and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a>. If a minister absent himself by leaving the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and be contumacious, without making any relevant excuse, a new citation is given him, and intimation is made at his own church when the congregation is met, that he is to be holden as confessed, since he refused to appear before them; and accordingly he is deposed from his office.

FAME

Pages 13-13

a heathen <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>, celebrated chiefly by the poets. She is feigned to have been the last of the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TITANS">Titans</a> produced by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, to have her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, and to have a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of eyes, ears, and tongues. She is mentioned by Hefiod, and particularly described by Ovid and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>.

FAMIA

Pages 13-14
or AFAMIA, the modern name of one of the ancient Apameas. See APAMEA. FAMILIARS of the INQUISITION, persons who assist in apprehending such as are accused, and carrying them to prison. They are assistants to the inquisitor, and called familiars, because they belong to his family. In some provinces of Italy they are called crofs-bearers, and in others the scholars of St Peter the martyr; and they wore a crofs before them on the outside garment. They are properly bailiffs of the inquisition; and the vile office is esteemed so honourable, that noblemen in the kingdom of Portugal have been ambitious of belonging to it. Nor is this surprising, when it is considered that Innocent III. granted very large indulgences and privileges to these familiars; and that the same plenary indulgence is granted by the pope to every single exercise of this office, as was granted by the Lateran council to those who succoured the Holy Land. When several persons are to be taken up at the same time, these familiars are commanded FAMILY denotes the persons that live together in one house, under the direction of one head or chief manager. It also signifies the kindred or lineage of a person; and is used by old writers for a hide or portion of land sufficient to maintain one family. See Hide.

FAMILY

Pages 14-14

in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by authors to express any order of animals, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other natural productions of the same class.

FAMINE

Pages 14-14

dearth, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> scarcity of food. For preservatives against <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HUNGER">hunger</a> in times of famine, see the article Hunger.

FAN

Pages 14-14

a machine used to raise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>, and cool the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> by agitating it. That the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the fan was known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> is very evident from what Terence says, *<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> hoc flabellum, et ventulum huic sic facio;* and from Ovid, Art. Amand. I. 161. *Profuit et tenues ventos movisse flabello.* The fans of the ancients were made of different materials; but the most elegant were composed of peacocks' feathers, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perhaps painted so as to represent a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s feather. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> which now prevails among the ladies, of wearing fans, was borrowed from the east, where the hot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> renders the use of fans and umbrellas almost indispensable. In the east they chiefly use <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> fans made of feathers, to keep off the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and the flies. In <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> they have a large sort of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> fans, suspended in the middle of their apartments, and particularly over the tables: these, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> at first given them, and which they retain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> on account of their perpendicular suspension, help to cool the air and drive off flies. In the Greek <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, a fan is put into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the deacons in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a> of their ordination, in allusion to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the deacon's office in that church, which is to keep the flies off the priests during the celebration of the sacrament. What is called a fan amongst us and throughout the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, is a thin skin, or piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, taffety, or other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> stuff, cut semicircularly, and mounted on several little sticks of wood, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a>, tortoiseshell, or the like. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> the paper be single, the sticks of the mounting are pasted on the least ornamented side; if <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a>, the sticks are placed between them. Before they proceed to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the sticks, which they call mounting the fan, the paper is to be plaited in such a manner, as that the plates may be alternately inward and outward. It is in the middle of each plait, which is usually about half an inch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, that the sticks are to be pasted; and these again are to be all joined and riveted together at the other end; they are very thin, and scarcely exceed one-third of an inch in breadth; and where they are pasted to the paper, are still narrower, continuing thus to the extremity of the paper. The two outer ones are bigger and stronger than the others. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of sticks rarely exceeds 22. The sticks are usually provided by the cabinetmakers or toymen; the fan-painters plait the papers, paint, and mount them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a> is either in colours or <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a>, applied on a silvered ground, both prepared by the goldbeaters. Sometimes they paint on a gold ground, but it is rarely; true gold being too dear, and false too paltry. To apply the silver leaves on the paper, they use a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, which they pretend is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> secret, but which appears to be no other than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> arabic, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDY">candy</a>, and a little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a>, melted in common <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and mixed with a little brandy. This composition is laid on with a sponge; then laying the silver leaves thereon, and pressing them gently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALL">ball</a> stuffed with cotton, they catch hold, and adhere together. When, instead of silver, gold ground is laid, the same method is observed. The ground being well dried, a number of the papers are well beaten together on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLOCK">block</a>, and by this means the silver or gold get a lustre as if they had been burnished. Fan is also an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> to winnow corn. The machine used for this purpose by the ancients seems to have been of a form similar to ours. The fan, which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> calls *mylica vanus lacchi*, was used at initiations into the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MYSTERIES">mysteries</a> of the ancients: for as the persons who were initiated into any of the mysteries, were to be particularly good, this instrument, which separates the wheat from the chaff, was the fittest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> that could be of setting apart the good and virtuous from the vicious and useless part of mankind. It is figuratively applied in a similar manner in Luke iii. 17.

FANATICS

Pages 14-14

wild, enthusiastic, visionary persons, who pretend to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">revelation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> called those *fanatici* who passed their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> (*fans*), and being often seized with a kind of enthusiasm, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> inspired by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, showed wild and antic gestures. Prudentius represents them as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> and slashing their arms with knives. Shaking the head was also <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> among the fanatici; for Lampridius informs us, that the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Heliogabalus was arrived at that pitch of madness, as to shake his head with the gashed fanatics. Hence the word was applied among us to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANABAPTISTS">Anabaptists</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUAKERS">Quakers</a>, &c., at their first rise, and is now an epithet given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> prophets, Muggletonians, &c.

FANIONS

Pages 14-14

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, small flags carried along with the baggage.

FANNERS

Pages 14-14

a machine for winnowing corn, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> for separating the chaff from the grain. See, for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">MECHANICS</a>.

FANSHAW

Pages 14-15

Sir Richard, famous for his embassies and writings, was the tenth and youngest son of Sir Henry Fanhaw of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WARE">Ware</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">Park</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HERTFORDSHIRE">Hertfordshire</a>, where it is supposed he was born about the year 1607. He distinguished himself so early by his abilities, that in 1635 he was taken into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> employments by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. and sent resident to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>; whence being recalled in the beginning of the troubles... troubles in 1641, he adhered to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, and was employed in several important matters of state. During his vacant hours he wrote <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> poems, and made several translations. At the Restoration it was expected he would have been made one of the secretaries of state; however, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the requisits; a station in those times of considerable profit. Afterwards, on account of his skill in the Latin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, he was made secretary for that tongue. In 1661, he was sent envoy to the king of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTUGAL">Portugal</a>. In 1662, he was again sent to that court with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a>, and negotiated the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> of his master King Charles II. with the infanta Donna Catherine. Upon his return he was made one of the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PRIVY_COUNCIL">privy <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>.
