Xenophon's work on horsemanship, 30 Y. Yeats, 393, f. Yellow, 441 Z. Zinc, 295, h. --- **F A R** Farthing, a small English copper coin, amounting to one-fourth of a penny. It was anciently called fourthing, as being the fourth of the integer or penny. Farthing of Gold, a coin used in ancient times, containing in value the fourth part of a noble, or 20d. silver. It is mentioned in the stat. 9 Hen. V. cap. 7, where it is enacted, that there shall be good and just weight of the noble, half-noble, and farthing of gold. Farthing of Land seems to differ from Farding-deal. For in a survey-book of the manor of West-Hampton in Devonshire, there is an entry thus: A. B. holds six farthings of land at 126l. per annum. So that the farthing of land must have been a considerable quantity, far more than a rood. Fasces, in Roman antiquity, axes tied up together with rods or staves, and borne before the Roman magistrates as a badge of their office and authority. According to Florus, the use of the fasces was introduced by the elder Tarquin, the fifth king of Rome; and were then the mark of the sovereign dignity. In after times they were borne before the consuls, but by turns only, each his day; they had each of them 12, borne by as many lictors. These fasces consisted of branches, FASCINATION branches of elm; having in the middle a securis or axe, the head of which stood out beyond the rest. Publicans took the axe out of the fasces, as Plutarch affirms us, to remove from the people all occasion of terror. After the consuls, the praetors assumed the fasces. In the government of the decemvirs, it was the practice at first for only one of them to have the fasces. Afterwards each of them had twelve after the manner of the kings. When the magistrates who by right had the axes carried before them, had a mind to show some deference to the people, or some person of singular merit, they either sent away the lictors, or commanded them to lower the fasces before them, which was called submittere fasces. Many instances of this occur in Roman history. FASCIETS, in the art of making glass, are the irons thrust into the mouths of bottles, in order to convey them to the annealing tower. FASCIA, in antiquity, a thin skin which the Roman women wrapped round their bodies, next to the skin, in order to make them slender. Something of this sort seems also to have been in use amongst the Grecian ladies, if we can depend upon the representation given by Terence, Eun. act. ii. sc. 4. Haud similis est virginum nostrarum, quas matres student Demissis humeris effe—vinculo corpore, ut graciles sint. FASCIA, in Architecture, signifies any flat member having a considerable breadth and but a small projection, as the band of an architrave, larmier, &c. In brick buildings, the jutting out of the brick beyond the windows in the several stories except the highest are called facias or facies.

FASCINATION (from the Greek θαυμασίαν, to fascinate or bewitch), a sort of witchcraft supposed to operate either by the eye or the tongue. Ancient writers distinguish two sorts of fascination, one performed by looking, or the efficacy of the eye. Such is that spoken of by Virgil in his third eclogue: Nescio quis teneros oculos mihi fascinat agnos. The second by words, and especially by malignant praises. Such is that mentioned by the same poet in his seventh eclogue: Aut, si ultra placitum laudabit, baccare frontem Cingite, ne vati noceat mala lingua futuro. Horace alludes to both kinds in his first book of epistles: Non illic obliquo oculo mea commodia quiquam Limat, non odio obscuro, morfique venenat. FASCINATION of serpents, a faculty which these animals are supposed to possess of attracting birds from the air, and making them their prey. See ORTHOLOGY Fascines Index. FASCINES, in Fortification, faggots of small wood, of about a foot diameter, and six feet long, bound in the middle, and at both ends. They are used in raising batteries, making chandeliers, in filling up the moat to facilitate the passage to the wall, in binding the ramparts where the earth is bad; and in making parapets of trenches to screen the men. Some of them are dipped in melted pitch or tar; and, being set on fire, serve to burn the enemy's lodgments or other works. In corrupt Latin, fascenina, fascennia, and fascinaia, &c. are used to signify the pales, fascines, &c. used to enclose ancient cattle, &c. FASCIOLA, the Fluke or Gourd Worm, a genus belonging to the order of vermes intestina. See HELMINTHOLOGY Index. FASHION-Pieces, in the sea language, the aftmost or hindmost timbers of a ship, which terminate the breadth, and form the shape of the stern. They are united to the stern-post, and to the extremity of the wing-tranlom, by a rabbet, and a number of strong nails or spikes driven from without. FAST, in general, denotes the abstinence from food, (see FASTING); but is more particularly used for such abstinence on a religious account. Religious fasting has been practised by most nations from the remotest antiquity. Some divines even pretend its origin was in the earthly paradise, where our first parents were forbidden to eat of the tree of knowledge. But though this seems carrying the matter too far, it is certain that the Jewish church has observed fasts ever since its first institution. Nor were the neighbouring heathens, viz. the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Assyrians, without their fasts. The Egyptians, according to Herodotus, sacrificed a cow to Isis, after having prepared themselves by fasting and prayer; a custom which he likewise attributes to the women of Cyrene. Porphyry affirms, that the Egyptians, before their stated sacrifices, always fasted a great many days, sometimes for six weeks; and that the least behoved to be for seven days: during all which time the priests and devotees not only abstained from flesh, fish, wine, and oil; but even from bread, and some kinds of pulse. These austerities were communicated by them to the Greeks, who observed their fasts much in the same manner. The Athenians had the Eleusinian and Thesmophorian fasts, the observation of which was very rigorous, especially among the women, who spent one whole day sitting on the ground in a mournful dress, without taking any nourishment. In the island of Crete, the priests of Jupiter were obliged to abstain all their lives from fish, flesh, and baked meats. Apuleius informs us, that whoever had a mind to be initiated in the mysteries of Cybele were obliged to prepare themselves by fasting ten days; and, in short, all the pagan deities, whether male or female, required this duty of those that desired to be initiated into their mysteries, of their priests and priestesses that gave the oracles, and of those who came to consult them. Among the heathens fasting was also practised before some of their military enterprises. Aristotle informs us, that the Lacedemonians having resolved to succour a city of the allies, ordained a fast throughout the the whole extent of their dominions, without excepting even the domestic animals: and this they did for two ends: one to spare provisions in favour of the besieged; the other to draw down the blessing of heaven upon their enterprise. The inhabitants of Tarentum, when besieged by the Romans, demanded succours from their neighbours of Rhegium, who immediately commanded a fast throughout their whole territories. Their enterprise having had good success by their throwing a supply of provisions into the town, the Romans were obliged to raise the siege; and the Tarentines, in memory of this deliverance, instituted a perpetual fast. Fasting has always been reckoned a particular duty among philosophers and religious people, some of whom have carried their abstinence to an incredible length. At Rome it was practised by kings and emperors themselves. Numa Pompilius, Julius Caesar, Augustus, Vespasian, and others, we are told, had their stated fast days: and Julian the Apostate was so exact in this observance as to outdo the priests themselves, and even the most rigid philosophers. The Pythagoreans kept a continual fast; but with this difference, that they believed the use of fish to be equally unlawful with that of flesh. Besides their constant temperance, they also frequently fasted rigidly for a very long time. In this respect, however, they were all outdone by their master Pythagoras, who continued his fasts for no less than 40 days together. Even Apollonius Tyaneus, one of his most famous disciples, could never come up to him in the length of his fasts, though they greatly exceeded those of the ordinary Pythagoreans. The Gymnosophists, or Brahmans of the east, are also very remarkable for their severe fastings; and the Chinese, according to Father Le Comte, have also their stated fasts, with forms of prayer for preserving them from barrenness, inundations, earthquakes, &c. The Mahometans too, who possess so large a part of Asia, are very remarkable for the strict observance of their fasts; and the exactness of their dervishes in this respect is extraordinary. Fasting was often used by the heathens for superstitious purposes; sometimes to procure the interpretations of dreams; at others, to be an antidote against their pernicious consequences. A piece of superstition prevails to this day among the Jews; who, though expressly forbidden to fast on Sabbath-days, think themselves at liberty to dispense with this duty when they happen to have fruitful and unlucky dreams the night preceding, that threatened them with great misfortunes. On these occasions they observe a formal fast the whole day; and at night the patient, having invited three of his friends, addresses himself to them seven times in a very solemn manner, saying, "May the dream I have had prove a lucky one!" And his friends answer as many times, "Amen, may it be lucky, and God make it so!" After which, in order to encourage him, they conclude the ceremony with these words of Ecclesiastes, "Go eat thy bread with joy;" and then sit themselves down to table. They have also added several fasts not commanded in the law of Moses, particularly three, in memory of sore distresses their nation has suffered at different times. The abstinence of the ancient Jews commonly lasted 27 or 28 hours at a time; beginning before sunset, and not ending till some hours after sunset next day. On these days they were obliged to wear white robes in token of grief and repentance; to cover themselves with sackcloth, or their worst clothes; to lie on ashes; to sprinkle them on their head, &c. Some spent the whole night and day following in the temple or synagogue, in prayers and other devotions, barefooted, with a scourge in their hands, of which they sometimes made a good use in order to raise their zeal. Lastly, in order to complete their abstinence, at night they were to eat nothing but a little bread dipped in water, with some salt for seasoning; except they chose to add to their repast some bitter herbs and pulse. The ancients, both Jews and Pagans, had also their fasts for purifying the body, particularly the priests and such as were any way employed at the altars; for when nocturnal disorders happened to these, it was unlawful for them to approach all the next day, which they were bound to employ in purifying themselves. On this account, at great festivals, where their ministry could not be dispensed with, it was usual for them, on the eve thereof, not only to fast, but also to abstain from sleep, for the greater certainty. For this purpose the high priest had under officers to wake him, if overtaken with sleep; against which other preservatives were also made use of. FASTERMANS, or FASTING-MEN, q. d. homines habentes, was used in our ancient customs for men in repute and substance; or rather for pledges, sureties, or bondsmen, who, according to the Saxon polity, were fast bound to answer for one another's peaceable behaviour. FASTI, in Roman antiquity, the calendar wherein were expressed the several days of the year, with their feasts, games, and other ceremonies. There were two sorts of fasti, the greater and lesser: the former being distinguished by the appellation fasti magistrales, and the latter by that of fasti calendares. 1. The fasti calendares, which were properly and primarily called fasti, are defined by Feftus Pompeius to be books containing a description of the whole year: i.e. ephemerides, or diaries, distinguishing the several kinds of days, fasti, profasti; fasti, nefasti, &c. The author of these was Numa, who committed the care and direction of the fasti to the pontifex maximus, whom the people used to consult on every occasion. This custom held till the year of Rome 459, when C. Flavius, secretary to the pontifices, exposed in the forum a list of all the days on which it was lawful to work; which was so acceptable to the people, that they made him curule edile. These lesser fasti, or fasti calendares, were of two kinds, urbani and rustic. The fasti urbani, or fasti of the city, were those which obtained or were observed in the city. Some will have them thus called, because they were exposed publicly in divers parts of the city; though by the various inscriptions or gravings thereof on antique stones, one would imagine that private persons had them likewise in their houses. Ovid undertook to illustrate these fasti urbani, and comment on them, in his Libri Fastorum.

FASCIETS

Pages 190-190

FASCIETS, in the art of making glass, are the irons thrust into the mouths of bottles, in order to convey them to the annealing tower. FASCIA, in antiquity, a thin skin which the Roman women wrapped round their bodies, next to the skin, in order to make them slender. Something of this sort seems also to have been in use amongst the Grecian ladies, if we can depend upon the representation given by Terence, Eun. act. ii. sc. 4. Haud similis est virginum nostrarum, quas matres student Demissis humeris effe—vinculo corpore, ut graciles sint. FASCIA, in Architecture, signifies any flat member having a considerable breadth and but a small projection, as the band of an architrave, larmier, &c. In brick buildings, the jutting out of the brick beyond the windows in the several stories except the highest are called facias or facies. FASCIA Latina, in Anatomy, a muscle of the leg, called also semi-membranous. See ANATOMY, Table of the Muscles. FASCLE, in Astronomy, the belts seen on the disk of the superior planets, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.—See ASTRONOMY, passim. FASCIALIS, in Anatomy, one of the muscles of the thigh, called fatorius. See ANATOMY, Table of the Muscles.

FASCINATION branches of elm; having in the middle a securis or axe, the head of which stood out beyond the rest. Publicans took the axe out of the fasces, as Plutarch affirms us, to remove from the people all occasion of terror. After the consuls, the praetors assumed the fasces. In the government of the decemvirs, it was the practice at first for only one of them to have the fasces. Afterwards each of them had twelve after the manner of the kings. Fascines Index. FASCINES, in Fortification, faggots of small wood, of about a foot diameter, and six feet long, bound in the middle, and at both ends. They are used in raising batteries, making chandeliers, in filling up the moat to facilitate the passage to the wall, in binding the ramparts where the earth is bad; and in making parapets of trenches to screen the men. FAST, in general, denotes the abstinence from food, (see FASTING); but is more particularly used for such abstinence on a religious account. Religious fasting has been practised by most nations from the remotest antiquity. Some divines even pretend its origin was in the earthly paradise, where our first parents were forbidden to eat of the tree of knowledge. But though this seems carrying the matter too far, it is certain that the Jewish church has observed fasts ever since its first institution. Nor were the neighbouring heathens, viz. the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Assyrians, without their fasts. The Egyptians, according to Herodotus, sacrificed a cow to Isis, after having prepared themselves by fasting and prayer; a custom which he likewise attributes to the women of Cyrene. Porphyry affirms, that the Egyptians, before their stated sacrifices, always fasted a great many days, sometimes for six weeks; and that the least behoved to be for seven days: during all which time the priests and devotees not only abstained from flesh, fish, wine, and oil; but even from bread, and some kinds of pulse. These austerities were communicated by them to the Greeks, who observed their fasts much in the same manner. The Athenians had the Eleusinian and Thesmophorian fasts, the observation of which was very rigorous, especially among the women, who spent one whole day sitting on the ground in a mournful dress, without taking any nourishment. In the island of Crete, the priests of Jupiter were obliged to abstain all their lives from fish, flesh, and baked meats. Among the heathens fasting was also practised before some of their military enterprises. Religious fasting has been practised by most nations from the remotest antiquity. Some divines even pretend its origin was in the earthly paradise, where our first parents were forbidden to eat of the tree of knowledge. But though this seems carrying the matter too far, it is certain that the Jewish church has observed fasts ever since its first institution. Nor were the neighbouring heathens, viz. the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Assyrians, without their fasts. The Egyptians, according to Herodotus, sacrificed a cow to Isis, after having prepared themselves by fasting and prayer; a custom which he likewise attributes to the women of Cyrene. Porphyry affirms, that the Egyptians, before their stated sacrifices, always fasted a great many days, sometimes for six weeks; and that the least behoved to be for seven days: during all which time the priests and devotees not only abstained from flesh, fish, wine, and oil; but even from bread, and some kinds of pulse. These austerities were communicated by them to the Greeks, who observed their fasts much in the same manner. The Athenians had the Eleusinian and Thesmophorian fasts, the observation of which was very rigorous, especially among the women, who spent one whole day sitting on the ground in a mournful dress, without taking any nourishment. In the island of Crete, the priests of Jupiter were obliged to abstain all their lives from fish, flesh, and baked meats. Apuleius informs us, that whoever had a mind to be initiated in the mysteries of Cybele were obliged to prepare themselves by fasting ten days; and, in short, all the pagan deities, whether male or female, required this duty of those that desired to be initiated into their mysteries, of their priests and priestesses that gave the oracles, and of those who came to consult them. Among the heathens fasting was also practised before some of their military enterprises. Aristotle informs us, that the Lacedemonians having resolved to succour a city of the allies, ordained a fast throughout the the whole extent of their dominions, without excepting even the domestic animals: and this they did for two ends: one to spare provisions in favour of the besieged; the other to draw down the blessing of heaven upon their enterprise. The inhabitants of Tarentum, when besieged by the Romans, demanded succours from their neighbours of Rhegium, who immediately commanded a fast throughout their whole territories. Their enterprise having had good success by their throwing a supply of provisions into the town, the Romans were obliged to raise the siege; and the Tarentines, in memory of this deliverance, instituted a perpetual fast. Fasting has always been reckoned a particular duty among philosophers and religious people, some of whom have carried their abstinence to an incredible length. At Rome it was practised by kings and emperors themselves. Numa Pompilius, Julius Caesar, Augustus, Vespasian, and others, we are told, had their stated fast days: and Julian the Apostate was so exact in this observance as to outdo the priests themselves, and even the most rigid philosophers. The Pythagoreans kept a continual fast; but with this difference, that they believed the use of fish to be equally unlawful with that of flesh. Besides their constant temperance, they also frequently fasted rigidly for a very long time. In this respect, however, they were all outdone by their master Pythagoras, who continued his fasts for no less than 40 days together. Even Apollonius Tyaneus, one of his most famous disciples, could never come up to him in the length of his fasts, though they greatly exceeded those of the ordinary Pythagoreans. The Gymnosophists, or Brahmans of the east, are also very remarkable for their severe fastings; and the Chinese, according to Father Le Comte, have also their stated fasts, with forms of prayer for preserving them from barrenness, inundations, earthquakes, &c. The Mahometans too, who possess so large a part of Asia, are very remarkable for the strict observance of their fasts; and the exactness of their dervishes in this respect is extraordinary. Fasting was often used by the heathens for superstitious purposes; sometimes to procure the interpretations of dreams; at others, to be an antidote against their pernicious consequences. A piece of superstition prevails to this day among the Jews; who, though expressly forbidden to fast on Sabbath-days, think themselves at liberty to dispense with this duty when they happen to have fruitful and unlucky dreams the night preceding, that threatened them with great misfortunes. On these occasions they observe a formal fast the whole day; and at night the patient, having invited three of his friends, addresses himself to them seven times in a very solemn manner, saying, "May the dream I have had prove a lucky one!" And his friends answer as many times, "Amen, may it be lucky, and God make it so!" After which, in order to encourage him, they conclude the ceremony with these words of Ecclesiastes, "Go eat thy bread with joy;" and then sit themselves down to table. They have also added several fasts not commanded in the law of Moses, particularly three, in memory of sore distresses their nation has suffered at different times. The abstinence of the ancient Jews commonly lasted 27 or 28 hours at a time; beginning before sunset, and not ending till some hours after sunset next day. On these days they were obliged to wear white robes in token of grief and repentance; to cover themselves with sackcloth, or their worst clothes; to lie on ashes; to sprinkle them on their head, &c. Some spent the whole night and day following in the temple or synagogue, in prayers and other devotions, barefooted, with a scourge in their hands, of which they sometimes made a good use in order to raise their zeal. Lastly, in order to complete their abstinence, at night they were to eat nothing but a little bread dipped in water, with some salt for seasoning; except they chose to add to their repast some bitter herbs and pulse. The ancients, both Jews and Pagans, had also their fasts for purifying the body, particularly the priests and such as were any way employed at the altars; for when nocturnal disorders happened to these, it was unlawful for them to approach all the next day, which they were bound to employ in purifying themselves. On this account, at great festivals, where their ministry could not be dispensed with, it was usual for them, on the eve thereof, not only to fast, but also to abstain from sleep, for the greater certainty. For this purpose the high priest had under officers to wake him, if overtaken with sleep; against which other preservatives were also made use of. FASTERMANS, or FASTING-MEN, q. d. homines habentes, was used in our ancient customs for men in repute and substance; or rather for pledges, sureties, or bondsmen, who, according to the Saxon polity, were fast bound to answer for one another's peaceable behaviour. FASTI, in Roman antiquity, the calendar wherein were expressed the several days of the year, with their feasts, games, and other ceremonies. There were two sorts of fasti, the greater and lesser: the former being distinguished by the appellation fasti magistrales, and the latter by that of fasti calendares. 1. The fasti calendares, which were properly and primarily called fasti, are defined by Feftus Pompeius to be books containing a description of the whole year: i.e. ephemerides, or diaries, distinguishing the several kinds of days, fasti, profasti; fasti, nefasti, &c. The author of these was Numa, who committed the care and direction of the fasti to the pontifex maximus, whom the people used to consult on every occasion. This custom held till the year of Rome 459, when C. Flavius, secretary to the pontifices, exposed in the forum a list of all the days on which it was lawful to work; which was so acceptable to the people, that they made him curule edile. These lesser fasti, or fasti calendares, were of two kinds, urbani and rustic. The fasti urbani, or fasti of the city, were those which obtained or were observed in the city. Some will have them thus called, because they were exposed publicly in divers parts of the city; though by the various inscriptions or gravings thereof on antique stones, one would imagine that private persons had them likewise in their houses. Ovid undertook to illustrate these fasti urbani, and comment on them, in his Libri Fastorum.

They have also added several fasts not commanded in the law of Moses, particularly three, in memory of sore distresses their nation has suffered at different times. The abstinence of the ancient Jews commonly lasted 27 or 28 hours at a time; beginning before sunset, and not ending till some hours after sunset next day. On these days they were obliged to wear white robes in token of grief and repentance; to cover themselves with sackcloth, or their worst clothes; to lie on ashes; to sprinkle them on their head, &c. Some spent the whole night and day following in the temple or synagogue, in prayers and other devotions, barefooted, with a scourge in their hands, of which they sometimes made a good use in order to raise their zeal. Lastly, in order to complete their abstinence, at night they were to eat nothing but a little bread dipped in water, with some salt for seasoning; except they chose to add to their repast some bitter herbs and pulse. The ancients, both Jews and Pagans, had also their fasts for purifying the body, particularly the priests and such as were any way employed at the altars; for when nocturnal disorders happened to these, it was unlawful for them to approach all the next day, which they were bound to employ in purifying themselves. On this account, at great festivals, where their ministry could not be dispensed with, it was usual for them, on the eve thereof, not only to fast, but also to abstain from sleep, for the greater certainty. For this purpose the high priest had under officers to wake him, if overtaken with sleep; against which other preservatives were also made use of. FASTERMANS, or FASTING-MEN, q. d. homines habentes, was used in our ancient customs for men in repute and substance; or rather for pledges, sureties, or bondsmen, who, according to the Saxon polity, were fast bound to answer for one another's peaceable behaviour. FASTI, in Roman antiquity, the calendar wherein were expressed the several days of the year, with their feasts, games, and other ceremonies. There were two sorts of fasti, the greater and lesser: the former being distinguished by the appellation fasti magistrales, and the latter by that of fasti calendares. 1. The fasti calendares, which were properly and primarily called fasti, are defined by Feftus Pompeius to be books containing a description of the whole year: i.e. ephemerides, or diaries, distinguishing the several kinds of days, fasti, profasti; fasti, nefasti, &c. The author of these was Numa, who committed the care and direction of the fasti to the pontifex maximus, whom the people used to consult on every occasion. This custom held till the year of Rome 459, when C. Flavius, secretary to the pontifices, exposed in the forum a list of all the days on which it was lawful to work; which was so acceptable to the people, that they made him curule edile. These lesser fasti, or fasti calendares, were of two kinds, urbani and rustic. The fasti urbani, or fasti of the city, were those which obtained or were observed in the city. Some will have them thus called, because they were exposed publicly in divers parts of the city; though by the various inscriptions or gravings thereof on antique stones, one would imagine that private persons had them likewise in their houses. Ovid undertook to illustrate these fasti urbani, and comment on them, in his Libri Fastorum.

FAST

Pages 190-190

FAST, in general, denotes the abstinence from food, (see FASTING); but is more particularly used for such abstinence on a religious account. Religious fasting has been practised by most nations from the remotest antiquity. Some divines even pretend its origin was in the earthly paradise, where our first parents were forbidden to eat of the tree of knowledge. But though this seems carrying the matter too far, it is certain that the Jewish church has observed fasts ever since its first institution. Nor were the neighbouring heathens, viz. the Egyptians, Phoenicians, and Assyrians, without their fasts. The Egyptians, according to Herodotus, sacrificed a cow to Isis, after having prepared themselves by fasting and prayer; a custom which he likewise attributes to the women of Cyrene. Porphyry affirms, that the Egyptians, before their stated sacrifices, always fasted a great many days, sometimes for six weeks; and that the least behoved to be for seven days: during all which time the priests and devotees not only abstained from flesh, fish, wine, and oil; but even from bread, and some kinds of pulse. These austerities were communicated by them to the Greeks, who observed their fasts much in the same manner. The Athenians had the Eleusinian and Thesmophorian fasts, the observation of which was very rigorous, especially among the women, who spent one whole day sitting on the ground in a mournful dress, without taking any nourishment. In the island of Crete, the priests of Jupiter were obliged to abstain all their lives from fish, flesh, and baked meats. Apuleius informs us, that whoever had a mind to be initiated in the mysteries of Cybele were obliged to prepare themselves by fasting ten days; and, in short, all the pagan deities, whether male or female, required this duty of those that desired to be initiated into their mysteries, of their priests and priestesses that gave the oracles, and of those who came to consult them. Among the heathens fasting was also practised before some of their military enterprises. Aristotle informs us, that the Lacedemonians having resolved to succour a city of the allies, ordained a fast throughout the the whole extent of their dominions, without excepting even the domestic animals: and this they did for two ends: one to spare provisions in favour of the besieged; the other to draw down the blessing of heaven upon their enterprise. The inhabitants of Tarentum, when besieged by the Romans, demanded succours from their neighbours of Rhegium, who immediately commanded a fast throughout their whole territories. Their enterprise having had good success by their throwing a supply of provisions into the town, the Romans were obliged to raise the siege; and the Tarentines, in memory of this deliverance, instituted a perpetual fast. Fasting has always been reckoned a particular duty among philosophers and religious people, some of whom have carried their abstinence to an incredible length. At Rome it was practised by kings and emperors themselves. Numa Pompilius, Julius Caesar, Augustus, Vespasian, and others, we are told, had their stated fast days: and Julian the Apostate was so exact in this observance as to outdo the priests themselves, and even the most rigid philosophers. The Pythagoreans kept a continual fast; but with this difference, that they believed the use of fish to be equally unlawful with that of flesh. Besides their constant temperance, they also frequently fasted rigidly for a very long time. In this respect, however, they were all outdone by their master Pythagoras, who continued his fasts for no less than 40 days together. Even Apollonius Tyaneus, one of his most famous disciples, could never come up to him in the length of his fasts, though they greatly exceeded those of the ordinary Pythagoreans. The Gymnosophists, or Brahmans of the east, are also very remarkable for their severe fastings; and the Chinese, according to Father Le Comte, have also their stated fasts, with forms of prayer for preserving them from barrenness, inundations, earthquakes, &c. The Mahometans too, who possess so large a part of Asia, are very remarkable for the strict observance of their fasts; and the exactness of their dervishes in this respect is extraordinary. Fasting was often used by the heathens for superstitious purposes; sometimes to procure the interpretations of dreams; at others, to be an antidote against their pernicious consequences. A piece of superstition prevails to this day among the Jews; who, though expressly forbidden to fast on Sabbath-days, think themselves at liberty to dispense with this duty when they happen to have fruitful and unlucky dreams the night preceding, that threatened them with great misfortunes. On these occasions they observe a formal fast the whole day; and at night the patient, having invited three of his friends, addresses himself to them seven times in a very solemn manner, saying, "May the dream I have had prove a lucky one!" And his friends answer as many times, "Amen, may it be lucky, and God make it so!" After which, in order to encourage him, they conclude the ceremony with these words of Ecclesiastes, "Go eat thy bread with joy;" and then sit themselves down to table. They have also added several fasts not commanded in the law of Moses, particularly three, in memory of sore distresses their nation has suffered at different times. The abstinence of the ancient Jews commonly lasted 27 or 28 hours at a time; beginning before sunset, and not ending till some hours after sunset next day. On these days they were obliged to wear white robes in token of grief and repentance; to cover themselves with sackcloth, or their worst clothes; to lie on ashes; to sprinkle them on their head, &c. Some spent the whole night and day following in the temple or synagogue, in prayers and other devotions, barefooted, with a scourge in their hands, of which they sometimes made a good use in order to raise their zeal. Lastly, in order to complete their abstinence, at night they were to eat nothing but a little bread dipped in water, with some salt for seasoning; except they chose to add to their repast some bitter herbs and pulse. The ancients, both Jews and Pagans, had also their fasts for purifying the body, particularly the priests and such as were any way employed at the altars; for when nocturnal disorders happened to these, it was unlawful for them to approach all the next day, which they were bound to employ in purifying themselves. On this account, at great festivals, where their ministry could not be dispensed with, it was usual for them, on the eve thereof, not only to fast, but also to abstain from sleep, for the greater certainty. For this purpose the high priest had under officers to wake him, if overtaken with sleep; against which other preservatives were also made use of. FASTERMANS

Pages 191-191
or FASTING-MEN, q. d. homines habentes, was used in our ancient customs for men in repute and substance; or rather for pledges, sureties, or bondsmen, who, according to the Saxon polity, were fast bound to answer for one another's peaceable behaviour.

FASTI

Pages 191-193

in Roman antiquity, the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALENDAR">calendar</a> wherein were expressed the several days of the year, with their feasts, games, and other ceremonies. There were two sorts of fasti, the greater and lesser: the former being distinguished by the appellation fasti magistrales, and the latter by that of fasti calendares. 1. The fasti calendares, which were properly and primarily called fasti, are defined by Feftus Pompeius to be books containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the whole year: i.e. ephemerides, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> diaries, distinguishing the several kinds of days, fasti, profasti; fasti, nefasti, &c. The author of these was Numa, who committed the care and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the fasti to the pontifex maximus, whom the people used to consult on every occasion. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> held till the year of Rome 459, when C. Flavius, secretary to the pontifices, exposed in the forum a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> of all the days on which it was lawful to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>; which was so acceptable to the people, that they made him curule edile. These lesser fasti, or fasti calendares, were of two kinds, urbani and rustic. The fasti urbani, or fasti of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, were those which obtained or were observed in the city. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have them thus called, because they were exposed publicly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the city; though by the various <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INSCRIPTIONS">inscriptions</a> or gravings thereof on antique <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, one would imagine that private persons had them likewise in their houses. Ovid undertook to illustrate these fasti urbani, and comment on them, in his Libri Fastorum. Fas, Faflorum, whereof we have the first six books still remaining; the last six, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> ever they were written, being lost. In the fafla rusticis, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> fasti, were expressed the several days, feasts, &c., to be observed by the country people: for as these were taken up in tilling the ground, fewer feasts, sacrifices, ceremonies, and holidays, were enjoined them than the inhabitants of cities; and they had also some peculiar ones not observed at Rome. These rustic fasti contained little more than the ceremonies of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KALENDS">kalends</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-NONES">nones</a>, and ides; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FAIRS">fairs</a>, signs of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZODIAC">zodiac</a>, incense and decrease of the days, the tutelary gods of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a>, and certain directions for rural works to be performed each month. 2. In the greater fasti, or fasti magistrates, were expressed the several feasts, with every thing relating to the gods, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and the magistrates; the emperors, their birth-days, offices, days consecrated to them, and feasts and ceremonies established in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a>, or for their prosperity, &c. With a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of such circumstances did flattery at length swell the fasti; when they became denominated Magni, to distinguish them from the bare calendar, or fasti kalendares. Fasti was also a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRONICLE">chronicle</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGISTER">register</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, where-in the several years were denoted by the respective consuls, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> events that happened during their consulates; these were called also fasti consulares, or consular fasti. Fasti, or Dies Fasti, also denoted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> days. The word fasti faflorum, is formed of the verb fari, "to speak," because during those days the courts were opened, causes might be heard, and the praetor was allowed fari, to pronounce the three words, do, dico, addico: The other days wherein this was prohibited were called nefasti: thus Ovid, Ille nefastus erit, per quem tria verba silentur: Fastus erit, per quem lege licet agi. These dieti fasti were noted in the calendar by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> F: but observe, that there were some days ex parte fasti, partly fasti, partly nefasti; i.e., <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> might be distributed at certain times of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, and not at others. These days were called intercali, and were marked in the calendar thus; F. P. faflor primo, where justice might be demanded during the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of that day. Fasting, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> from food. See Fast. Many wonderful stories have been told of extraordinary fasting; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> numbers of which undoubtedly must be false. Others, however, we have on very good authority, of which some are mentioned under the article Abstinence. Another we have in the Fasting Woman. A full account of this very uncommon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is given in the Phil. Trans. Vol. LXVII. Part I. the substance of which follows: The woman, whose name was Janet McLeod, an inhabitant of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINCARDINE">Kincardine</a> in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROSS_SHIRE">Ross-shire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> healthy till she was 15 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, when she had a pretty severe epileptic fit; after this she had an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTERVAL">interval</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> for four years, and then another epileptic fit which continued a whole day and a night. A few days afterwards she was seized with a fever, which continued with violence several weeks, and from which she did not perfectly recover for some months. At this fasting time she lost the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of her eyelids; so that she was under a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of keeping them open with the fingers of one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, whenever she wanted to look about her. In other respects she continued in pretty good health; only she never had any appearance of menes, but periodically spit up blood in pretty <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities, and at the same time it flowed from the nose. This discharge continued several years; but at last it ceased: and soon after she had a third epileptic fit, and after that a fever from which she recovered very slowly. Six weeks after the crisis, she stole out of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> unknown to her parents, who were buried in their <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> work, and bound the sheaves of a ridge before she was observed. In the evening she took to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>, complaining much of her heart (most probably her stomach, according to the phraseology of that country) and her head. From that time she never rose for five years, but was occasionally lifted out of bed. She seldom spoke a word, and took no little food that it seemed scarce sufficient to support a sucking infant. Even this small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> was taken by compulsion; and at last, about Whitunday 1763, she totally refused every kind of food or drink. Her jaw now became so fast locked, that it was with the greatest difficulty her father was able to open her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> a little, in order to admit a small quantity of gruel or whey; but of this so much generally run out at the corners of her mouth, that they could not be sensible any had been swallowed. About this time they got some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from a noted medicinal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> in Brae-Mar, some of which they attempted to make her swallow, but without effect. They continued their trials, however, for three mornings; rubbing her throat with the water, which run out at the corners of her mouth. On the third morning during the operation, she cried out, "Give me more water;" and swallowed with ease all that remained in the bottle. She spoke no more intelligibly for a year; though she continued to mutter some words, which her parents only understood, for 14 days. She continued to reject all kinds of food and drink till <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1765. At this time her father thought, by some figs he made, that she wanted her jaws opened; and this being done, not without violence, she called intelligibly for a drink, and drank with ease about an English pint of water. Her father then asked her why she would not make some signs when she wanted a drink? to which she answered, why should she when she had no desire. It was now supposed that she had regained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of speech; and her jaws were kept open for about three weeks by means of a wedge. But in four or five days she became totally silent, and the wedge was removed because it made her lips sore. She still, however, continued sensible; and when her eyelids were opened, knew everybody, as could be guessed from the signs she made. By continuing their attempts to force open her jaws, two of the under foreteeth were driven out; and of this opening her parents endeavoured to avail themselves by putting some thin nourishing drink into her mouth; but without effect, as it always returned by the corners. Sometimes they thought of thrusting a little dough of oatmeal through this <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol10.html#article-GAP">gap</a> of the teeth, which she would retain a few seconds, and then return with something like a straining to vomit, without one particle Fasting. ticle going <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. Nor were the family sensible of anything like swallowing for four years, excepting the small draught of Brae-Mar water and the English pint of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> water. For the last three years she had not any evacuation by stool or urine, except that once or twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> she passed a few drops of urine, about as much, to use the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of her parents, as would wet the surface of a halfpenny. In this situation she was visited by Dr Mackenzie, who communicated the account of her case to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. He found her not at all emaciated; her <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-KNEES">knees</a> were bent, and the hamstring tight, so that her heels almost touched her buttocks. She slept much, and was very quiet; but when awake, kept a constant whimpering like a newborn weakly infant. She never could remain a moment on her back, but always fell to one side or another; and her chin was clasped <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>, nor could it by any force be moved backwards. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> paid his first visit in the month of October; and five years afterwards, viz. in October 1772, was induced to pay her a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> visit, by hearing that she was recovering, and had begun to eat and drink. The account given him was most extraordinary. Her parents one day returning from their country labours (having left their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> fixed to her bed as usual), were greatly surprised to find her sitting upon her hams, on the side of the house opposite to her bed-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> with her mother's distaff. All the food she took at that time was only to crumble a little oat or barley cake in the palm of her hand, as if to feed a chicken. She put little crumbs of this into the gap of her teeth; rolled them about for some time in her mouth; and then sucked out of the palm of her hand a little water, whey, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and this only once or twice a-day, and even that by compulsion. She never attempted to speak; her jaws were fast locked, and her eyes shut. On opening her eyelids, the balls were found to be turned up under the edge of the os frontis; her countenance was ghastly, her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>, and her whole person emaciated. She seemed feeble, and tractable in every thing except in taking food. This she did with the utmost reluctance, and even cried before she yielded. The great change of her looks Dr Mackenzie attributed to her spinning <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAX">flax</a> on the distaff, which exhausted too much of the saliva; and therefore he recommended to her parents to confine her totally to the spinning of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>. In 1775, she was visited again, and found to be greatly improved in her looks as well as strength; her food was also considerably increased in quantity; though even then she did not take more than would be sufficient to sustain an infant of two years of age. The following remarkable instances of animals being able to live <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> without food, are related by Sir William <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAMILTON">Hamilton</a> in his account of the late earthquakes in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> (Phil. Transf. vol. lxxiii). "At Soriano (says he), two fattened hogs that had remained buried under a heap of ruins, were taken out alive the 42d day; they were lean and weak, but soon recovered." Again, "At Messina two mules belonging to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> de Belvil remained under a heap of ruins, one of them 22 days, and the other 23 days; they would not eat for some days, but drank water plentifully, and are now recovered. There are numberless instances of dogs remaining many days in the same situation; and a hen belonging to the British vice-<a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSUL">consul</a> at Messina, that had been closely shut up under the ruins of his house, was taken out the 22d day, and is now recovered; it did not eat for some days, but drank freely; it was emaciated, and showed little signs of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> at first. From these instances, and those related before of the hogs at Soriano, and several others of the same kind that have been related to me, but which being less remarkable I omit, one may conclude, that long fasting is always attended with great thirst and total loss of appetite." An instance of a similar kind, not less remarkable than either of the two preceding, we find in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">Gentleman</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGAZINE">Magazine</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1785, communicated by a correspondent, as follows: "During the heavy snow which fell in the night of the 7th of January 1779, a parcel of sheep belonging to Mr John Wolley, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATLOCK">Matlock</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>, which were pastured on that part of the East Moor that lies within the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> of Matlock, were covered with the drifted snow: in the course of a day or two all the sheep that were covered with the snow were found again, except two, which were consequently given up as lost; but on the 14th of February following (some time after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> of the snow in the valleys, and 38 days after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>), as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> was walking over a large parcel of drifted snow which remained on the declivity of a hill, a dog he had with him discovered one of the two sheep that had been lost, by winding (or scenting) it through a small aperture which the breath of the sheep had made in the snow; the servant thereupon dug away the snow, and released the captive from its prison; it immediately ran to a neighbouring spring, at which it drank for a considerable time, and afterwards rejoined its old companions as though no such accident had befallen it. On inspecting the place where it was found, it appeared to have stood between two large stones which lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> with each other at about two feet and a half distance, and probably were the means of protecting it from the great <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of the snow, which, in that place lay several yards thick: from the number of stones around it, it did not appear that the sheep had been able to pick up any food during its confinement. Soon afterwards its owner removed it to some low lands; but as it had nearly lost its appetite, it was fed with <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and milk for some time: in about a fortnight after its enlargement it lost its sight and wool; but in a few weeks afterwards they both returned again, and in the course of the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> it was quite recovered. The remaining sheep was found dead about a week after the discovery of the other." In the same publication is recorded the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of one Caleb Elliot, a visionary enthusiast, who meant to have fasted 40 days, and actually survived 16 without bituary food, having obstinately refused sustenance of every kind.

FASTOLF

Pages 193-194

Sir John, a valiant and renowned English officer, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a> banneret and of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARTER">garter</a>, who served in France under Henry IV. V. and VI. was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, and was born about the year 1377. He was as much distinguished for his virtue at home as for his valour abroad; and became no less amiable in his private, than he had been admirable in his public character. He died in 1457, upwards of 80 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, as we learn. learn from his noted <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTEMPORARY">contemporary</a> William Caxton the first English printer. By an unaccountable mistake it has been alleged, that Shakespeare's Falstaff was drawn to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a> this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>; and this has made judicious biographers more studious to preserve his reputation.

FAT

Pages 194-194

an oily concrete substance, deposited in different parts of animal bodies. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>, supernatural <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, an acrimonious state of the juices, and other like causes, by which the oily parts of the blood are attenuated, resolved, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> evacuated, prevent the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> of fat; labours of the mind also have this effect, as well as labour or intemperance of the body. Hence rest and plentiful food are sufficient to fatten <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUTES">brutes</a>; but with men it is often otherwise. It is surprising how soon some birds grow fat; ortolans, it is said, in 24 hours, and larks still sooner. Fats may be divided, from their consistence, into three kinds: (1.) The soft and thin, which grow perfectly liquid in a very small heat; (2.) The thick and consistent, which liquefy less readily; and, (3.) The hard and firm, which require a still stronger heat to melt them. The first is called Pinguedo; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, Avengia; and the third, Adeps, as taken from the animal; and Selum, or Sevum, when freed from the skins, &c. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the names, however, is not constant, some employing them differently. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fats have been kept in the shops, for making ointments, plasters, and other medicinal compositions; as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOG">hog</a>'s <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-LARD">lard</a>, the fat of the boar, the fox, the hare, dog, wild cat, Alpine moufe, beaver; that of hens, ducks, geese, storks; of the whale, pike, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERPENTS">serpents</a>, viper, &c. as also <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> fat.—In regard to all these kinds of substances, however, much depends upon the manner of purifying or trying, and of keeping them. To obtain fat pure, it must be cut into pieces, and cleaned from the interposed membranes and vessels. It must then be cleansed from its gelatinous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> by washing with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, till the water comes from it colourless and insipid; it is afterwards to be melted with a moderate heat in a proper vessel with a little water; and it is to be kept thus melted till the water be entirely evaporated, which is known by the discontinuance of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, which is caused by the water only, and which lasts till not a drop of it remains; it is afterwards to be put into an earthen pot, where it fixes; then it is exceedingly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, sufficiently pure for the purposes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHARMACY">pharmacy</a> or chemical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>. Fat thus purified has very little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and a weak, but peculiar smell. For its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> and chemical properties, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. One of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> uses of fat probably is, to receive into its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, to blunt and correct, a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a> of the aliments, and which are more than are requisite to the composition of the nutritive juice, or which <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> could not otherwise expel. This is certain, that the greater the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of aliments taken by healthy animals, above what is necessary for their nourishment and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-REPRODUCTION">reproduction</a>, the fatter they become. Hence animals which are castrated, which are not much exercised, or which are come to an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> when the loss and production of the seminal fluid is less, and which at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> consume much succulent aliment, generally become fatter, and sometimes exceedingly so. Although fat be very different from truly animalized substances, and appears not easily convertible into nutritive juices, it being generally difficult of digestion, and apt to become rancid, as <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> does in the stomachs of many persons; yet in certain <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> it serves to the nourishment and reparation of the body. Animals certainly become lean, and live upon their fat, when they have too little food, and when they have diseases which prevent digestion and the production of the nutritive juice; and in these cases the fatter animals hold out longer than the leaner. The fat appears to be then absorbed by the vessels designed for this use, and to be transformed into nutritive juice. Fat, in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, signifies the same with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>. Thus a ship is said to have a fat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the trussing in or tuck of her quarter be deep.

FAT LIKEWISE

Pages 194-195

t likewise denotes an uncertain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity. Thus a fat of inglands contains from 3½ hundred <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> to 4 hundred weight; a fat of unbound books, half a maund <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> four bales; of wire, from 20 to 25 hundred weight; and of yarn, from 220 to 221 bundles. Fat, or VAT, is used also for several utensils: as, 1. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> wooden vessel, employed for measuring of malt, and containing a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> or eight bushels. 2. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a> vessel, used by brewers to run their wort in. 3. A leaden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">pan</a> or vessel for the making of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DROITWICH">Droitwich</a>. FATA MORGANA; a very singular phenomenon, mentioned by different philosophical writers and travellers, particularly by Brydone and Swinburne. They inform us that it is seen in the straits of Messina, and sometimes denominated the castles of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAIRY">Fairy</a> Morgana. The accounts of this phenomenon differ considerably from each other, and travellers are not unanimous as to the causes which are necessary for its production. It would perhaps be difficult to determine how far the imagination of those who have spoken of it may be considered capable of producing astonishment, yet the actual existence of such a phenomenon admits of no dispute. The first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> of Minasi, in his Dissertation on the Fata Morgana, speaks of this phenomenon in the following manner. When the rising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> thins from that point whence its incident ray forms an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of 45° on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REGGIO">Reggio</a>, and the bright surface of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> is not disturbed either by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> or the current, the spectator being placed on an eminence of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, with his back to the sun and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> to the sea; on a sudden there appear in the water, as in a catoptric <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a>, various multiplied objects, that is to say, numberless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of pilasters, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a>, castles well delineated, regular columns, lofty towers, superb palaces, with balconies and windows, extended alleys of trees, delightful plains with herbs and flocks, armies of men on foot and horseback, and many other strange images, in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> colours and proper actions, passing rapidly in succession along the surface of the sea during the whole of the short <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> while the above-mentioned causes remain. "But <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a>, in addition to the circumstances before described, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> be highly impregnated with vapour and dense exhalations, not previously dispersed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of the wind or waves, or rarefied by the sun, it..." it then happens that in this vapour, as in a curtain extended along the channel to the height of about 30 palms, and nearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the sea, the observer <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> behold the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCENE">scene</a> of the same objects not only reflected from the surface of the sea, but likewise in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, though not so distinct or well defined as the former objects from the sea. "If the air be slightly hazy and opake, and at the same time dewy and adapted to form the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">iris</a>, then the above-mentioned objects will appear only at the surface of the sea, as in the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, but all vividly coloured, or fringed with <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, green, blue, and other prismatic colours." From this account of Minasi it appears, that there are three different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Fata Morgana; the first appearing at the surface of the sea, denominated the Marine Morgana; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in the air, called the Aerial Morgana, and the third only at the surface of the sea, or Morgana fringed with prismatic colours. The same ingenious author attempted to trace the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a> of the word Morgana, which he thinks is derived from μοργανής, τριγύρης, and γαλακτοσ, λευκότητος αφίξιος. This splendid sight affects all descriptions of men with such joy, that they run towards the sea, exclaiming Morgana, Morgana! This etymology of Minasi may seem at first view to be a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> in terms; but it will appear most natural, when we consider the joy which the Morgana inspires, and the corresponding sorrow or dejection which must be felt when it vanishes away. Our author informs us, that he beheld this magnificent appearance three times, and would rather behold it again than the "most superb theatrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> in the world." In his physical and astronomical remarks on this phenomenon, he observes that the sea in the straits of Messina exhibits the appearance of a large inclined speculum; that, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERNATE">alternate</a> current or tide which flows and returns in the straits for six hours each way, and is constantly attended by an opposite current along shore to the medium distance of about half a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a>, there are many eddies and irregularities at the time of the change of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; and that the Morgana usually appears at this period. He describes the effects produced by it to the supposed inclination of the surface of the sea, and its subdivision into different planes by the contrary eddies. The effects produced in the air he considers as the result of saline and other effluvia suspended in the air. These appearances are produced by a calm sea, and one or more <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of superincumbent air differing in refractive, and consequently in reflective power, rather than from any considerable change in the surface of the water, with the laws of which we are much better acquainted than with those of the atmosphere. To the above account we shall add the following, given by M. Houel, whose judgment and veracity render his authority highly respectable. "In fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> days, when the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> is calm, there rises above the great current a vapour, which acquires a certain density, so as to form in the atmosphere <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> prisms, whose sides are disposed in such a manner, that when they come to their proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection, they reflect and represent successively, for some time (like a moveable mirror), the objects on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> or in the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>. They exhibit by turns the city and suburbs of Messina, trees, animals, men, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. They are certainly beautiful aerial moving pictures. There are sometimes two or three prisms, equally perfect; and they continue in this state eight or ten minutes. After this, some shining inequalities are observed upon the surface of the prism, which render confused to the eye the objects which had been before so accurately delineated, and the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PICTURE">picture</a> vanishes. The vapour forms other <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMBINATIONS">combinations</a>, and is dispersed in air. Different accounts have been given of this singular appearance; which for my <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> I <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> to a bitumen that issues from certain rocks at the bottom of the sea, and which is often seen to cover a part of its surface in the strait of Messina. The subtile parts of the bitumen being attenuated, combined, and exhaled with the aqueous globules that are raised by the air, and formed into bodies of vapour, give to this condensed vapour more consistence; and contribute, by their smooth and polished particles, to the formation of a kind of aerial crystal, which receives the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, reflects it to the eye, and transmits to it all the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> the objects exhibited in this phenomenon, and render them visible."

FATE

Pages 195-195

denotes an inevitable <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> depending upon a superior cause. The word is formed à fando, "from speaking," and primarily implies the same with effatum, viz. a word <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DECREE">decree</a> pronounced by God; or a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENTENCE">sentence</a> whereby the Deity has prescribed the order of things, and allotted to every person what shall befall him. The Greeks called it ναυπάτρια, as it were a chain or necessary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of things indissolubly linked together. It is also used to express a certain unavoidable designation of things, by which all agents, both necessary and voluntary, are swayed and directed to their ends. See NECESSITY. In this last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, fate is distinguished into, 1. Astrological fate, arising from the influence and position of the heavenly bodies; which (it was supposed) gave laws both to the elements and mixed bodies, and to the wills of men. 2. Stoical fate, defined by Cicero an order or series of causes, wherein, cause being linked to cause, each produces another, and thus all things flow from one prime cause. To this fate the Stoics subject even the gods. Fate is divided by later authors into physical and divine. Physical fate is an order and series of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> causes appropriated to their effects. By this fate it is that fire warms, bodies communicate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> to each other, &c. and the effects of it are all the events and phenomena of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. 2. Divine fate is what is more usually called <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">PROVIDENCE</a>. See PROVIDENCE.

FATHEMITES

Pages 195-195

FATHEMITES, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> FATHIMITES, the descendants of Mahomet by Fatima, or Fatima, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>. They never enjoyed the caliphate of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAGDAD">Bagdad</a>, but reigned in Barbary and <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGYPT">Egypt</a>. See the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of these countries.

FATHER

Pages 195-196

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of relation denoting a person who hath begot a child. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">PARENT</a> and CHILD. By the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>, a father had an unlimited power over his children. Amongst the Lacedemonians, as we learn from <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>'s Politics, the father of three children was excused from the duty of mounting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> for the security of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>; and a father of four children was exempted from every public burden. The Poppean <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, granted many valuable privileges to the fathers of three chil- Father dren; amongst which one was, that he should be excused from civil offices, and that the mother should have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a>, in her father's lifetime, to make a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and manage her estate without the authority of tutors. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> Father, is he who has illegitimate children. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASTARD">Bastard</a>; and Law <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Adoptive Father, is he who takes the children of some other, and acknowledges them as his own. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADOPTION">Adoption</a>. Putative Father, is he who is only the reputed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> supposed father. <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> was putative father of our Saviour. Father-in-law, is a person married to a woman who has children by a former husband, &c., to which children he is said to be a father-in-law. Father is also used in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> for the First Person in the Trinity. Father is also used in a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> on <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> moral and spiritual occasions. Thus, it is applied to the patriarchs; as we say <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADAM">Adam</a> was the father of all mankind, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABRAHAM">Abraham</a> the father of the faithful, &c. Father, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, is applied to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors who have preserved in their writings the traditions of the church. Thus St Chrysostom, St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a>, &c., are called Greek fathers, and St Augustine and St <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBROSE">Ambrose</a> Latin fathers. No author who wrote later than the 12th century is dignified with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Father. Father, is also a title of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> given to prelates and dignitaries of the church, to the superiors of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CONVENTS">convents</a>, to congregations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ECCLESIASTICS">ecclesiastics</a>, and to persons venerable for their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Thus we say, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> reverend father in God, the father general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEDICTINES">Benedictines</a>, the fathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> of Nice, father of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, &c.

FATHERLASHER

Pages 196-197

a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fishes belonging to the genus cottus. See Cottus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fathom, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing six feet, used chiefly at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> for measuring the length of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> and cordage. Fatness.
