To explain this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> a little farther: The word felony, or felonia, is of undoubted feudal original, being frequently to be met with in the books of feuds, &c.; but the derivation of it has much puzzled the juridical lexicographers, Prateus, Calvinus, and the rest: some deriving it from the Greek, παράστης, "an impostor or deceiver;" others from the Latin, fallo, fefelli, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTER">counter</a>- Felony, nance which they would have it called fellonia. Sir Edward Coke, as his manner is, has given us a still stranger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETYMOLOGY">etymology</a>; that it is crimen animo felleo perpetratum, "with a bitter or gallish inclination." But all of them agree in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a>, that it is such a crime as works a forfeiture of all the offender's lands or goods. And this gives <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> to Sir Henry Spelman's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEUTONIC">Teutonic</a> or German derivation of it: in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, indeed, as the word is clearly of feudal origin, we ought rather to look for its signification, than among the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Felon then, according to him, is derived from two northern words: FEE, which signifies (we well know) the fief, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FEUD">feud</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENEFICIARY">beneficiary</a> estate; and LON, which signifies price or value. Felony is therefore the same as pretium feudii, the consideration for which a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> gives up his fief; as we say in common speech, such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> is as much as your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> or estate is worth. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> clearly signify the feudal forfeiture, or act by which an estate is forfeited, or escheats to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a>. To confirm this, we may observe, that it is in this sense, of forfeiture to the lord, that the feudal writers constantly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it. For all those acts, whether of a criminal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> or not, which at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> are generally forfeitures of copyhold estates, are styled felonies in the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal law</a>: "si scilicet, per quas feudum amittitur." As "si dominus deferviret nobiorem si per annum et diem essaverit in petenda invictura si dominum ejuravit, i.e. negavit se a domino feudum habere si a domino in jus eum vacante, ter citatus non comparuerit:"—all these, with many others, are still causes of forfeiture in our copyhold estates, and were denominated felonies by the feudal constitutions. So likewise injuries of a more substantial or criminal nature were denominated felonies, that is, forfeitures: as assaulting or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the lord; vitiating his wife or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a>, "si dominum cucurbitaverit," i.e. cum uxor ejus concubuerit; all these are esteemed felonies, and the latter is expressly so denominated, "si fecerit feloniam, dominum forte cucurbitando." And as these contempts, or smaller offences, were felonies or acts of forfeiture, of course greater crimes, as <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a> and robbery, fell under the same denomination. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the lord might be guilty of felony, or forfeit his feignory to the vassal, by the same act as the vassal would have forfeited his feud to the lord. "Si dominus commisit feloniam, per quam vassalus amitteret feudum si cam committerit in dominium, feudii proprietatem etiam dominus perdere debet." One instance given of this sort of felony in the lord is beating the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> of his vassal, so that he loses his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; which seems merely in the nature of a civil injury, so far as it respects the vassal. And all these felonies were to be determined, "per laudamentum five judicium parium suorum," in the lord's <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>; as with us forfeitures of copyhold lands are presentable by the homage in the court-baron. Felony, and the act of forfeiture to the lord, being thus <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SYNONYMOUS">synonymous</a> terms in the feudal law, we may callily trace the reason why, upon the introduction of that law into England, those crimes which induced such forfeiture or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> of lands (and, by a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFECTION">defection</a> from the original sense, such as induced the forfeiture of goods also) were denominated felonies. Thus it was that suicide, robbery, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAPE">rape</a>, were felonies; that is, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of such crimes was forfeiture; till by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> use we began to signify by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of felony the actual crime committed, and not the penal consequence. And upon this system only can we account for the cause, why treason in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> times was held to be a species of felony; viz. because it induced a forfeiture. Hence it follows, that capital punishment does by no means enter into the true idea and definition of felony. Felony may be without inflicting capital punishment, as in the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> instances of self-murder, excusable homicide, and petit-larceny: and it is possible that capital punishments may be inflicted, and yet the offence be no felony; as in case of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> by the common law, which, though capital, never worked any forfeiture of lands or goods, an inseparable incident to felony. And of the same nature was the punishment of standing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUTE">mute</a>, without pleading to an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>; which at the common law was capital, but without any forfeiture, therefore such standing mute was no felony. In short, the true criterion of felony is forfeiture: for, as Sir Edward Coke justly observes, in all felonies which are punishable with death, the offender loses all his lands in fee-simple, and also his goods and chattels; in such as are not punishable, his goods and chattels only. The idea of felony is indeed so generally connected with that of capital punishment, that we find it hard to separate them; and to this usage the interpretations of the law do now conform. And therefore, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a statute makes any new offence felony, the law implies that it shall be punished with death, viz. by hanging, as well as with forfeiture: unless the offender pays the benefit of clergy; which all felons are entitled once to have, unless the same is expressly taken away by statute. Felonies by statute are very numerous; and as this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> will not admit of a proper enumeration, we must refer to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of the quarto edition of the Statutes, where they are set forth in alphabetical order.

FELTING

Pages 206-207

the method of working up <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> into a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of cloth, independent of either <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">weaving</a>. Felting in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is not much practised, except in the manufacturing of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-HATS">hats</a>; and as the generality even of those who are employed in making them, are unacquainted with the principles on which they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, a few observations on the method of felting may, to such, be both useful and agreeable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> wool, the hair of a rabbit, hare, beaver, or <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a>-hair, be examined with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a> of the greatest magnifying power, the surface of each hair appears perfectly smooth, or if any inequalities are observed, they do not appear so much to arise from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a> surface, as from some peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> and transparency of the substances examined; for if their image be viewed by a solar microscope, it terminates in even <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, without the smallest vestige of any roughness. Yet nothing is more evident than that the surfaces of hairs are not perfectly smooth, but either composed of lamellae covering each other from the root to the point, resembling the scales of fishes; or what some have deemed more more probable, of zones placed over each other, similar to the structure of horns; and to this texture, hair, wool, &c., owe their disposition for what is denominated felting. Let a person take hold of a hair by the root with one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and draw it between two fingers of the other, from the root towards the point, he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> scarcely perceive any friction, or hear any <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a>; but should he hold the hair by the point, and draw it between his fingers from the point towards the root, he will feel a sensible opposition or resistance which could not be felt before. A sort of tremulous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> is likewise produced, which can be distinguished by the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EAR">ear</a>. From this simple experiment it is obvious that the texture of the surface of a hair is not the same from the point to the root, as it is from the root to the point. If a hair is taken hold of by the fore-finger and thumb, and rubbed in a longitudinal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, a progressive motion is the result, which is invariably towards the root. This is wholly independent of the texture or <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the skin of the fingers; for if the hair be turned, and the point of it placed where the root formerly was, the movement becomes contrary, or, in other words, it is still directed towards the root. It is found a very difficult task to untie a knot made in the middle of a hair, on account of its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> thinness; but if the hair is placed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> of the hand, the knot being in a line with the little finger, and if the hair is grasped by closing the hand, and the fist struck several times against the knee, the knot is thereby opened, because the asperities of one end of the hair are in a contrary direction to those of the other, by which means each end of it recedes a little. By the introduction of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> into the eye thus formed at the knot, it is easily untied. Although these observations have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> reference to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> hair; yet they are equally applicable to wool, furs, and almost every species of animal hair. The surfaces of all these consist of hard lamellae, placed upon each other like tiles, in the direction from the root to the point. By attending to these remarks, it is easy to see why the contact of woollen stuffs is rough to the skin. The asperities on the surface of the fibres of wool produce a disagreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>, by fixing themselves in the skin, which can only be endured by being accustomed to feel it frequently. The injury done to wounds by the application of wool, is not the result of any chemical <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>, but is entirely occasioned by the asperities of its surface. A hatter separates the hairs from each other, by striking the wool with the string of his bow, causing them to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> up in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> in every possible direction, forming a layer of a particular thickness, which is covered by the workmen with a cloth, pressing it with his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and moving the hairs backwards and forwards in different directions. In this manner the hairs are brought against each other, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of contact considerably multiplied, and the agitation gives each hair a progressive motion towards the root, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the hairs become twisted together. As the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASS">mass</a> becomes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, the pressure ought to be increased, in order to keep up the progressive motion and twisting of the hairs, which is then performed with greater difficulty. The hair designed for the manufacturing of hats is always cut off with a sharp <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a>, and not pulled out by the roots, because the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> of the hair which would come out with it in the latter <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, would render the end which was fixed in the skin very obtuse, and nearly destroy its disposition to unite with the adjacent hairs. But in addition to the tendency of hairs to move progressively towards the root, they should not be straight like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NEEDLES">needles</a>, for in this case they could not produce any compactness in the stuff. The fibres of wool having naturally a crooked form, that substance is well adapted to the operation of felting. The hair of beavers, rabbits, hares, &c., being straight, it cannot be employed in felting by itself, till it has been subjected to a previous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>, viz. rubbing and combing on the skin, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> being dipped in a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a> in nitric acid. This substance, by acting only on one side of the hairs, gives them that disposition to felting which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> to wool. When it is not intended that the hairs shall enter into the body of the mass, but serve only as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> coating, which is sometimes given to the outer surface of hats, the operation with the nitric acid need not be performed. They must be uniformly spread upon the surface to which the coating is to be applied, and being covered with a cloth, it is pressed with the hands, and agitated for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They receive a particular direction afterwards by means of a brush, and are enabled to keep it by having a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> passed over them. Woollen cloth is thickened by fulling, on the same principles that wool and hair become capable of felting. Felt-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">Spar</a> or Feld-Spar, a mineral substance. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Feltria, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">Ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town on the borders of Rhaetia towards <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. Now Feltria, in the territory of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a>, on the Piava. E. Long. 12. 16. N. Lat. 46. 0. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FELUCCA">Felucca</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> affairs, a little vessel rowed with six oars, frequent in the Mediterranean; which has this peculiarity, that its helm may be applied either in the head or stern, as occasion requires. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">Female</a>, (feminina), a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> peculiar to animals, signifying that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEX">sex</a> which conceives and generates its young within itself. See Sex and <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">Generation</a>. Female is also applied, figuratively, to things without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, from the resemblance they bear to the females of animals. Thus we say a Female Screw. See Screw. Female Flower. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMININE">Feminine</a> Flos. Female Plant. See Feminine Planta. Femme <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COVERT">covert</a>, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, a married woman. See Coverture. Femme sole, an unmarried woman, whose debts, contracted before <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>, become those of her husband after it. A femme sole merchant, is where a woman, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, uses a trade alone, without her husband; on which account she shall be <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGED">charged</a> without him. Feminine, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">Grammar</a>, one of the genders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOUNS">nouns</a>. See Gender.

FEN

Pages 208-208

a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> overflowed with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> abounding with bogs. See Bog and Draining, in <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fens are either made up of a congeries of bogs; or consist of a multitude of pools or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, with dry spots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> intermixed, like so many little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>. Several statutes have been made for the draining of fens, chiefly in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGESHIRE">Cambridgeshire</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEDFORDSHIRE">Bedfordshire</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>; and by a late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, 11 Geo. II. commissioners shall be appointed for the effectually draining and preserving of the fens in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a>, who are authorized to make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAINS">drains</a>, dams, and proper works thereon; and they may <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> the landholders therein with a yearly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>-tax, and in default of payment, sell the defender's lands. The wet grounds called *fens*, in Lincolnshire and elsewhere in England, bring many advantages to the inhabitants of those counties. Fowl and fish are very plentiful in them. The pike and eels are <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and easily caught, but they are usually coarse. The duck, mallard, and teal, are in such plenty as is scarce to be conceived. They are taken by decoys in prodigious flocks at a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. They send these fowl from Lincolnshire to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, twice a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, on horseback, from Michaelmas to Lady-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; and one decoy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> furnish 20 dozen, or more, twice a-week, for the whole season in this manner. The decoy-men <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with the people, who bring them to London at a certain rate, and they are obliged to take off their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> that is catched. Two teal are usually reckoned equal to one duck; and five ducks and twelve teal are accounted a dozen of wild fowl; and the usual market price is about 9s. for such a dozen. About midsummer, during the moulting season, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> number also are destroyed by the people in the neighbourhoods. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> birds at this season are neither able to swim nor fly well; and the people going in with boats among the reeds where they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, knock them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a>. A little before Michaelmas, vast flights of these birds arrive at the decoys from other places; they soon grow fat in them, and continue there a prey to the masters or owners, as long as the decoys are unfrozen; but, when they are iced over, they fly away again, and go to the neighbouring seas for food. The fens also abound in a sort of herbage that is very nourishing to cattle. Sheep and horses always grow fat upon it. The fens are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, and the owners of cattle mark them that they may be known. It is remarkable, that, though all is open, the cattle used to one particular spot of ground seldom leave it, but the owner may always find them in or near the same place. The fens have many large and deep drains. In these the pike and eel grow to a vast size; and they are full of geese which feed on the grass; but these eat <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and muddy, and may even be found as soon as a person comes into the room where they are roosting. But the people have another very great advantage from these birds besides the eating of them, namely, their feathers and quills; and the produce of these is so great, that the customhouse books in the town of Bollton show, that there are frequently sent away in one year 300 bags of feathers, each containing a hundred and a half <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>. Each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> of feathers brings in the owner twopence; and it may be thought strange by people unacquainted with these things, but it is a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a>, that the owners pull them five or six times a year for the feathers, and three times for the quills. Each pulling comes to about a pound, and many people have 1000 geese at a time, or more. They are kept at no charge, except in deep snowy <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, when they are obliged to feed them with corn. Oats also grow very well in many of the fen countries, and in good seasons bring great increase and advantage to the owners. There is also another vegetable of great profit to them. This is the *rapum fibrofre*; the feed of which they call *cole-feed*; and they make an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> from it of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in trade. They grind the feed between two large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, the one standing perpendicularly on the other. The stones are made of a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> marble, and are brought from Germany. They sometimes turn them by sails, and sometimes by the drains which carry off the water from the fen lands. The fens lying low, and being of a vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, are very subject to be overflowed by waters from the neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> countries; and though great care and expense is used to keep them dry, they are often like a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>; and the sheep are obliged to be carried off in boats, and the people to live in their upper rooms, and to be supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> also with boats.

FENCE

Pages 208-209

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a> and Husbandry, a hedge, wall, ditch, <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other enclosure, made round gardens, fields, woods, &c. In hot climates, where they have not occasion for walls to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> their fruit, their gardens <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> open, where they can have a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> fence, and prospects; or else they bound their gardens with groves, in which are fountains, walks, &c., which are much more pleasing to the sight than a dead wall; but, in colder countries, we are obliged to have walls to shelter and ripen our fruit, although they take away much from the pleasant prospect of the garden. Brick walls are accounted the best and warmest for fruit: and these walls, being built panel-wise, with pillars at equal distances, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SAVE">save</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, in that the walls may be built thinner than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they were made plain without these panels, for then it would be necessary to build them thicker everywhere; and, besides, these panels make the walls look the handsomer. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a> walls, however, on account of their durability, are to be preferred to those of brick, especially those of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> hewn <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Those that are made of rough stones, though though they are very dry and warm, yet, by reason of their unevenness, are inconvenient to nail up trees to, except pieces of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> be laid in them here and there for that purpose. But, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> gardens, it is better to have the prospect open to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> garden; which should be surrounded with a fence, that from the garden the adjacent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> may be viewed. But this must depend on the situation of the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: for, if the prospect from the garden is not good, it had better be shut out from the sight than be open. As also, when a garden lies near a populous town, and the adjoining grounds are open to the inhabitants; if the garden is open, there will be no walking there in good <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, without being exposed to the view of all passersby, which is very disagreeable. Where the fences are made round a garden which is situated in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, they are extremely proper; because hereby the prospect of the park will be obtained in the garden, which renders those gardens much more agreeable than those that are confined.—In the making these fences there have been many inventions; but, upon the whole, none seem preferable to those which have an upright wall next the garden, which (where the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> will admit of a deep trench) should be five or six feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>; and, from the foot of this wall, the ground on the outside should rise with a gradual easy slope, to the distance of 18 or 20 feet; and where it can be allowed, if it slopes much farther it will be easier, and less perceptible as a ditch, to the eye, when viewed at a distance; but, if the ground is naturally wet, so as not to admit a deep fence, then, in order to make a fence against cattle, if the wall be four feet high, and flight posts of three feet high are placed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> behind the wall, with a small chain carried on from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> to post, no cattle or deer will ever attempt to jump against it; therefore it will be a secure fence against them; and if these are painted green, they will not be discerned at a distance, and at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the chain will secure persons walking in the garden from tumbling over. In places where there are no good prospects to be obtained from a garden, it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> to make the enclosure of park palings; which, if well performed, will last many years, and has a much better appearance than a wall; and this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> may be hid from the sight within, by plantations of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-EVERGREENS">evergreens</a>; or there may be a quick hedge planted within the pale, which may be trained up, so as to be an excellent fence by the time the pales begin to decay. Fences round parks are generally of palings; which, if well made of winter-fallen oak, will last many years. But a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> thing to be observed, in making these pales, is not to make them too heavy: for, when they are so, their own <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> will cause them to decay; therefore the pales should be cleft thin; and the rails should be cut triangular, to prevent the wet lodging upon them; and the posts should be good, and not placed too far asunder. If these things are observed, one of these pales will last, with a little care, upwards of 40 years very well. The common way of making these fences is, to have every other pale <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten inches above the intermediate ones; so that the fence may be six feet and a half high, which is enough for fallow deer; but, where there are <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> deer, the fence should be one foot higher, otherwise they will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> over. Some enclose their parks with brick walls; and in countries where stone is cheap, the walls are built with this material; some with, and others without, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KITCHEN">kitchen</a> garden, if rightly contrived, will contain walling enough to afford a supply of such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> as require the affluence of walls, for any family; and this garden, being situated on one side, and quite out of sight of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, may be surrounded with walls which will screen the kitchen garden from the sight of persons in the pleasure garden; and, being locked up, the fruit will be much better preserved than it can be in the public garden; and the having too great a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of walling is often the occasion that so many ill managed trees are frequently to be seen in large gardens. The height of garden walls should be 12 feet, which is a moderate proportion; and, if the soil be good, it may in time be well furnished with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> wood in every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, especially that part planted with pears, notwithstanding of the branches being trained horizontally from the bottom of the walls. With regard to the different kinds of fences, see <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fence-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">Month</a>, the month wherein deer begin to fawn, during which it is unlawful to hunt in the forest. It commences 15 days before Midsummer, and ends 15 days after it. This month, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> foresters, is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>-month. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FENCING">Fencing</a>, the art of making a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWORD">sword</a>, as well for attacking an enemy as for defending one's self. This art is acquired by practicing with foils, called in Latin rudes; whence fencing is also denominated gladiatura rudaria.—It is one of the exercises learnt in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> (see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">Exercise</a> and Academy); and is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACCOMPLISHMENT">accomplishment</a> both agreeable and useful;—agreeable, as it affords gentlemen a noble and distinguished amusement;—useful, as it forms their body; and furnishes them with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACULTY">faculty</a> of defense, whether it be of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> or their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, when the one or the other is attacked by those turbulent and dangerous persons whose correction is of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> in general. Pyrard affirms us, that the art of fencing is so highly esteemed in the East Indies, that none but princes and noblemen are allowed to teach it. They wear a badge or cognizance on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> arms, called in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> efaru; which is put on with great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, like the badges of our orders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHTHOOD">knighthood</a>, by the kings themselves. Fencing is divided into two parts, simple and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. Simple is that performed directly and nimbly, on the same line; and is either offensive or defensive.—The principal object of the first, is whatever may be attempted, in pushing or making palls, from this or that point, to the most uncovered part of the enemy. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> consists in parrying and repelling the thrusts aimed by the enemy. The compound includes all the possible arts and inventions to deceive the enemy, and make him leave that part we have a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> on bare and unguarded, upon finding

FENELON

Pages 209-210

FRANCIS DE SALIGNAC DE LA MOTTE, was of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and illustrious family, and born at the castle of Fenelon in Perigord in 1651. In 1689, he was appointed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a> to the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a> and Anjou; and in 1655 was consecrated archbishop of Cambrai. After this preferment, a storm arose against him, that obliged him to leave the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> forever, occasioned by his performance entitled, An Explanation of the Maxims of the Saints concerning the Interior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a>; in which he supposed to favour the extravagant notions of Madame Guyon, and the principles of Quietism. A controversy on this occasion was for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> carried on between him and M. Boiflet, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAUX">Meaux</a>; which terminated in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPEAL">appeal</a> to the pope; when his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLINESS">holiness</a> condemned the archbishop's book, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIEF">brief</a> dated <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 12, 1699. Some friends indeed pretend, that there was more of court policy than <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> zeal in this affair; but be this as it may, the archbishop submitted patiently to this determination; and, retiring to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIOCESE">diocese</a> of Cambrai, acquitted himself punctually in all the duties of his station, and led a most exemplary life. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> that gained him the greatest reputation, and which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> render his <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> immortal, is his Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TELEMACHUS">Telemachus</a>; the style of which is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a>, the fictions well contrived, the moral sublime, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> maxims tending all to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> of mankind. Hence it is thought, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTING">printing</a> of this work was stopped at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, that the prelate's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERESY">heresy</a> was in politics instead of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>; and though his disgrace was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to this work, he had, while he was tutor to the young princes, taught them the same principles affected and exemplified in Telemachus. Fenelon died in 1715; and a collection of all his religious works was afterwards printed at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROTTERDAM">Rotterdam</a>, under the care of the marquis de Fenelon his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a>-nephew, when <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBASSADOR">ambassador</a> to the States-General. FENNEL. See ANETHUM, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FENTON

Pages 210-210

Elijah, defended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SHELTON">Shelton</a> near <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEWCASTLE">Newcastle</a>, but in what year is uncertain. He was the youngest of 12 children, and was intended for the ministry; but embracing principles contrary to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, while at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, he became disqualified for entering into Fenugreek holy orders. After he quitted the university, he was secretary to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORRERY">Orrery</a>; but seems to have spent the most of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> amongst his friends and relations, and used to pay an annual visit to his elder <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> who enjoyed an estate of 1000l. a-year. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> tenderness and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMANITY">humanity</a>, enjoyed the utmost reputation, and was much esteemed by Mr Pope; who, when he died in 1730, paid him the tribute of a very elegant epitaph. He published a volume of poems in the year 1717; and in 1723 was acted his tragedy of Mariamne, built upon his story collected from Josephus in the third volume of the Spectator. FENUGREEK. See TRIGONELLA, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">BOTANY</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FEOD

Pages 210-210
or FEUD, is defined to be a right which a vassal hath in lands or some immovable thing of his lord's, to use the same, and take the profits thereof hereditarily, rendering unto the lord such feudal duties and services as belong to military tenure, &c., and the property of the soil always remaining to the lord.

FEODAL SYSTEM

Pages 210-217

the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of FEIFS <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> FEUDS. About 12 centuries ago, this system was so universally received in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, that Sir Henry Spelman calls it the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW_OF_NATIONS"><a class="xref</a>" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of nations in our western world. Hence it deserves our <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> in a particular manner; a knowledge of the different feuds being indispensably requisite for a proper understanding either of the civil <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of our own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, or of the laws by which its landed <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> is regulated. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> policy of the Celtic or northern nations, known by the names of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOTHS">Goths</a>, Vandals, Franks, Huns, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOMBARDS">Lombards</a>, furnished the original constitution or system of feuds. These people pouring out in vast multitudes from the same officina gentium or "storehouse of nations," overran all the European countries on the declension of the Roman empire. They brought the feudal system along with them from the countries out of which they emigrated; and, supposing it to be the most proper method of securing their new conquests, they introduced it into their more southerly colonies. According to this system, the victorious general allotted considerable tracts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers; while they, in like manner, divided their possessions among the inferior officers, and even those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SOLDIERS">soldiers</a> who were thought to be the most deserving. Allotments of this kind were named feoda, fiefs, fees, or feuds, from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of words, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> of these barbarians, signifying a reward or stipend bestowed on certain conditions (a). The condition upon which these rewards were given was, that the possessors should faithfully serve the person from whom they were received, both at home and abroad, in the military way. To this they engaged themselves by a juramentum fidelitatis, or oath of fealty;† in the event of a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of which, either by not performing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> due, or by transposing these two northern syllables, (A) We were informed by Pontopiddan, that odh in these northern languages is the same with proprietas, and dovall: in ALL with totum in the Latin. Hence among the northern nations, he tells us, that odhall signifies <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> 2, and hence we may conjecture that the udal right in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FINLAND">Finland</a> is derived †. By transposing these two northern syllables, service agreed upon, by deserting their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>, &c., the lands were to return to their original possessor. Thus the possessors of feudal allotments became interested in the defense of them; and not only the receivers but those who gave them, were equally and mutually bound to defend their possessions, none of them being able to pretend any right but that of conquest. For this purpose government and subordination were absolutely necessary; it being impossible to conduct any system of defense where every thing was tumultuous and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>. Every person, therefore, who was a feudatory, i.e. who had received lands, was bound to do everything in his power to defend the lord of his fee; while, on the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the latter was no less subordinate to his immediate superior; and so on to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> himself. In like manner a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RECIPROCAL">reciprocal</a> bond of defense existed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> from the prince to the lowest feudists. Such were the foundations on which the feudal system was properly established; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> was, a military subjection throughout the whole <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-COMMUNITY">community</a>. The prince could always collect an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> of feudatories ready to defend not only the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> in general, but the particular possessions of each person; and the propriety of this constitution was soon apparent in the strength which these newly erected kingdoms acquired, and the valor with which their conquests were defended. Besides these feudal grants, however, which were held only on the terms of military service above mentioned, there were others called allodial, which were given upon more enlarged principles. To these every free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a>; and could not only claim his territory as well as the rest, but dispose of it at his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> (n); and this freedom was denominated allodality. These allodials, however, were not exempted from military service. A part of their freedom consisted in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> to go to the wars; for this, in the barbarous times we speak of, was the only way to acquire any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of renown. Only the slaves were defined to follow the arts of peace; while every free person was not only at liberty to defend his country, but under an obligation to do it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of any urgent <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. Thus there was a feudal and a national <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MILITIA">militia</a>. The feudal and free people only were allowed to possess property; the national feudal vassals constituted the army, properly so called; militia, while the national militia was composed of the allodial proprietors. This allodality, however, was not confined to landed property, but included likewise moveable estates or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>; so that proprietors of the latter kind were obliged also in times of danger to bear arms and appear in the field. Between the feudal and different allodial proprietors, however, there was this farther situation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that the latter had no concern with any of the feudal lords themselves; so that they were never obliged to appear in the field unless when called forth by the sovereign against the enemies of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a>. This circumstance we might suppose to be an advantage, but it ultimately operated otherwise; becoming the means of changing the allodial right into a feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a>. For some time the holders of fiefs had an eminent advantage over the allodial proprietors. This was owing to the imperfection of government in those days; so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOBLES">nobles</a> had it in their power to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> their own quarrels, while the weak were equally exposed to the insults of both parties. The lord and his vassals therefore were always formidable; but the allodial --- (b) The author of *A View of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a> in Europe*, has traced the remote sources of the feudal laws in an elegant and spirited manner (book i. chap. ii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a>. i.) Tacitus informs us, that the individuals of each of the German nations cultivated by turns a tract of land proportionate to their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the whole; after which each individual received such an allotment of the cultivated tract as his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIGNITY">dignity</a> seemed to require. These nations had not altered their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> principles at the time they overran the Roman empire; and hence the provinces of it were then divided after the same manner. The most considerable allotment was bestowed on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, as being the most dignified person in the community, and this allotment was styled his domain; while the shares of citizens and warriors, which were likewise in proportion to the merit or dignity of each, constituted what was called allodality. But as it often happened that all the land was not exhausted by these partitions, what remained was considered as the property of the community, and in the barbaric codes was called the lands of the fisc. In such German nations as had thus obtained a settlement, it was necessary that there should be a more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> connexion betwixt the sovereign and the chiefs, as well as between the chiefs and people, than in others. This was effected by means of the lands of the fisc; for of these the sovereign took possession, dealing them out to the chiefs under the burden of appearing in arms whenever he should please to call; while the chiefs in like manner dealt out lands to those called their retainers, who were also obliged to supply them with military <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLIANCE">alliance</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of necessity. Hence a political system was founded, which had a prodigious effect on society in all those countries where it prevailed. The intention and tendency of this system was to render the nation independent both at home and abroad; for, while the people were all armed in their common defense, individuals were also properly guarded against the attacks of depopulation. The power of the chiefs, who formed a regular <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, was a counterpoise to that of the sovereign; while the number of the retainers and vassals, constituting the greatness and power of the nobility, was a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> against aristocratical oppression; for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> who oppressed his vassals evidently acted against his own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. Feudal proprietors had scarce any means of defending themselves. The reason of this was, in the first <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that the law did not allow them to commit any hostilities; and in the next, they were too distant and unconnected to form any proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAGUE">league</a> for mutual defense; and hence proceeded the necessity already hinted at, of converting allodial property into feudal tenure. This was indeed owing in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> to the absurdity and violence of the times, by which gifts of property, burdened with service, and which might return to the person who granted them, were rendered superior in value to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> and unconditional possession of a subject. Other considerations, however, besides those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> mentioned, contributed to produce the same effect. As in those dark ages no right existed but what had its origin in conquest, it thence followed, that the greatest conqueror or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WARRIOR">warrior</a> was the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> person. The king, in whom the whole exploits of the community centered, as being their head, was the most honourable person: all others derived from him that portion of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> which they enjoyed, and which was most nicely adjusted in proportion as they approached him. Allodial proprietors, therefore, having no pretensions of this kind, were treated with contempt as a kind of poltroons. From this disagreeable situation they wished to free themselves, by converting their allodial property into feudal tenures; while the princes, supposing it their interest to extend those tenures as much as possible, discouraged the allodial possessions. As the feudists supported the conversion of the nation and dignity of the monarch, of allodium it was not thought proper to allow the allodial proprietors any greater compensations than what were given to vassals in similar cases. Thus they were exposed to continual mortifications in the courts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>: they were neglected by the king; denied sufficient protection from the laws; exposed not only to continual insults; but to have their property on all occasions destroyed by the great: so that they were without resource except from the feudal tenures, and were obliged even to solicit the privileges which were bestowed in other cases on vassals. In these unhappy circumstances, they were glad to yield up their lands to any superior whom they thought most agreeable, and to receive them back from him as a feudal gift. Thus the landed property was everywhere changed into feudal tenures, and fiefs became universal (c). For some time the feudal system was not only useful in itself, but honourable in its principles; but this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> no longer than while the importers of it into Europe adhered to their original simple and noble maxims. During that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, the lord exercised his bounty. (c) It has been an object of inquiry to the learned, in what nation of barbarians fiefs had their origin? But it is probable, that they took place in all these nations nearly about the same time, on the same principles; and were continued by reason of a similarity of manners, conquests, &c., so that we cannot ascribe the prevalence of them to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>. In France, we find mention made of fiefs as early as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of Childebert. They were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> by the Lombards; amongst whom the customs and laws relating to fiefs seem very early to have made rapid advances*. They were introduced into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> before the invasion of the Moors and Saracens in the year 710. Lands were granted for service and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> among the Goths; among whom also the person who received the gift was the retainer of him who granted it. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> he refused his service, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANT">grant</a> was forfeited, and he was said to receive it in patronio; he also swore fealty to his lord; and on this footing the national militia was regulated†. There can be very little doubt that the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol9.html#article-FEUDAL_LAW">feudal law</a> was known in England in the Saxon times, as is mentioned in the text. In Scotland, however, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of fiefs is still more uncertain than anywhere else; which has been ascribed partly to the mutilated state of the Scottish records, and partly to the want of able antiquaries in the nation. But, according to a late writer‡, allodiality and feudalism have existed ever since the foundation of the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONARCHY">monarchy</a>, and have most probably arisen from a familiarity of the manners and customs in Scotland to those of other nations. It has indeed been supposed, that these customs were introduced from some foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> by Malcolm II. According to some, they were introduced directly from England; and the policy of Malcolm in establishing them has been highly extolled: but, according to our author, there is no foundation for any notion of that kind. Both the opinions just mentioned either directly assert or imply, that the feudal maxims were introduced into this country upon the principle of imitation; but it is very improbable that they could be imported from one people to another, on account of their excessive <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRARIETY">contrariety</a> to the common usages and precepts of government among mankind. It must undoubtedly have been very absurd, if not altogether impracticable, to transplant the feudal tenures when the grants of land were precarious, or depending entirely on the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> of the prince, to a country which had never known superiority or vassalage. This would have required an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> of all the orders of society from the king to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEASANT">peasant</a>; while the whole chain of customs, as well as the jurisdiction of the kingdom, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> and low, must have sustained a corresponding alteration, in order to conform them to the new system. It is likewise obvious, that no conquest could be made on purpose to obtain a settlement by any nation who had already received the knowledge of fiefs. The establishment of them implied, that the people had already a fixed and settled residence; and accordingly history does not furnish us with any account of a nation among whom fiefs were known, who ever migrated from the country they already possessed, to seek for one in which they might <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a>. Feudal institutions must have originated wherever they have been observed to flourish.—Scotland was formerly a feudal kingdom, and we know pretty nearly the time when the fiefs were <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a> there; but in that form they could not be introduced by the sovereign; and there was not any nation among whom fiefs were already known who conquered, or made an establishment by conquest, in Scotland. Fiefs therefore must have gradually advanced to such a state of perfection. The progress they made may be likewise easily bounty to the vassal, which the latter repaid by acts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a>; so that the intercourse between them was of the most tender and affectionate kind; and this gave rise to what are called the feudal incidents. The expectants of fiefs were educated in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a> of the superior, while the tenures were precarious or only for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; and even when they became hereditary, the lord took care of the son and estate of his deceased vassal; not only protecting his person, but taking <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a>, and directing the management of his affairs. He took pleasure in observing his approach to maturity; and when he came of age, never failed to deliver to him the lands, with the care of which he had been intrusted, and which he had been careful to improve. This was called the incident of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARDSHIP">wardship</a>. The incident of relief was founded upon the gratitude of the vassal; who, upon entering on his fief, brought a present to his lord, as an acknowledgment of his care of him during the early part of his life; and in order to conciliate his future regard. The incident of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> proceeded also upon the principle of gratitude on the part of the vassal. The latter, conscious of the favours he had received, did not choose to ally himself with a family inimical to his chief; while the superior himself, ambitious to aggrandize and augment the importance of his family, sought how to find the most advantageous <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-MATCH">match</a> for his vassal. Sometimes the superior himself was reduced in his circumstances by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> or other accident; but from whatever cause his distress proceeded, even though it had arisen from his own extravagance or prodigality, or when only destitute of means to support his ambition or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANDEUR">grandeur</a>, his vassals were bound to support and relieve him according to their circumstances; and this was called the incident of aid. The incident of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESCHEAT">escheat</a> took place on the part of the vassal, when, through cowardice, treachery, or any remarkable misbehaviour, he rendered himself unworthy of his fief. In that case, the taking it from him, and giving it to one more worthy, was called an escheat. While the lords and vassals thus vied with one another in mutual acts of friendship and benevolence, universal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a>, liberty, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, were diffused throughout the society. The vassals behaved courteously towards the retainers, who were immediately below them; while they again were courted by the lords as constituting their importance and strength; the lords, lastly, giving a like importance and dignity to the sovereign himself. Thus a regular, powerful, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> system of government took place; an unanimity and attention pervaded the various departments of state; so that, while the subjects were free, the nation at large was formidable. During this happy state of affairs, the members of the national <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSEMBLY">assembly</a> in every country in Europe appeared there in arms, whether they came personally or by their representatives. Such particularly was the case under the Anglo-Saxon government; and the happiness they at that time enjoyed made the oppression and tyranny of the Normans appear the more intolerable. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of time, however, the state of society began to suffer a remarkable alteration. The high and disinterested notions, from which the happiness above mentioned took its origin, declined; the romantic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IDEAS">ideas</a> of chivalry ceased; and much more interested notions of property came in their stead. The separation of the interests of the lords from their vassals was the first step towards the destruction of the feudal system. Thus the incidents, which, as has just now been mentioned, promoted their happiness, did the very reverse. Property being now looked upon as a distinction superior to personal merit, naturally introduced the most mercenary views. In consequence of these the infant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WARD">ward</a>, the care of whom was wont to be considered as a sacred and honorary trust, was now only looked upon as a means of procuring emolument to the superior. The latter now regarded the profits of his vassals as so many diminutions of his own wealth. Instead of taking care to improve the estate of his ward as formerly, he impoverished it; not only neglecting the education of the heir, but offering insults to himself; inasmuch that the relations of the unfortunate vassal were frequently obliged to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RANSOM">ransom</a> from the avaricious superior both his person and effects. By merchandise of this kind the coffers of princes were filled, and wardships let out to strangers, who might <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> their rapacity with greater freedom. When the vassal at last attained the years of maturity, he came to the possession of his land without any of that joy and festivity which usually took place on the occasion. He received an inheritance wasted and destroyed, while new grievances daily presented themselves to augment the horrors of his situation. All the incidents, which in former times oppressed were so many expressions of gratitude on the part of the situation of vassal, were now changed into taxes which might be exacted at the pleasure of the lord. Before the vassal was invested in his land, the superior exacted from him a certain sum or other gift, to be measured only by his own rapacity; and in case of delay or inability to pay this demand, the superior continued in possession of the estate. Such scandalous oppression could not but produce the greatest discontent and clamour. Applications were made to the law without success; nor were even the laws regarded which were fabricated on purpose for their relief. The incident of marriage now proved a source of the most dreadful oppression. The lord assumed a right of marrying his vassal to whom he pleased; and he not only exerted this right himself, but would sell it to a stranger, or allow the vassal to buy it himself; while the penalty annexed to a marriage without out the consent of the superior involved no less <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUNISHMENT">punishment</a> than the loss of the estate itself, or some grievous infliction as for a crime of the first magnitude. The case was still worse with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> ward; whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and accomplishments became a source of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> to the superior, or were sacrificed to please his whims or caprices; so that her relations were frequently obliged to buy from him the privilege of marrying her to the person she or they thought most proper. In like manner the aid, which was formerly a voluntary gift from the vassal in cases of distress happening to his lord, now became an unavoidable tax. An aid formerly was demanded when the eldest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of the superior was married, when his eldest son was knighted, or when the superior himself was taken prisoner in battle. These were the only legal causes of making a demand of this kind; but in the subsequent times of degeneracy, the most frivolous pretences were every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> made use of by the prince to oppress the lords, and by the lords to oppress their vassals; demanding subsidies at pleasure, which their inferiors were always obliged to comply with. Lastly, the efcheat, which in former times took place only in cases of cowardice, treachery, or some other heinous crime, was now inflicted on the most trifling occasions. If the vassal happened to be too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in attending the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of his superior to take the oath of fealty; if he committed any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> which could in the least be construed an infringement of the oath; if he neglected to give his lord warning of any misfortune which he might suppose was about to befall him; revealed any thing concerning him; made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> to his sister or daughter, &c.; or even if he should grant a tenure of land to another person in form different from that in which he held his own; all these, nay others still more ridiculous, were judged sufficient reasons for the superior to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEIZE">seize</a> on the estate of the vassal, and involve him and his family in ruin. Notwithstanding these oppressions, however, the vassal was still obliged to submit to his lord; to own him as his superior; and even, in appearance, to pay him the same respect as formerly when the greatest unanimity and cordial affection subsisted between them. Still he was obliged to perform the same military service; because a failure in that respect would have subjected him to a forfeiture of lands according to the original agreement. A vast difference, however, now took place in the valour and activity which inspired the army. The vassals, forced into the field with desponding hearts, were indifferent as to the success of the cause in which they were engaged, and frequently obstructed instead of forwarding the operations of the field. Hence the sovereign found himself embarrassed; and, though nominally at the head of a martial and powerful people, was frequently unable to effect anything, by reason of the mutual hatred and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> which everywhere prevailed. Thus the feudal states of Europe became unnaturally weak: a remedy was necessary; and it is remarkable that the same remedy was applied all over the continent. This was, in short, the making fiefs hereditary, which till now had only been granted for a long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> of years; and, in return, burdening the lands with a certain number of soldiers, which were not to be refused upon any pretence whatever. Hence was derived the tenure of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KNIGHT">knight</a>-service. A certain portion of land, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> burdened with the service of one soldier or knight, was called a knight's fee; and thus an estate, furnishing any service, number of soldiers, was paid to contain as many knight's fees; so that now the manors, baronies, &c., became powerful according to the number of soldiers they were bound to furnish. In the grants from the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, the nobility were obliged to furnish a certain number of soldiers for the service of the sovereign; and in those from the nobility to their vassals, the like service was required. Even the commons who had grants from the crown furnished a certain proportion of knights. The force of the nation was called into action by grants in capitae, or from the sovereign and nobility. A numerous and powerful army was instantly assembled, and at once ready for action. Of this army the king was the general, the nobility the officers, and the vassals soldiers; the whole being exactly arranged, and capable of entering upon any expedition without the least delay. Thus a remedy was found in some measure for the weaknesses of the feudal sovereigns; but though the knights' tenure could accomplish this, it could not bring back the former affection and cordiality which subsisted between the various ranks of people. On the contrary, by uniting them more firmly to one another by legal ties, it rendered matters rather worse. The oppression originating from the operation of the feudal incidents, still continued with unremitting violence. The grants of knights' tenure were attended with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OATHS">oaths</a> of homage and fealty; the same incidents of relief, wardship, marriage, aid, and efcheat, with the feudal tenures. The princes promised to abate somewhat of their rigour in demanding the feudal perquisites, but did not keep their word. Laws were occasionally promulgated, and for some time had an effect; but palliatives soon became ineffectual, and a new state of weakness began to commence. The two remarkable eras in the feudal history are, the time before the invention of knight-service (D), and the history that during which it continued. Fiefs were in a state of fluctuation from the destruction of the Roman empire till the ninth century; but they were rendered perpetual in France about the year 877, and were generally become so in every country of Europe about the beginning of the tenth. Du Cange, voce Militia, gives us an example of a knight fee in the year 830. By the year 987, when Hugh Capet was raised to the throne of France, knight service was become general all over Europe, and was introduced into England after having introduced its appearance in other countries (E). In England, however, there have been several doubts and inquiries land, into England. quires among the learned concerning the introduction of the feudal laws. Many are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that they were first introduced by William the Conqueror; and consequently, that they were entirely unknown to the Anglo-Saxons: but others think, that they existed among the latter in the same form under which they were continued by the Normans. Dr Stuart is of opinion that the Saxons who settled in England could not be strangers to fiefs. He supposes the conformity of manners, which undoubtedly prevailed between the Saxons and other barbarians, a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> that the hereditary grant of land, as well as the fluctuating state of feudal tenures which preceded it, were known to the former. Collateral proofs are derived from the spirit and tenure of the Anglo-Saxon laws, but especially from the grants of hereditary estates on condition of military service (f). The condition of fiefs under the Anglo-Saxons was very different from what it was afterwards. In their times we find no mention made of these oppressions of which so much notice has already been taken; and this may easily be accounted for from the alteration of the feudal spirit in different ages. During the time that a warm and generous affection subsisted between the feudal superiors and vassals, the incidents were marks of generosity on the one part, and gratitude on the other; but as soon as a variance had taken place, by reason of the interested disposition which the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> produced, the same incidents became sources of the most flagrant oppression. This was remarkably the case in the time of William the Conqueror; and, during the reign of King John, matters were come to such a crisis, that the people everywhere complained loudly, and demanded the restoration of the laws of Edward the Confessor (c). "What these laws of Edward the Confessor were (says Mr Hume), which the English every reign during a century and a half desired so passionately to have restored, is much disputed by antiquarians; and our <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> of them seems one of the greatest defects of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> English history." Dr Stuart has offered an explanation; but this is in fact no more than a conflation of conjecture, that "by the laws or customs of the Confessor, then by that condition of felicity was expressed which had been enjoyed during the fortunate state of the feudal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a>. The cordiality, equality, and independence, which then prevailed among all ranks in society, continued to be remembered in less prosperous times, and occasioned an ardent desire for the revival of those laws and usages which were the sources of so much happiness." Besides the great distinction (of which an account Distinction has already been given) between the state of fiefs under concerning the Anglo-Saxons and under the Normans, they were fiefs in no less distinguished by the introduction of knight-service.
