Consult Mr Evelyn's Sylva, the Philosophical Transactions, the French <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">Memoirs</a>, and Dr Stahl's Philosophical Principles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>; but a proper set of accurate experiments seems still wanting in this view.

FERULA

Pages 224-224

Fennel-giant, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the pentandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 45th order, Umbellatae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The drug asafoetida is obtained from a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of ferula.

FESCENNIA

Pages 224-224
or FESCENNIUM, in Ancient Geography, a town of Etruria, above Falerii; where the Fescennine verses were first invented. Now Galese, in the Ecclesiastical State, near the Tiber.

FESCENNINE VERSES

Pages 224-224

in antiquity, were a kind of satirical verses, full of wanton and obscene expressions, sung <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rehearsed by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a>, with many indecent gestures and dances, at the solemnization of a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; (Hor. lib. v. ep. i. 145.) The word is borrowed, according to Macrobius, from facinum, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARM">charm</a>;" the people taking such songs to be proper to drive away witches, or prevent their effect; but its more probable origin is from Felcennium, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Campania, where such verses were first used.

FESSE WAYS

Pages 224-224
or in FESSE, denotes any thing borne after the manner of a fesse; that is, in a rank across the middle of the shield. Party per FESSE, implies a parting across the middle of the shield, from side to side, through the fesse point.

FESTI DIES

Pages 224-224

in Roman antiquity, certain days in the year devoted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the gods. Numa, when he distributed the year into 12 months, divided the same into the dies festi, dies profliti, and dies intercifi. The festi were again divided into days of sacrifices, banquets, games and feriae. See FERIE. The profliti were those days allowed to men for the administration of their affairs, whether of a public <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> private <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>: these are divided into fasti, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMITIA">comitia</a>, leis, &c. See FASTI, COMITIALES, &c. The intercifi were days <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> both to gods and men, some parts of which were allotted to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of the one, and some to that of the other.

FESTINO

Pages 224-224

in Logic, the third mood of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of the syllogism, the first proposition whereof is an universal <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NEGATIVE">negative</a>, the second a particular affirmative, and the third a particular negative; as in the following example: FES No bad <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can be happy. TI Some rich men are bad men. NO Ergo, Some rich men are not happy.

FESTIVAL

Pages 224-224

a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of feasting. See FEAST.—The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is particularly applied to anniversaries days of civil <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> joy.

FESTOON

Pages 224-224

in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">Sculpture</a>, &c., an ornament in form of a garland of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, and leaves, intermixed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twisted together. It is in the form of a string or collar, somewhat bigger in the middle, where it falls <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a>; being extended by the two ends, the extremities of which hang down perpendicularly. Festoons are now chiefly used in friezes, and other vacant places which want to be filled up and adorned; being done in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> clutters of flowers, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> placed on the doors of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPLES">temples</a> and houses on festival occasions.

FESTUCA

Pages 224-224

FESCUE GRASS, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the triandria clas, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 34th order, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAMINA">Gramina</a>. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FESTUS Pompeius, a celebrated grammarian of antiquity, who abridged a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> of Verrius Flaccus, De Significatione Verborum; but took such liberties in citation and criticism, as Gerard Vossius observes, are not favourable to the reputation of his author. A complete edition of his fragments was published by M. Dacier in 1681, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the Dauphin. Scaliger says, that Festus is an author of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> use to those who would attain the Latin tongue with accuracy.

FETLOCK

Pages 224-224

in the Manege, a tuft of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> growing behind the pastern <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> of many horses; for those of a low size have scarce any such tuft.

FETTI

Pages 224-225

Domenico, an eminent painter in the style of Julio Romano, was born at Rome in 1589, and educated under Ludovico Civioli of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a>. He painted but little for churches, but excelled in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>; his pictures are much sought after, and are scarce.—He abandoned himself to disorderly courses; and put an end to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> by excesses, in the 35th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. FÉTUS. See FOETUS.

FEU-DUTY

Pages 225-225

in Scots <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is the annual rent <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> duty which a vassal, by the tenor of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>, becomes bound to pay his superior. FEU-Holding, in Scots Law, is that particular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENURE">tenure</a> by which a vassal is taken bound to pay an annual rent or feu-duty to his superior. FEVER. See Medicine <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> deified the diseases as well as the passions and affections of men. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a> places them in the entrance into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HELL">hell</a>, Aen. vi. 273. Among these Fever had a temple on Mount Palatine, and two other parts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> Rome; and there is still extant an inscription to this <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a>. FEBRI. SANCTÆ. FEBRI. MAGNÆ. CAMILLA. AMATA. PRO. FILIO. <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">MALE</a>. AFFECTO.

FEUD

Pages 225-225

in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> customs, is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> quarrel <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> enmity, not to be satisfied but with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the enemy; and thence usually called deadly feud.—Feud, called also feida, and faida, in the original German, signifies guerram, i.e. bellum, "<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>." Lambert writes it feith, and <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> it signifies capitales inimicitias, or "implacable hatred." In Scotland, and the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> of England, feud is particularly used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of kindred, to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVENGE">revenge</a> the death of any of their blood, against the killer and all his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>, or any other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> enemy.

FEUDAL

Pages 225-225
or FEODAL, of or belonging to a feud or fee. See FEODAL.

FEUDATORY

Pages 225-225
or FEODATORY, a tenant who formerly held his estate by feudal service. See Feodal Tenure.

FEVER

Pages 225-225

in Farriery. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FEVERFEW. See Matricaria, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index.

FEVERSHAM

Pages 225-225

a town of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a> in England, situated on a branch of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a>, which is navigable for <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOY">hoy</a>. It was a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> demesne A.D. 811, and called in Kenulf's <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a>'s little Town, though it is now a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> one. It was inhabited by the Britons <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before the invasion of Caesar. In 903, King Athelstan held a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a> here. King Stephen erected a stately <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>, 1147, whose <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a> sat in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a>; and he was buried in it, together with Maud his <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a>, and Eustace his son; but of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> gate-houses are all that now remain. The town was first incorporated by the name of the barons of Feverham, afterwards by Henry VIII. with the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of the mayor and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>, and lastly, by that of the mayor and jurats and commonalty. It is a populous flourishing <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, consisting chiefly of two long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> streets, with a market-<a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the centre, built 1574. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> was rebuilt in 1754, at the expense of £2000. but was originally built in Edward II's reign. There is a free <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-GRAMMAR">grammar</a> school in the place, built and endowed by Queen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> in 1582; also two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>. It is a member of the cinque-port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, and has a manufactory of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUNPOWDER">gunpowder</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a> are supplied from hence with abundance of apples and cherries, and the best oysters for stewing. These last were at one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> carried away in such quantities by the Dutch, that many men and boats were employed in the winter to dredge for them; and it is said they carried home as many as amounted to above 2000l. a-year. The fishermen admit none to take up their freedom but married men.

FEVILDEA

Pages 225-225

a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the dicotyledonous order, Cucurbitaceae. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FEVRE

Pages 225-225
Claude le, an eminent French painter, was born at Fontainebleau in 1633, and studied in the palace there, and then at Paris under Le Sueur and Le Brun; the latter of whom advised him to adhere to portraits, for which he had a particular talent, and in his style equalled the best masters of that country. He died in England in 1675, aged 42.

FEZ

Pages 225-227

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of the same name in Barbary, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>. It is described as a very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, surrounded with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> walls, within which there are hills and valleys, only the middle being <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> and flat. The river, which runs through the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, is divided into two streams, from which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> are cut into every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the town; so that the mosques, colleges, palaces, and the houses of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> men, are amply supplied with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. They have generally <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> marble basins in the middle of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of their houses, which are supplied with water by marble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through the walls. They constantly run over, and the stream returns back into the street, and so into the river. The houses are built with brick <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>; and are adorned on the outside with fine mosaic <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, or tiles like those of <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>. The wood work and ceilings are carved, painted and gilt. The roofs are flat; for they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> on the tops of the houses in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. Most of the houses houses are two stories high, and some three. There are plazas and galleries running all round the court on the inside, so that you may wander cover from one apartment to another. The pillars are of brick, covered with glazed tiles, or of marble, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARCHES">arches</a> between. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> work is carved and painted with gay colours, and most of the rooms have marble cisterns of water. Some of the great men build towers over their houses several stories high, and spare no expense to render them beautiful; from hence they have a fine prospect all over the city. There are in this city 700 mosques, great and small; 50 of which are magnificent, and supported with marble pillars, and other ornaments. The floors are covered with mats, as well as the walls to the height of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. Every mosque has a tower or minaret, like those in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, with a gallery on the top, from whence they call the people to prayers. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> mosque is near a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half in circumference. The middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a> is 150 yards in length, and 80 in breadth, with a tower proportionally high. Round this to the east, west, and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a>, there are great colonnades 30 or 40 yards <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>. There are 900 lamps lighted every night; and in the middle of the mosque are large branches, which are capable of holding 500 lamps each. Along the walls are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> pulpits, from which the doctors of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> teach the people. The business of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> is only to read prayers, and distribute alms to the people; to support which, there are large revenues. Besides the mosques, there are two colleges built in the Moorish manner, and adorned with marble and paintings. In one of them there are 100 rooms, besides a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>. In this there is a great marble vase full of water, adorned with marble pillars of various colours, and finely polished. The capitals are gilt, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROOF">roof</a> shines with <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, azure, and purple. The walls are adorned with Arabic verses in gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>. The other colleges are not near so beautiful, or rather are all gone to ruin since the neglect of learning. There are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HOSPITALS">hospitals</a> in the city, where formerly all strangers were maintained three days gratis. But the estates belonging to them have been confiscated for the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>. There are above 100 public <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATHS">baths</a>, many of which are stately buildings. People of the same trade or business live in streets by themselves. Though the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> about Fez is pleasant and fertile, and in many places abounding with corn and cattle, yet a great part of it lies waste and uncultivated, not so much for want of inhabitants as from the oppression of the governors; which makes the people choose to live at some distance from the high <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-ROADS">roads</a>, where they cultivate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> as is necessary for their own subsistence. Round the city there are fine marble tombs, monuments, and gardens full of all manner of fruit trees. Such are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> accounts of this city. The following are given by M. Chenier, in his Recherches Historiques sur les Maures. Fez was built in the end of the eighth century by Edris, a descendant of Mahomet and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALI">Ali</a>; whose father, in order to avoid the proclivities of the caliph Abdallah, retired to the extremity of Africa, and was proclaimed sovereign by the Moors. Sidy Edris, having succeeded to the throne of his father, built the city of Fez in the year 793. He caused a mosque to be erected, in which his body was interred, and the city ever afterwards became an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASYLUM">asylum</a> for the Moors, and a place of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. In the first moments of fervour which a new worship inspires, another mosque was built called caroub, which is perhaps one of the largest and most beautiful edifices in Africa. Several others were successively built, besides colleges and hospitals; and the city was held in such veneration, that when the pilgrimage to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECCA">Mecca</a> was interrupted in the fourth century of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEGIRA">Hegira</a>, the western Mahometans substituted that of Fez in its stead, while the eastern people went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JERUSALEM">Jerusalem</a>. When the Arabs had spread <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, Africa, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, they brought to Fez the little knowledge they had acquired in the sciences and arts; and that capital conjoined, with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> where <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> was taught, together with medicine and <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>. This last gradually degenerated; <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> brought astrology into repute, and this quickly engendered the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAGIC">magic</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINATION">divination</a>. Fez soon became the common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> of all Africa. The Mahometans went thither for the purposes of devotion; the affluence of strangers introduced a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; libertinism quickly followed; and, as its progress is most rapid in warm countries, Fez, which had been the nurse of sciences and arts, became a harbour for every kind of vice. The public baths, which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, cleanliness, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, had rendered necessary, and which were everywhere respected as sacred places, became scenes of debauchery; where men introduced themselves in the habits of women; youths in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISGUISE">disguise</a>, with a dittoff in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, walked the streets at sunset in order to entice strangers to their inns, which were less a place of repose than a convenience for prostitution. The usurpers who disputed the kingdom of Fez after the 16th century overlooked these abuses, and contented themselves with subjecting the masters of the inns to furnish a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COOKS">cooks</a> for the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>. It is to this laxity of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> that Fez owed its first splendour. As the inhabitants are beautiful, the Africans flocked thither in crowds; the laws were overturned, morals despised, and vice itself turned into an engine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLITICAL">political</a> resource. The same spirit, the same inclinations, the same depravity, still exist in the hearts of all the Moors. But libertinism is not now encouraged; it wears there, as in other places, the mask of hypocrisy; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DARES">dares</a> not venture to show itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. The Mahometans of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANDALUSIA">Andalusia</a>, those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRANADA">Granada</a> and Cordova, migrated to Fez during the different revolutions that agitated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>: they carried with them new customs and new arts, and perhaps some slight <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of civilization. The Spanish Moors carried from Cordova to Fez the art of staining goat and sheep skins with a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, which were then called Cordova <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>, and now <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MOROCCO">Morocco</a> leather, from that city where the art is less perfect. They manufacture gauzes at Fez, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> stuffs, and girdles elegantly embroidered with gold and silk, which show how far their ingenuity might be carried <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> industry were more encouraged. There is still some taste for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> preserved at Fez, and the Arabic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> is spoken there in greater purity. purity than in any other part of the empire. The rich Moors send their children to the schools at Fez, where they are better instructed than they could be elsewhere. Leo Africanus, in the 16th century, gave a magnificent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of this city, from which most of those that have been afterwards made are copied; but its situation, its schools, and the industry and great urbanity of its inhabitants, are the only circumstances that give it any preference to the other cities of the empire. There are some pretty convenient inns here, consisting of two or three stories. The houses have no elegance externally: the streets are ill paved, and so strait that two persons riding abreast can hardly pass. The shops are like stalls; and have no more room in them than is sufficient to serve for the owner, who is always seated with his wares around him, which he shows to the passengers. But though the Moors of Fez are more civilized than the rest, they are vain, superstitious, and intolerant; and an order must be obtained from the emperor before a Christian or a Jew can be allowed to enter the city. The situation of Fez is exceedingly singular. It lies in the bottom of a valley surrounded by little hills in the shape of a funnel; the declivities are divided into gardens planted with tall trees, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHRUBS">shrubs</a>, and all sorts of fruit trees; a river meanders along the declivity, and turns a number of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MILLS">mills</a>, which distribute the water abundantly to all the gardens, and almost to every <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> to the city, which stands in the centre, is long; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROAD">road</a> lies through these gardens, which it traverses, in a serpentine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The gardens, seen from the city, form a most delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>. Formerly each garden had a house in which the inhabitants spent the summer. These houses were destroyed in the times of the civil wars, and in the revolutions to which Fez has been subject, and few individuals have restored them. The situation of Fez, however, cannot be healthful; moist vapours fill the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> in summer, and fevers are exceedingly common. On the height above Fez, in a plain susceptible of rich cultivation, stands New Fez, finely situated, and enjoying excellent air, containing some old palaces, in which the children of the emperor live, and where he sometimes resides himself. New Fez is inhabited by some Moorish families, but by a greater number of Jews. Fez is seated on the river Cebu, W. Long. 4° 25'. N. Lat. 33° 8'.

FEZZAN

Pages 227-228

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFRICA">Africa</a>, about 300 miles <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, and 200 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> from east to west. It is bounded on the east by the Harutich and line of the deserts; by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> of the Tibboes on the south and south-east; by that of the Nomadic Tuaregs on the south-west; and the country which forms the western boundary, is inhabited by Arabs. It contains 101 <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> and villages, of which Mourzouk is the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> of this kingdom is neither temperate nor agreeable at any season whatever; for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> is almost intolerable, even to the inhabitants, especially when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> blows from the south; and the prevalence of the north wind during winter makes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> so intense, as not only to chill the natives, but those also who visit it from northern Fezzan regions. <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">Rain</a> falls but seldom in this country, and in very small quantities. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-THUNDER">Thunder</a> is also a rare phenomenon: Mr Horneman affirms us that there was not a single storm from November 1798 to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1799; and that on the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1799 there were some faint flashes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHTNING">lightning</a> unaccompanied by any claps of thunder. Winds, however, blow very frequently, both from the north and south, whirling up the dust and sand in such a manner as to give the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a> a yellowish appearance. There is neither river nor rivulet of any <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> in the whole country, according to Mr Horneman, who informs us that the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> is a deep sand, beneath which is found calcareous rock <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and sometimes a stratum of an argillaceous subfusance. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DATE">Date</a> trees may be considered as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> production of Fezzan, in the western parts of which some fenana grows, of a superior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> to that which is imported from the country of the Tibboes. Culinary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, and almost every vegetable peculiar to the garden, are met with in abundance. Wheat and barley seem well adapted to the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the soil, as well as to the climate; yet corn is not raised in sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> for home consumption, which is brought from those parts of Africa bordering on the northern parts of the kingdom. This is most probably owing to the native indolence of the people, the despotism of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a>, and the difficulties inseparable from their peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of tillage. They bestow little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> on the rearing of cattle, which are only found in the most fertile parts of the country, and even in these their numbers are but small. They are made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of to draw <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> from the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a>, and are never killed but in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animal is the goat; and although sheep are reared in the southern parts of the country, the most abundant supply is furnished by the Arabs on the borders. They make coarse cloths of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a>, which constitute the apparel of the inhabitants in general. Their horses are not numerous, as they make most use of asses, either for carriage, draught, or burthen. Camels bear a most extravagant price, being only made use of by the higher ranks, or by opulent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a>; and the common food of all those animals is the fruit of the date tree. Although the trade of Fezzan consists entirely of foreign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>, it is nevertheless considerable. Mourzouk is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> market and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of general <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> for different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARAVANS">caravans</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIRO">Cairo</a>, Bengasi, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRIPOLI">Tripoli</a>, and other places, between the months of October and February. The caravans which come to Mourzouk from the west or south, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> in ostrich feathers, tiger skins, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> dust, and also in furs of both sexes as articles of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a> and snuff, with other articles manufactured in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURKEY">Turkey</a>, are brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> by the merchants from Bengasi; and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, fire-arms, sabres, knives, and woollen cloth, are conveyed to it from Tripoli. Fezzan is governed by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">sultan</a>, a descendant of the family of the Sheriffs; and according to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a> of the country, his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCESTORS">ancestors</a> came from the western parts of Africa, invaded and made a conquest of it about 500 years ago. He reigns over his dominions with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">ab</a>- Fezzan. Solute power, but is at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> tributary to the bailhaw of Tripoli, who annually receives from him the sum of 4000 dollars by the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of an officer appointed for that purpose. The sultan who was upon the throne when Mr Horne <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> in 1798 visited the country, assumed the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of "Sultan Muhammed ben Sultan Manfur," engraved on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEAL">seal</a> which is applied to all public acts, and also to correspondence within his dominions; but he makes use of a smaller seal when he writes to the bailhaw of Tripoli. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> is <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HEREDITARY">hereditary</a>; yet it descends not in all cases from father to son, for when the heir apparent dies, a nephew may succeed in preference to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> son, which is frequently the occasion of much bloodshed, when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of succession comes to be warmly contested. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> of the sultan is within the walls of the fortress of the capital, where he leads a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> of retirement attended by his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUNUCHS">eunuchs</a>. The harem is near the palace, into which he never enters, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> whom he inclines to see is conducted to his apartment. The harem consists of the sultana and about 40 female slaves, which last he frequently dispenses of, and replaces them by others, unless they bear him children, or become the objects of his ardent <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a>, either by their personal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> or other accomplishments. Those who wish for an audience with the sultan, approach the throne, which is an old elbow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> raised a few steps from the ground, kiss his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and raise it so as to touch their forehead, and then kneel before him to give a statement of their business in common <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, taking care, however, to intermix it with such exclamations as these: "God prolong thy life, God protect thy country," and to offer him some small present. The <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the sultan consists of a first and second minister, the general of his forces, a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>, and a few <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> slaves. Some of the black slaves who are purchased while boys, and educated according to their distinctions and talents, often acquire considerable influence with the sultan. The dress of the sultan, when he appears in state, consists of a white frock of stuff, ornamented with gold and silver, and sometimes of satin interwoven with silver. The appearance of his turban is remarkable, which <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a> not less than three feet from the fore to the hinder <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, and two feet in breadth. His revenue arises from certain taxes on all gardens and cultivated lands, and from fines and requisitions imposed in an arbitrary manner. The slaves who are employed in collecting these are often rigorous in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a>, but it is often possible to procure their lenity by means of a bribe. The expenditure of this revenue is chiefly confined to the support of the sultan, his court and palace, for the cadi and department of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers of government, are supported by the produce of date-tree woods and gardens. The administration of justice is vested in the hands of a cadi, whose decisions are guided by the Mohammedan <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, by antiquated customs, and established practice; but judgment in all criminal cases is purely arbitrary, or is referred to the sultan. The office of cadi has been hereditary in one family, ever since the conquest of the country by the ancestors of the present sultan; and when he dies, his place is filled up by one who is most eminent for learning, or who can best read and write, which is all the learning that he is ever possessed of. It is difficult to ascertain anything like an accurate statement of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a> of Fezzan, but Mr Horne man conjectures that they may amount to about 75,000, all of them professing the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> of Mahomet. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPLEXION">complexion</a> of the people varies considerably; those in the northern parts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> in this respect a striking resemblance to the Arabians, while those in the southern districts are very much like the Tibboes and Tuaregs. Those who are strictly indigenous are of ordinary stature, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIMBS">limbs</a> far from being muscular; of a deep <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, short black <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> formed like the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>, and their nose not so flat as that of the negro. Their walk, mein and gesture, indicate a total want of energy, either of body or mind. The women of this country are in general fond of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a>, and the wanton manners and public freedoms in which they are permitted to indulge, are frequently astonishing, even to Mahometans from other countries; and the men are very much addicted to the vice of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>, using the juice of the date-tree, or a drink that is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAYA">baya</a>, which is of an intoxicating nature. Different <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of the venereal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> prevail in this country, but that which is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUDAN">Soudan</a> is reckoned the most virulent. The common lues venerea is called franzi, for the cure of which they make use of salts and colocynth as powerful cathartics, healing the sores with natron water or dissolved soda. They are sometimes afflicted with hemorrhoids, the cure of which is no doubt rendered more difficult by the too liberal use of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>; and a fever and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-AGUE">ague</a> which are very pernicious to foreigners. They are entirely unacquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHLEBOTOMY">phlebotomy</a>, yet they sometimes draw blood by means of cupping; and some are as much acquainted with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">surgery</a> as to be able to cure a simple fracture. Their houses are miserable structures, composed of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> or bricks mixed with clay, and dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, and the hands of the labourer are all the tools which are employed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>. When the walls are finished, they are covered over with <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> made of calcareous earth, which is also done with the hand. Their houses are extremely low, and there is no other entrance for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> but by the door. They are uncommonly abstemious in respect of diet. Indeed they can never abstain from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTCHER">butcher</a> meat when it is placed before them; but this is not an article of food with the generality, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> for a rich man is, "that he eats <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> and meat every day." FEWEL. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUEL">FUEL</a>.

FIASCONE

Pages 228-228

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, in the territories of the pope, remarkable for its good wine. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 13. 12. N. Lat. 42. 20.

FIBRE

Pages 228-230

in Anatomy, a perfectly simple body, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> at least as simple as any thing in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> structure; being fine and slender like a thread, and serving to form other parts. Hence some fibres are hard, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONY">bony</a> ones; and others soft, as those defined for the formation of all the other parts. The fibres are divided also, according to their position and Fibre and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>, into such as are straight, oblique, transverse, annular, and spiral; as they are arranged in these directions in different parts of the body. Fibre is also used to denote the slender Filaments which compose other bodies, whether animal, vegetable, or mineral; but more especially the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CAPILLARY">capillary</a> roots of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Fibrose, or <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">Fibrous</a>, something consisting of fibres, as the roots of plants. See Root. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIBULA">Fibula</a>, in Anatomy, the outer and smaller of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a> of the leg. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fibula, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> for the cloting of gaping wounds.—Celsus speaks of the fibula as to be used when the wound was so patent as not easily to admit of being sewed. (Op. lib. vii. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 25. apud <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a>.) Fibula, in Antiquity, was a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTON">button</a>, buckle, or clasp, made use of by the Greeks and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> for keeping clothe or tying up some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of their clothes. They were of various forms, and often adorned with precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>. Men and women wore them in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> and at their shoes. Players and musicians, by way of preserving the voices of children put under their care to learn their arts, used to keep clothe the prepuce with a fibula, lest they should have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> with women. Ficinus, Marsilius, a celebrated Italian, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLORENCE">Florence</a> in 1433, and educated at the expense of Laurence de Medicis. He attained a perfect knowledge of the Greek and Latin tongues, and became a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a>, a great physician, and a great divine. He was in the highest favour with Laurence and Cosmo de Medicis, who made him a canon of the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-CATHEDRAL">cathedral</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of Florence. He applied himself intensely to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>; and while others were striving who should be the deepest read in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOTLE">Aristotle</a>, who was then the philosopher in fashion, he devoted himself wholly to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>. He was indeed the first who restored the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATONIC">Platonic</a> philosophy in the west; for the better effecting of which he translated into Latin the whole works of Plato. There goes a story, but we know not how true it is, that when he had finished his translation, he communicated it to his friend Marcus Maturus, to have his approbation of it; but that, Maturus disliking it, he did it all over again. He next translated <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOTINUS">Plotinus</a>; and afterwards the works, or part of them at least, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCLUS">Proclus</a>, Jamblicus, Porphyrius, and other celebrated Platonists.—In his younger years, Ficinus lived like a philosopher; and too much so, as is said, to the neglect of piety. However, Savonarola coming to Florence, Ficinus went with every body else to hear his sermons; and while he attended them for the sake of the preacher's eloquence, he imbibed a strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, and devoted himself henceforward more especially to the duties of it. He died at Correggio in 1499; and as Baronius assures us upon the testimony of what he calls credible authors, appeared immediately after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> to his friend Michael Mercatus: to whom, it seems, he had promised to appear, in order to confirm what he had taught concerning the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IMMORTALITY">immortality</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>. His writings, sacred and profane, which are very numerous, were collected and printed at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VENICE">Venice</a> in 1516, at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASIL">Basil</a> in 1561 and 1576, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> 1641, in two vols. folio. Twelve books of his Epistles, among which are many treatises, were printed separately in folio at Venice 1495, and at <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> 1497, in folio 4to. Ficoideae, the specific name given to several plants, as the mefembryanthemum, mufa, and opuntia. See Mefembryanthemum, &c. <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> Index. Fiction. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FABLE">Fable</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">Poetry</a>. Ficus, the fig-tree: A genus of plants, belonging to the polygamia clas; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> method ranking under the 53d order, Scabridae. See Botany Index. The ficus religiosa, or Banian tree, is a native of several parts of the East Indies. It has a woody stem, branching to a great height and vast <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>, with heart-shaped entire leaves ending in acute <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a>. Of this tree the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> contain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> equally beautiful and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>: There soon they chose The fig tree; not that tree for fruit renown'd, But such as, at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> to Indians known In Malabar or Decan, spreads her arms, Branching so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, that in the ground The bended twigs take root, and daughters grow About the mother tree, a pillar'd <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">High</a> overarch'd, and echoing walks between: There oft' the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> herdman, thumping heart, Shelters in cool, and tends his pasturing herds At loop-holes cut through thickest shade. Par. Lost, Book ix. l. 1100. The Banian tree, or Indian fig, is perhaps the most beautiful of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">Nature</a>'s productions in that genial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a>, where she sports with the greatest profusion and variety. Some of these trees are of amazing size and great extent, as they are continually increasing, and, contrary to most other things in animal and vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, they seem to be exempted from decay. Every branch from the main body throws out its own roots; at first, in small tender fibres, several yards from the ground; these continually grow thicker until they reach the surface; and there striking in, they increase to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> trunks, and become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out new branches from the top; these in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> suspend their roots, which, swelling into trunks, produce other branches; thus continuing in a state of progression as long as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, the first parent of them all, contributes her sustenance. The Hindoos are particularly fond of the Banian tree; they look upon it as an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EMBLEM">emblem</a> of the Deity, from its long <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DURATION">duration</a>, its outstretching arms, and overshadowing beneficence; they almost pay it divine honours, and Find a fane in every sacred <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROVE">grove</a>. Near these trees the most esteemed pagodas are generally erected; under their shade the Brahmins spend their lives in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> solitude; and the natives of all castes and tribes are fond of reclining in the cool recesses, beautiful walks, and lovely vistas of this unbraggious canopy, impervious to the hottest beams of a tropical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. A remarkable large tree of this kind grows on an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the river Nerbudda, ten miles from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of Baroche in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Guzerat; a flourishing settlement lately in possession of the East <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">Company</a>, but ceded by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENGAL">Bengal</a>, at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of peace concluded with the Mahattas in 1783, to Mahadajee Scindia a Mahratta <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a>. It is distinguished by the name of Cubbeer Burr, which was given it in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of a famous saint. It was once much larger than at present; but high floods have carried away the banks of the island where it grows, and with them such parts of the tree as had thus far extended their roots: yet what remains is about 2000 feet in circumference, measured round the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> stems; the overhanging branches, not yet struck <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, cover a much larger space. The chief trunks of this single tree (which in size greatly exceed our English elms and oaks), amount to 350; the smaller stems, forming into stronger supporters, are more than 3000; and every one of these is calling out new branches, and hanging roots, in time to form trunks, and become the parents of a future progeny. Cubbeer Burr is famed throughout Hindostan for its great extent and surpassing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>: the Indian armies generally encamp around it; and, at stated seasons, solemn jatarras, or Hindu festivals, are held there, to which thousands of votaries repair from various parts of the Mogul empire.—It is said that 7000 persons find ample room to repose under its shade. The English gentlemen, on their hunting and shooting parties, used to form extensive encampments, and spend weeks together under this delightful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVILION">pavilion</a>, which is generally filled with green wood pigeons, doves, peacocks, and a variety of feathered songsters; crowded with families of monkeys performing their antics tricks; and shaded by bays of a large size, many of them measuring upwards of six feet from the extremity of one wing to the other. This tree not only affords shelter, but sustenance, to all its inhabitants, being covered amid its bright foliage with small figs of a rich scarlet, on which they all regale with as much delight, as the lords of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a> on their more costly fare in their parties.

FIDDES

Pages 230-230

RICHARD, a learned divine and polite writer, was born in 1671, and educated at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>. He was presented to the living of Halfham in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, where he was so admired for the sweetness of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> and the gracefulness of his delivery, that the people for several miles round flocked to his sermons. Coming to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> in 1712, he was by the favour of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">Dean</a> Swift, introduced to the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of Oxford, who made him one of his chaplains, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> soon after appointed him chaplain to the garrison at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HULL">Hull</a>: but losing his patrons upon the change of the ministry, he lost his chaplainship; and being obliged to apply himself to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, composed, 1. A body of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">Divinity</a>; 2. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Wolsey; 3. A Treatise of Morality, &c. He died in 1725. FIDE-JUSSORES Affidui. See ASSIDUUS.

FIDEI-COMMISSUM

Pages 230-230

in Roman antiquity, an estate left in trust with any person, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of another. See TRUSTEE.

FIDEJUROR

Pages 230-230

in the Civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, is a surety, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> one that obliges himself in the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>, for the greater security of the creditor or stipulator.

FIDENA

Pages 230-230
or FIDENÆ, in Ancient Geography, a town of the Sabines, five miles to the north of Rome, where traces of it are still to be seen. Fidenates, the people (Livy.)

FIDES

Pages 230-230
FAITH or FIDELITY, one of the virtues deified by the Pagans. She had a temple near the Capitol, founded by Numa Pompilius; but no animals were offered, or blood spilt, in her sacrifices. During the performance of her rites, her priests appeared in white vestments, with their heads and hands covered with linen, to show that fidelity ought to be sacred.

FIDIUS

Pages 230-230

in Pagan worship, a god who presided over alliances and promises. This deity, which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> borrowed from the Sabines, was also called Sanctus, Semon, and Semi-Pater.

FIELD

Pages 230-230

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, is the whole surface of the shield <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the continent, so called because it containeth those achievements anciently acquired in the field of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. It is the ground on which the colours, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a>, furs, charges, &c. are represented. Among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> heralds, field is less frequently used in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> than shield or escutcheon. See SHIELD, &c. FIELD-Book, in Surveying, a book in which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, stations, distances, &c., are set <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>. FIELD-Colours, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAMP">Camp</a>-Colours, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">War</a>, are small flags of about a foot and a half <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>, which are carried along with the quartermaster general, for marking out the ground for the squadrons and battalions. FIELD-Fare, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-ORNITHOLOGY">Ornithology</a>. See TURDUS, ORNITHOLOGY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FIELD-Officers, in the art of war. See OFFICER. FIELD-Pieces, small cannons, from three to twelve pounders, carried along with an <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> in the field. FIELD-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">Staff</a>, a weapon carried by the gunners, about the length of a halbert, with a spear at the end; having on each side ears screwed on, like the cock of a matchlock, where the gunners screw in lighted matches when they are upon command; and then the field-staffs are said to be armed. FIELD-Works, in Fortification, are those thrown up by an army in besieging a fortress, or by the besieged to defend the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. Such are the fortifications of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMPS">camps</a>, highways, &c. Elysian-Fields. See ELYSIAN.

FIELDING

Pages 230-231

HENRY, a well-known writer of the present <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general Fielding who served under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARLBOROUGH">Marlborough</a>, was born in 1707. He had four <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SISTERS">sisters</a>; of whom Sarah is well known, as writer of The Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAVID">David</a> Simple. On the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of his mother, his father married again; and Sir John Fielding, who succeeded him in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> of the peace for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIDDLESEX">Middlesex</a>, is his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> by this <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a>. Henry was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEYDEN">Leyden</a>; but a failure in his remittances obliged him to return in two years, when his own propensity to gaiety and profusion drove him to write for the stage at 20 years of age. His first dramatic piece, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">Love</a> in several Masques, which was well received, appeared in 1727; and all his plays and farces, to the amount of 18, were written before before the year 1737, and many of them are still acted with applause. While he was thus employed, he married a young lady with £500 fortune, and inherited an estate of £200 a-year from his mother; all which, though on the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> of retiring into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, he contrived to dispense in three years; and then applied himself to the study of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> for a maintenance. In losing his fortune, he acquired the gout; which, rendering it impossible for him to attend the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAR">bar</a>, he with a shattered <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> had recourse to many extempore applications of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> for immediate supplies; until, soon after the rebellion in 1745, he accepted the office of acting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> for Middlesex, an employment much more profitable than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> in the public esteem. Reduced at length by the fatigues of this office, and by a complication of disorders, he, by the advice of his physicians, went to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LISBON">Lisbon</a>, where he died in 1754. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of fugitive pamphlets and periodical essays; but is chiefly distinguished by his Adventures of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOSEPH">Joseph</a> Andrews, and <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of Tom Jones. His works have been collected and published, with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> prefixed, by Mr Murphy.

FIENUS

Pages 231-231

Thomas, an ingenious and learned physician, born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1566. He went into <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> physic under Mercantius and Aldrovandus; and on his return distinguished himself so much in the university of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUVAIN">Louvain</a>, that he was there chosen professor of physic, and was afterwards made physician to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAVARIA">Bavaria</a>. He wrote several works, among which were, De viribus imaginationis; and Deformatione factur. He died at Louvain in 1631.

FIERI FACIAS

Pages 231-231

in Latin, a writ that lies where a person has recovered judgment for debt <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> damages in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s courts against one, by which the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> is commanded to levy the debt and damages on the defendant's goods and chattels.

FIGURE

Pages 238-240

figure of speech, every circumstance ought to be avoided that agrees with the proper sense only, not with the figurative sense: for it is the latter that expresses the thought, and the former serves for no other purpose but to make harmony: Zacynthus green with ever-shady groves, And Ithaca, presumptuous boast their loves; Obtruding on my choice a second lord, They press the Hymenean rite abhorred. *Odyssey*, book xix. l. 152. Zacynthus here standing figuratively for the inhabitants, the description of the island is quite out of place: it puzzles the reader, by making him doubt whether the word ought to be taken in its proper or figurative sense. Write, my queen, And with mine eyes I'll drink the words you send, Though ink be made of gall. *Cymbeline*, act i. sc. 2. The difficult one has to drink ink in reality, is not to the purpose where the subject is drinking ink figuratively. 4. To draw consequences from a figure of speech, as if the word were to be understood literally, is a gross absurdity; for it is confounding truth with fiction: Be Moubray's sins so heavy in his bosom, That they may break his foaming courser's back, And throw the rider headlong in the lists, A caitiff recreant to my cousin Hereford. *Ricard II.*, act i. sc. 3. Sin may be imagined heavy in a figurative sense: but weight in a proper sense belongs to the accessory only; and therefore to describe the effects of weight, is to defer the principal subject, and to convert the accessory into a principal: Cromwell. How does your Grace? Wolsey. Why, well; Never so truly happy, my good Cromwell. I know myself now, and I feel within me A peace above all earthly dignities, A still and quiet conscience. The king has cur'd me, I humbly thank his Grace: and, from these shoulders, These ruin'd pillars, out of pity, taken A load would sink a navy, too much honour. *Henry VIII.*, act iii. sc. 6. Ulysses speaking of Hector— I wonder now how yonder city stands, When we have here the base and pillar by us. *Troilus and Cressida*, Act. iv. Sc. 9. Othello. No; my heart is turned to stone: I strike it, and it hurts my hand. *Othello*, act. iv. sc. 5. Nor lest, even in this delusive show, Than when my name fill'd Afric with affrights, And froze your hearts beneath your torrid zone. *Don Sebastian King of Portugal*, act. i. How long a space, since first I lov'd, it is! To look into a glas I fear, And am surpris'd with wonder, when I miss Gray hairs and wrinkles there. *Cowley*, vol. i. p. 86. I chose the flourishing't tree in all the park, With freshest boughs and fairest head; I cut my love into its gentle bark, And in three days behold 'tis dead; My very written flames so violent be, They've burnt and wither'd up the tree. *Cowley*, vol. i. p. 136. Ah, mighty Love, that it were inward heat Which made this precious limbeck sweat! But what, alas! ah, what does it avail, That she weeps tears so wondrous cold, As scarce the ass's hoof can hold, So cold, that I admire they fall not hail! *Cowley*, vol. i. p. 132. Such a play of words is pleasant in a ludicrous poem. Almeria. O Alphonso, Alphonso! Devouring seas have wash'd thee from my sight, No time shall raze thee from my memory: No, I will live to be thy monument: The cruel ocean is no more thy tomb; But in my heart thou art interr'd. *Mourning Bride*, act i. sc. 1. This would be very right, if there were any inconsistence in being interred in one place really, and in another place figuratively. From considering, that a word used in a figurative sense suggests at the same time its proper meaning, we discover a fifth rule, That we ought not to employ a word in a figurative sense, the proper sense of which is inconsistent or incongruous with the subject: for every inconsistence, and even incongruity, though in the expression only and not real, is unpleasant: Interca genitor Tyberini ad flaminis undam, Vulnera fecerat lymphis. *Æneid*, book x. l. 833. Tres adeo incertus creca caligine soles Erramus pelago, totidem sine fidele noctes. *Æneid*, book iii. l. 293. The foregoing rule may be extended to form a sixth, That no epithet ought to be given to the figurative sense of a word that agrees not also with its proper sense: Dicat Opuntice Frater Megilla, quo beatus Vulnere. *Horat.* Carm. lib. i. ode 27. Parcus deorum cultor, et infrequens, Isonenitium dum sapientiae Consultus erro. *Horat.* Carm. lib. i. ode 54. Seventhly, The crowding into one period or thought different figures of speech, is not less faulty than crowding metaphors in that manner; the mind is distracted in the quick transition from one image to another, and is puzzled instead of being pleased: I am of ladies most deject and wretched, That fuck'd the honey of his music vows. *Hamlet.* My bleeding bosom fickens at the sound. *Odyssey*, book i. l. 439. Ah mihi, Quanta laboras in Charybdi! Digne puer meliore flamma. Quae faga, quis te solvere Thelalis Magus veniens, qua poterit Deus: Vix illigatum tetriformi Pegasus expedit Chimera. *Horat.* Carm. lib. i. ode 27. Eighthly, If crowding figures be bad, it is still worse to graft one figure upon another: For instance, While his keen falchion drinks the warriors lives. *Iliad*, book xi. l. 271. A falchion drinking the warriors blood, is a figure built upon resemblance, which is passable. But then in the expression, lives is again put for blood; and by thus grafting one figure upon another, the expression is rendered obscure and unpleasant. Ninthly, Intricate and involved figures, that can scarce be analyzed, or reduced to plain language, are least of all tolerable: Votis incendimus aras. *Æneid*, book iii. l. 279. Onerentique canistris Dona laborate Cereris *Æneid*, book viii. l. 180. Vulcan to the Cyclops: Arma acri facienda viro: nunc viribus usus, Nunc manibus rapidis, omni nunc arte magistra: Precipitate moras. *Æneid*, book viii. l. 441. Huic gladio, perque area scuta, Per tunicum squalentem auro, latus haurit apertum. *Æneid*, book x. l. 313. Scriberis Vario fortis, et hosfium Victor, Mæonii carminis alie. *Horat.* Carm. lib. i. ode 6. Elfe shall our fates be number'd with the dead. *Iliad*, book v. l. 294. Communal death the fate of war confounds. *Iliad*, book viii. l. 85, and book xi. l. 117. Speaking of Proteus: Instant he wears, elusive of the rape, The mimic force of every savage shape. *Odyssey*, book iv. l. 563. Rolling convulsive on the floor, is seen The piteous object of a prostrate queen. *Ibid.* book iv. l. 652. The mingling tempest weaves its gloom. *Autumn*, l. 337. A various sweetness swells the gentle race. *Ibid.*, l. 640. The distant waterfall swells in the breeze. *Winter*, l. 738. In the tenth place, When a subject is introduced by its proper name, it is absurd to attribute to it the properties of a different subject to which the word is sometimes applied in a figurative sense: Hear me, Oh Neptune! thou whose arms are hurl'd From shore to shore, and gird the fold world. *Odyssey*, book ix. l. 617. Neptune is here introduced personally, and not figuratively, for the ocean; the description therefore, which is only applicable to the latter, is altogether improper. It is not sufficient that a figure of speech be regularly constructed, and be free from blemish; it requires taste to discern when it is proper, when improper; and taste perhaps is our only guide. One, however, may gather from reflections and experience, that ornaments and graces suit not any of the disfiguring passions, nor are proper for expressing anything grave and important. In familiar conversation, they are in some measure ridiculous: Prospero, in the *Tempest*, speaking to his daughter Miranda, says, The fringed curtains of thine eyes advance, And say what thou feel'st fond. No exception can be taken to the justness of the figure; and circumstances may be imagined to make it proper: but it is certainly not proper in familiar conversation. In the last place, Though figures of speech have a charming effect when accurately constructed and properly introduced, they ought, however, to be scattered with a sparing hand; nothing is more ludicrous, and nothing consequently more fatiguing, than redundant ornaments of any kind. Figure is used, in Theology, for the mysteries represented or delivered obscurely to us under certain types, or actions in the Old Testament. Thus manna is held a figure or type of the eucharist; and the death of Abel a figure of the suffering of Christ. Many divines and critics contend, that all the actions, histories, ceremonies, &c. of the Old Testament, are only figures, types, and prophecies, of what was to happen under the New. The Jews are supposed Figure to have had the figures or shadows, and we the substance. Figure is also applied in a like sense to profane matters; as the emblems, enigmas, fables, symbols, and hieroglyphics, of the ancients.

FIGURED

Pages 240-240

FIGURED, in general, something marked with figures. The term figured is chiefly applied to stuffs, whereon the figures of flowers, and the like, are either wrought or stamped. Figured, in Music, is applied either to simple notes or to harmony: to simple notes, as in these words figured bass, to express a bass whose notes carrying chords are subdivided into many other notes of lesser value; to harmony, when, by supposition and in a diatonic procedure, other notes than those which form the chord are employed. See Supposition. To figure is to put several notes for one; to form runnings or variations; to add some notes to the air, in whatever manner it be done; in short, it is to give to harmonious sounds a figure of melody, by connecting them with other intermediate sounds.

FILAGO

Pages 240-240

FILAGO, a genus of plants, belonging to the syn-genesia clas; and in the natural method ranking under the 49th order, Compositae. See Botany Index.

FILAMENT

Pages 240-242

FILAMENT, in Anatomy, Natural History, &c., a term used in the same sense with fibre, for those fine threads whereof the flesh, nerves, skin, plants, roots, &c., are composed. See Fibre. Vegetable Filaments form a substance of great use in the arts and manufactures; furnishing thread, cloth, cordage, &c. For these purposes the filamentous parts of the Cannabis and Linum, or hemp and flax, are employed among us. But different vegetables have been employed in different countries for the same uses. Putrefaction destroys the pulpy or flabby matter, and leaves the tough filaments entire: By putrefying the leaf of a plant in water, we obtain the fine flexible fibres, which constituted the basis of the ribs and minute veins, and which now form as it were a skeleton of the leaf. Alkaline lye, in some degree, produce similar effects to putrefaction.
