He observed, as might indeed have been imagined from the nature of the material, that the flame disappeared wherever the mixture fell, and that the saline, metallic, and earthy matters formed an impenetrable layer round the hot combustible matter, which prevented the access of the air, and consequently the renewal of the destructive process. It is scarcely probable that this practice in the large way, with an engine throwing upwards of 200 gallons (value about £1. 10s.) each minute, would be thought of or adopted, or that a sufficient store of the materials would be kept in readiness; since at this rate the expenditure for an hour would demand a provision to the amount of £10l. sterling. But in country places the process, or some variation of it, might be applied with sufficient profit in the result; more especially if it be considered that common salt or alum, or such saline matter as can be had and mixed with the water, together with clay, chalk, or lime, ochreous earth or common mud, or even these last without any salt, may answer the purpose of the late with more or less effect, and extinguish an accidental fire with much greater speed and certainty than clear water would do. Water-Engine for Extinguishing Fire. See Hydrostatics. In using this machine we have the following improvement by Dr Hoffman, which promises to be of great efficacy. As soon as the engine is in readiness to work, stir into the water that immediately is to be discharged, seven or eight pounds of pearl ashes in powder, and continue to add it in this manner as occasion requires; taking care that it be directed against the timber or wainscot, &c. just beginning to burn, and not waited against the brick-work: or, where time will admit, dissolve any quantity of pearl ashes in a copper with water, and as fast as it dissolves, which will be in a few minutes, mix a palpit with the water in the engine, pretty often; and whatever burning wood it is played upon, will be extinguished as if it was dipped in water, and will not burn afresh in the part extinguished. Easy Method of Extinguishing Fire in Chimneys. It is well known, that the inner parts of chimneys easily take fire; the foot that kindles therein emits a greater flame, according as the tunnel is more elevated, because the inferior air feeds the fire. If this air could therefore be suppressed, the fire would soon be extinguished. In order to this, some discharge a pitfall into the chimney, which produces no effect; others lay...

FIRING

Pages 267-267

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> art, denotes the discharge of the fire-arms; and its object is to do the utmost execution to the enemy. The method of firing by platoons is said to have been invented by Guglielmo Adolphus, and first used about the year 1618; the reason <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> given for this method is, that a constant fire may be always kept up. There are three different ways of platoon firing; viz. standing, advancing, and retreating. But previous to every kind of firing, each regiment <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> battalion must be told off in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">grand</a> divisions, subdivisions, and platoons, exclusively of the grenadiers, which form two subdivisions or four platoons of themselves. In firing standing, either by divisions or platoons, the first fire is from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> or platoon on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a>; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> fire from the left; the third from the right again; and so on alternately, till the firing comes to the centre platoon, which is generally called the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> platoon, and does not fire, remaining as a reserve for the colours. Firing advancing is performed in the same manner, with this addition, that before either division or platoon fires, it advances three paces forward. Firing retreating varies from either of the former methods; for before either division or platoon fires, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> they are marching from the enemy, it must go to the right about, and after firing, to the left about again, and continue the retreat as slow and orderly as possible. In hedge firing the men are drawn up two deep, and in that order both ranks are to fire standing. Oblique firing is either to the right and left, or from the right and left to the centre, according to the situation of the object. The Prussians have a particular contrivance for this purpose; if they are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> to the right, the rear ranks of every platoon make two quick but small paces to the left, and the body of each soldier turns one-eighth of a circle, and vice versa. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARAPET">Parapet</a> firing depends on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the parapet over which the men are to fire, and also upon that of the attack made to protect it. This method of firing is sometimes performed by single ranks stepping on the banquette and firing; each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> instantly handing his arms to the centre <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the same <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FILE">file</a>, and taking his back in the room of it; and the centre rank giving it to the rear to load, and forwarding the arms of the rear to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> rank; by which means the front rank men can fire six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROUNDS">rounds</a> in a minute with exactness. Parapet firing may also be executed two deep, when the banquette is three feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a>, or in field works where no banquettes are made. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a> firing is performed by a regiment or body of men drawn up in a hollow square, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> each front is generally divided into four divisions or firings, and the flanks of the square, being the weakest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, are covered by four platoons of grenadiers. The first fire is from the right division of each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a>; the second from the left division of each face, &c. and the grenadiers make the last fire. Street firing is practised in two ways; either by making the division or platoon that has fired to wheel by half-rank to the right and left outwards from the centre, and to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a> in that order by half divisions <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the flanks on each side of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a>, and to draw up in the rear, and go on with their priming and loading; or, to make the division or platoon, after firing, to face to the right and left outwards from the centre, and one half rank to follow the other; and in that order to march in one centre file down on each side of the column into the rear, and there draw up as before. Firing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">Iron</a>, in Farriery, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> not unlike the blade of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>; which being made <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> hot is applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hams, or other places standing in need of it, as in preternatural swellings, farcy, knots, &c. in order to disperse them.

FIRKIN

Pages 267-267

an English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of capacity for things liquid, being the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>: it contains eight gallons of ale, loap, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> herrings; and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> gallons of beer.

FIRLOT

Pages 267-267

a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> used in Scotland. The oat firlot contains 21 1/3 th pints of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; the wheat firlot contains about 22 1/3 cubical inches; and the barley firlot, 31 standard pints. Hence it appears that the Scotch wheat firlot exceeds the English bushel by 33 cubical inches.

FIRMAMENT

Pages 267-267

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a>, the eighth heaven <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> sphere; being that wherein the fixed stars were supposed to be placed. It is called the eighth, with respect to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> heavens or spheres of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a> which it surrounds. It is supposed to have two motions; a diurnal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, given it by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIMUM_MOBILE">primum <a cla</a>ss="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MOBILE">mobile</a>, from east to west, about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> of the ecliptic; and another opposite motion from west to east; which last it finishes, according to Tycho, in 25,412 years; according to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PTOLEMY">Ptolemy</a>, in 36,000; and according to Copernicus, in 258,000; in which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the fixed stars return to the same precise <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> wherein they were at the beginning. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a>'s year, or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> year. In various places of Scripture the word firmament is used for the middle region of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> allowed, with the moderns, that the firmament is a fluid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>; though they, who gave it the denomination of firmament, must have taken it for a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> one.

FIRMAN

Pages 267-267

is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASSPORT">passport</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> permit granted by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> Mogul to foreign vessels, to trade within the territories of his jurisdiction.

FIRMICUS

Pages 267-270

Maternus Julius, an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> writer, who lived about the middle of the fourth century. Nothing is known with certainty respecting his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, profession, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> character, as we find no mention made of him in the writings of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> authors. Some say that he was by birth a Sicilian, and practised in the forum as a barrister for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, becoming a convert to Christianity when far advanced in years; which appears to derive considerable support from different <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PASSAGES">passages</a> in his writings. He was author of a treatise De errore profanarum religionum, which was dedicated to the emperors Constantius and Constans. This <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>... Firmness must have been written between 340 and 350, in which Confutans was slain by Magnentius. It is allowed to be a learned, able, and well written performance, in which the reasonableness of the Christian <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> is strongly contrasted with the absurdity and immorality of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENTILE">gentile</a> creed. It must not be dissembled, however, that he sometimes betrays such a spirit of intolerance as is wholly incompatible with the genius of the Christian religion, which breathes nothing but benevolence towards the whole <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. The arguments employed by him in its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a> are disgraced by an exhortation to the civil power to propagate it by force of arms, and to crush the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADVOCATES">advocates</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> by severe edicts. This work was first published at Straßburg in 1562, at <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol5.html#article-HEIDELBERG">Heidelberg</a> in 1559, and at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1610. The greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of critics ascribe to him a work entitled *Afronimorum, seu de Mathesi*, lib. viii. In it he treats of the power and influence of the stars, agreeably to the doctrine of the Egyptians and Babylonians, blending a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of mathematical knowledge with the unmeaning jargon of judicial astrology. Those who imagine that so good a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> as Firmicus could not have been the author of such an absurd performance, should remember that it was probably composed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIOR">prior</a> to his conversion, when such absurdities would constitute a part of his creed. **Firmness**, denotes the consistence of a body, or that state wherein its sensible parts cohere in such a manner, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of one part induces a motion in the rest. **First-born.** See Primogeniture, for the literal meaning of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>. In Scripture it is also used often in a figurative <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> for that which is first, most excellent, most distinguished in any thing. Thus it is said of Christ (Col. i. 5.), that he is "the first-born of every creature;" and in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REVELATION">Revelation</a> (i. 5.) he is called "the first-begotten of the dead;" that is, according to the commentators, begotten of the Father before any creature was produced; and the first who rose from the dead by his own power. "The first-born of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>," (Isa. xiv. 30.) signifies, The most miserable of all the poor; and in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOB">Job</a> (xviii. 13.) "The first-born of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>;" that is, The most terrible of all deaths. **First <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">Fruits</a> (primitive),** among the Hebrews, were oblations of part of the fruits of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a>, offered to God as an acknowledgment of his sovereign dominion. The first of these fruits was offered in the name of the whole <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, being either two loaves of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, or a sheaf of barley which was threshed in the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of the temple. Every private person was obliged to bring his first fruits to the temple; and these consisted of wheat, barley, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, figs, apricots, olives, and dates. There was another sort of first fruits which were paid to God. When bread was kneaded in a family, a portion of it was set apart and given to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a> or Levite who dwelt in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> there was no priest or Levite there, it was <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the oven, and consumed by the fire. These offerings made a considerable part of the revenues of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> priesthood. First Fruits are frequently mentioned in ancient Christian writers as one part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> revenue. One of the councils of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a> enjoins, that they should consist only of grapes and corn; which shows, that this was the practice of the African church. **First Fruits,** in the church of England, are the profits of every spiritual benefice for the first year, according to the valuation thereof in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s books. **Fisc,** (Fiscus), in the Civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURY">treasury</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> or state; or that to which all things due to the public do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>. The word is derived from the Greek φίσκος, "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BASKET">basket</a>," used when they went to market.—By the civil law, none but a sovereign prince has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to have a fisc or public treasury. At Rome, under the emperors, the term ararium was used for the revenues destined for support of the charges of the empire; the fiscus for those of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a>'s own family. The treasury, in effect, belonged to the people, and the fiscus to the prince. Hence the goods of condemned persons, if appropriated to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the public, were said publicari; if to the support of the emperor or prince, conficari. **Fiscal,** in the Civil Law, something relating to the pecuniary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of the prince or people. The officers appointed for the management of the fisc, were called procuratores fisci, and advocati fisci; and among the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> enumerated in the constitutions of the empire where it was their business to plead, one is against those who have been condemned to pay a fine to the fisc on account of their litigionsnels or frivolous appeals. **Fiscus.** See Fisc. **Fish,** in <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, an animal that lives in the waters as the natural place of its abode. Fishes form the fourth class of animals in the Linnaean system. Their most general or popular <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> is into fresh and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> ones. Some, however, are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that all fishes naturally inhabit the salt waters, and that they have mounted up into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> only by accident. A few <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> only swim up into the rivers to deposit their spawn; but by far the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> keep in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, and would soon expire in fresh water. There are about 400 species of fishes (according to Linnæus) of which we know something; but the unknown ones are supposed to be many more; and as they are thought to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> in great depths of the sea remote from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, it is probable that many species <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> remain for ever unknown. For the subdivisions, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, and natural history of this class of animals, see <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. **Blowing of Fish,** is a practice similar to that of blowing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POULTRY">poultry</a>, and pigs, and adopted for the same deceitful purposes. The method of blowing fish, especially cod and whitings, is by placing the end of a quill or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">tobacco</a>-pipe at the vent, and pricking a hole with a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a> which is next the gill; thereby making the fish appear to the eye <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and full, which when dressed will be flabby, and little else than skin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>. But this imposition may be discovered by placing the finger and thumb on each side of the vent, and squeezing it hard; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> may be perceived to go out, the skin will fall in, and the fish appear lank, and of little value. **Breeding of Fishes** may be turned to great advantage; for, besides furnishing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, obliging one's friends, and raising <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, the land will be thereby greatly greatly improved, so as to yield more this way than by any other employment whatever. See Fish Pond. <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASTRATION">Castration</a> of Fish, is a method first practised by Mr Tull, in order to prevent the excessive increase of fish in some of his ponds, where the numbers did not permit any of them to grow to an advantageous size. But he afterwards found, that the castrated fish grew much larger than their usual size, were more fat, and always in season. This operation may be performed both on <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> fish; and the most eligible time for it is when the ovaries of the female have their ova in them, and when the vessels of the male, analogous to these, have their seminal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> in them; because, at this time, these vessels are more easily distinguished from the ureters, which convey the urine from the kidneys into the bladder, and are situated near the seminal vessels on each side of the spine; which, without sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>, may be mistaken for the ovaries, especially when these last are empty. The time least proper for this operation, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> after they have spawned, because the fish are then too weak and languid to bear, with success, so severe an operation; however, with skill and care, it may be performed almost at any time. When a fish is to be castrated, it must be held in a wet cloth, with its belly upwards; then with a sharp penknife, having its point bent backwards, the operator cuts through the integuments of the rim of the belly, taking care not to wound any of the intestines. As soon as a small aperture is made, he carefully inserts a hooked <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a>-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, and with this dilates the aperture from between the two fore-fins almost to the anus. He then, with two small blunt silver hooks, five or six inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, and of this form P, by the help of an assistant, holds open the belly of the fish; and with a spoon or spatula, removes carefully the intestines from one side. When these are removed, you see the ureter, a small vessel, nearly in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of the spine, and also the ovary, a larger vessel, lying before it, nearer the integuments of the belly. This last vessel is taken up with a hook of the same kind with those before mentioned, and, after detaching it from the side far enough for the purpose, divided transversely with a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of sharp scissors, care being taken that the intestines are not wounded or injured. After one of the ovaries has been divided, the operator proceeds to divide the other in the same manner; and then the divided integuments of the belly are sewed with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, the stitches being inserted at a small distance from one another. Mr Tull observes farther, that the spawning time is very various; that trouts are full about Christmas; perch in February; pikes in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, and carp and tench in May; and that allowance must be made for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLIMATE">climate</a> and situation, with regard to the spawning of fish. When the fish are castrated, they are put into the water where they are intended to continue; and they take their chance in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with other fish, as though they were not castrated. With tolerable care, few die of the operation. Phil. Trans. vol. xlviii. Part 2. Art. 106. Although we could not properly avoid inserting the above detail, it is presumed that few will be pleased with the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a>. The operation is peculiarly cruel, and the purpose of it only a detestable piece of Apician refinement. Feeding of Fishes. When they are fed in large pools or ponds, either malt boiled, or fresh grains, is the best food; thus carps may be raised and fed like capons, and tenches will feed as well. The care of feeding them is best committed to a gardener or the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTLER">butler</a>, who should be always at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. When fed in a stew, any sort of grain boiled, especially peas, and malt coarsely ground, are proper food; also the grains after <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREWING">brewing</a>, while fresh and sweet; but one bullock of malt not brewed will go as far as two of grains. Stealing of Fish, by persons armed and disguised, is felony without benefit of clergy, by 9 Geo. I. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 22. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">Black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">Act</a>. And by 5 Geo. III. cap. 14, the penalty of transportation for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years is inflicted on persons stealing or taking fish in any water, within a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARK">park</a>, paddock, orchard, or yard; and on the receivers, aiders, and abettors; and a forfeiture of five pounds to the owner of the fishery is made payable by persons taking or destroying (or attempting so to do) any fish in any river or other water within any enclosed ground, being private <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a>. Preserving of Fish for Cabinets. Linnaeus's method is, to expose them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>; and when they acquire such a degree of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> that the skin loses its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> to the body of the fish, it may be slid off almost like a glove; the two sides of this skin may then be dried upon <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> like a plant, or one of the sides may be filled with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of Paris to give the subject a due plumpness. A fish may be prepared, after it has acquired this degree of putrefaction, by making a longitudinal incision on the belly, and carefully dissecting the fleshy part from the skin, which is but slightly attached to it in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of the putrefaction. The skin is then to be filled with cotton and the antiseptic powder as directed for birds; and, lastly, to be sewed up where the incision was made. <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">Gold</a> Fish. See Cyprinus, Ichthyology Index. Gilding on Fish. In the posthumous papers of Mr Hooke, a method is described of gilding live craw fish, carps, &c., without injuring the fish. The cement for this purpose is prepared, by putting some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">burgundy</a> pitch into a new earthen pot, and warming the vessel till it receives so much of the pitch as will stick round it; then strewing some finely powdered <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a> before the pitch when growing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, adding a mixture of three pounds of linseed <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> and one of oil of turpentine, covering the vessel, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> them for an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> over a gentle fire, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> the mixture, as it is wanted, with so much pumice-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> in fine powder as will reduce it to the consistence of paint. The fish being wiped dry, the mixture is spread upon it; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLD_LEAF">gold-<a c</a>lass="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> being then laid on, and gently pressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>, the fish may be immediately put into water again, without any danger of the gold coming off, for the matter quickly grows firm in water. Fish, in a ship, a plank or piece of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a>, fastened to a ship's mast or yard, to strengthen it; which is done by nailing it on with <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> spikes, and winding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a> hard about them. Fishes, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, are the emblems of silence and watchfulness; and are borne either upright, inwound, extended, endorsed respecting each other, surmounting one another, fretted, &c. In <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLAZONING">blazoning</a> fishes, those borne feeding, should be termed devouring; all fishes borne upright and having fins, Fisher, fins, should be blazoned hauriant; and those borne transverse the escutcheon, must be termed naiant. Fish Ponds, those made for the breeding or feeding of fish. Fish ponds are no small improvement of watery and boggy lands, many of which are fit for no other use. In making of a pond, its head should be at the lowest part of the ground, that the trench of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a>-gate or sluice, having a good fall, may not be too long in emptying. The best way of making the head secure, is to drive in two or three rows of stakes above six feet long, at above four feet distance from each other, the whole length of the pond head, whereof the first row should be rammed at least about four feet deep. If the bottom is false, the foundation may be laid with quicklime; which flaking, will make it as hard as a stone. Some lay a layer of lime, and another of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> dug out of the pond, among the piles and stakes; and when these are well covered, drive in others as they see occasion, ramming in the earth as before, till the pond head be of the height designed. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAM">dam</a> should be made sloping on each side, leaving a waite to carry off the over abundance of water in times of floods or rains; and as to the depth of the pond, the deepest part need not exceed six feet, rising gradually in shoals towards the sides, for the fish to run themselves, and lay their spawn. Gravelly and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> bottoms, especially the latter, are best for breeding; and a fat <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a> with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fat water, as the washings of hills, commons, streets, finks, &c. is best for fattening all sorts of fish. For storing a pond, carp is to be preferred for its goodmels, quick growth, and great increase, as breeding five or six times a-year. A pond of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>, if it be a feeding and not breeding one, will every year feed 200 carps of three years old, 300 of two years old, and 400 of a year old. Carps delight in ponds that have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARL">marl</a> or clay bottoms, with plenty of weeds and grass, whereon they feed in the hot months. Ponds should be drained every three or four years, and the fish sorted. In breeding ones, the smaller ones are to be taken out, to store other ponds with; leaving a good stock of females, at least eight or <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> years old, as they never breed before that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. In feeding ponds, it is best to keep them pretty near of a size.

FISHER

Pages 270-270

JOHN, bishop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROCHESTER">Rochester</a>, was born at Beverly in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORKSHIRE">Yorkshire</a>, in the year 1459, and educated in the collegiate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of that <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>. In 1484, he removed to Michael <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, of which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> he was elected <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> in the year 1495. Having applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, he took orders; and, becoming eminent as a divine, attracted the notice of Margaret countess of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-RICHMOND">Richmond</a>, mother of Henry VII., who made him her chaplain and confessor. In 1501, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of divinity, and the same year was elected <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHANCELLOR">chancellor</a> of the university. In the year following, he was appointed Lady Margaret's first divinity professor; and in 1504, consecrated bishop of Rochester; which small bishopric he would never resign, though he was offered both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELY">Ely</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a>. It is generally allowed, that the foundation of the two colleges of Christ church and St John's, in Cambridge, was entirely owing to Bishop Fisher's persuasion and influence with the countess of Richmond: he not only formed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, but superintended the execution. On the promulgation of Martin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUTHER">Luther</a>'s doctrine, our bishop was the first to enter the lists against him. On this occasion he exerted all his influence, and is generally supposed to have written the famous book by which Henry VIII. obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Defender of the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">Faith</a>. Hitherto he <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> in favour with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>; but in 1527, opposing his divorce, and denying his supremacy, the implacable Harry determined, and finally effected, his destruction. In 1543, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> found him guilty of misprision of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASON">treason</a>, for concealing certain prophetic speeches of a fanatical impostor, called the Holy Maid of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, relative to the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>; and condemned him, with five others, in lots of goods, and imprisonment during his majesty's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; but he was released on paying 300l. for the king's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. King Henry being now married to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANNE">Anne</a> Boleyn, his obsequious parliament took an oath of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALLEGIANCE">allegiance</a> proper for the occasion. This oath the bishop of Rochester steadily refused; alleging, that his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONSCIENCE">conscience</a> could not be convinced that the king's first <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> was against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of God. For refusing this oath of succession, he was attainted by the parliament of 1534; and committed to the Tower, where he was cruelly treated, and were he would probably have died a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> death, had not the pope created him a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">cardinal</a>. The king, now positively determined on his destruction, sent Rich, the solicitor general, under the pretence of consulting the bishop on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of conscience, but really with a design to draw him into a conversation concerning the supremacy. The honest old bishop spoke his mind without suspicion <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> reserve, and an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> and conviction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> treason was the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a>. He was beheaded at Tower Hill, on the 22d of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a> 1535, in the 77th year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. Thus died this good old prelate; who, notwithstanding his inflexible enmity to the Reformation, was undoubtedly a learned, pious, and honest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. He wrote several treatises against Luther, and other works, which were printed at Wurtzburg, in 1597, in one volume folio.

FISHERY

Pages 271-278

Y denotes also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a> of fish, more particularly the catching them for <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a>. Were we to enter into a very minute and particular consideration of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, as at present established in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, this article would swell beyond its proper bounds; because, to do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> to a subject of such concernment to the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a>, requires a very ample and distinct discussion. We shall, however, observe, that since the Divine <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROVIDENCE">Providence</a> hath so eminently stored the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a> with the most valuable fish; and since fisheries, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> successful, become permanent nurseries for breeding expert fishermen; it is not only a duty we owe to the Supreme Being, not to despise the wonderful plenty he hath afforded us, by neglecting to extend this branch of commerce to the utmost; but it is a duty we owe to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, for its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> security, which depends upon the strength of our <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>. No nation can have a navy where there is not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUND">fund</a> of benefits to breed and employ fishermen without any expense to the public, and no trade is so well calculated for training up these useful members of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> as fisheries. The situation of the British coasts is the most advantageous in the world for catching fish: the Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a>, particularly those to the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> and west, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> most commodious for carrying on the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> trade to perfection; for no country in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> can pretend to come up to Scotland in the abundance of the finest fish, with which its various creeks, bays, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAKES">lakes</a>, and coasts, are replenished. Of these advantages the Scots seem indeed to have been abundantly sensible; and their traffic in herrings, the most valuable of all the fisheries, is noticed in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> so early as the ninth century. The frequent laws which were enacted in the reigns of James III., IV., and V., discover a steady determined zeal for the benefit of the native subjects, and the full restoration of the fisheries, which the Dutch had latterly found means to engross; and do <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a> of those patriots whom <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times affect to call barbarians. The expedition of James V. to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBRIDES">Hebrides</a> and western parts of the Highlands and his assiduity in exploring and founding the harbours, discovered a fixed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a>, to civilize the inhabitants, to promote the valuable fisheries at their doors, and to introduce general industry. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, at an early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>, and the subsequent <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> and civil commotions in the kingdom, frustrated those wise designs, and the western fisheries remained in their original state of neglect. At length, 1602, James VI. returned the national purposes which had been thus chalked out by his grandfather. "Three <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> (says Dr Robertson) which might serve as a retreat for the industrious, and a nursery for arts and commerce, were appointed to be built in different parts of the Highlands; one in <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAITHNESS">Caithness</a>, another in Lochaber, and a third in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">isle</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a>; and in order to draw the inhabitants thither, all the privileges of the royal boroughs were to be conferred upon them. Finding it, however, to be no easy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> to inspire the inhabitants of those countries with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> of industry, a resolution was taken to plant amongst them colonies of people from the more industrious counties. The first experiment was made in the isle of Lewis; and as it was advantageously situated for the fishing trade (a source from which Scotland ought naturally to derive great wealth), the colony transported thither was drawn out of Fife, the inhabitants of which were well skilled in that branch of commerce. But before they had remained there <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> enough to manifest the good effects of this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTITUTION">institution</a>, the islanders, enraged at seeing their country occupied by those intruders, took arms, and surprising them in the night <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, murdered some of them, and compelled the rest to abandon the settlement. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> being soon turned to other objects, particularly to his succession to the English <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a>, we hear no more of this salutary project." The Scottish fisheries were, however, resumed by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> I. who "ordained an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ASSOCIATION">association</a> of the three kingdoms, for a general fishing within the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIL">hail</a> seas and coasts of his majesty's said kingdoms; and for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> of the said association, ordained, that there should be a standing committee chosen and nominated by his majesty, and his successors from time to time." &c. &c. Several persons of distinction embarked in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a>, which the king honoured with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRONAGE">patronage</a>, and encouraged by his bounty. He also ordered <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to be more strictly observed; prohibited the importation of fish taken by foreigners; and agreed to purchase from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> his naval stores and the fish for his fleets. Thus the scheme of establishing a fishery in the Hebrides began to assume a favourable aspect; but all the hopes of the adventurers were frustrated by the breaking out of the civil wars, and the very tragic death of their benefactor. In 1661, Charles II., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Clarendon, and other persons of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> and fortune, resumed the business of the fisheries with greater vigour than any of their predecessors. For this purpose the most salutary laws were enacted by the parliaments of England and Scotland; in virtue of which, all materials used in, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> depending upon, the fisheries, were exempted from all duties, excises, or imposts whatever. In England, the company were authorized to set up a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOTTERY">lottery</a>, and to have a voluntary collection in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARISH">parish</a> churches; houses of entertainment, as taverns, inns, ale-houses, were to take one or more barrels of herrings, at the stated price of 30s. per <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARREL">barrel</a>; and 2s. 6d. per barrel was to be paid to the stock of this company on all imported fish taken by foreigners. Some Dutch families were also invited, or permitted, to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> in Stormont: the herrings cured by the Royal English company gave general satisfaction, and, as mentioned above, brought a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> price for those days. Every circumstance attending this new establishment seemed to be the result of a judicious <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> and thorough knowledge of the business, when the necessities of the king obliged him to withdraw his subscription or bounty; which gave such umbrage to the parties concerned, that they soon after dissolved. In 1677, a new royal company was established in England, at the head of which was the duke of York, the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">earl</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a>, &c. Besides all the privileges which former companies had enjoyed, the king granted this new company a perpetuity, with power to purchase lands; and also £20,000 to be paid them annually, out of the customs of the port of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, for every dogger or buss they should build and send out for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> years to come. A stock of 15,980l. was immediately advanced, and afterwards 1600l. more. This small <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> was soon exhausted in purchasing and fitting out busses, with other incidental expenses. The company, made, however, a successful beginning; and one of their busses or doggers actually took and brought home 32,000 cod fish; other vessels had also a favourable fishery. Such favourable beginnings might have excited fresh subscriptions, when an unforeseen event ruined the whole design beyond the possibility of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>. Most of the busses had been built in <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOLLAND">Holland</a>, and manned with Dutchmen; on which pretence the French, who were then at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> with Holland, seized six out of seven vessels, with their cargoes and fishing tackle: and the company being now in debt, sold, in 1680, the remaining stores, &c. A <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of gentlemen and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> raised a new subscription of 60,000l. under the privileges and immunities of the former <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>. This attempt also came to nothing, owing to the death of the king, and the troubles of the subsequent reign. Soon after the Revolution this business was again resumed, and upon a more extensive <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a>; the proposed capital being 300,000l., of which 100,000l. was to have been raised by the surviving patentees or their successors, and 200,000l. by new subscribers. Copies of the letters patent, the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a> of the company, and terms of subscription, were lodged at sundry places in London and Westminster, for the perusal of the public, while the subscription was filling. It is probable, that King William's partiality to the Dutch fisheries, the succeeding war, or both of these circumstances, frustrated this new attempt; of which we have no farther account in the annals of that reign or since. The Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> had also, during the three last reigns, passed sundry acts for erecting companies and promoting the fisheries; but the intestine commotions of that country, and the great exertions which were made for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARIEN">Darien</a> establishment, enfeebled all other attempts, whether collectively or by individuals, within that kingdom. In 1749, his late majesty having, at the opening of the parliament, warmly recommended the improvement of the fisheries, the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of commons appointed a committee to inquire into the state of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HERRING">herring</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fisheries, and to consider of the most probable means of extending the same. All ranks of men were elevated with an idea of the boundless <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICHES">riches</a> that would flow into the kingdom from this source. A subscription of 500,000l. was immediately filled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, by a body of men who were incorporated for 21 years by the name of The Society of the Free British Fishery. Every encouragement was held out by government, both to the society, and to individuals who might embark in this national business. A bounty of 30s. per ton was to be paid annually out of the customs, for 14 years, to the owners of all decked vessels or busses, from 20 to 80 tons burden, which should be built after the commencement of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>, for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of, and fitted out and employed in, the said fisheries, whether by the Society or any other persons. At the same time numerous pamphlets and newspaper essays came forth; all pretending to elucidate the subject, and to convince the public with what facility the herring fisheries might be transferred from Dutch to British <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>. This proved, however, a more arduous task than had been foreseen by superficial speculators. The Dutch were frugal in their expenditures and living; perfect masters of the arts of fishing and curing, which they had carried to the greatest height and perfection. They were in full possession of the European <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARKETS">markets</a>; and their fish, whether delivered or otherwise, had the reputation of superior qualities to all others taken in our seas. With such advantages, the Dutch not only maintained their ground against this formidable company, but had also the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> of seeing the capital gradually sinking, without having procured an adequate return to the adventurers; notwithstanding various aids and efforts of government from time to time in their favour, particularly in 1757, when an advance of 20s. per ton was added to the bounty. In 1780 the public attention was again called to the state of the British fisheries, by the suggestions of Mr Dempster in the house of commons, and by different publications that appeared upon the subject; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which the minister suffered a committee to be named; to inquire into this great source of national wealth. To that committee it appeared, that the best way of improving the fisheries was to encourage the inhabitants living nearest to the seat of them to become fishers: And it being found that the north-western <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a> of the kingdom, though abounding with fish and with fine harbours, was utterly destitute of towns, an act was passed for incorporating certain persons therein named, by the style of "The British Society for extending the fisheries and improving the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> coasts of the kingdom;" and to enable them to subscribe a <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JOINT">joint</a> stock, and therewith to purchase lands, and build thereon free towns, villages, and fishing stations, in the Highlands and islands in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Great Britain called Scotland, and for other purposes. The isle of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MULL">Mull</a>, Loch <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROOM">Broom</a>, the isles of Sky and of Cannay, have already been pitched upon as proper situations for some of these towns. The progress of such an undertaking from its <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> must be slow, but still slower when carried on with a limited capital arising from the subscriptions of a few public-spirited individuals. But it is not to be doubted but that it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> ultimately tend to the increase of our fisheries, and to the improvement of the Highland part of this kingdom. Its tendency is also to lessen the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMIGRATION">emigration</a> of a brave and industrious <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of inhabitants, too many of whom have already removed with their families to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a>. I. Anchovy Fishery. The anchovy is caught in the months of May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, on the coasts of Catalonia, Provence, &c., at which season it constantly repairs up the straits of Gibraltar, into the Mediterranean. Collins says they are also found in plenty on the western coasts of England and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WALES">Wales</a>. The fishing for them is chiefly in the night time; when a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> being put on the stern of their little fishing vessels, the anchovies flock round, and are caught in the nets. But then it is asserted to have been found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that anchovies taken thus by fire, are neither so good, so firm, nor so proper for keeping, as those which are taken without fire. When the fishery is over, they cut off the heads, take out their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GALL">gall</a> and guts, and then lay them in barrels, and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> them. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> way of eating anchovies is with <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VINEGAR">vinegar</a>, &c. in order to which they are first boned, and the tails, fins, &c. slipped off.—Being put on the fire, they dissolve almost in any liquor. Or they are made into a sauce by mincing them with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, &c. Some also pickle anchovies in small delft or earthen pots, made on purpose, of two or three pounds <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, more or less, which they cover with <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> to keep them the better. Anchovies should be chosen small, fresh pickled, white on the outside and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> within. They must have a round back; for those which are flat or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> are often nothing but sardines. Besides these qualities, the pickle, on opening the pots or barrels, must be of a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, and not have lost its flavour. 2. Cod Fishery. There are two kinds of cod fish; the one green or white cod, and the other dried or cured cod; though it is all the same fish, differently prepared; the former being sometimes salted and barrelled, then taken out for use; and the latter, having lain some competent time in salt, dried in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>. We shall therefore speak of each of these apart; and first of the Green. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> fisheries for green cod are in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BAY">bay</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANADA">Canada</a>, on the great <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> of Newfoundland, and on the isle of St <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PETER">Peter</a>, and the isle of Sable; to which places vessels <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a> from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts both of Europe and America. They are from 100 to 150 tons burden, and will catch between 30,000 and 40,000 cod each. The most essential part of the fishery is, to have a <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> who knows how to cut up the cod, one who is skilled to take off the head properly, and above all a good falter, on which the preserving of them, and consequently the success of the voyage depends. The best season is from the beginning of February to the end of April; the fish, which in the winter retire to the deepest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, coming then on the banks, and fattening extremely. What is caught from <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> to June keeps well; but those taken in July, August, and September, when it is warm on the banks, are apt to spoil soon. Every fisher takes but one at a time: the most expert will take from 350 to 400 in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>; but that is the most, the weight of the fish and the great coldness on the bank fatiguing very much. As soon as the cod are caught, the head is taken off; they are opened, gutted, and salted; and the falter flows them in the bottom of the hold, head to tail, in beds a fathom or two <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>; laying layers of salt and fish alternately, but never mixing fish caught on different days. When they have lain thus three or four days to drain off the water, they are replaced in another part of the ship, and salted again; where they remain till the vessel is loaded. Sometimes they are cut in thick pieces, and put in barrels for the convenience of carriage. Dry. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> fishery for this article is, from <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">Cape</a> Rose to the Bay des Exports, along the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACENTIA">Placentia</a>, in which compass there are divers commodious ports for the fish to be dried in. These, though of the same kind with the fresh cod, are much smaller, and therefore fitter to keep, as the salt penetrates more easily into them. The fishery of both is much alike; only this latter is most expensive, as it takes up more time and employs more hands, and yet scarce half so much salt is spent in this as in the other. The bait is herrings, of which great quantities are taken on the coast of Placentia. When several vessels meet and intend to fish in the same part, he whose flotilla first touches ground becomes entitled to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> and privileges of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a>: he has the choice of his station, and the refusal of all the wood on the coast at his arrival. As fast as the masters arrive, they unrig all their vessels, leaving nothing but the throats to sustain the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MASTS">masts</a>; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> time the mates provide a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TENT">tent</a> on shore, covered with branches of trees, and falls over them, with a scaffold of great trunks of pines, 12, 15, 16, and often 20 feet high, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> from 40 to 60 feet long, and about one-third as much in breadth. While the scaffold is preparing, the crew are a-fishing; and as fast as they catch, they bring their fish ashore, and open and salt them upon moveable benches; but the main salting is performed on the scaffold. When the fish have taken salt, they wash and hang them to drain on rails; when drained, they are laid on kinds of flages, which are small pieces of wood laid across, and covered with branches of trees, having the leaves stripped off for the passage of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. On these flages, they are disposed, a fish thick, head against tail, with the back uppermost, and are turned carefully four times every 24 hours. When they begin to dry, they are laid in heaps 10 or 12 thick, in order to retain their warmth; and every day the heaps are enlarged till they become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> their first bulk; then two heaps are joined together, which they turn every day as before: lastly, they are salted again, beginning with those first salted; and being laid in huge piles, they remain in that situation till they are carried on board the ships, where they are laid on the branches of trees disposed for that purpose, upon the ballast, and round the ship, with mats to prevent their contracting any moisture. There are four sorts of commodities drawn from cod, viz. the founds, the tongues, the roes, and the oil extracted from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. The first is salted at the fishery together with the fish, and put in barrels from 600 to 700 pounds. The tongues are done in like manner, and brought in barrels from 400 to 500 pounds. The roes are also salted in barrels, and serve to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> into the sea to draw fish together, and particularly pilchards. The oil comes in barrels, from 400 to 520 pounds, and is used in dressing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. In Scotland, they catch a small kind of cod on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUCHAN">Buchan</a>, and all along the Murray frith on both sides; as also in the friths of Forth, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLYDE">Clyde</a>, &c. which is much esteemed. They salt and dry them in the sun upon rocks, and sometimes in the chimney. 3. Coral Fishery. See Coral. 4. Herring 4. Herring Fishery. Our great stations for this fishery are off the Shetland and Western Isles, and off the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a>, in which the Dutch also share. There are two seasons for fishing herring; the first from June to the end of August; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> in autumn, when the fogs become very favourable for this kind of fishing. The Dutch begin their herring fishing on the 24th of June, and employ a vast number of vessels therein, called buffles, being between 45 and 60 tons burden each, and carrying three or four small cannon. They never sail out of port, without a convoy, unless there be enough together to make about 18 or 20 cannon among them, in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> they are allowed to go in company. Before they go out they make a verbal agreement, which has the same force as if it were in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>. The regulations of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a> of Holland are partly followed by the French and other nations, and partly improved and augmented with new ones; as, that no fisher shall cast his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a> within 100 fathoms of another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>; that while the nets are cast, a light shall be kept on the hind part of the vessel; that when a boat is by any accident obliged to leave off fishing, the light shall be cast into the sea; that when the greater part of a fleet leaves off fishing, and casts <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>, the rest shall do the same, &c. Mr Anderson gives to the Scots a knowledge of great antiquity in the herring fishery. He says that the Netherlanders resorted to these coasts as early as A.D. 836, to purchase salted fish of the natives, but, imposing on the strangers, they learned the art, and took up the trade, in after-times of such immense emolument to the Dutch. Sir Walter Raleigh's observations on that head, extracted from the same author, are extremely worthy the attention of the curious, and excite reflections on the vast strength resulting from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a> of well-applied industry. In 1603, he remarks, the Dutch sold to different nations as many herrings as amounted to £1,759,000 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STERLING">sterling</a>. In the year 1615, they at once sent out 2000 buffles, and employed in them 37,000 fishermen. In the year 1618, they sent out 3000 ships, with 50,000 men to take the herrings, and 9000 more ships to transport and sell the fish; which by sea and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> employed 150,000 men, besides those first mentioned. All this wealth was gotten on our coasts, while our attention was taken up in a distant whale fishery. The Scottish monarchs for a long time seemed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> all their attention to the preservation of the salmon fishery, probably because their subjects were such novices in sea affairs. At length James III. endeavoured to stimulate his great men to these patriotic undertakings; for by an act of his third parliament, he compelled "certain lords spiritual and temporal, and burrows, to make ships, buffles, and boats, with nets and other pertinents, for fishing." That the same should be made in each burgh; in number according to the substance of each burgh, and the least of them to be of twenty tons: and that all idle men be compelled by the sheriffs in the country to go on board the same." Numerous indeed have been the attempts made at different periods to secure this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TREASURE">treasure</a> to ourselves, but without success. In the late reign, a very strong effort was made, and bounties allowed for the encouragement of British adventurers: the first was of 30s. per ton to every baffle of 70 tons and upwards. This bounty was afterwards raised to 50s. per ton, to be paid to such adventurers as were entitled to it by claiming it at the places of rendezvous. The buffles are from 20 to 90 tons burden, but the best size is 80. A vessel of 80 tons ought to take ten lasts, or 120 barrels of herrings, to clear expenses, the price of the fish to be admitted to be a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUINEA">guinea</a> a barrel. A ship of this size ought to have 18 men, and three boats: one of 20 tons should have six men; and every five tons above require an additional <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>. To every ton are 280 yards of nets; so a vessel of 80 tons carries 20,000 square yards: each net is 12 yards long, and 10 deep, and every boat takes out from 20 to 30 nets, and puts them together, so as to form a long train; they are sunk at each end of the train by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, which weighs it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a>: the top is supported by buoys, made of sheepskin, with a hollow stick at the mouth fastened tight: through this the skin is blown up, and then stopped with a peg, to prevent the escape of the air. Sometimes these buoys are placed at the top of the nets: at other times the nets are suffered to sink deeper, by the lengthening the cords fastened to them, every <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> being for that purpose 10 or 12 fathoms long. But the best fisheries are generally in more shallow water. Of the Scots fishery in the Western Isles, the following account is given by Mr Pennant. "The fishing is always performed in the night, unless by accident. The buffles remain at anchor, and send out their boats a little before sunset; which continue out, in winter and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, till day light; often taking up and emptying their nets, which they do 10 or 12 times in a night, in case of good success. During winter it is a most dangerous and fatiguing employ, by reason of the greatness and frequency of the gales in these seas, and in such gales are the most successful captures: but by the Providence of heaven, the fishers are seldom lost; and, what is wonderful, few are visited with illness. They go out well prepared, with a warm great coat, boots, and skin aprons, and a good provision of beef and spirits. The same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOOD_FORTUNE">good fortune</a> attends the buffles, which in the tempestuous season, and in the darkest nights, are continually shifting, in these narrow seas, from harbour to harbour. Sometimes 80 barrels of herrings are taken in a night by the boats of a single vessel. It once happened, in Loch Slappan, in Sky, that a baffle of 80 tons might have taken 200 barrels in one night, with 10,000 square yards of net; but the matter was obliged to desist, for want of a sufficient number of hands to preserve the capture. The herrings are preserved by salting; after the entrails are taken out. This last is an operation performed by the country people, who get three halfpence per barrel for their trouble; and sometimes, even in the winter, can <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> fifteen pence a-day. This employs both women and children; but the salting is only intrusted to the crew of the buffles. The fish are laid on their backs in the barrels, and layers of salt between them. The entrails are not lost, for they are boiled into an oil: 8000 fish will yield ten gallons, valued at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> the gallon. A vessel of 80 tons takes out 144 barrels of salt; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWBACK">drawback</a> of 2s. 8d. is allowed for each barrel used by the foreign or Irish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPORTATION">exportation</a> of the fish; but there is a duty of 1s. per barrel for the home consumption, and the same..." for those sent to Ireland. The barrels are made of oak slaves chiefly from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGINIA">Virginia</a>; the hoops from several parts of our own <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a>, and are either of oak, birch, hazel or willow; the last from Holland, liable to a du- ty. The barrels cost about 3s. each, they hold from 500 to 800 fish, according to the size of the fish; and are made to contain 32 gallons. The barrels are in- spected by proper officers; a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COOPER">cooper</a> examines if they are statutable and good; if faulty, he destroys them, and obliges the maker to stand to the loss. "Loch Broom has been celebrated for three or four centuries as the resort of herrings. They generally appear here in July; those that turn into this bay are part of the brigade that detaches itself from the west- ern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> of that great <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> which annually defers the vast depths of the arctic circle, and comes, heaven- directed, to the seats of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POPULATION">population</a>, offered as a cheap food to millions, whom wasteful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>-hearted avarice hath deprived, by enhancing the price, of the wonted supports of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIGRATION">migration</a> of these fish from their northern retreat is regular; their visits to the Western isles and coasts certain; but their at- tachment to one particular loch extremely precarious. All have their turns: that which swarmed with fish one year, is totally deserted the following; yet the next loch to it may be crowded with the shoals. These changes of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> give often full employ to the buffes, who are continually shifting their harbour in quest of news respecting these important wanderers. They commonly appear here in July; the latter end of August they go into deep water, and continue there for some time, without any apparent cause: in November, they return to the shallows, when a new fishery commences, which continues till <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a>: at that time the herrings become full of roe, and are use- ful as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> of commerce. Some doubt, whether these herrings that appear in November are not part of a new migration; for they are as fat, and make the same appearance, as those that composed the first. The signs of the arrival of the herrings are flocks of gulls, who catch up the fish while they skim on the surface, and of gannets, who plunge and bring them up from considerable depths. Both these birds are closely attended to by the fishers. Cod fish, haddock, and dog fish, follow the herrings in vast multitudes: these voracious fish keep on the outsides of the col- umns, and may be a concurrent reason of driving the shoals into bays and creeks. In summer, they come into the bays generally with the warmest <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, and with easy gales. During winter, the hard gales from north-west are supposed to assist in forcing them into shelter. East winds are very unfavourable to the fishery." Herrings are cured either white or pickled, or red. Of the fish, those done by the Dutch are the most esteemed, being distinguished into four sorts, ac- cording to their sizes; and the best are those that are fat, flethy, firm, and white, salted the same day they are taken, with good salt, and well barrelled. The British cured herrings are little inferior, if not equal, to the Dutch: for in spite of all their endeavours to conceal the secret, their method of curing, lasting, or calking the herrings, has been discovered, and is as follows.
