After they have hauled in their nets, which they drag in the stern of their vessels backwards forwards in traversing the coast, they throw them upon the ship's deck, which is cleared of every thing for that purpose: the crew is separated into sundry divi- sions, and each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVISION">division</a> has a peculiar task; one part opens and guts the herrings, leaving the milt and roes; another cures and salts them, by lining or rub- bing their inside with salt; the next packs them, and between each row and division they sprinkle handfuls of salt; lastly, the cooper puts the finishing hand to all, by heading the casks very tight, and flowing them in the hold. Red herrings must lie 24 hours in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRINE">brine</a>, in- asmuch as they are to take all their salt there; and when they are taken out, they are spitted, that is, strung by the head on little wooden spits, and then hung in a chimney made for that purpose. After which, a fire of brushwood, which yields a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of smoke, but no <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>, being made under them, they remain there till sufficiently smoked and dried, and are afterwards barrelled up for keeping. 5. Lobster Fishery. Lobsters are taken along the British channel, and on the coast of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORWAY">Norway</a>, whence they are brought to London for sale; and also in the firth of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>, and on the coast of Northumber- land. By 10 and 11 W. III. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>. 24, no lobster is to be taken under eight inches in length, from the peak of the nose to the end of the middle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIN">fin</a> of the tail; and by 9 G. II. cap. 33, no lobsters are to be taken on the coast of Scotland from the 1st of June to the 1st of September. 6. Mackerel Fishery. The mackerel is a summer fish of passage, found in large shoals, in divers parts of the ocean, not far north; but especially on the French and English coasts. The fishing is usually in the months of April, May, and June, and even July, ac- cording to the place. They enter the English chan- nel in April, and proceed up to the straits of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> as the summer advances; so that by June they are on the coasts of Cornwall, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, Normandy, Picardy, &c. where the fishery is most considerable. They are an excellent food fresh; and not to be despised, when well prepared, pickled, and put up in barrels; a me- thod of preserving them chiefly used in Cornwall. The fish is taken two ways; either with a line or nets: the latter is the more considerable, and is usually performed in the night-time. The rules observed in the fishing for mackerel are much the same as those already mentioned in the fishery of herrings. There are two ways of pickling them: the first is, by opening and gutting them, and filling the belly with salt, crammed in as hard as possible with a stick; which done, they range them in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> or rows, at the bottom of the vessel, interweaving salt between the layers. In the second way, they put them immediately into tubs full of brine, made of fresh water and salt; and leave them to steep, till they have imbibed salt enough to make them keep; after which, they are taken out, and barrelled up, taking care to press them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> down. Mackerel are not cured or exported as merchandise, except a few by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> and Leoftoff merchants, but are generally consumed at home; especially in the city of London, and the sea-ports between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> and Yarmouth, east, and the Land's End of Cornwall, west. 7. Oyster Fishery. This fishery is principally carried on at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLCHESTER">Colchester</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ESSEX">Essex</a>; Feverham and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILTON">Milton</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>; the Isle of Wight; the Swales of the Medway; and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TENBY">Tenby</a> on the coast of Wales. From Feverham, and adjacent parts, the Dutch have sometimes loaded a hundred large hoyes with oysters in a year. They are also taken in great quantities near <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORTSMOUTH">Portsmouth</a>, and in all the creeks and rivers between Southampton and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHICHESTER">Chichester</a>: many of which are carried about by sea to London and to Colchester, to be fed in the pits about Wavenhoe and other places. 8. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEARL">Pearl</a> Fishery. See Pearl, <a class="xref" href="../1815/vol6.html#article-CONCHOLOGY">Conchology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>, and Ceylon. 9. Pilchard Fishery. The chief pilchard fisheries are along the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DALMATIA">Dalmatia</a>, on the coast of Bretagne, and along the coasts of Cornwall and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>. That of Dalmatia is very plentiful: that on the coasts of Bretagne employs annually about 300 ships. Of the pilchard fishery on the coast of Cornwall the following account is given by Dr Borlase: "It employs a great number of men on the sea, training them thereby to naval affairs; employs men, women, and children, on land, in salting, pressing, washing and cleaning; in making boats, nets, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, casks, and all the trades depending on their <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> and sale. The poor are fed with the offals of the captures, the land with the refuse of the fish and salt; the merchant finds the gains of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSION">commission</a> and honest commerce, the fisherman the gains of the fish. Ships are often freighted hither with salt, and into foreign countries with the fish, carrying off at the same time part of our tin. Of the usual produce of the great number of hogheads exported each year for ten years from 1747 to 1756 inclusive, from the four ports of Fowey, <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FALMOUTH">Falmouth</a>, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PENZANCE">Penzance</a>, and St Ives, it appears that Fowey has exported yearly 1732 hogheads; Falmouth, 14,631 hogheads and two thirds; Penzance and Mounts-Bay 12,149 hogheads and one third; St Ives, 1280 hogheads: in all amounting to 29,795 hogheads. Every hoghead for ten years last past, together with the bounty allowed for each hoghead exported, and the oil made out of each hoghead, has amounted, one year with another at an <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-AVERAGE">average</a>, to the price of 1l. 13s. 3d.; so that the cash paid for pilchards exported has, at a medium, annually amounted to the sum of 49,532l. 10s."—The numbers that are taken at one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOOTING">shooting</a> out of the nets are amazingly great. Mr Pennant says, that Dr Borlase assured him, that on the 5th of October 1767, there were at one time enclosed in St Ives's Bay 7000 hogheads, each hoghead containing 35,000 fish, in all 245 millions. The pilchards naturally follow the light, which contributes much to the facility of the fishery; the season is from June to September. On the coasts of France they make use of the roes of the cod fish as a bait; which, thrown into the sea, makes them rise from the bottom, and run into the nets. On our coasts there are persons posted ashore, who, spying by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the water where the shoals are, make signs to the boats to go among them to cast their nets. When taken, they are brought on shore to a warehouse, where they are laid up in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> piles, supported with backs and sides; and as they are piled, they salt them with bay salt; in which lying to soak for 30 or 40 days, they run out a deal of blood, with dirty pickle and bitters; then they wash them clean in sea water; and, when dry, barrel and press them hard down to squeeze out the oil, which issues out at a hole in the bottom of the casks. 10. Salmon Fishery. The chief salmon fisheries in Europe are in England, Scotland, and Ireland, in the rivers, and sea coasts adjoining to the river mouths. The most distinguished for salmon in Scotland are, the river Tweed, the Clyde, the Tay, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEE">Dee</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DON">Don</a>, the Spey, the Ness, the Bewly, &c. in most of which it is very common, about the height of summer, especially if the weather happens to be very hot, to catch four or five score salmon at a draught. The chief rivers in England for salmon are, the Tyne, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRENT">Trent</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a>, and the Thames. The fishing is performed with nets, and sometimes with a kind of locks or weirs made on purpose, which in certain places have iron or wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATES">grates</a> disposed, in an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>, that being impelled by any force in a contrary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> to the course of the river, they may give way and open a little at the point of contact, and immediately shut again, closing the angle. The salmon, therefore, coming up into the rivers, are admitted into these grates, which open, and suffer them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through, but shut again, and prevent their return. The salmon is also caught with a spear, which they dart into him when they see him <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> near the surface of the water. It is customary likewise to catch them with a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> and lanthorn, or wisp of straw set on fire; for the fish naturally following the light, are struck with the spear, or taken in a net spread for that purpose, and lifted with a sudden jerk from the bottom. "The capture of salmon in the Tweed, about the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of July (says Mr Pennant) is prodigious. In a good fishery, often a boat load, and sometimes near two, are taken in a tide: some few years ago there were above 700 fish taken at one haul, but from 50 to 100 is very frequent. The cooperers in Berwick then begin to talt both salmon and grilles in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> and other large vessels, and afterwards barrel them to send abroad, having then far more than the London markets can take off their hands. "Most of the salmon taken before April, or to the setting in of the warm weather, is sent fresh to London in balkets: unless now and then the vessel is disappointed by contrary winds of failing immediately; in which case the fish is brought ashore again to the cooper's offices, and boiled, pickled, and kitted, and sent to the London markets by the same ship, and fresh salmon put in the balkets in lieu of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> ones. At the beginning of the season, when a ship is on the point of failing, a fresh clean salmon will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from a shilling to eighteen pence a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; and most of the time that this part of the trade is carried on, the prices are from five to <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> shillings per stone; the value rising and falling according to the plenty of fish, or the prospect of a fair or foul <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. Some fish are sent in this manner to London the latter end of September, when the weather grows cool; but then the fish are full of large roes, grow very thin bellied, and are not esteemed either palatable or wholesome. "The season for fishing in the Tweed begins November 3rd, but the fishermen <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> very little till after Christmas: it ends on Michaelmas day; yet the corporation of Berwick (who are conservators of the river) There are on the river 41 considerable fisheries, extending upwards about 14 miles from the mouth, (the others above being of no great value), which are rented for near £500l. per annum; the expense attending the servants <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WAGES">wages</a>, nets, boats, &c. amount to £500l. more; which together makes up the sum £10,500l. Now, in consequence, the produce must defray all, and no less than 20 times that sum of fish will effect it; so that 208,000 salmon must be caught there one year with another. Scotland possesses great numbers of fine fisheries on both sides of that kingdom. The Scotch in early times had most severe laws against the killing of this fish; for the third offence was made capital, by a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> of James IV. Before that, the offender had power to redeem his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. They were thought in the time of Henry VI. a present worthy of a crowned head; for in that reign the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of Scotland sent to the duchess of Clarence 10 casks of salted salmon; which Henry directed to pass duty free. The salmon are cured in the same manner as at Berwick, and a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> is sent to London in the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>; but after that time, the adventurers begin to barrel and export them to foreign countries; but we believe that commerce is far less lucrative than it was in former times, partly owing to the great increase of the Newfoundland fishery, and partly to the general relaxation of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISCIPLINE">discipline</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSTINENCE">abstinence</a> in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>. Ireland (particularly the north) abounds with this fish; the most considerable fishery is at Cranna, on the river Ban, about a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILE">mile</a> and a half from Coleraine. When I made the tour of that hospitable kingdom in 1754, it was rented by a neighbouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> for £60l. a-year; who assured me, that the tenant, his predecessor, gave £600l. per annum, and was a much greater gainer by the bargain, for the reasons before mentioned, and on account of the number of the poachers who destroy the fish in the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">fence</a> months. The mouth of this river faces the north; and is finely situated to receive the fish that roam along the coast in search of an inlet into some fresh water, as they do all along that end of the kingdom which opposes itself to the northern ocean. We have seen near Ballincastle, nets placed in the sea at the foot of the promontories that jut into it, which the salmon strike into as they are wandering close to shore; and numbers are taken by that method. In the Ban they fish with nets 18 score yards long, and are continually <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> night and day the whole season, which we think lasts about four months, two sets of 16 men each alternately relieving one another. The best drawing is when the tide is coming in: we were told, that at a single draught there were once 840 fish taken. A few miles higher up the river is a wear where a considerable number of fish that escape the nets are taken. We were lately informed, that, in the year 1760, about 320 tons were taken in the Cranna fishery. Curing Salmon. When the salmon are taken, they open them along the back, take out the guts and gills, and cut out the greatest part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, endeavouring to make the inside as smooth as possible: they then salt the fish in large tubs for the purpose, where they lie a considerable time soaking in brine; and about October, they are packed close up in barrels, and sent to London, or exported up the Mediterranean. They have also in Scotland a great deal of salmon salted in the common way, which after soaking in brine a competent time, is well pressed, and then dried in smoke: this is called kipper, and is chiefly made for home consumption; and if properly cured and prepared, is reckoned very delicious. Sturgeon Fishery. The greatest sturgeon fishery is in the mouth of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOLGA">Volga</a>, on the Caspian sea; where the Muscovites employ a great number of hands, and catch them in a kind of enclosure, formed by huge stakes representing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> Z repeated several times. These fisheries are open on the side next the sea, and close on the other; by which means the fish ascending in its course up the river, is embarrassed in these narrow angular retreats, and is easily killed with a harping iron. Sturgeons, when fresh, eat deliciously; and in order to make them keep, they are salted or pickled in large pieces, and put up in casks from 30 to 50 pounds. But the great object of this fishery is the roe, of which the Muscovites are extremely fond, and of which is made the caviar, or kavia, so much esteemed by the Italians. Tunny Fishery. The tunny (a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of Scomber), was a fish well known to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, and made a great article of commerce: And there are still very considerable tunny fisheries on the coasts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SICILY">Sicily</a>, as well as several other parts of the Mediterranean. The nets are spread over a large space of sea by means of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CABLES">cables</a> fastened to anchors, and are divided into several compartments. The entrance is always directed, according to the season, towards that part of the sea from which the fish are known to come. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> placed upon the summit of a rock high above the water, gives a signal of the fish being arrived; for he can discern from that elevation what passes under the waters infinitely better than any person nearer the surface. As soon as notice is given that the shoal of fish has penetrated as far as the inner compartment, or the chamber of death, the netting is drawn close, and the slaughter begins. The undertakers of these fisheries pay an acknowledgment to the king, or the lord upon whose land they fix the main stay or foot of the tonnare; they make the best bargain they can: and, till success has crowned their endeavours, obtain this leave for a small consideration; but the rent is afterwards raised in proportion to their capture. The tunny enters the Mediterranean about the vernal equinox, travelling in a triangular phalanx, so as to cut the waters with its point, and to present an extensive base for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TIDES">tides</a> and currents to act against, and impel forwards. These fish repair to the warm seas of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREECE">Greece</a> to spawn, steering their course thither along the European shores, but as they return, approach the African coast; the young fry is placed in the van of the squadron as they travel. They come back from the east in May, and abound on the coast of Sicily and <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CALABRIA">Calabria</a> about that time. In autumn they steer northward, and frequent the neighbourhood of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMALFI">Amalfi</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAPLES">Naples</a>; but during the whole season stragglers are occasionally caught. When taken in May, the usual time of their appearance in the Calabrian bays, they are full of spawn, and their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> is then esteemed unwholesome, apt to occasion headaches and vapours; the milts and roes are particularly so at that season. To prevent these bad effects, the natives fry them in oil, and afterwards salt them. The quantity of this fish consumed annually in the Two Sicilies almost exceeds the bounds of calculation. From the beginning of May to the end of October it is eaten fresh, and all the rest of the year it is in use salted. The most delicate part is the muzzle. The belly salted was called tarantallum, and accounted a great delicacy by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>; its present name is Surra. The rest of the body is cut into slices, and put into tubs. Turbot Fishery. Turbots grow to a large size, some of them weighing from 23 to 30 pounds. They are taken chiefly off the north coast of England, and others off the Dutch coast. The large turbot (as well as several other kinds of flat fish) are taken by the hook and line, for they lie in deep water; the method of taking them in weirs or flaked nets being very precarious. When the fishermen go out to fish, each person is provided with three <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>, which are coiled on a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> piece of wicker work; the hooks being baited, and placed regularly in the centre of the coil. Each line is furnished with 14 score of hooks, at the distance of six feet two inches from each other. The hooks are fastened to the lines upon heads of twisted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> 27 inches in length. When fishing, there are always three men in each coble, and consequently nine of these lines are fastened together, and used in one line, extending in length near three miles, and furnished with 2520 hooks. An anchor and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUOY">buoy</a> are fixed at the first end of the line, and one more of each at the end of each man's lines; in all four anchors, which are common perforated <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, and four buoys made of leather or cork. The line is always laid across the current. The tides of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> and ebb continue an equal time upon our coast, and, when undisturbed by winds, run each way about six hours; they are so rapid that the fishermen can only throw and haul their lines at the turn of tide, and therefore the lines always remain upon the ground about six hours; during which time the myxine glutinosa of Linnaeus will frequently penetrate the fish that are on the hooks, and entirely devour them, leaving only the skin and bones. The same rapidity of tides prevents their using hand lines; and therefore two of the people commonly wrap themselves in the sail, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SLEEP">sleep</a> while the other keeps a strict look-out, for fear of being run down by ships, and to observe the weather. For storms often rise so suddenly, that it is with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> difficulty they can sometimes escape to the shore, leaving their lines behind. Besides the coble, the fishermen have also a five men boat, which is 40 feet long and 15 broad, and 25 tons burden; it is so called, though navigated by five men and a boy, because one of the men is commonly hired to cook, &c., and does not share in the profits with the other five. This boat is decked at each end, but open in the middle, and has two large lug sails. All our able fishermen go in these boats to the herring fishery at Yarmouth in the latter end of September, and return about the middle of November. The boats are then laid up till the beginning of Lent, at which time they go off in them to the edge of the Dogger, and other places, to fish for turbot, cod, ling, skates, &c. They always take two cobs on board; and when they come upon their ground, anchor the boat, throw out the cobs, and fish in the same manner as those who go from the shore in a coble; with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> only, that here each man is provided with double the quantity of lines, and instead of waiting the return of the tide in the coble, return to their boat and bait their other lines; thus hauling one net and shooting another every turn of tide. They commonly run into harbour twice a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> to deliver their fish. The best bait is fresh herring cut in pieces of a proper size; the five men boats are always furnished with nets for taking them. Next to herrings are the lesser lampreys. The next baits in esteem are small haddock cut in pieces, sand <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and limpets, here called fiddlers; and when none of these can be had, they use bullock's liver. The hooks are two inches and a half long in the shank, and near an inch wide between the shank and the point. The line is made of small cording, and is always tanned before it is used. Turbots are extremely delicate in their choice of baits; for if a piece of herring or haddock has been 12 hours out of the sea, and then used as bait, they will not touch it. Whale Fishery. See Balæna, Cetology Index. Whales are chiefly caught in the north seas; the largest sort are found about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREENLAND">Greenland</a> or Spitzbergen. At the first discovery of this country, whales not being used to be disturbed, frequently came into the very bays, and were accordingly killed almost close to the shore; so that the blubber being cut off was immediately boiled into oil on the spot. The ships in those times took in nothing but the pure oil and the whalebone, and all the butinels was executed in the country; by which means a ship could bring home the product of many more whales than she can, according to the present method of conducting this trade. The fishery also was then so plentiful, that they were obliged sometimes to send other ships to fetch off the oil they had made, the quantity being more than the fishing ships could bring away. But time and change of circumstances have shifted the situation of this trade. The ships coming in such numbers from Holland, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DENMARK">Denmark</a>, Hamburgh, and other northern countries, all intruders upon the English, who were the first discoverers of Greenland, the whales were disturbed, and gradually, as other fish often do, forsaking the place, were not to be killed so near the shore as before; but are now found, and have been so ever since, in the openings and spaces among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ICE">ice</a>, where they have deep water, and where they go sometimes a great many leagues from the shore. The whale fishery begins in May, and continues all June and July; but whether the ships have good or bad success, they must come away, and get clear of the ice, by the end of August; so that in the month of September at farthest they may be expected home; but a ship that meets with a fortunate and early fishery in May may return in June or July. But, for the manner of taking whales, and for a farther account of the whale fishery, as a trade, see Cetology.

FISHGARD

Pages 278-278
or FISGARD, a town of Pembroke-shire, situated on a steep cliff on the sea-shore, 254 miles from

FISHING

Pages 278-281

in general, the art of catching fish, whether by means of nets, of spears, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> of the line and hook. FISHING in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a>, performed by the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, spear, or harpoon, for fish that go in shoals, has been explained in the preceding article. That performed by the rod, line, and hook, for solitary fish, is usually termed <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANGLING">ANGLING</a>: See that article; and for the particular manner of angling for the different kinds of fish, see their respective names, as DACE, EEL, PERCH, under <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">ICHTHYOLOGY</a>. Here we shall give an account of the following: 1. The Barbel, so called on account of the barb or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARD">beard</a> that is under his chops), though a coarse fish, gives considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a> to the angler's ingenuity. They swim together in great shoals, and are at their worst in April, at which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> they spawn, but come soon in season; the places whither they chiefly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESORT">resort</a>, are such as are weedy and gravelly rising grounds, in which this fish is said to dig and root with his nose like a swine. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> he frequents the strongest, swiftest, currents of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; as deep bridges, weirs, &c., and is apt to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SETTLE">settle</a> himself among the piles, hollow places, and mows, or weeds; and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> remain there immoveable; but in the winter he retires into deep waters, and helps the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> to make a hole in the sands to hide her spawn in, to hinder its being devoured by other fish. He is a very curious and cunning fish; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> his baits be not sweet, clean, well scoured, and kept in sweet mows, he will not bite; but well ordered and curiously kept, he will bite with great eagerness. The best bait for him is the spawn of a salmon, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TROUT">trout</a>, or any other fish; and if you would have good sport with him, bait the places where you intend to fish with it a night or two before, or with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a> cut in pieces; and the earlier in the morning or the later in the evening that you fish, the better it will be. Your rod and line must be both strong and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, with a running plummet on the line; and let a little bit of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> be placed a foot or more above the hook, to keep the bullet from falling on it; so the worm will be at the bottom, where they always bite; and when the fish takes the bait, your plummet will rise and not choke him. By the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDING">bending</a> of your rod you may know when he bites, as also with your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> you will feel him make a strong snatch; then strike, and you will rarely fail, if you play him well; but if you manage him not dexterously, he will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> your line. The best time for fishing is about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in the morning, and the most proper season is the latter end of May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, and the beginning of August. 2. The Bleak, is an eager fish, caught with all sorts of worms bred on trees or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; as also with flies, paste, sheep's blood, &c. They may be angled for with half a score of hooks at once, if they can be all fastened on; he will also in the evening take a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fly. If the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> be warm and clear, there is no fly so good for him as the small fly at the top of the water, which he will take at any time of the day, especially in the evening; but if the day is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> and cloudy, gentles and caddis are the best; about two feet under water. No fish yields better sport to a young angler than the bleak. It is so eager, that it will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> out of the water for a bait. There is another way of taking bleak, which is by whipping them in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a>, or on a <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BANK">bank</a> side in fresh water in a summer's evening, with a hazel top about five or six feet long and a line twice the length of the rod. But the best method is with a drabble, thus: Tie eight or ten small hooks across a line two inches above one another; the biggest hook the lowermost, (whereby you may sometimes take a better fish), and bait them with gentles, flies, or some small <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> worms, by which means you may take half a dozen or more at a time. 3. For the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-BREAM">Bream</a>, observe the following directions, which will also be of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in carp fishing.—Procure about prins, i.e., a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUART">quart</a> of large red worms; put them into fresh mows, well washed and dried every three or four days, feeding them with fat mould and chopped fennel, and they will be thoroughly scoured in about three weeks. Let your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a>, but all silk is the best; let the floats be either swan-quills or goose-quills. Let your plumb be a piece of lead in the shape of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEAR">pear</a>, with a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> at the little end of it; fasten the lead to the line, and the line hook to the lead, about ten or twelve inches space between lead and hook will be enough; and take care the lead be heavy enough to sink the float. Having baited your hook well with a strong worm, the worm will draw the hook up and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> in the bottom, which will provoke the bream to bite the more eagerly. It will be best to fit up three or four rods and lines in this manner, and let them as will be directed, and this will afford you much the better sport. Find the exact depth of the water if possible, that your float may swim on its surface directly over the lead; then provide the following ground bait. Take about a peck of sweet grofs-ground malt; and having boiled it a very little, strain it hard through a bag, and carry it to the water side where you have founded; and in the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where you suppose the fish frequent, there throw in the malt by handfuls squeezed hard together, that the stream may not separate it before it comes to the bottom; and be sure to throw it in at least a yard above the place where you intend the hook shall <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a>, otherwise the stream will carry it down too far. Do this about nine o'clock at night, keeping some of the malt in the bag, and go to the place about three the next morning; but approach very warily, lest you should be seen by the fish; for it is certain that they have their sentinels watching on the top of the water, while the rest are feeding below. Having baited your hook so that the worm may crawl to and fro, the better to allure the fish to bite, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> it in at the place where you find the fish to stay most, which is generally in the broadest and deepest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the river, and so that it may rest about the midst of your bait that is on the ground. Cast in your <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> line so that it may rest a yard above that, and a third about a yard below it. Let your rods lie on the bank with some <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> to keep them down at the great ends; and then withdraw yourself, yet not so far but that you can have your eye upon Fishing. upon all the floats; and when you see one bitten and carried away, do not be too hasty to run in, but give time to the fish to tire himself, and then touch him gently. When you perceive the float link, creep to the water side, and give it as much line as you can. If it is a bream or carp, they will run to the other side; which strike gently, and hold your rod at a bent a little while; but do not pull, for then you will spoil all; but you must first tire them before they can be landed, for they are very fly. If there are any carps in the river, it is an even wager that you take one or more of them; but if there are any pike or perch, they will be sure to visit the ground bait, though they will not touch it, being drawn thither by the great resort of the small fish; and until you remove them, it is in vain to think of taking the bream or carp. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, bait one of your hooks with a small bleak, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ROACH">roach</a>, or gudgeon, about two feet deep from your float, with a little red worm at the point of your hook; and if a pike be there, he will be sure to snap at it. This sport is good till nine o'clock in the morning; and, in a gloomy day, till night; but do not frequent the place too much, lest the fish grow fly. 4. The carp +. A person who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> for carp must arm himself with abundance of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATIENCE">patience</a>, because of its extraordinary subtlety and policy; they always choose to lie in the deepest places, either of ponds or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a>, where there is but a small running stream. Further, observe, that they will seldom bite in cold <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>; and you cannot be too early or too late at the spot in hot weather; and if he bite, you need not fear his hold; for he is one of those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>-mouthed fish that have their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> in their throat. Neither must you forget, in angling for him, to have a strong rod and line; and since he is so very wary, it will be proper to entice him, by baiting the ground with a coarse paste. He seldom refuses the red worm in <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a>, the caddis in June, or the grasshopper in June, April, and September. This fish does not only delight in worms, but also in sweet paste; of which there is great variety; the best is made of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and ought to be thrown into the water some hours before you begin to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a>; neither will small pellets thrown into the water two or three days before be worse for this purpose, especially if chickens' guts, garbage, or blood mixed with bran and cow dung, be also thrown in. But more particularly, as to a paste very proper for this use, you may make it in the manner following: Take a sufficient <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of flour, and mingle it with veal, cut small, making it up with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a> of honey; then <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> all together in a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a> till they are so tough as to hang upon the hook without wailing off. In order to effect which the better, mingle whitish <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> with it; and if you keep it all the year round, add some virgin wax and clarified honey. Again, If you fish with gentles, anoint them with honey, and put them on your hook, with a deep scarlet dipped in the like, which is a good way to deceive the fish. Honey and crumbs of wheat <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a>, mixed together, make also a very good paste. In taking a carp either in pond or river, if the angler intends to add profit to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, he must take a peck of ale-grains, and a good quantity of any blood to mix with the grains, baiting the ground with it where he intends to angle. This food will wonderfully attract the feafe-fills, as carp, tench, roach, dace, and bream. Let him angle in a morning, plumbing his ground, and angling for carp with a strong line: the bait must be either paste or a knotted red worm; and by this means he will have sport enough. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">Description</a> of proper Baits for the several sorts of Fish referred to in the annexed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Flies.] 1. <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a> fly, found under hollow stones at the sides of rivers, is of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, with <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> streaks on the back and belly, has large wings, and is in season from April to July. 2. Green drake, found among stones by river sides, has a yellow body ribbed with green, is long and slender, with wings like a butterfly, its tail turns on his back, and from May to Midsummer is very good. 3. Oak-fly, found in the body of an oak or ash, with its head downwards, is of a brown colour, and excellent from May to September. 4. Palmer fly or worm, found on leaves of plants, is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called a caterpillar, and when it comes to a fly is excellent for trout. 5. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">Ant</a> fly, found in ant hills from June to September. 6. The May fly is to be found playing at the river side, especially against <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a>. 7. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> fly is to be found upon every hawthorn after the buds are come off. Paste.] 1. Take the blood of sheep's hearts, and mix it with honey and flour worked to a proper consistence. 2. Take old cheese grated, a little <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a> sufficient to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> it, and colour it with saffron: in winter use rusty <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">bacon</a> instead of butter. 3. Crumbs of bread chewed or worked with honey or sugar, moistened with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> ivy water. 4. Bread chewed, and worked in the hand till stiff. Worms.] 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> bob, found in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> ground after ploughing; it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, with a red head, and bigger than a gentle: another is found in heathy ground, with a blue head. Keep them in an earthen vessel well covered, and a sufficient quantity of the mould they harbour in. They are excellent from April to November. 2. Gentles, to be had from putrid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a>: let them lie in wheat bran a few days before used. 3. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">Flag</a> worms, found in the roots of flags; they are of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> yellow colour, are longer and thinner than a gentle, and must be covered like them. 4. Cow-turd bob, or clap bait, found under a cow turd from May to Michaelmas; it is like a gentle, but larger. Keep it in its native earth like the earth bob. 5. Caddis worm, or cod bait, found under loose stones in shallow rivers; they are yellow, bigger than a gentle, with a black or blue head, and are in season from April to July. Keep them in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> bags. 6. Lob worm, found in gardens; it is very large, and has a red head, a streak down the back, and a flat <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> tail. 7. Marth-worms, found in marshy ground; keep them in moss ten days before you use them: their colour is a bluish red, and are a good bait from March to Michaelmas. 8. Brandling red worms, or blood worms found in rotten dunghills and tanners bark; they are small red worms, very good for all small fish, have sometimes a yellow tail, and are called tag-tail. Fishing. Fish and Insects. 1. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINNOW">Minnow</a>. 2. Gudgeon. 3. Roach. 4. Dace. 5. Smelt. 6. Yellow frog. 7. Snail flit. 8. Grasshopper. Fishing Fly, a bait used in angling for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds of fish. See Fishing. The fly is either natural or artificial. I. Natural flies are innumerable. The more usual for this purpose are mentioned in the preceding page. There are two ways to fish with natural flies; either on the surface of the water, or a little underneath it. In angling for chub, roach, or dace, move not your natural fly swiftly when you see the fish make at it; but rather let it glide freely towards him with the stream; but if it be in a still and slow water, draw the fly slowly sidewise by him, which will make him eagerly pursue. II. The artificial fly is seldom used but in blustering weather, when the waters are so troubled by the winds, that the natural fly cannot be seen, nor rest upon them. Of this artificial fly there are reckoned no less than 12 sorts, of which the following are the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a>. 1. For March, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUN">dun</a> fly; made of dun wool, and the feathers of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a>'s wing; or the body made of black wool, and the feathers of a black drake. 2. For April, the stone fly; the body made of black wool, dyed yellow under the wings and tail. 3. For the beginning of May, the ruddy fly; made of red wool, and bound about with black silk, with the feathers of a black <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPON">capon</a> hanging dangling on his sides next his tail. 4. For June, the greenish fly; the body made of black wool, with a yellow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIST">list</a> on either side, the wings taken off the wings of a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUZZARD">buzzard</a>, bound with black broken <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a>. 5. The moorish fly, the body made of darkish wool, and the wings of the blackfish mail of a drake. 6. The tawny fly, good till the middle of June; the body made of tawny wool, the wings made contrary one against the other of the whitish mail of a white drake. 7. For July, the wasp fly; the body made of black wool, cast about with yellow silk, and the wings of drakes feathers. 8. The <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEEL">steel</a> fly; good in the middle of July; the body made with greenish wool, cast about with the feathers of a <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-PEACOCK">peacock</a>'s tail, and the wings made of those of the buzzard. 9. For August, the drake fly; the body made with black wool cast about with black silk; his wings of the mail of a black drake, with a black head. The best rules for artificial fly fishing are, 1. To fish in a river somewhat disturbed with rain; or in a cloudy day, when the waters are moved by a gentle breeze; the fourth <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> is best; and if the wind blow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, yet not so but that you may conveniently <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> your tackle, the fish will rise in plain deeps; but if the wind be small, the best angling is in swift streams. 2. Keep as far from the water side as may be; fish down the stream with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> at your back, and touch not the water with your line. 3. Ever angle in clear rivers, with a small fly and slender wings; but in muddy places, use a larger. 4. When, after rain, the water becomes brownish, use an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> fly; in a clear day, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>-colored fly; a dark fly for dark waters, &c. 5. Let the line be twice as long as the rod, unless the river be encumbered with wood. 6. For every sort of fly, have several of the same differing in colour, to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> with the different complexions of several waters and weathers. 7. Have a nimble eye, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> hand, to strike presently with the rising of the fish; or else he will be apt to spue out the hook. 8. Let the fly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> first into the water, and not the line, which will scare the fish. 9. In slow rivers, or still places, cast the fly across the river, and let it sink a little in the water, and draw it gently back with the current. Salmon flies should be made with their wings standing one behind the other, whether two or four. This fish delights in the gaudiest colours that can be; chiefly in the wings, which must be long, as well as the tail.

FISHING BY

Pages 281-283

g by means of birds, a method peculiar to the Chinese, who train certain birds for the purpose in the same manner as falcons are taught to pursue <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAME">game</a>. For this purpose they have trained a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of pelican, resembling the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> corvornant, which they call the Lew-tze, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>. Sir George Staunton, who, when the embassy was proceeding on the southern branch of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> canal, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> those birds employed, tells us, that on a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> lake, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> to the east side of the canal, are thousands of small boats and rafts, built entirely for this species of fishery. On each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or raft are ten or a dozen birds, which, at a signal from the owner, plunge into the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and it is astonishing to see the enormous size of fish with which they return, grasped within their bills. They appeared to be so well trained, that it did not require either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CORD">cord</a> about their throats to prevent them from swallowing any portion of their prey, except what their <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> was pleased to return to them for encouragement and food. The boat used by these fishermen is of a remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> make, and is often carried to the lake, together with the fishing birds, by the men who are there to be supported by it. The same author saw the fishermen busy on the great lake Wee-chaung-hee; and he gives the following account of a very singular method practised by them for catching the fish of the lake without the aid of birds, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NET">net</a>, or of hooks. To one side of a boat a flat board, painted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, is fixed, at an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLE">angle</a> of about 45 degrees, the edge inclining towards the water. On moonlight nights the boat is so placed that the painted board is turned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a>, from whence the rays of light striking on the whitened surface, give to it the appearance of moving water; on which the fish being tempted to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> as on their element, the boatmen raising with a string the board, turn the fish into the boat. Water-fowl are much sought after by the Chinese, and are taken upon the same lake by the following ingenious device. Empty jars or gourds are suffered to float about upon the water, that such objects may become familiar to the birds. The fisherman then wades into the lake with one of those empty vessels upon his head, and walks gently towards a bird; and lifting up his arm, draws it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> below the surface of the water without any disturbance or giving alarm to the rest, several of whom he treats in the same manner, until he fills the bag he had brought to hold his prey. The contrivance itself is not so singular, as it is that the same exactly should have occurred in the new continent, as An Epitome of the whole art of **Fishing**, wherein is shown (at one view), the harbours, seasons, and depths, for catching all sorts of fish usually angled for; also the various baits for each, so digested as to contain the essence of all the treatises ever written on the No° | Fish and Insects No° | | 1 | 3 | 1 to 7 | 8 | | 2 | | 2 6 7 | | | 1 2 | 2 | 2 3 8 | | | 1 3 4 | | 1 2 3 4 7 | | | 2 3 8 4 | | | | | 1 to 5 | 2 3 8 4 | | | | Ditto | Wh. fro. and snip | Ditto | | 5 6 7 | | | | | 1 5 6 7 | | | | | 1 1 | | | | | 2 3 9 | | | | | 1 3 4 | | | | | 1 2 3 4 7 | | | | | 1 2 | | | | | 1 2 | | | | **FISHERY.** *Fishing, Ulga affinis*, to the natives of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CARTHAGENA">Carthagena</a>, upon the lake Cienega de Yefos, *Fisingum Fluminis*, are little appendages to the line, smooth, serving to keep the hook and bait suspended at the proper depth, when the fish has hold of them. Of these there are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> kinds, some made of Mulcory cluck quills, which are the bait for the thank, yet somewhat thick in the circumference; flow waters; but for fishing flames, found cork, wimple, made of fluffs or holes, bored through with a hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, minus. For setting the hook on, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> strong but small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, laying the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> on the inside of your hook; for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be on the outside, the silk <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> fret and cut it asunder. There are several sizes of these fishing hooks, some big, some little; and of these, some have peculiar names; as, 1. Single hooks. 2. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">Double</a> hooks; which have two bendings, one contrary to the other. 3. Snappers, or gorgers, which are the hooks to whip the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> fly upon, or bait with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> fly. 4. Springers, or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> hooks; a kind of double hooks, with a spring, which flies open upon being struck into any fish, and so keeps its mouth open. Fishing-Line, is either made of hair twisted; or silk; or the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> grass. The best colours are the sotrel, white, and gray; the two last for clear waters, the first for muddy ones. Nor is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a> watery green desirable; this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> is given artificially, by steeping the hair in a liquor made of <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, root, and the juice of walnut leaves, boiled together. Fishing-Rod, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> slender rod or wand, to which the line is fastened, for <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANGLING">angling</a>.—Of these there are several sorts; as, 1. A troller, or trolling rod, which has a ring at the end of the rod, for the line to go through when it runs off a reel. 2. A whipper, or whipping rod; a top rod, that is weak in the middle, and top heavy, but all slender and fine. 3. A dropper; which is a strong rod and very light. 4. A snapper, or snap rod; which is a strong pole, peculiarly used for the pike. 5. A bottom rod; being the same as the dropper, but somewhat more pliable. 6. A frizzling or procking stick; a forked stick, having a short strong line, with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a>, baited with a lob worm: this is only for eels in their holes. Fishing-Frog, or Angler. See Lophius. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">Right</a> of Fishing, and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of fish. It has been held, that where the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANOR">manor</a> hath the foil on both sides of the river, it is a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVIDENCE">evidence</a> that he hath a right of fishing; and it puts the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> upon him who claims liberam piscariam: but where a river ebbs and flows, and is an arm of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, there it is common to all, and he who claims a privilege to himself must prove it; for if the trespass is brought for fishing there, the defendant may justify, that the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where is brachium maris, in quo unumquique fidelibus domini regis habet et habere debet liberam piscariam. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVERN">Severn</a> the foil belongs to the owner of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> on each side; and the foil of the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THAMES">Thames</a> is in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, but the fishing is common to all. He who is owner of the foil of a private river, hath separatis piscaria; and he that hath libera piscaria, hath a property in the fish, and may bring a possession <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> for them; but communis piscaria is like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of all other commons. One that has a clove pond in which there are fish, may call them piscis suos, in an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a>, &c. but he cannot call them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONA">bona</a> et catalla, if they be not in trunks. There needs no privilege to make a fish pond, as there doth in the case of a warren. See Franchise.

FISSURES

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOLOGY">Geology</a>, certain interruptions, that in a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> manner divide the several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STRATA">strata</a> of which the body of our globe is composed. See Geology <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fissure of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">Bones</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, is when they are divided either transversely or longitudinally, not quite through, but cracked after the manner of glas, by any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> force. See Surgery.

FISTULA

Pages 283-283

in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> music, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind, resembling our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">flute</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flageolet. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> wind instruments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, were the tibia and the fistula. But how they were constituted, wherein they differed, or how they were played upon, does not appear. All we know is, that the fistula was at first made of reeds, and afterwards of other matters. Some had holes, some none; some again were single <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; others a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMBINATION">combination</a> of several; witness the syringa of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. Fistula, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, a deep, narrow, and callous ulcer, generally arising from abscesses. It differs from a sinus, in its being callous, the latter not. See Surgery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fistula, in Farriery. See Farriery Index. Fistularia, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TOBACCO">Tobacco</a>-Pipe Fish; a genus of fishes, belonging to the order of abdominales. See <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> Index. FIT. See Paroxysm. Dr Cheyne is of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, that fits of all kinds, whether epileptic, hysterical, or apoplectic, may be cured solely by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a> diet, of about two quarts of cows milk a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, without any other medicine. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FITCHES">Fitches</a>, in Husbandry, a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PULSE">pulse</a>, more generally known by the name of chick-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>. See Cicer, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index. Fitches are cultivated either for feeding cattle, or improving the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>. They make a wholesome and nourishing food, whether given in the straw or thrashed out. When sown only to improve the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">soil</a>, they are ploughed in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as they begin to blossom, by which means a tough stiff clay soil is much enriched.

FITCHET

Pages 283-283

a name used in some places for the weasel, called also the faunari. See Mustela, <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MAMMALIA">Mammalia</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FITCHY

Pages 283-283

in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, (from the French fishe, i.e. fixed); a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> applied to a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> when the lower branch ends in a sharp point; and the reason of it Mackenzie supposes to be, that the primitive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHRISTIANS">Christians</a> were wont to carry crosses with them wherever they went; and when they stopped on their journey at any <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, they fixed those portable crosses in the ground for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>'s sake.

FITZ-STEPHEN

Pages 283-284

William, a learned monk of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANTERBURY">Canterbury</a>, of Norman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a>, but born of respectable parents in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. He lived in the 12th century; and being attached to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> of Archbishop Becket, was present at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MURDER">murder</a>. In the year 1174, he wrote in Latin, *The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">Life</a> of St. Thomas, archbishop and <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARTYR">martyr</a>*; in which, as Becket was a native of the <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>, he introduces a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the city of London, with a miscellaneous detail of the manners and usages of the citizens: this is deservedly considered as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> curiosity, being the earliest professed account of London extant. Fitz-Stephen died in 1191.

FITZHERBERT

Pages 283-283

Sir Anthony, a very learned lawyer in the reign of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> Henry VIII. was descended from an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family, and born at Norbury in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DERBYSHIRE">Derbyshire</a>. He was made one of the judges of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-COMMON_PLEAS"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> pleas in 1523; and distinguished himself by many valuable works, as well as by such an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOURABLE">honourable</a> discharge of the duties of his office, as made him esteemed an oracle of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>. His writings are, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAND">Grand</a> Abridgement; The Office and Authority of Justices of Peace; the Office of Sheriffs, Bailiffs of Liberties, Escheators, Constables, Coroners, &c.; Of the Diversity of Courts; The New Natura Brevium; Of the Surveying of Lands, and The Book of Husbandry. He died in 1538.

FIVES

Pages 284-284
or VIVES.** See FARRIERY. **FIXATION,** in Chemistry, the rendering any volatile substance fixed, so as not to fly off upon being exposed to a great heat: hence, **FIXED BODIES,** are those which bear a considerable degree of heat without evaporating, or losing any of their weight. Some of the most fixed bodies are diamonds, gold, &c. **Fixed, or Fixable Air,** an invisible and permanently elastic fluid, superior in gravity to common atmospheric air and most other aerial fluids, exceedingly destructive to animal life; produced in great quantities, naturally from combustible bodies, and artificially by many chemical processes. From its acid properties it has obtained the name of *aerial acid,* *cretaceous acid,* and *carbonic acid:* from its noxious qualities, it has been called *mephitic air* or *mephitic gas:* and, from the circumstance of being produced in vast quantities during the combustion of charcoal, it first obtained from Van Helmont the name of *gas syloxyfre.* The term fixed air has been given from its property of readily losing its elasticity, and fixing itself in many bodies, particularly those of the calcareous kind; and though some objected to the propriety of the term, the fluid in question is so well known by the name of fixed air, that we choose still to retain it. See Chemistry Index. For an account of the apparatus for impregnating water with fixed air or carbonic acid, see Materia Medica Index. **Fixed Stars,** are such as constantly retain the same position and distance with respect to each other; by which they are distinguished from *erratic* or *wandering* stars, which are continually shifting their situation and distance. The fixed stars are properly called *flares:* the rest have the peculiar denomination of *planet* and *comet.* See Astronomy Index. **FIXITY,** or **FIXEDNESS,** in Chemistry, is in a peculiar manner used for the affection opposite to volatility; i.e. the property whereby bodies bear the action of the fire, without being dissipated in fumes.

FIXMILLNER

Pages 284-285

PIACIDUS,** an eminent astronomer, was born at Achleiten near Linz, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>, on the 28th of May, 1720. He received the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDIMENTS">rudiments</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> of Kremnitz, of which his uncle Alexander was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABBOT">abbot</a>. Here he studied during five years, and delighted so much in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> straight and curved figures, that his mother called him the *<a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALMANACK">almanack</a>-maker.* He went afterward to <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALZBURG">Salzburg</a>, where he studied a regular course of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and particularly turned his <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> to <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a> under a professor Stuard, whose method of teaching that science was truly extraordinary, as he never made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of any figures, and yet conveyed such a clear idea of every proposition as made it perfectly easy. He was admitted as a novice into Kremnitz in 1737, and the next year he took the solemn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOW">vow</a> in presence of his uncle. After being two years in this monastery, during which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> he devoted every leisure <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of mathematics and philosophy, he went to Salzburg to finish his studies in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURISPRUDENCE">jurisprudence</a>, acquiring at that time a competent knowledge of oriental and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> languages, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> and antiquities. In the year 1745, he obtained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of D.D., after which he received <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIEST">priest</a>'s orders in his own monastery, and was created professor of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, which office he held for 40 years, discharging the duties belonging to it till within a few days of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>. He was also chosen <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAN">dean</a> of the higher <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SCHOOLS">schools</a>, and regent of the young <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, which he retained during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>. He wrote a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMENTARY">commentary</a> on the *Jus Canonicum,* notwithstanding his extensive epistolary correspondence, and the management of the whole business of the monastery; but this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> was never published. He was, by the intrigues of his friends, induced to publish his *Reipublicae sacrae origines divinae, seu Ecclesiae Christi exterior junctura, imperium, et hierarchia, ex primigenia ejus institutione eruta et demonstrata.* His commendable diligence procured him universal esteem, but it was his knowledge of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">astronomy</a> which rendered him illustrious. His uncle Alexander fitted up an apartment for containing the instruments necessary for the dissemination of mathematical knowledge, and he also erected an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OBSERVATORY">observatory</a>, which was begun in 1748, and completed in 1758, under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a> of Anhelm Dering of Emstorf, a celebrated <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol3.html#article-ARCHITECT">architect</a>. While the observatory was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, Fixmillner led a life of retirement and severe study; his favourite subject during these ten years being astronomy. When it was finished, one Dobler, a celebrated mathematician, was appointed first astronomer; but the successors of Fixmillner's uncle having discovered his extensive mathematical knowledge, made him an offer of the astronomical department, and the sole direction of the observatory: This <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> he accepted in the year 1762, still retaining his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> as professor of ecclesiastical law. He was not yet <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the learning which practical astronomy requires, to remedy which defect he attentively perused Lalande's *Exposition du Calcul Astronomique,* soon after which he obtained the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> astronomical work of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>, and in 1766 he published his *Meridianus Speculæ Astronomicæ Cremifanensis,* by which he acquired considerable reputation. Ten years after this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> he gave the world his *Decennium Astronomicum,* containing many curious and important particulars respecting the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> and practice of astronomy. His *Acta Astronomicæ Cremifanensis,* which did not appear till after his decease, still farther increased his astronomical reputation; and he was a large contributor to many periodical publications in different countries. He made and collected a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of observations of the planet <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">Mercury</a>, which were at that period both scarce and difficult, the importance of which was publicly acknowledged by Lalande, as they greatly assisted him in constructing his tables of that planet. Fixmillner was one of the first astronomers who calculated the orbit of the new planet Uranus (Georgium Sidus), and his tables reflecting it may be seen in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BERLIN">Berlin</a> almanack for 1789. He also proved the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> of what was formerly conjecture, that the 34th <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of Taurus, which Flamsteed observed in 1690, was the new planet. It may be said of most philosophers, that they observe a great great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, and calculate little, but the conduct of Fixmillner was exactly the reverse. He turned his attention to the observation of the solar spots more than any of his predecessors, which he noticed in the years 1767, 1776, 1777, 1778, and 1782, from which he deduced important inferences respecting the revolution of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> on its axis. He had a genius uncommonly adapted to the study of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, by which he was enabled to invent a new micrometer, and a machine for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRINDING">grinding</a> concentric circles. As an additional <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of his profound inventive genius, he resided in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, by which means he was in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> deprived of literary affluence, yet to the very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of life he was a singular instance of the most indefatigable zeal, diligence, and perseverance. He was little subject to the influence of the turbulent passions;—perhaps less so than most other men. Like the laws of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> which it was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> delight to study, he was simple, uniform, and constant; and such were the mildness and integrity of his character, that he could not fail to acquire the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOVE">love</a> and esteem of mankind. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> reputation never inspired him with vanity, and he rather wished to conceal than to propagate what was written in his praise. It gave general joy to his monastic brethren to celebrate the anniversary of the fiftieth year of his residence in it, which he did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> survive. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> was very much impaired by his intense application, and he finished his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> on the 27th of August 1791, in the 71st year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>.

FLACCUS

Pages 285-285
CAIUS VALERIUS, an ancient Latin poet, of whom we have very imperfect accounts remaining. He wrote a poem on the Argonautic expedition; of which, however, he did not live to finish the eighth book, dying at about 30 years of age. John Baptist Pius, an Italian poet, completed the eighth book of the Argonautics; and added two more from the fourth of Apollonius; which supplement was first added to Aldus's edition in 1523.

FLAG

Pages 285-286

in the marine, a certain banner <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> standard, by which an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ADMIRAL">admiral</a> is distinguished at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> from the inferior ships of his squadron; also the colours by which one <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> is distinguished from another. See Plate CCXVIII.
