In the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVY">navy</a>, flags are either <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, or blue; and are displayed from the top of the main-mast, fore-mast, or mizen-mast, according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of the admiral. When a flag is displayed from the flag-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a> on the main-mast, the officer distinguished thereby is known to be an admiral; when from the fore-mast, a vice-admiral; and when from the mizen-mast a rear-admiral. The first flag in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">Great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a> is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> standard, which is only to be hoisted when the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> are on board the vessel; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a> of hope, which characterizes the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> admiral, or lords commissioners of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ADMIRALTY">admiralty</a>; and the third is the union flag, in which the crosses of St George and St Andrew are blended. This last is appropriated to the admiral of the fleet, who is the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILITARY">military</a> officer under the lord high admiral. The next flag after the union is that of the white squadron at the main-mast head; and the last, which characterizes an admiral, is the blue, at the same mast head. For a vice-admiral, the first flag is the red, the second the white, the third the blue, at the flag staff on the fore-mast. The same order proceeds with regard to the rear admirals, whose flags are hoisted on the top of the mizen-mast: the lowest flag in our navy is accordingly the blue on the mizen mast. To Lower or Strike the Flag, in the marine, is to pull it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a>, or to take it in, out of the respect, or submission, due from all ships or fleets inferior to those any way justly their superiors. To lower or strike the flag in an engagement is a sign of yielding. The way of leading a ship in triumph is to tie the flags to the shrouds, or the gallery, in the hind <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the ship and let them hang down towards the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to tow the vessels by the stern. Livy relates, that this was the way the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> used those of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARTHAGE">Carthage</a>. To Heave out the Flag, is to put out or put abroad the flag. To Hang out the White Flag, is to ask <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a>; or it shows when a vessel is arrived on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>, that it has no hostile intention, but comes to trade, or the like. The red flag is a sign of defiance and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a>. Flag is also used for a fedge, a kind of rush. Corn-Flag. See Gladiolus, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Sweet-scented Flag. See Acorus, Botany Index. Flag-Officers, those who command the several squadrons of a fleet; such are the admirals, vice-admirals, and rear admirals. The flag officers in our pay, are the admiral, vice-admiral, and rear-admiral, of the white, red, and blue. See Admiral, Flag, and Fleet. Flag-Ship, a ship commanded by a general or flag-officer, who has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to carry a flag, in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTRADICTION">contradiction</a> to the secondary vessels under the command thereof. Flag-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">Stone</a>, a kind of <a class="xref" href="../1823/vol0.html#article-SAND_STONE">sand-stone</a> of a flat structure, on account of which it is much employed for the purpose of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAVING">paving</a> foot paths or the floors of apartments in which wood is unsuitable. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLAGELLANTES">Flagellantes</a>, a set of wild fanatics who chastised and disciplined themselves with whips in public. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> of the Flagellantes had its rise in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> in the year 1260; its author was one Ranier a hermit; and it was propagated from hence through almost all the countries of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. It was in all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROBABILITY">probability</a> no more than the effect of an indiscreet zeal. A great <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons of all ages and sexes made processions, walking two by two with their shoulders bare, which they whipped till the blood ran down, in order to obtain mercy from God, and appease his indignation against the wickedness of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>. They were then called the devout; and having established a superior, he was called the general of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVOTION">devotion</a>. Though the primitive Flagellantes were exemplary in point of morals. Flagolet morals, yet they were joined by a turbulent rabble, who were infected with the most ridiculous and impious opinions; so that the emperors and pontiffs thought proper to put an end to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> frenzy, by declaring all devout whipping contrary to the divine <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, and prejudicial to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUL">soul</a>'s eternal <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>. This sect revived in Germany towards the middle of the next century, and rambling through many provinces, occasioned great disturbances. They held, among other things, that flagellation was of equal virtue with <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BAPTISM">baptism</a> and the other sacraments; that the forgiveness of all sins was to be obtained by it from God without the merits of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JESUS">Jesus</a> Christ; that the old law of Christ was soon to be abolished, and that a new law enjoining the baptism of blood to be administered by whipping was to be substituted in its <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>: upon which Clement VII., by an injudicious as well as unrighteous policy, thundered out anathemas against the Flagellantes, who were burnt by the inquisitors in several places; but they were not easily extirpated. They appeared again in Thuringia and Lower <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAXONY">Saxony</a> in the 15th century; and rejected not only the sacraments, but every branch of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> worship; and placed their only hopes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALVATION">salvation</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a> and flagellation, to which they added other strange doctrines concerning evil spirits. Their leader <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONRAD">Conrad</a> Schmidt and many others were committed to the flames by German inquisitors in and after the year 1414.

FLAGOLET

Pages 286-286
or Flajeulet, a little flute, used chiefly by shepherds and country people. It is made of box or other hard wood, and sometimes of ivory; and has six holes besides that at the bottom, the mouth-piece, and that behind the neck.

FLAGS

Pages 285-285

in the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, are small banners of distinction stuck in the baggage wagons to distinguish the baggage of one brigade from another; and of one battalion from another; that they may be marshalled by the waggon-<a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> general according to the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> of their brigades, to avoid the confusion that might otherwise arise.

FLAIL

Pages 286-286

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for thrashing corn. It consists of the following parts. 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAFF">staff</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> piece held in the thrasher's hand. 2. The twiple, or that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> which strikes out the corn. 3. The caplins, or strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> leathers, made fast to the tops of the hand-staff and twiple. 4. The middle band, being the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a> thong or fish skin that ties the caplins together.

FLAIR

Pages 286-286

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. The seamen say that the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> doth flair over, when a ship is housed in near the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, so that the work hangs over a little too much, and this is let out broader aloft than the due proportion <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> allow.

FLAKE

Pages 286-286

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a name given by the florists to a sort of carnations which are of two colours only, and have very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> stripes, all of them going quite through the leaves. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Flake, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">Painting</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> corroded by means of the pressing of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAPES">grapes</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a ceruse prepared by the acid of grapes. It is brought from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>; and far surpasses, both with regard to the purity of its whiteness and the certainty of its standing, all the ceruse or white lead made with us in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>. It is used in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VARNISH">varnish</a> painting for all purposes where a very clean white is required. The white flake should be procured in lumps as it is brought over, and levigated by those who <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> it; because that which the journeymen fell in a prepared state is levigated and mixed up with <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, and often with white lead, and worse sophifications.

FLAMBEAU

Pages 286-286
or Flamboy, a luminary made of several thick wicks, covered over with wax, serving to burn at nights in the streets; as also at funeral processions, illuminations, &c. Flambeaux differ from links, torches, and tapers.—They are made square, sometimes of white wax and sometimes of yellow. They usually consist of four wicks or branches near an inch thick, and about three feet long, made of a sort of coarse hemp yarn half twisted. They are made with the ladle much as torches or tapers are; viz. by first pouring the melted wax on the top of the several suspended wicks, and letting it run down to the bottom. This they repeat twice. After each wick has thus got its proper cover of wax, then lay them to dry; then roll them on a table and to join four of them together by means of a red hot iron. When joined, they pour on more wax till the flambeau is brought to the size required, which is usually from a pound and half to three pounds. The last thing is to finish their form or outside, which they do with a kind of polishing instrument of wood by running it along all the angles formed by the union of the branches. The flambeaux of the ancients were different from ours. They were made of woods dried in furnaces or otherwise. They used divers kinds of wood for this purpose; the wood most usual was pine. Pliny says, that in his time they frequently also burnt oak, elm, and hazel. In the seventh book of the Aeneid, mention is made of a flambeau of pine; and Servius on that passage remarks, that they also made them of the cornel-tree. FLAMBOROUGH head, in Geography, a cape or promontory on the eastern coast of Yorkshire, five miles east of Burlington, and 216 from London.—E. Long. 2°. N. Lat. 54. 15.—This was the Fleamburg of the Saxons; so called, as some think, from the lights made on it to direct the landing of Ina, who in 547 joined his countrymen in these parts with a large reinforcement from Germany, and founded the kingdom of Northumberland. In the time of Edward the Confessor, Flamborough was one of the manors of Harold, earl of the West Saxons, afterwards king of England. On his death, the Conqueror gave it to Hugh Lupus; who, in perpetual alms, bestowed it on the monastery of Whitby.—The town is on the north side; and consists of about 150 small houses, entirely inhabited by fishermen; few of whom, as is said, die in their beds, but meet their fate in the element they are so conversant in. The cliffs of the Head are of a tremendous height and amazing grandeur. Beneath are several vast caverns; some closed at the end, others pervious, formed with a natural arch. In some places the rocks are insulated, and of a pyramidal figure, soaring up to a vast height. The bases of most are solid, but in some pierced through and arched. The colour of all these rocks is white, from the dust of the innumerable flocks of migratory birds, which quite cover the face of them, filling every little projection, every hole that will give them leave to rest.

FLAME

Pages 286-287

is a general name for every kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUMINOUS">luminous</a> vapour, provided the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> it emits hath any considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of intensity. The name flame, how- ever, is most generally applied to such as are of a conical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, like those arising from our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> fires; without this, they are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called luminous vapours, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> simply lights. According to Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton, flame is only <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a>-hot <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, or the vapour of any substance raised from it by fire, and heated to such a degree as to emit light copiously. This <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> seems to be the most accurate and expressive of any. It is certain, that bodies are capable of emitting flame only in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of vapour that rises from them. Thus wood, coals, &c., which emit a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantity of vapour, flame violently; while <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a>, tin, &c., which emit but a small fume, can scarce be perceived to flame at all. This rule, however, is by no means to be depended upon in all <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>. Some vapours seem to be in their own <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> inflammable, and capable of extinguishing flame; as those of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, the mineral <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACIDS">acids</a>, sal-ammoniac, arsenic, &c.; while others take fire on the slightest approach of a flaming substance; such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ETHER">ether</a>, spirit of wine, &c. These last mentioned substances also exhibit a remarkable phenomenon; namely, that they cannot be made to flame without the approach of some substance actually in flames beforehand. Thus, spirit of wine poured on a red-hot <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, though instantly dissipated in vapour, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not flame; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BURNING">burning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CANDLE">candle</a> touches its surface, the whole is set in flame at once. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is otherwise with oils, especially those of the grocer's kind; for the vapours will readily be changed into flame by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERE">mere</a> increase of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, without the approach of any flaming substance. There is, however, no kind of vapour, perhaps, that is incapable of being converted into flame, provided it is exposed to a sufficient degree of heat. Thus the vapour of water made to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> through burning coals produces an exceedingly strong and bright flame.—It is remarkable, that this kind of vapour seems to be more powerful than almost any other in absorbing heat, and retaining it in a latent state. When any quantity of aqueous vapour is condensed, more heat will be separated from it than would have been sufficient to heat an equal bulk of iron red-hot.—It is most probably to this <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> which all vapours have of absorbing heat, and detaining it in a latent state, that we are to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATTRIBUTE">attribute</a> the phenomena of flame, and also the exceeding great elasticity of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a>. It is certain, that vapours, of water at least, have a much greater power of absorbing and retaining heat, than the water from which they are raised. In open vessels, water cannot be heated more than to 212 degrees of Fahrenheit's thermometer; but in Papin's digester, where the vapour is forcibly confined, it has been heated to 400 of the same degrees; and, no doubt, might have been heated a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> more, had the vessels been strong enough to bear the expansive force of the steam. On opening the vessels, however, the excess of heat was found to have resided entirely in the vapour; for the water in the vessel very soon sunk <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to 212, while the steam issued forth with great violence. From these experiments it appears, that the steam of water, after it has absorbed as much heat in a latent state as it can contain, continues to absorb, or detain among its particles, an unlimited quantity of sensible heat; and if the steam could be confined till this quantity became great enough to be visible by its emission of light, there cannot be the least doubt that the vapour would then be converted into flame. In what manner the heat is detained among the particles of steam, is perhaps impossible to be explained; but to this heat we must undoubtedly ascribe the violent expansive force of steam of every kind. It seems probable, that when smoke is converted into flame, the latent heat with which the vapour had combined, or rather that which made an essential <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it, breaks forth, and adds to the quantity of sensible heat which is already present. This seems probable, from the sudden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPLOSION">explosion</a> with which all flames <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> out. If a vessel full of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> is set over the fire, a smoke or vapour begins to arise from it; which grows gradually thicker and thicker; and at last begins to thine in some places very near the surface of the oil, like an electric light, or sulphur <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> kindled. At this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> the oil is very hot, as well as the steam which issues from it. But this last is continually giving off its sensible heat into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATMOSPHERE">atmosphere</a>; so that at the distance of an inch or two from the surface of the oil, the heat of the steam will not exceed 400 degrees of Fahrenheit, or perhaps may not be so much; but if a burning candle is held in the steam for a moment, the whole is immediately converted into flame, with something like an explosion; after which, the oil burns quietly until it is all consumed. The flame, as soon as it appears, is not only much hotter than the steam from whence it was produced, but even than the oil which lies below it. Whence, then, has this sudden and great increase of heat arisen? It could not be the sensible heat of the vapour, for that was greatly inferior; nor could it be communicated from the oil, for that could communicate no more than it had to itself. The candle, indeed, would communicate a quantity of heat to the vapour which touched its flame; but it is impossible that this quantity should extend permanently over a surface perhaps 100 times larger than the flame of the candle, in such a manner as to make every part of that surface equally hot with the flame of the candle itself; for this would be to suppose it to communicate 100 times more heat than really was in it. The heat therefore must have originally resided in the vapour itself; and as, in the freezing of water, its latent heat is extricated and becomes sensible, and the water thereupon loses its fluidity; so, in the ascension of vapour, the latent heat breaks forth with a bright flash, and the vapour is then totally decomposed, and converted into foot, ashes, or water, according to the different nature of the substances which produce it, or according to the intensity of the heat.—Several other hypotheses have been invented to solve the phenomena of burning and flaming bodies; for an account of which, see <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNITION">Ignition</a> and Heat, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flames are of different colours, according to the substances from which they are produced. Thus, the flame of sulphur and spirit of wine is blue; the flame of nitre and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZINC">zinc</a>, of a bright <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; that of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, of a greenish blue, &c.—These varieties afford an opportunity of making a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of agreeable representations in fireworks, which could not be done if the flame produced from every different substance was of the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>. See Pyrotechnics.

FLAMEN

Pages 287-288

in Roman antiquity, the name of an order order of priests, instituted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Numa; authors not being agreed on this head. They were originally only three, viz. the Flamen Dialis, Flamen Martialis, and Flamen Quirinalis. The Flamen Dialis was sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUPITER">Jupiter</a>, and a person of the highest <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> and authority in the state. He discharged several <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> duties which properly belonged to the kings, and was honoured with many eminent privileges beyond all other officers, but was obliged to observe several superstitious restraints. The Flamen Martialis was sacred to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MARS">Mars</a>, and was ordained to inspect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RITES">rites</a> of that god. The Flamen Quirinalis was sacred to, and superintended the rites of, Quirinus Romulus. The Flamines last mentioned, though of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> authority, were much inferior to the Flamen Dialis. All three were chosen by the people, and consecrated by the Pontifex Maximus.—In latter times several priests of the same order and name were added to them, but inferior in power. The whole <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> at last amounted to 15: the three first of whom were senators, and called Flamines majores; the other 12, taken from among the people, being denominated Flamines minores.—Some authors tell us the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> had a Flamen for every deity they worshipped. The greater Flamines wore the robe edged with purple, like the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> magistrates; had an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IVORY">ivory</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a>, and a seat in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>. They wore a little band of thread about their heads, whence their name is said to be derived, quasi Filamines.—The wife of the Flamen Dialis was called Flaminia, and wore a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAME">flame</a>-coloured <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, on which was painted a thunderbolt, and above her head-dress she had green oak boughs, to indicate that she belonged to Jupiter the thunderer, to whom the oak was sacred. The Flamines wore each of them a hat or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAP">cap</a> called Flammum or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APEX">Apex</a>.

FLAMINIUS

Pages 288-288
or FLAMININUS, T. Q. a celebrated Roman, raised to the consulship in the year of Rome 554, though under the age of 30. He was trained in the art of war against Hannibal; and he showed himself capable in every respect to discharge with honour the great office with which he was intrusted. He was sent at the head of the Roman troops against Philip king of Macedon, and in his expedition he met with uncommon success. The Greeks gradually declared themselves his firmest supporters; and he totally defeated Philip on the confines of Epirus, and made all Locris, Phocis, and Thessaly, tributary to the Roman power. He granted peace to the conquered monarch, and proclaimed all Greece free and independent at the Isthmian games. This celebrated action procured the name of Patron of Greece to the Romans, and infallibly paved their way to universal dominion. Flaminius behaved among them with the greatest policy; by his ready compliance to their national customs and prejudices, he gained uncommon popularity, and received the name of father and deliverer of Greece. He was afterwards sent ambassador to King Prusias, who had given refuge to Hannibal; and there his prudence and artifice hastened out of the world a man who had long been the terror of the Romans. Flaminius was found dead in his bed, after a life spent in the greatest glory, in which he had imitated with success the virtues of his model Scipio. Flaminius or Flaminio, Mark Antony, one of Flaminius the best Latin poets in the 16th century, of Imola in Italy, son and grandson of very learned men. The pope had chosen him secretary to the council in 1545; but he refused that employment, because, favouring the new opinions, he would not employ his pen in an assembly where he knew these opinions were to be condemned.—He paraphrased 38 of the psalms in Latin verse, and also wrote notes on the Psalms; and some letters and poems which are esteemed. He died at Rome in 1550.

FLAMSTEED

Pages 288-289

JOHN, an eminent English astronomer, and the first who obtained the appointment of astronomer-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DERBY">Derby</a> in the year 1646. He was educated at the free school of Derby, where he was head scholar at 14 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, at which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a> his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, naturally tender and delicate, was much tried by a severe illness. When some of his companions went to the university, the state of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> prevented him from accompanying them. He afterwards met with a book De Sphera, written by John Sacrobosco, which was perfectly suited to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> turn of his genius, and therefore he perused it with uncommon satisfaction, translating as much of it into English as he thought would be necessary for him; and from the Astronomia Carolinae of Strut he learned the method of calculating eclipses, and ascertaining the places of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANETS">planets</a>. Mr Hatton, a mathematician, sent him Kepler's Tabula Rudolphinae, and Riccioli's Almagestum Novum, together with some other astronomical works to which he was as yet a stranger. In 1669 he calculated an eclipse of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>, which had been omitted in the Ephemerides for the following year, together with five apulses of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOON">moon</a> to fixed stars, and sent them to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Brouncker, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the Royal <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>, who submitted them to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> of that learned body, by which they were greatly applauded, and he received a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LETTER">letter</a> of thanks from Mr Oldenburg the secretary. He likewise received a letter of thanks from Mr Collins, one of the members. In 1670 he was invited to come up to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> by his father, that he might become personally acquainted with his learned correspondents, of which he gladly accepted, and had an interview with Mr Oldenburg and Mr Collins, by the latter of whom he was introduced to Sir Jonas Moore, who became the warm friend and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">patron</a> of Mr Flamsteed. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of this journey he became acquainted with many astronomical instruments, and was presented by Sir Jonas Moore with Townley's micrometer, who also assisted him in procuring glasses at a moderate rate for the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTRUCTION">construction</a> of telescopes. On his way home again he returned by <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he paid a visit to the celebrated Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARROW">Barrow</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a> is a perfectly champaign <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, with not a rising ground <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> hill in it, and watered with many fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. Its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> commodities are fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAPESTRY">tapestry</a>. In this country some important arts were invented and improved. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEAVING">Weaving</a> in general was greatly improved, and that of figures of all sorts in linen was invented; also the art of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-DYEING">dyeing</a> cloths and stuffs, and of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> colours; the curing of herrings, &c. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a> of this country are not now in the flourishing state they were formerly; yet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, cotton, and woollen stuffs, brocades, camlets, tapestry, lace, and linen, are still manufactured here in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> quantities. This <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> had counts of its own from the ninth century to the year 1369, when it went by <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">marriage</a> to the dukes of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>; and afterwards from them, by marriage also, to the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-AUSTRIA">Austria</a>. France, in 1667, seized the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>; and the states general obtained the northern, partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUNSTER">Munster</a>, and partly by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARRIER">barrier</a> treaty of 1715. For a more particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a> of Flanders, with a continuation <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to the present times, see the article <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">NETHERLANDS</a>.

FLANEL

Pages 289-290
or FLANNEL, a kind of slight, loose, woollen stuff, composed of a woof and warp, and woven on a loom with two treddles, after the manner of baize. Dr Black assigns as a reason why flannel and other substances of the kind keep the body warm, that they compose a rare and spongy mass, the fibres of which touch each other so slightly, that the heat moves slowly through the interstices, which being filled only with air, and that in a stagnant state, give little affluence in conducting the heat. From the experiments of Count Rumford, it appears, that there is a relation betwixt the power which the substances usually worn as clothing have of absorbing moisture, and that of keeping the body warm. Having provided a quantity of each of these substances mentioned below, he exposed them, spread out upon clean China plates, for the space of 24 hours to the warm and dry air of a room which had been heated by a German stove for several months, and during the last six hours had raised the thermometer to 85° of Fahrenheit; after which he weighed equal quantities of the different substances with a very accurate balance. They were then spread out upon a China plate, and removed into a very large uninhabited room upon the second floor, where they were exposed 48 hours upon a table placed in the middle of the room, the air of which was at 45° of Fahrenheit. At the end of this space they were weighed, and then removed into a damp cellar, and placed on a table in the middle of the vault, where the air was at the temperature of 45°, and which by the hygrometer seemed to be fully saturated with moisture. In this situation they were suffered to remain three days and three nights; the vault being all the time hung round with wet linen cloths, to render the air as completely damp as possible. At the end of three days they were weighed, and the weights at the different times were found as in the following table. | Material | Weight after being dried in the hot room | Weight after coming out of the cold room | Weight after remaining 72 h. in the vault | |---------------------------|------------------------------------------|----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------| | Sheep's wool | 1084 | 1163 | | | Beaver's fur | 1072 | 1125 | | | The fur of a Ruffian hare | 1065 | 1115 | | | Eider down | 1067 | 1112 | | | Raw single thread | 1057 | 1107 | | | Silk | | | | | Ravellings of white taffety | 1054 | 1103 | | | Parts | | | | | Fine lint | 1046 | 1102 | | | Linen | | | | | Ravelling of fine linen | 1044 | 1082 | | | Cotton wool | 1043 | 1089 | | | Ravellings of silver lace | 1000 | 1000 | | On these experiments our author observes, that though linen, from the apparent ease with which it receives dampness from the atmosphere, seems to have a much greater attraction for water than any other; yet it would appear from what is related above, that those bodies which receive water in its unelastic form with the greatest ease, or are most easily wet, are not those which in all cases attract the moisture of the atmosphere with the greatest avidity. "Perhaps (says he), the apparent dampness of linen to the touch, arises more from the ease with which that substance parts with the water it contains, than from the quantity of water it actually holds: in the same manner as a body appears hot to the touch, in consequence of its parting freely with its heat; while another body which is really at the same temperature, but which withholds its heat with great obstinacy, affects the sense of feeling much less violently." It is well known that woollen clothes, such as flannels, &c., worn next the skin, greatly promote insensible perspiration. May not this arise principally from the strong attraction which subsists between wool and the watery vapour which is continually issuing from the human body? That it does not depend entirely on the warmth of that covering, is clear; for the same degree of warmth produced by wearing more clothing of a different kind, does not produce the same effect. The perspiration of the human body being absorbed by a covering of flannel, it is immediately distributed through the whole thickness of that substance, and by that means exposed, by a very large surface, to be carried off by the atmosphere; and the loss of this watery vapour which the flannel sustains on the one side by evaporation, being immediately restored from the other, in consequence of the strong attraction between the flannel and this vapour, the pores of the skin are disencumbered, and they are continually surrounded by a dry and salubrious atmosphere."

FLANK

Pages 290-290

in Fortification, is a line drawn from the extremity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FACE">face</a> towards the inside of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">Or</a>, flank is that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of a battalion which reaches from the curtain to the face, and defends the opposite face, the flank, and the curtain. See FORTIFICATION. Oblique or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">Second</a> Flank, or Flank of the Curtain, is that part of the curtain from whence the face of the opposite battalion can be seen, being contained between the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a> rafant and fichant, or the greater and lesser lines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEFENCE">defence</a>; or the part of the curtain between the flank and the point where the fichant line of defence terminates. Covered, Low, or Retired Flank, is the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-PLATFORM">platform</a> of the casement, which lies hid in the battalion; and is otherwise called the Orillon. Fichant Flank, is that from whence a cannon playing, fires directly on the face of the opposite battalion. Rafant or Rozant Flank, is the point from whence the line of defence begins, from the conjunction of which with the curtain, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> only rafeth the face of the next battalion, which happens when the face cannot be discovered but from the flank alone.

FLAT

Pages 290-290

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> ground lying at a small depth under the surface of the sea, and is also called a shoal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> shallow. Flat-bottomed Boats are such as are made to swim in shallow <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and to carry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of troops, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTILLERY">artillery</a>, ammunition, &c. They are constructed with a 12 pounder, bow-chafe, and an 18 pounder, stern-chafe; their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a> is from 90 to 100 feet, and from 12 to 24 feet beam: they have one mast, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> main-fail, and a jib-fail; are rowed by 18 or 20 oars, and can carry 400 men each. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> takes up one bow, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">bridge</a> the other, over which the troops are to <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">march</a>. Those that carry horses have the fore-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> made to open when the men are to mount and ride over a bridge.

FLATUS

Pages 290-291

FLATULENCE, in Medicine; vapours <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATED">generated</a> in the stomach and intestines, chiefly occasioned by a weakness of these parts. They occasion distensions, uneasy <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and sickness, and often a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of pain. See MEDICINE <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLAVEL

Pages 291-291

JOHN, an eminent non-conformist minister, was educated at University-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>; and became minister first of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DEPTFORD">Deptford</a>, and afterwards of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DARTMOUTH">Dartmouth</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, where he resided the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, much respected and admired for his preaching; although he was persecuted on account of his principles, when in 1685, several of the aldermen of the town, attended by the rabble, carried about a ridiculous effigy of him, to which were affixed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">Bill</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-EXCLUSION">Exclusion</a> and the Covenant. Upon this occasion, he thought it prudent to withdraw from the town; not knowing what treatment he might meet with from a riotous mob, headed by magistrates who were themselves among the lowest of mankind. Part of his Diary, printed with his Remains, must give the reader a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> idea of his piety. He died in 1691, aged 61; and after his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a>, his works, which consisted of many pieces of practical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVINITY">divinity</a>, were printed in two volumes folio. Among these, the most famous are his "<a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">Navigation</a> Spiritualized, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> a New Compass for Seamen, consisting of 32 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> of pleasant observations and serious reflections," of which there have been several editions in 8vo; and his "Husbandry Spiritualized, &c. with occasional meditations upon beasts, birds, trees, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and several other objects," of which also there have been many editions in octavo.

FLAX

Pages 291-302

in <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>. See LINUM, BOTANY <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. The following particulars with regard to the manner of raising flax, have been some years past warmly recommended by the <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-TRUSTEES">trustees</a> for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol9.html#article-FISHERIES">fisheries</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MANUFACTURES">manufactures</a>, and improvements in Scotland. Of the choice of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOIL">Soil</a>, and preparing the Ground for Flax. A skilful flax-raiser always prefers a free open deep loam; and all grounds that produced the preceding year a good crop of turnip, cabbage, potatoes, barley, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> clover, or have been formerly laid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> rich, and kept for some years in pasture. A clay soil, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or third crop after being limed, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> answer well for flax; provided, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the ground be still stiff, that it be brought to a proper mould, by tilling after <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HARVEST">harvest</a> to expose it to the winter frosts. All new grounds produce a strong crop of flax, and pretty free of weeds. When a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> many <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLE">mole</a> heaps appear upon new ground, it answers the better for flax, after one tilling. Flax seed ought never to be sown on grounds that are either too wet or dry; but on such as retain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> moisture: and such grounds as are inclined to weeds ought to be avoided, unless prepared by a careful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> fallow. If the linseed be sown early, and the flax not allowed to stand for seed, a crop of turnip may be got after the flax that very year; the second year a crop of bear or barley may be taken; and the third year, grass seeds are sometimes sown along with the linseed. This is the method mostly practised in and about the counties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLN">Lincoln</a> and Somerset, where great quantities of flax and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEMP">hemp</a> are every year raised, and where these crops have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> been <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. There, old ploughed grounds are never sown with linseed, unless the soil be very rich and clean. A certain worm, called in Scotland the coup worm, abounds in grounds newly broken up, and greatly hurts every crop but flax. In small enclosures surrounded with trees or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hedges, the flax, for want of free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, is subject to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> before it be ripe; and the droppings of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEW">dew</a> from the trees prevent the flax, within the reach of the trees, from growing to any perfection. Of preceding crops, potatoes and hemp are the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> for flax. In the fens of Lincoln, upon proper ground of old tillage, they sow hemp, dunging well the first year; the second year, hemp without dung; the third year, flax without dung; and that same year, a crop of turnip eaten on the ground by sheep; the fourth year, hemp with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> coat of dung; and so on for ever. If the ground be free and open, it should be but once ploughed; and that as shallow as possible, not deeper than 2½ inches. It should be laid flat, reduced to a fine garden mould by much harrowing, and all <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> and lods should be carried off. Except a little pigeons dung for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> or four ground, no other dung should be used preparatory for flax; because it produces too many weeds, and throws up the flax thin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> upon the stalk. Before sowing, the bulky clods should be broken, or carried off the ground; and stones, quickenings, and every other thing that may hinder the growth of the flax should be removed. Of the choice of Linseed. The brighter in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, and heavier the seed is, so much the better; that which when bruised appears of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> or yellowish green, and fresh in the heart, oily and not dry, and smells and tastes sweet, and not fusty, may be depended upon. Dutch seed of the preceding year's growth, for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, answers best; but it seldom succeeds if kept another year. It ripens sooner than any other foreign seed. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILADELPHIA">Philadelphia</a> seed produces fine lint and few bolls, because sown thick, and answers best in wet cold soils. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGA">Riga</a> seed produces coarser lint, and the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of seed. Scots seed, when well winned and kept, and changed from one kind of soil to another, sometimes answers pretty well; but should be sown thick, as many of its grains are bad, and fail. It <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> well, and its flax is sooner ripe than any other; but its produce afterwards is generally inferior to that from foreign seed. A kind has been lately imported called Memmel seed; which looks well, is short and plump, but seldom grows above eight inches, and on that account ought not to be sown. Of Sowing Linseed. The quantity of linseed sown should be proportioned to the condition of the soil; for if the ground be in good heart, and the seed sown thick, the crop will be in danger of falling before it is ready for pulling. From 11 to 12 pecks Linlithgow <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> of Dutch or Riga seed, is generally sufficient for one Scots <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACRE">acre</a>; and about 10 pecks of Philadelphia seed, which, being the smallest grained, goes farthest. Riga linseed, and the next year's produce of it, is preferred in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINCOLNSHIRE">Lincolnshire</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> for sowing linseed is from the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> to the end of April, as the ground and season answers. answers; but the earlier the seed is sown, the less the crop interferes with the corn harvest. Late sown linseed may grow long, but the flax upon the stalk will be thin and poor. After sowing, the ground ought to be harrowed till the seed is well covered, and then (supposing the soil, as before mentioned, to be free and reduced to a fine mould) it ought to be rolled. When a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> sows a large quantity of linseed, he may find it proper to sow a part earlier and part later, that in the future operations of weeding, pulling, watering, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRAFTING">grafting</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> may be the easier and more conveniently gone about. It ought always to be sown on a dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a>. Of Weeding Flax. It ought to be weeded when the crop is about four inches long. If longer deferred, the weeder will too much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> and crook the stalks, that they will never perhaps recover their straightness again; and when the flax grows crooked, it is more liable to be hurt in the rippling and swinging. Quicken grass should not be taken up; for, being strongly rooted, the pulling of it always loosens a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> of the lint. If there is an appearance of a settled drought, it is better to defer the weeding, than by that operation to expose the tender roots of the flax to the drought. How soon the weeds are got out, they ought to be carried off the field, instead of being laid in the furrows, where they often take root again, and at any rate obstruct the growth of the flax in the furrows. Of Pulling Flax. When the crop grows so short and branchy, as to appear more valuable for seed than flax, it ought not to be pulled before it be thoroughly ripe; but if it grows long and not branchy, the seed should be disregarded, and all the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> given to the flax. In the last <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> it ought to be pulled after the bloom has fallen, when the stalk begins to turn <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and before the leaves fall, and the bolls turn hard and sharp pointed. When the stalk is small, and carries few bolls, the flax is fine; but the stalk of coarse flax is grofs, <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a>, branchy, and carries many bolls. When the flax has fallen, and lies, such as lies ought to be immediately pulled, whether it has grown enough or not, as otherwise it will rot altogether. When parts of the same field grow unequally, so that some parts are ready for pulling before other parts; only what is ready should be pulled, and the rest should be suffered to stand till ready. The flax-raiser ought to be at pains to pull and keep by itself, each different kind of lint which he finds in his field; what is both long and fine, by itself; what is both long and coarse, by itself; what is both short and fine, by itself; what is both short and coarse, by itself; and in like manner every other kind by itself that is of the same size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. If the different kinds be not thus kept separate, the flax must be much damaged in the watering and the other succeeding operations. What is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> called under-growth may be neglected as useless. Few persons that have seen pulled flax, are ignorant of the method of laying it in handfuls across each other; which gives the flax sufficient air, and keeps the handfuls separate and ready for the rippler. Of Stacking up Flax during the Winter, and Winning the Seed. If the flax be more valuable than the seed, it ought by no means to be stacked up; for its own natural juice affords it greatly in the watering; whereas, if kept long unwatered, it looses that juice, and the harle adheres so much to the boon, that it requires longer time to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and even the quality of the flax becomes thereby harsher and coarser. Besides, the flax attacked over year, is in great danger from vermine and other accidents; the water in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> is not so soft and warm as in harvest; and near a year is thereby lost of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of the lint: but if the flax be so short and branchy as to appear most valuable for seed, it ought, after pulling, to be stooked and dried upon the field, as is done with corn; then stacked up for winter, rippled in spring; and after wheeling, the seed should be well cleaned from bad seeds, &c. Of Rippling Flax. After pulling, if the flax is to be regarded more than the seed, it should be allowed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> some hours upon the ground to dry a little, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> some firmness, to prevent the skin or harle, which is the flax, from rubbing off in the rippling; an operation which ought by no means to be neglected, as the bolls, if put into the water along with the flax, breed vermine there, and otherwise spoil the water. The bolls also prove very inconvenient in the dressing and breaking. In Lincolnshire and <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRELAND">Ireland</a>, they think that rippling hurts the flax; and therefore, in <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of rippling, they strike the bolls against a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>. The handfuls for rippling should not be great, as that endangers the lint in the rippling comb. After rippling, the flax-raiser will perceive, that he is able to afford each size and quality of the flax by itself more exactly than he could before. Of Watering Flax. A running stream wastes the lint, makes it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>, and frequently carries it away. Lochs, by the great quantity and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of the water, also whiten and whiten the flax, though not so much as running streams. Both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and lochs water the flax quicker than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a>. But all flax ought to be watered in canals, which should be dugged in clay ground if possible, as that soil retains the water best: but if a firm retentive soil cannot be got, the bottom or sides of the canal, or both the bottom and sides, may be lined with clay; or instead of lining the sides with clay, which might fall down, a ditch may be dug without the canal, and filled with clay, which will prevent both extraneous water from entering, and the water within from running off. A canal of 40 feet long, six broad, and four deep, will generally water the growth of an acre of flax. It ought to be filled with fresh soft water from a river or brook, if possible, two or three weeks before the flax is put in, and exposed all that time to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a>. The greater way the river or brook has run, the softer, and therefore the better, will the water be. Springs, or short runs from hills, are too cold, unless the water is allowed to stand long in the canal. Water from coal or <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> is very bad for flax. A little of the powder of <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a> thrown into a glass of water, will will immediately discover if it comes from minerals of that kind, by <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> it into a dark colour, more or less tinged in proportion to the quantity of vitriol it contains. The canal ought not to be under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHADE">shade</a>; which, besides keeping the sun from softening the water, might make part of the canal cooler than other parts, and so water the flax unequally. The flax-raiser will observe, when the water is brought to a proper heat, that small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> will be rising quickly in it, numbers of small insects and reptiles will be generating there, and bubbles of air rising on the surface. If no such signs appear, the water must not be warm enough, or is otherwise unfit for flax. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOLD">Mold</a> holes, when neither too deep nor too shallow, frequently answer well for watering flax, when the water is proper, as before described. The proper season for watering flax is from the end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> to the end of August. The advantage of watering flax as soon as possible after pulling, has been already mentioned. The flax being forced after rippling, as before mentioned, should next be put in beets, never larger than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> can grasp with both his <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a>, and tied very slack with a band of a few stalks. Dried rushes answer exceedingly well for binding flax, as they do not rot in the water, and may be dried and kept for use again. The beets should be put into the canals slopewise, or half standing upon end, the root end uppermost. Upon the crop ends, when uppermost, there frequently breeds a deal of vermine, destructive of the flax, which is effectually prevented by putting the crop end downmost. The whole flax in the canal ought to be carefully covered from the sun with divots; the grassy side of which should be next the flax, to keep it clean. If it is not thus covered, the sun will discolour the flax, though quite covered with water. If the divots are not weighty enough to keep the flax entirely under water, a few stones may be laid above them. But the flax should not be pressed to the bottom. When the flax is sufficiently watered, it feels soft to the gripe, and the harle parts easily with the boon or bow, which last is then become brittle, and looks whitish. When these signs are found, the flax should be taken out of the water, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> after beat; each gently rinsed in the water, to cleanse it of the nastiness which has gathered about it in the canal; and as the lint is then very tender, and the beat slackly tied, it must be carefully and gently handled. Great care ought to be taken that no part be overdone; and as the coarsest waters soonest, if different kinds be mixed together, a part will be rotted, when the rest is not sufficiently watered. When lint taken out of the canal is not found sufficiently watered, it may be laid in a heap for 12, 18, or 24 hours, which will have an effect like more watering; but this operation is nice, and may prove dangerous in unskilful hands. After the flax is taken out of the canal, fresh lint, should not be put a second time into it, until the former water be run off, and the canal cleaned, and supplied with fresh water. Of Grafting Flax. Short heath is the best field for grafting flax; as, when wet, it fattens to the heath, and is thereby prevented from being blown away by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a>. The heath also keeps it a little above the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and so exposes it the more equally to the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. When such heath is not to be got, links or clean old <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> ground is the next best. Long grass grounds should be avoided, as the grafts growing through the lint frequently spots, tenders, or rots it; and grounds exposed to violent winds should also be avoided. The flax, when taken out of the water, must be spread very thin upon the ground; and being then very tender, it must be gently handled. The thinner it is spread the better, as it is then the more equally exposed to the weather. But it ought never to be spread during a heavy shower, as that would wash and waste the harle too much, which is then excessively tender, but soon after becomes firm enough to bear the rains, which, with the open air and sunshine, cleans, softens, and purifies the harle to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> wanted, and makes it bliter from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOOM">boom</a>. In short, after the flax has got a little firmness by being a few hours spread in dry weather, the more rain and sunshine it gets the better. If there be little danger of high winds carrying off the flax, it will be much the better of being turned about once a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>. If it is not to be turned, it ought to be very thin spread. The spreading of flax and hemp requires a deal of ground, and enriches it greatly. The skilful flax-raiser spreads his first row of flax at the end of the field opposite to the point from whence the most violent wind commonly comes, placing the root-ends foremost; he makes the root-ends of every other row overlap the crop ends of the former row three or four inches, and binds down the last row with a rope; by which means the wind does not easily get below the lint to blow it away; and as the crop ends are seldom so fully watered as the root ends, the aforesaid overlapping has an effect like giving the crop ends more watering. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">Experience</a> only can fully teach a person the signs of flax being sufficiently grafted: then it is of a clearer colour than formerly; the harle is blittered up, and easily parts with the boon, which is then become very brittle. The whole should be sufficiently grafted before any of it is lifted; for if a part be lifted sooner than the rest, that which remains is in great danger from the winds. A dry <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> ought to be chosen for taking up the flax; and if there is no appearance of high wind, it should be loosed from the heath or grafts, and left loose for some hours, to make it thoroughly dry. As a great quantity of flax can scarcely be all equally watered and grafted, and as the different qualities will best appear at lifting the flax off the grafts; therefore at that time each different kind should be gathered together, and kept by itself; that is, all of the same colour, length, and quality. The smaller the beets lint is made up in, the better for drying, and the more convenient for stacking, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSING">housing</a>, &c. and in making up these beets, as in every other operation upon flax, it is of great <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> that the lint be laid together as it grew; the root ends together, and the crop ends together. Follows an estimate of the Expence, Produce, and Profit of a Scots Acre of Flax—supposing the season favourable, that no accidental losses happen, and that the farmer is neither unskillful nor negligent. | Ground rent, labouring the ground, and leading the flax Linseed from 2l. to 4l. per hoghead, the medium 3s. 4d. per peck | A medium crop. | A great crop. | An extra crop. | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Clodding and sowing | L. 2 10 | L. 3 10 | L. 5 0 | | Weeding | 1 16 8 | 1 10 0 | 1 6 8 | | Pulling, rippling, putting in, and covering in the water | 0 2 0 | 0 2 0 | nothing. | | Taking out of the water, grassing, and stacking | 0 14 0 | 0 15 0 | 1 0 0 | | Breaking and fetching, at 2s. per stone | 0 8 0 | 0 12 0 | 0 18 0 | | Total expense | L. 9 2 8 | L. 10 17 | L. 14 6 8 | | Produce at 10s. per stone. | L. 15 0 | L. 20 0 | L. 30 0 | | Linseed sold for <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> at 1s. per peck | for 30 stones. | for 40 stones. | for 60 stones. | | The chaff of the bolls is well worth the expence of drying the seed; as it is good food, when boiled and mixed with bear, for horses. | 0 16 0 | 0 18 0 | 1 0 0 | | Total produce | L. 15 10 | L. 20 18 | L. 31 0 | | <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BALANCE">Balance</a> for profit | L. 6 14 4 | L. 10 1 | L. 16 13 4 | The above estimate being made several years ago, the expence and profit are now different; but the proportions of each are probably the same. There is nothing stated here as expence of the canal in which the flax is watered; because that varies much according to circumstances. It is a certain fact, that the greater the crop is, the better is the quality of the same kind of flax. The advantage of having both a crop of flax and a crop of turnip the same year—or of sowing grass seeds along with the linseed—and of reducing the ground to a fine garden mould, free of weeds, ought to be attended to. For Cambrie and fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAWN">Lawn</a>. The ground must be a rich light soil, rather <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a>, but cannot be too rich. It ought to be ploughed in September, or the beginning of October, first putting a little hot rotten dung upon it. In <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> it ought to have a second ploughing, after a hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FROST">frost</a>; and when you intend to sow it, <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLOUGH">plough</a> it a third time, or rather hoe it, reducing the clods very fine; but make no furrows: the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> must be made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> like a garden; but never work the land when wet. The seed should be sown the beginning of April, and about <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> the quantity that is generally sown by our farmers; if the land be very rich, it will require rather more than double. As soon as sown (if the weather be dry) it will be necessary to roll the ground. The lint must be weeded very clean when about three inches high; directly after which you must set forked sticks, of about one and a half inch thick (which ought to be prepared before), every four or five feet, according to the length of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLES">poles</a> you are to lay upon them; they should be well fixed in the ground, the forked part to receive the poles about six or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> inches above the lint; each row of poles should be two, three, or four feet slumber, according to the length of the brushwood you are to lay upon them. The poles ought to be from 10 to 15 feet long, and strong enough to support the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a> across the poles; take the longest brushwood you can get, the more branchy the better, very thick, filling up the vacancies with smaller brush, and any of the branches that rise higher than 18 or 20 inches ought to be lopped off to make the brush lie as level as possible: any sort of brush will do except oak, as that tinges the lint. Your lint must be pulled as soon as the seed is fully formed, which is a few days after it is out of the bloom, before the lint turn yellow. It must be pulled above the brushwood, and every handful laid upon it as soon as possible: if it is fine weather, leave it four or five hours in that manner: then carry it to a screen near a barn, to put it under cover in case of rain; there it must be spread four or five days, and always put in the barn at night, or when it appears to rain: the bundles must be opened in the barn, or made hollow, to prevent it from heating. These operations must be performed until the lint is perfectly dry, and out of danger of heating; taking care all the time to keep the roots as even as possible, and if possible keep it from rain or wet: if you cannot prevent it from being wet, it will be better to leave it on the grass till dry; because when once wet, the putting it under cover before dry will make it turn <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a>; a thing which must be prevented at all events. If any of the lint upon the border, or through the piece of ground, be coarser than another, it must be separated from the rest. The utmost care must be taken to preserve the flax entire or unbroken; for this reason they beat off the feed with a round <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALLET">mallet</a> or bittle. The most proper ground is summer fallow, or after potatoes or lea; if possible near a wood, to prevent the expense of carrying brush. As soon as the feed is off, if you intend to water it that season, it must be tied in bundles about as large as you can grasp with your two hands. The water proper for it, is a very small rivulet or soft spring free of any metallic ore; taking care that no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">flood</a> or foul water enters your pit; which must be at least five feet deep, about <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> or ten broad at the top, and seven or eight at the bottom; the length will depend on the quantity of flax you have to water. A very small stripe of water, when clear, should always be running in and off from your pit when the lint is in it. The pit ought to be made three or four months before it is used. You must drive poles about four inches thick, with a hook inclining downwards, in this form 7, all along the sides of the pit, above five feet asunder. The hooks must be level with, or rather under, the surface of the water. A long pole, the whole length of the pit, must be fixed into these hooks on each side; and crofs poles put under that, to keep the lint under water; but the crofs poles are not used till the lint is put in. You must order it so, that all the lint should be three or four inches under water. You next bring your lint to the sides of the pit; then put your fleaves head to head, causing each to overlap the other about one-third, and take as many of these as make a bundle of two or two and a half feet broad, laying the one above the other till it is about four or four and a half feet high; then you tie them together in the middle, and at each root end: after this you wrap your bundle in straw, and lay it in the water, putting the thin or broad side undermost, taking care that none of your lint touch the earth; after it is fully preffed under water, put in your crofs poles to keep it under. The bundles ought to lie in the pit a foot separate from each other. This renders it easy to take out; for, if the bundles entangle, they will be too heavy to raise. The time of watering depends so much upon the weather, and softness or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARDNESS">hardness</a> of the water, that it is impossible to fix any certain time. This must be left to the skill of the farmer. If the flax is intended for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPINNING">spinning</a> yarn soft and fit for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIC">cambric</a>, it ought to be spread upon short grass for four or five days before you put it into the water; but if for lawns, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LACE">lace</a>, or thread, it is best to dry it outright. In either case, avoid as much as possible to let it get rain; as much rain blanches and wastes out the oil, which is necessary to preserve the strength. The great <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of this flax is to be fine and long. Thick sowing raises all plants fine and slender; and when the ground is very rich, it forces them to a great length. Pulling green prevents that coarse hardness which flax has when let stand till it be full ripe, and gives it the fine silky property. The brushwood, when the flax springs up catches it by the middle, and prevents it from lying down and rotting; infallible consequences of sowing thick upon rich ground. It likewise keeps it straight, moist, and soft at the roots; and by keeping it warm, and shaded from the sun, greatly promotes its length. The keeping it from rain, heating, taking proper care of your water, preserves the colour, and prevents those bars in cloth so much complained of by bleachers. **Flax-Dressing.** For many ages it was the practice to separate the boon or core from the flax, which is the bark of the plant, by the following simple <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> methods. First, for breaking the boon, the stalks in small parcels were beat with a mallet; or, more dexterously, the break (Plate CCXVIII. fig. 1. and 2.) was used thus: The flax being held in the left hand across the three under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEETH">teeth</a> or swords of the break (A, fig. 1. and a fig. 2.), the upper teeth (B, fig. 1. and b, fig. 2.) were with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> hand quickly and often forced down upon the flax, which was artfully shifted and turned with the left hand. Next, for clearing the flax of the broken boon: the workman with his left hand held the flax over the flock (fig. 3. and 4.), while with his right hand he struck or thrashed the flax with the scutchers (fig. 5.) These methods of breaking and scutching the flax being slow and very laborious, a water-mill was invented in Scotland about the year 1750; which, with some improvements, makes great despatch, and in skilful and careful hands gives satisfaction. It has been generally constructed to break the boon by three dentled rollers, placed one above the other. The middle one of which, being forced quickly round, takes the other two along with it, and one end of the handfuls of the flax being by the workmen directed in between the upper and middle rollers, the flax is immediately drawn in by the rollers; a curved board or plate of tin behind the rollers directs the flax to return again between the middle and undermost rollers;—and thus the operation is repeated until the boon be sufficiently broke. Great weights of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIMBER">timber</a> or stone at the ends of levers, press the upper and under rollers towards the middle one. The scutching is next carried on by the mill in the following manner: Four arms, something like the hand-scutchers before described, project from a perpendicular axle; a box around the axle encloses these projecting scutchers; and this box is divided among the workmen, each having sufficient room to stand and handle his flax, which, through slits in the upper part and sides of the box, they hold in to the stroke of the scutchers; which, moving <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> horizontally, strike the flax across at right <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a>, and so thrash out or clear it of the boon. The breaking of the flax by rollers is scarcely subject to any objection, but that it is dangerous to workmen not sufficiently on their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a>, who sometimes allow the rollers to take hold of their fingers, and thereby their whole arm is instantly drawn in: thus many have lost their arms. To avoid this danger, a break, upon the general principles of the hand-break before described, has been lately adapted to water-machinery, and used in place of rollers.
