"If the vessel be loaded quite up to the line <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AB">AB</a>, and the specific gravity of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> and burden be the same, then the point G is simply the centre of gravity of the section ABCD; but if not, the centres of gravity of the boat and burden must be found separately, and reduced to one by the common method, namely, by dividing the sum of the momenta by the sum of weights, or areas, which in this case are as the weights. The point R is always the centre of gravity of the section MMCD, which, if consisting of different figures, must also be found by dividing the sum of the momenta by the sum of the weights as common. These two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> being found, the next thing necessary is to determine the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AREA">area</a> of the two equal triangles MXE, M XF, their centres of gravity o, o, and the perpendicular projected distance n n of these points on the water line EF. This being done, through R and parallel to EF draw RT = a fourth <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPORTIONAL">proportional</a> to the whole area MMCD, either triangle MXE or M XF, and the distance n n; through T, and at right angles to RT or EF, draw TS meeting the vertical axis of the vessel in S the metacentre; also through the points G, B, and parallel to ST, draw NGW and BV; moreover through S, and parallel to EF, draw WSV, meeting the two former in V and W; then SW is as the stability of the vessel, which will be positive, nothing, or negative, according as the point S is above, coincident with, or below, the point G. If now we suppose W to represent the weight of the whole vessel and burden (which will be equal to the section MMCD multiplied by the length of the vessel), and P to represent the required weight applied at the gunwale B to sustain the vessel at the given angle or inclination; we shall always have this proportion: as VS : SW :: W : P; which proportion is general, whether SW be positive or negative; it must only in the latter case be supposed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> upward to prevent an overturn. "In the rectangular vessel, of given weight and dimensions, the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is so evident, that any farther explanation would be unnecessary. In the trapezoidal vessel, after having found the points G and R, let <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AD">AD</a>, BC be produced until they meet in K. Then, since the two sections MMCD, EFDC are equal; the two triangles MMK, EFK are also equal; and therefore the rectangle EK × KF = KM × KM = KM²; and since the angle of inclination is supposed to be known, the angles at E and F are given. Consequently, if a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> proportional be found between the sines of the angle at E and F, we shall have the following proportions: "As the mean proportional thus found: fine ∠E :: KM : KF, and in the said mean proportional: fine ∠F :: KM : KE; therefore ME, MF become known; from whence the area of either triangle MXE or M XF, the distance n n, and all the other requisites, may be found. "In the mixtilinear section, let AB = 9 feet = 108 inches, the whole depth = 6 feet = 72 inches, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTITUDE">altitude</a> of MM the line of floatation 4 feet or 48 inches; also let the two curvilinear parts be circular quadrants of two feet, or 24 inches radius each. Then the area of the two quadrants = 904.7808 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> inches, and the distance of their centres of gravity from the bottom = 13.8177 inches very nearly; also the area of the included rectangle abie = 1440 square inches, and the altitude of its centre of gravity 12 inches; in like manner, the area of the rectangle ABCD will be found = 5184 square inches, and the altitude of its centre of gravity 48 inches: therefore we shall have Momentum of the two quadrants = 904.7808 × 13.8177 = 12501.9896016 Moment of the rectangle abie = 1440 × 12 = 17280 Moment of the rectangle ABCD = 5184 × 48 = 248832 Now the sum of the momenta, divided by the sum of the areas, will give \(\frac{2786139896016}{75287808} = 37006\) inches, the altitude of G, the centre of gravity of the section. Floating section ABCD above the bottom. In like manner, Bodies the altitude of R, the centre of gravity of the section Flooding, MMCD, will be found to be equal \[ \frac{12309378966016}{49367808} = 24'934 \text{ inches; and consequently their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, or the value of GR } = 12'072 \text{ inches, will be found.} \] Suppose the vessel to heel 15°, and we shall have the following proportion; namely, As radius : tangent of 15° :: MX = 54 inches : 14'469 inches = ME or MF; and consequently the area of either triangle MXE or MXF = 39°663 square inches. Therefore, by theorem 4th, as 49367808 : 39°663 :: 72 = n = \( \frac{3}{4} \) AB : 5'6975 inches = RT; and, again, as radius: fine of 15° :: 12'072 = GR : 3'1245 inches = RN; consequently RT - RN = 5'6975 - 3'1245 = 2'573 inches = SW, the stability required. Moreover, as the fine of 15° : radius :: 5'6975 = RT : 22'013 = RS, to which, if we add 24'934, the altitude of the point R, we shall have 46'947 for the height of the metacentre, which taken from 72, the whole altitude, there remains 25'033; from which, and the half width = 54 inches, the distance BS is found = 59'529 inches very nearly, and the angle SBV = 80° - 56' - 4'2"; from whence SV = 58'645 inches. Again: Let us suppose the mean length of the vessel to be 40 feet, or 480 inches, and we shall have the weight of the whole vessel equal to the area of the section MMCD = 49367808 multiplied by 480 = 2360654784 cubic inches of water, which weighs exactly 85708 pounds avoirdupois, allowing the cubic foot to weigh 62.5 pounds. And, finally, as SV : SW (i.e.) as 58'645 : 2'573 :: 85708 : 3760 + , the weight on the gunwale which will sustain the vessel at the given inclination. Therefore a vessel of the above dimensions, and weighing 38 tons 5 cwt. 28 lbs. will require a weight of 1 ton 13 cwt. 64 lbs. to make her incline 15°. In this example the deflecting power has been supposed to act perpendicularly on the gunwale at B; but if the vessel is navigated by sails, the centre velique must be found; with which and the angle of deflection, the projected distance thereof on the line SV may be obtained; and then the power calculated as above, necessary to be applied at the projected point, will be that part of the wind's force which causes the vessel to heel. And conversely, if the weight and dimensions of the vessel, the area and altitude of the sails, the direction and velocity of the wind be given, the angle of deflection may be found.* * Phil. Mag. 1:393. Flooding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. See Bridge. Flock Paper. See Paper. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOD">Flood</a>, a deluge or inundation of waters. See Deluge. Flood is also used in speaking of the tide. When the water is at lowest, it is called ebb; when rising, young flood; when at highest, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> flood; when beginning to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a>, ebb water. Flood-mark, the mark which the sea makes on the shore at flowing water and the highest tide; it is also called high-water mark. Flook of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">anchor</a>. See Anchor. Fooking, among miners, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used to express a peculiarity in the load of a mine. The load or quantity of ore is frequently intercepted in its course by the crossing of a vein of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, or some different metallic substance; in which case the load is moved to one side, and this transient part of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> is called a flooding. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">Floor</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, the underside of a room, or that part we walk on. Floors are of several sorts; some of earth, some of brick, others of stone, others of boards, &c. For brick and stone Floors, see Pavement. For boarded Floors, it is observable that the carpenters never floor their rooms with boards till the carcass is set up, and also enclosed with walls, lest the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> should injure the flooring. Yet they generally rough-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANE">plane</a> their boards for the flooring before they begin any thing else about the building, that they may let them by to dry and season, which is done in the most careful manner. The best wood for flooring is the fine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a> well seasoned, which when well laid, will keep its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> while; whereas the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> sort becomes <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> by often washing, and looks very bad. The <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of the boards are commonly made plain, so as to touch each other only; but, when the fluff is not quite dry, and the boards shrink, the water runs through them whenever the floor is walked, and injures the ceiling underneath. For this reason they are made with feather edges, so as to cover each other about half an inch, and sometimes they are made with grooves and tenons; and sometimes the joints are made with dove tails; in which case the lower edge is nailed down, and the next drove into it, so that the nails are concealed. The manner of measuring floors is by squares of 10 feet on each side, so that taking the length and breadth, and multiplying them together and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off two decimals, the content of a floor in square will be given. Thus 18 by 16 gives 288 or 2 squares and 88 decimal parts. Earthen Floors, are commonly made of loam, and sometimes, especially to make malt on, of lime, and brook sand, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUN">gun</a> dust, or anvil dust from the forge. Ox blood and fine clay, tempered together, Sir Hugh Plat says, make the finest floor in the world. The manner of making earthen floors for plain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> habitations is as follows: Take two-thirds of lime, and one of coal ashes well fitted, with a small quantity of loam clay; mix the whole together, and temper it well with water, making it up into a heap: let it <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a> or ten days, and then temper it over again. After this, heap it up for three or four days, and repeat the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERING">tempering</a> very high, till it become smooth, yielding, tough, and gluey. The ground being then levelled, lay the floor therewith about 2½ of 3 inches thick, making it smooth with a trowel: the hotter the season is, the better; and when it is thoroughly dried, it will make the best floor for houses, especially malt houses. If any one would have their floors look better, let them take lime made of rag <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, well tempered with whites of eggs, covering the floor about half an inch thick with it, before the under-flooring is too dry. If this be well done, and thoroughly dried, it will look when rubbed with a little <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a> as transparent as metal or glass. In elegant houses, floors of this nature are made of stucco, or of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLASTER">plaster</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> beaten and sifted, and mixed with other ingredients. Floor of a Ship, strictly taken, is only so much of her bottom as she rests on when <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGROUND">aground</a>. Such ships as have long, and withal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> floors, lie on the ground with most security, and are not apt to heel, or tilt on one side; whereas others, which are narrow in the floor, or in the sea phrase, cranked by the ground, cannot be grounded without danger of being overturned. Floor Timbers, in a ship, are those parts of a ship's timbers which are placed immediately across the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEEL">keel</a>, and upon which the bottom of the ship is framed; to these the upper parts of the timbers are united, being only a continuation of floor timbers upwards.

FLORA

Pages 310-310

the reputed <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, was, according to Lactantius, only a lady of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>, who having gained <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> sums of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> by prostituting herself, made the Roman people her heir, on condition that certain games called Floralia might be annually celebrated on her birthday. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards, however, such a foundation appearing unworthy the majesty of the Roman people, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENATE">senate</a>, to ennoble the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CEREMONY">ceremony</a>, converted Flora into a goddess, whom they supposed to preside over flowers; and so made it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a> to render her propitious, that it might be well with their gardens, vineyards, &c. But Vossius (de Idol. lib. i. c. 12.) can by no means allow the goddess Flora to have been the courtezans above mentioned: he <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> rather have her a Sabine deity, and thinks her worship might have commenced under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMULUS">Romulus</a>. His reason is, that Varro, in his fourth book of the Latin tongue, ranks Flora among the deities to whom Tatius <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> of the Sabines offered up vows before he joined <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>. Add, that from another passage in Varro it appears, that there were priests of Flora, with sacrifices, &c. as early as the times of Romulus and Numa. The goddess Flora was, according to the poets, the wife of Zephyrus. Her image in the temple of <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAIUS">Caius</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POLLUX">Pollux</a> was draped in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, and she held in her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> the flowers of peas and beans: but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> poets and painters have been more lavish in setting off her charms, considering that no parts of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> offered such innocent and exquisite entertainment to the sight and smell, as the beautiful variety which adorns, and the odour which embalms, the floral <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CREATION">creation</a>.

FLORALES LUDI

Pages 310-310
or FLORAL GAMES, in antiquity, were games held in honour of Flora, the goddess of flowers.—They were celebrated with shameful debaucheries. The most licentious dissolute were not enough, but the courtezans were called together by the sound of a trumpet, made their appearance naked, and entertained the people with indecent shows and postures: the comedians appeared after the same manner on the stage. Val. Maximus relates, that Cato being once present in the theatre on this occasion, the people were ashamed to ask for such immodest representations in his presence; till Cato, apprised of the reservedness and respect with which he inspired them, withdrew, that the people might not be disappointed of their accustomed diversion. There were several other sorts of shows exhibited on this occasion; and, if we may believe Suetonius in Galba, c. 6. and Vopiscus in Carinus, these princes presented elephants dancing on ropes on these occasions. The ludi florales, according to Pliny, lib. xviii. c. 29., were instituted by order of an oracle of the Sibyls, on the 28th of April; not in the year of Rome 1066, as we commonly read it in the ancient editions of that author; nor in 1044, as E. Hardouin has corrected it, but, as Vossius reads it, in 513: though they were not regularly held every year till after 580. They were chiefly held in the night time, in the Patrician street: some will have it there was a circus for the purpose on the hill called Hortulorum.

FLORALIA

Pages 310-310

in antiquity, a general name for the feasts, games, and other ceremonies, held in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GODDESS">goddess</a> Flora: See FLORA and FLORALES LUDI.

FLORENCE

Pages 310-312

the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUSCANY">Tuscany</a>, and one of the finest cities in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. It is surrounded on all sides but one with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> hills, which rise insensibly, and at last join with the lofty <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> called the Apennines. Towards <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISA">Pisa</a>, there is a vast plain of 40 miles in length; which is so filled with villages and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> houses, that they seem to be a continuation of the suburbs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>. Independent of the churches and palaces of Florence, most of which are very magnificent, the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a> of the houses in general is in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>; and the streets are remarkably clean, and paved with <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> chiseled so as to prevent the horses from sliding. The city is divided into two unequal parts by the river Arno, over which there are no less than four bridges in sight of each other. That called the Ponte della Trinità, which is uncommonly elegant, is built entirely of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> marble, and ornamented with four beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STATUES">statues</a> representing the Seasons. The quays, the buildings on each side, and the bridges, render that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of Florence through which the river runs by far the finest. Every corner of this beautiful city is full of wonders in the arts of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, statuary, and architecture. The streets, squares, and fronts of the palaces, are adorned with a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of statues; some of them by the best <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> masters, Michael Angelo, Bandinelli, Donatello, Giovanni di <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLOGNA">Bologna</a>, Benvenuto Cellini, and others. Some of the Florentine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> formerly were men of vast wealth, and lived in a most magnificent manner. One of them, about the middle of the fifteenth century, built that noble fabric, which, from the name of its founder, is still called the Palazzo Pitti. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> was ruined by the prodigious expense of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BUILDING">building</a>, which was immediately purchased by the Medici family, and has <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> ever since to be the residence of the sovereigns. The gardens belonging to this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> are on the declivity of an eminence. On the summit there is a kind of fort, called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BELVEDERE">Belvedere</a>. From this, and from some of the higher walks, you have a complete view of the city of Florence, and the beauteous vale of Arno, in the middle of which it stands. This palace has been enlarged since it was purchased from the ruined family of Pitti. The furniture is rich and curious, particularly some tables of Florentine <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, which are much admired. The most precious ornaments, however, are the paintings. The walls of what is called the Imperial Chamber, are painted in fresco, by various painters; the subjects are allegorical, and in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> of Lorenzo of Medicis distinguished. Florence, distinguished by the name of the Magnificent. The famous gallery attracts every stranger. One of the most interesting parts of it, in the eyes of many, is the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> of Roman emperors, from Julius Caesar to Gallienus, with a considerable number of their empresses, arranged opposite to them. This series is almost complete; but wherever the bust of an <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> is wanting, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> is filled up by that of some other distinguished Roman. The celebrated Venus of Medici, which has been removed to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, is thought to be the standard of taste in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> and proportion, and stood formerly in a room called the Tribunal. The inscription on its base mentions its being made by Cleomenesian Athenian, the son of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APOLLODORUS">Apollodorus</a>. It is of white marble, and surrounded by other masterpieces of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-SCULPTURE">sculpture</a>, some of which are said to be the works of Praxiteles and other Greek masters. In the same room are many valuable curiosities, besides a collection of admirable pictures by the best masters. There are various other rooms, whose contents are indicated by the names they bear; as, the Cabinet of Arts, of <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">Natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a>, of Medals, of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PORCELAIN">Porcelain</a>, of Antiquities; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SALOON">Saloon</a> of the Hermaphrodite, so called from a statue which divides the admiration of the amateurs with that in the Borghese villa at Rome, though the excellence of the execution is disfigured by the vileness of the subject; and the Gallery of Portraits, which contains the portraits of the most eminent painters (all executed by themselves) who have flourished in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a> during the three last centuries. Our limits <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> not admit of a detail of the hundredth part of the curiosities and buildings of Florence. We must not however omit mentioning the chapel of St Lorenzo, as being perhaps the finest and most expensive habitation that ever was reared for the dead; it is incrusted with precious stones, and adorned by the workmanship of the best modern sculptors. Mr Addison remarked, that this chapel advanced so slowly, that it is not impossible that the family of Medici may be extinct before their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">burial</a> place is finished. This has actually taken place: the Medici family is extinct, and the chapel remains still unfinished. Florence is a place of some strength, and contains an archbishop's see and an university. The number of inhabitants is calculated at 80,000. They boast of the improvements they have made in the Italian tongue, by means of their Academia della Crusca; and several other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a> are now established at Florence. Though the Florentines affect great state, yet their <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a> and gentry drive a retail trade in wine, which they sell from their cellar windows, and sometimes they even hang out a broken flask, as a sign where it may be bought. They <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, besides wine and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> and silver stuffs. The Jews are not held in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of odium, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> subjected to the same humiliating distinctions here, as in most other cities of Europe; and it is said that some of the richest merchants are of that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>. As to the manners and amusements of the inhabitants, Dr Moore informs us, that "besides the conversations which they have here, as in other <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-TOWNS">towns</a> of Italy, a number of the nobility meet every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> at a <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> called the Cafino. This <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">society</a> is pretty much on the same footing with the clubs in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. The members are elected by ballot. They meet at no particular <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>, but go at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> that is convenient. They play at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILLIARDS">billiards</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDS">cards</a>, and other games, or continue conversing the whole evening, as they think proper. They are served with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a>, coffee, lemonade, ices, or what other refreshments they choose; and each person pays for what he calls for. There is one material <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between this and the English clubs, that women as well as men are members. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of both sexes behave with more frankness and familiarity to strangers as well as to each other, than is customary in public assemblies in other parts of Italy. The <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> is a place where the people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a> pay and receive visits, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONVERSE">converse</a> as freely as at the Cafino above mentioned. This occasions a continual passing and repassing to and from the boxes, except in those where there is a party of cards formed; it is then looked on as a piece of ill manners to disturb the players. From this it may be guessed, that here, as in some other towns in Italy, little <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the music by the company in the boxes, except at a new opera, or during some favourite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. But the dancers command a general attention: as soon as they begin, conversation ceases; even the card-players lay <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> their cards, and fix their eyes on the ballette. Yet the excellence of Italian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DANCING">dancing</a> seems to consist in feats of strength, and a kind of jerking agility, more than in graceful movement. There is a continual contest among the performers, who shall <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> highest. You see here none of the sprightly alluring gaiety of the French comic dancers, or of the graceful attitudes and smooth flowing motions of the performers in the serious opera at Paris. It is surprising that a people of such taste and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSIBILITY">sensibility</a> as the Italians, should prefer a parcel of athletic jumpers to elegant dancers. On the evenings on which there is no opera, it is usual for the genteel company to drive to a public walk immediately without the city, where they remain till it begins to grow dark." E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 12. 24. N. Lat. 43. 34. Florence, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> piece of English gold <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>. Every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of standard gold was to be coined into 50 Florences to be current at six shillings each; all which made in tale 15 pounds; or into a proportionate number of half Florences, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> pieces, by indenture of the mint: 18 Edw. III. Florentia, in Ancient <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOGRAPHY">Geography</a>, a town of Etruria, on the Arno; of great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a> in Sylla's wars. Now called Firenze or Fiorenza by the Italians; Florence in English. E. Long. 11. Lat. 43. 30. Florentine marble. See Citadanesca. Florescentia (from floresco, "to flourish or bloom"); the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of flowering, which Linnaeus and the sexualists compare to the act of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a> in animals; as the ripening of the fruit in their <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> resembles the birth. See Flower. Florid style, is that too much enriched with figures and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">rhetoric</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLORIDA">Florida</a>, the most southerly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of the British empire in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> before the last <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a>, bounded on the south by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GULF">gulf</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEXICO">Mexico</a>, on the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> by the Appalachian mountains, on the east by the province of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEORGIA">Georgia</a>, and on the west by the river <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MISSISSIPPI">Mississippi</a>. It was first discovered, in 1497, by Sebastian Cabot, a Venetian, then in the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a>; whence a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> was claimed by the kings of England; and this province, as well as Georgia, was included in the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a> granted by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> II. to Carolina. In 1512, however, Florida was more fully discovered by Ponce de Leon, an able Spanish navigator, but who undertook his voyage from the most absurd motives that can be well imagined. The Indians of the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARIBBEE_ISLANDS">Caribbee <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLANDS">islands</a> had among them a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRADITION">tradition</a>, that somewhene on the continent there was a fountain whose waters had the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of restoring youth to all old men who tasted them. The romantic imaginations of the Spaniards were delighted with this idea. Many embarked in voyages to find out this imaginary fountain, who were never afterwards heard of. Their superstitious countrymen never imagined that these people had perished. They concluded that they did not return, only because they had drunk of the immortalizing liquor, and had discovered a spot so delightful, that they did not choose to leave it. Ponce de Leon set out with this extravagant view as well as others, and fully persuaded of the existence of a third world, the conquest of which was to immortalize his name. In the attempt to discover this country, he rediscovered Florida; but returned to the place from whence he came, visibly more advanced in years than when he set out. For some time this country was neglected by the Spaniards, and some Frenchmen settled in it. But the new colony being neglected by the ministry, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a> having accustomed himself to think that he was the sole proprietor of America, fitted out a fleet at <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CADIZ">Cadiz</a> to destroy them. His orders were executed with barbarity. The French intrenchments were forced, and most of the people killed. The prisoners were hanged on trees; with this inscription, "Not as Frenchmen, but as Heretics." This cruelty was soon after revenged by Dominie de Gourgues, a skilful and intrepid seaman of Gascony, an enemy to the Spaniards, and passionately fond of hazardous expeditions and of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a>. He held his estate; built some ships; and with a select band of adventurers like himself embarked for Florida. He drove the Spaniards from all their posts with incredible valour and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>; defeated them in every encounter; and by way of retaliation, hung the prisoners on trees, with this inscription, "Not as Spaniards, but as Assassins." This expedition was attended with no other consequences; Gourgues blew up the forts he had taken, and returned home, where no notice was taken of him. It was conquered in 1539 by the Spaniards under Ferdinand de Soto, not without a great deal of bloodshed; as the natives were very warlike and made a vigorous resistance. The settlement, however, was not fully established till the year 1565; when the town of St Augustine, the capital of the colony while it remained in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of the Spaniards, was founded. In 1586, this place was taken and pillaged by Sir Francis Drake. It met with the same fate in 1665, being taken and plundered by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">Captain</a> Davis and a body of buccaneers. In 1702, an attempt was made upon it by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLONEL">Colonel</a> More, governor of Carolina. He set out with 500 English and 700 Indians; and having reached St Augustine, he besieged it for three months; at the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPIRATION">expiration</a> of which, the Spaniards having sent some ships to the relief of the place, he was obliged to retire. In 1740 another attempt was made by General Oglethorpe; but he being outwitted by the Spanish governor, was forced to raise the siege with loss; and Florida continued in the hands of the Spaniards till the year 1763, when it was ceded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREATY">treaty</a> to Great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRITAIN">Britain</a>. During the American war, which terminated in 1783, it was again reduced by his Catholic majesty, and was guaranteed to the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROWN">crown</a> of Spain at the peace.

FLORILEGE

Pages 312-312

is also particularly used for a kind of breviary, in the Eastern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, compiled by Arcadius, for the conveniency of the Greek priests and monks, who cannot carry with them, in their travels and pilgrimages, all the volumes wherein their office is dispersed. The florilegium contains the general rubrics, psalter, canticles, the horologium, and the office of the feriae, &c.

FLORILEGIUM

Pages 312-312

FLORILEGE, a name the Latins have given to what the Greeks call ἀθηναῖος, anthology; viz. a collection of choice pieces, containing the finest and brightest things in their kind.

FLORIN

Pages 312-312

is sometimes used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COIN">coin</a>, and sometimes for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> of account. Florin, as a coin, is of different values, according to the different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-METALS">metals</a> and different countries where it is struck. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a> florins are most of them of a very coarse alloy, some of them not exceeding thirteen <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> fourteen carats, and none of them seventeen and a half. See Money <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">Table</a>. Florin, as a money of account, is used by the Italian, Dutch, and German <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKERS">bankers</a>, but admits of divisions in different places. Ibid.

FLORINIANS

Pages 312-312
or FLORIANI, a sect of heretics, of the second century, denominated from its author Florinus, or Florianus, a priest of the Roman church, deposed along with Blastus for his errors. Florinus had been a disciple of St Polycarp, along with Irenaeus. He made God the author of evil; or rather asserted, that the things forbidden by God are not evil, but of his own appointing. In which he followed the errors of Valentinus, and joined himself with the Carpocratians. They had also other names given them. Philastrius says, they were the same with the Carpophorians. He adds that they were also called soldiers, militiae, quia de militarius fuerunt. St Irenaeus calls them Gnostics; St Epiphanius Phibionites; and Theodoret, Barbarites, on account of the impurities of their lives. Others call them Zaccheans; others Coddians, &c. though for what particular reasons, it is not easy to say, nor perhaps would be worth while to inquire.

FLORIS

Pages 312-312

FRANCIS, an eminent historical painter, was born at <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTWERP">Antwerp</a> in 1520. He followed the profession of a statuary till he was twenty years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; when preferring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAINTING">painting</a>, he entered the school of Lambert Lombard, whose manner he imitated very perfectly. He afterwards went to <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, and completed his studies from the most eminent masters. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> progress he made in historical painting, at his return procured him much employment; and his countrymen complimented him with the flattering appellation of the Flemish Raphael. He got much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a>, and might have rendered his acquaintance more worthy of the <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> of the great, had he not debauched himself by frequent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRUNKENNESS">drunkenness</a>. He died 1570, aged 50.

FLORIST

Pages 312-313

a person curious <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> skilled in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>; their kinds, names, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a>, culture, &c. It is also applied to an author who writes what is called the flora, flora of any particular <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, that is, a catalogue of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> and trees which are found spontaneously growing there.

FLORUS

Pages 313-313

LUCIUS ANNÆUS, a Latin historian, of the same family with Seneca and Lucan. He flourished in the reigns of Trajan and Adrian; and wrote an <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ABRIDGMENT">abridgment</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROMAN_HISTORY">Roman <a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, of which there have been many editions. It is composed in a florid and poetical style; and is rather a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PANEGYRIC">panegyric</a> on many of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> actions of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a>, than a faithful and correct recital of their history. He also wrote <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, and entered the lists against the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Adrian, who satirically reproached him with frequenting taverns and places of dissipation.

FLORY

Pages 313-313

FLOWERY, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> Fleury, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> that has <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> at the end circumflex and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a>; different from the potence, in as much as the latter stretches out more like that which is called patee.

FLOS

Pages 313-313

FLOWER. See Flower, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Feminus Flos, a flower which is furnished with the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PISTIL">pistil</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a> organs of <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GENERATION">generation</a>, but wants the stamens or <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MALE">male</a> organ. Female <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> may be produced apart from the male, either on the same root or on distinct <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>. Birch and mulberry are examples of the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, willow and poplar of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>. Mæculus Flos, a male flower. By this name Linnaeus and the sexualists distinguish a flower which contains the stamen, reckoned by the sexualists the male organ of generation; but not the stigma or female organ. All the plants of the clas diercia of Linnaeus have male and female flowers upon different roots; those of the clas monoeica bear flowers of different sexes on the same root. The plants, therefore of the former are only male and female; those of the latter are androgynous; that is, contain a mixture of both male and female flowers. Flos, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>, the most subtle <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of bodies separated from the more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROSS">gross</a> parts by sublimation in a dry form.

FLOTA

Pages 313-313
or Flotta, fleet; a name the Spaniards give particularly to the ships which they send annually from Cadiz to the port of Vera Cruz, to fetch thence the merchandizes gathered in Mexico for Spain. It consists of the captains, admiral, and patach, or pinace, which go on the king's account; and about 16 ships, from 400 to 1000 tons, belonging to particular persons. They set out from Cadiz about the month of August, and are 18 or 20 months before they return. Those sent to fetch the commodities prepared in Peru are called galleons. The name flotilla is given to a number of ships, which get before the rest in their return, and give information of the departure and cargo of the flota and galleons.

FLOTSON

Pages 313-313
or Flotsom, goods that by shipwreck are lost, and floating upon the sea; which, with jeton and lagan, are generally given to the lord admiral: but this is the case only where the owners of such goods are not known. And here it is to be observed, that jeton signifies any thing that is cast out of a ship when in danger, and afterwards is beat on the shore by the water, notwithstanding which the ship perishes. Logan is where heavy goods are thrown overboard, before the wreck of the ship, and sink to the bottom of the sea.

FLOUNDER

Pages 313-313

FLUKE, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> BUT. See Pleuronectes, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flounders may be fished for all <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a>, either in a swift stream, or in the still deep <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but best in the stream in the months of April, May, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUNE">June</a>, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>: the most proper baits are all sorts of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, wasps, and gentles.

FLOUR

Pages 313-313

the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> of wheat-corn, finely ground and sifted. See Meal. The grain itself is not only subject to be eaten by insects in that state; but, when ground into flour, it gives birth to another <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a> of destroyers, who eat it unmercifully, and increase so fast in it, that it is not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> before they wholly destroy the substance. The finest flour is most liable to breed these, especially when <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STALE">stale</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> ill prepared. In this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be examined in a good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be observed to be in continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>, and on a nicer inspection there will be found in it a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of little animals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> of the flour, and very nimble. If a little of this flour is laid on the plate of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>, the insects are very distinctly seen in great numbers, very brisk and lively, continually crawling over one another's backs, and playing a thousand antic tricks together; whether in diversion, or in search of food, is not easy to be determined. These animals are of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> and slender form; their heads are furnished with a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUNK">trunk</a> or hollow tube, by means of which they take in their food, and their body is composed of several rings. They do vast mischief among magazines of flour laid up for armies and other public uses. When they have once taken possession of a parcel of this valuable commodity, it is impossible to drive them out; and they increase so fast, that the only method of preventing the total loss of the parcel is to make it up into <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> as soon as can be done. The way to prevent their breeding in the flour, is to preserve it from damp: nothing gets more injury by being put up damp than flour; and yet nothing is more frequently put up so. It should be always carefully and thoroughly dried before it is put up, and the barrels also dried into which it is to be put; then, if they are placed in a room tolerably warm and dry, they will keep it well. Too dry a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> never does flour any hurt, though one too moist almost always spoils it. Flour when carefully analyzed, is found to be composed of three very different substances. The first and most abundant is pure <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STARCH">starch</a>, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> fecule, insoluble in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, but soluble in hot <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and of the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of mucous substances; which, when dissolved, form water-glues. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> is the gluten, most of whose properties have been described under the article Bread. The third is of a mild nature, perfectly soluble in cold water, of the nature of faccharine extractive mucous matters. It is susceptible of the spirituous <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>, and is found but in small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> in the flour of wheat. See Bread, Gluten, Starch, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">Sugar</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>.

FLOWER

Pages 313-317

Flos, among botanists and gardeners, the most beautiful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of trees and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, containing the organs <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> parts of fructification. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">Flowers</a>, designed for medical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a>, should be plucked when they are moderately blown, and on a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> before noon: for conserves, roles must taken in the bud. Flowers, in antiquity. We find flowers in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> request at the entertainments of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a>, being provided by the <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a> of the feast, and brought in before the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> course; or, as some are of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a>, at the beginning of the entertainment. They not only adorned their heads, necks, and breasts, with flowers, but often bedewed the beds whereon they lay, and all parts of the room with them. But the head was chiefly regarded. See Garland. Flowers were likewise used in the bedecking of tombs. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURIAL">Burial</a>. Eternal Flower. See Xeranthemum, Everlasting Flower. See Gnaphalium, Flower-<a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FENCE">Fence</a>. See Poinciana, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">Sun</a>-Flower. See Helianthus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SULTAN">Sultan</a>-Flower. See Cyamus, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TRUMPET">Trumpet</a>-Flower. See Bignonia, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">Wind</a>-Flower. See Anemonf. Flower-de-lis, or Flower-de-luce, in <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HERALDRY">Heraldry</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> representing the lily called the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">queen</a> of flowers, and the true hieroglyphic of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> majesty; but of late it is become more <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a>, being borne in some coats one, in others three, in others five, and in some fleurs or spread all over the escutcheon in great numbers. The arms of France are, three flowers-de-lis or, in a field azure. Flower-de-Luce. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRIS">Iris</a>, Botany Index. Flowers, in Heraldry. They are much used in coats of arms; and in general signify hope, or denote <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> frailty and momentary prosperity. Flowers, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a>. By this name are generally understood bodies reduced into very fine parts, either spontaneously, or by some operation of art; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> is chiefly applied to volatile <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> substances, reduced into very fine parts, or into a kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> by sublimation.—Some flowers are nothing else than the bodies themselves, which are sublimed entire, without suffering any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALTERATION">alteration</a> or decomposition; and other flowers are some of the constituent parts of the body subjected to sublimation. Colours of Flowers. See the article <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">Colour</a> (of Plants). Colours extracted from Flowers. See Colour-Making. Preserving of Flowers. The method of preserving flowers in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> through the whole year has been much sought after by many people. Some have attempted it by gathering them when dry and not too much opened, and burying them in dry sand; but this, though it preserves their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> well, takes off from the liveliness of their colour. Muntingius prefers the following method to all others. Gather roses, or other flowers, when they are not yet thoroughly open, in the middle of a dry day; fill the vessel up to the top with them; and when full sprinkle them over with some good French wine, with a little <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> in it; then set them by in a cellar, tying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the mouth of the pot. After this they may be taken out at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; and, on setting them in the sun, or within reach of the fire, they <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> open as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> growing naturally; and not only the colour, but the smell also will be preserved. The flowers of plants are by much the most difficult parts of them to preserve in any tolerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of perfection; of which we have instances in all the collections of dried plants, or horti seci. In these the leaves, stalks, roots, and seeds of the plants, appear very well preserved; the strong texture of these parts making them always retain their natural form, and the colours in many <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> naturally remaining. But where these fade, the plant is little the worse for us as to the knowing the species by it. But it is very much otherwise in regard to flowers; these are naturally by much the most beautiful parts of the plants to which they belong; but they are so much injured in the common way of drying, that they not only lose, but change their colours one into another, by which means they give a handle to many errors; and they usually also wither up, so as to lose their very form and natural shape. The primrose and cowslip kinds are very eminent instances of the change of colours in the flowers of dried specimens; for those of these clasps plants easily dry in their natural shape; but they lose their <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a>, and, instead of it, acquire a fine green colour, much superior to that of the leaves in their most perfect state. The flowers of all the violet kind lose their beautiful blue, and become of a dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>: so that in dried specimens there is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> between the blue-flowered violet and the white-flowered kinds. Sir Robert Southwell has communicated to the world a method of drying plants, by which this defect is proposed to be in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> remedied, and all flowers preserved in their natural shape, and many in their natural colours.—For this purpose two plates of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> are to be prepared of the size of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> half sheet of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, or larger, for particular occasions; these plates must be made so thick as not to be apt to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a>; and there must be a hole made near every corner for the receiving a screw to fasten them <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> together. When these plates are prepared, lay in readiness several sheets of paper, and then gather the plants with their flowers when they are quite perfect. Let this be always done in the middle of a dry day; and then lay the plant and its flower on one of the sheets of paper doubled in half, spreading out all the leaves and petals as nicely as possible. If the stalk is thick, it must be pared or cut in half, so that it may <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> flat; and if it is woody, it may be peeled, and only the bark left. When the plant is thus expanded, lay round about it some loose leaves and petals of the flower, which may serve to complete any part that is deficient. When all is thus prepared, lay several sheets of paper over the plant, and as many under it; then put the whole between the iron plates, laying the papers smoothly on one, and laying the other evenly over them; screw them close, and put them into an oven after the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> is drawn, and let them lie there two hours. After that, make a mixture of equal parts of aquafortis and common brandy; shake these well together, and when the flowers are taken out of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a> of the plates, rub them lightly over with a camel's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENCIL">pencil</a> dipped in this liquor; then lay them upon fresh <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> paper, and covering them with some other sheets, press them between this and other papers with a handkerchief till the Flower, the wet of these liquors is dried wholly away. When Flowering, the plant is thus far prepared, take the bulk of a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUM">gum</a> dragon; put this into a pint of fair <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and let it stand 24 hours; it will in this <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> be wholly dissolved; then dip a fine hair pencil in this liquor, and with it daub over the back sides of the leaves, and lay them carefully down on half a sheet of white paper fairly expanded, and press them down with some more papers over them. When the gum-water is fixed, let the presser and papers be removed, and the whole <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> is finished. The leaves retain their verdure in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, and the flowers usually keep their natural colours. Some care, however, must be taken, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the oven be not too great. When the flowers are thick and bulky, some art may be used to pare off their backs, and dispose the petals in a due order; and after this, if any of them are wanting, their places may be supplied with some of the superfluous ones dried on purpose; and if any of them are only faded, it will be prudent to take them away, and lay down others in their stead: the leaves may be also disposed and mended in the same manner. Another method of preserving both flowers and fruit found throughout the whole year is also given by the same author. Take <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALTPETRE">saltpetre</a>, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POUND">pound</a>; Armenian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOLE">bole</a>, two pounds; clean common sand, three pounds; mix all well together. Then gather fruit of any kind that is not fully ripe, with the stalk to each; put these in, one by one, into a wide-mouthed glass, laying them in good order. Tie over the top with an <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>-cloth, and carry them into a dry cellar, and set the whole upon a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> of the prepared <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of four inches thick in a box. Fill up the remainder of the box with the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a>; and let it be four inches thick all over the top of the glass, and all round its sides. Flowers are to be preserved in the same sort of glasses, and in the same manner; and they may be taken up after a whole year as plump and fair as when they were buried. <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">Artificial</a> Flowers of the Chinese. See TONG-TSAO. Flowers, in the animal economy, denote women's monthly purgations or menes.—Nicod derives the word in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>, from fluere, q. d. flows. Others will have the name occasioned hence, that women do not conceive till they have had their flowers; so that these are a sort of forerunners of their fruit. Flowers, in <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RHETORIC">Rhetoric</a>, are figures or ornaments of discourse, by the Latins called floreuli. FLOWERING of Bulbous Plants. These plants will grow and flower in water alone, without any <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and make a very elegant appearance. We daily see this practised in single roots; but there is a method of doing it with several roots in the same vessel. Take a common small garden pot; stop the hole at the bottom with a cork, and late in the cork with putty, that no water can get through; then fit a board to the top of the pot, and bore five or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes in it at equal distances, to <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> the bulbs in; and as many smaller ones near them to receive sticks, which will serve to tie up the flowers. Then fill up the pot with water to the board; and place tulips, jonquils, narcissuses, and the like plants in the root upon the holes, so that the bottom of the roots may touch the water; thus will they all flower early in the season, and be much more beautiful than any pot of gathered flowers, and will last many weeks in their full perfection. After the season of flowering is over, the roots will gradually shrink through the holes of the board, and get loose into the water; but, instead of being spoiled there, they will soon increase in size; so that they cannot return through the holes, and will produce several offsets. It is natural to try from this the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of keeping the roots under water during the whole time of their blowing; and in this way they have been found to succeed very well, and flower even stronger and more beautifully than when in the ground. They may thus, also, with proper care in the degree of heat in the room, he kept flowering from before Christmas till <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> or April. It is not easy, in this last manner, to manage the keeping the boards under water, for which reason, it is better to procure some sheet-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> of about four pounds to the foot, and cut this to the size of the mouth of the pot. In this there should be bored holes for the bulbs, and other holes for the sticks; and, in order to keep the sticks quite firm, it is proper to have another plate of lead shaped to the bottom of the pot, with holes in it, answering to those of the upper plate made for the sticks. The sticks will by this means be always kept perfectly steady; and the roots, being kept under water by the upper plate of lead, will flower in the most vigorous and beautiful manner imaginable. Some have thought of adding to the virtues of the water by putting in nitre in small quantities, and others have added earth and sand at the bottom; but it has always been found to succeed better without any addition. It may be more agreeable to some to use glass jars in this last method with the leads, instead of earthen pots. The bulbs succeed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> as well in these; and there is this advantage, that the progress of the roots is seen all the while, and they are managed better as to the supply of water. By repeated experiments in this way on dried bulbs, and on those taken fresh out of the ground, the former have been found to succeed the best. For those taken fresh out of the ground being full of moisture, will not soon, upon changing their element, be nourished fully by a new one; and the fibres which they had struck in the ground, always rot when put into the water, and new ones must be formed in their places; so that it requires more time for them to come to flowering. The bulbs themselves will not rot in this manner; but they will never be so strong as those which were put into the water dry, which gradually fill themselves with moisture from it, and regularly plump up. The best method of managing the whole <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> is this: Place the bulbs at first only on the surface of the water; for thus they will strike out their fibres most strongly. When they have stood thus six weeks, pour in the water so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> as to cover them entirely, and keep them thus till they have done flowering. Sometimes the roots will become mouldy in several parts while they stand above the water, and the cleaning them of it is no purpose; for it will eat and spread the farther, and frequently eat through two or three of their coats. In this case they must be immediately covered with water; when the mould will be stopped, Flowering stopped, and the roots become found, and flower as well as those which never had any such distemper. If the roots are suffered to remain in water all the year, they will not decay; but will flower again at their proper season, and that as vigorously as those which have been taken out and dried. The old fibres of those roots never rot till they are ready to push forth new ones. It is found by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, that the hyacinth, and many other plants, grow to a greater degree of perfection when thus in water than when in the ground. There is a peculiar species of hyacinth called Keyser's <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JEWEL">jewel</a>; this never, or very rarely, produces seed-vessels in the common way of flowering in the ground; but it will often produce some pods when blown in water. Mr Millar has intimated, in the Philosophical Transactions, that bulbs set in glasses grow weaker, and should be renewed every other year; but it is found, that, when managed in this manner, and kept under water, at the time of taking them up, they are as large, and some of them larger, than when planted; and if these be dried at a proper season, they will flower, year after year, as well as fresh ones. Ranunculus and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-ANEMONE">anemone</a> roots have been found to shoot up their stalks very well in this way; but the flowers are usually blasted, which seems to arise from want of free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. Pinks will flower very well in this manner; auriculas also may, with care, be brought to flower, but not strongly. Roses, jessamines, and honeysuckles, may also be made to flower this way, and will thrive and send out suckers; the best pieces to plant, are suckers cut off about three inches under ground, without any fibres. The succulent plants may also be raised this way; for instance, the opuntia or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> fig. If a fragment of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of this plant be cut, and laid by to dry for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> till it is an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> skin, as soon as it is put in this manner into water, it begins to plump up, and soon sends out <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-FIBROUS">fibrous</a> roots, and produces new leaves as quickly as it would do in the ground. This is the more singular in these sorts of plants, because in their natural state in the ground, they cannot bear much water. This method of growing in water is not peculiar to the bulbous-rooted ones, but others may even be raised from feed by it. A bean or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEA">pea</a>, let in this manner, will grow up to its proper standard, and will flower and produce pods which will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIPEN">ripen</a> their seed. The smaller seeds may be also raised in this manner, by the help of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WOOL">wool</a> to support them. No vegetable transplanted out of the earth into water will thrive kindly; but any plant, whether raised from the root or feed in water, may be transplanted to the earth, and will succeed very well. It may be possible, therefore, from this method of raising plants in water, to come at a better way than is usually practised of raising some roots in the earth which are subject to rot there; such as anemones, ranunculuses, and hyacinths. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BULB">bulb</a> dropped by chance upon the ground, will strike out both stronger and more numerous fibres than those which are planted in the usual way in the ground. On this principle, it may be proper to take out the earth of the bed where the bulbs are to stand at the time of <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLANTING">planting</a> them, to such a depth as they are to be placed under it when set for flowering. The bulbs are then to be set in their places, on the surface of this low ground; and to stand there till they have <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHOT">shot</a> out their fibres and their head; then the earth is to be added over them by degrees, till they are covered as high above the head as they are in the usual manner of planting them; thus they would be preserved from the danger of rotting; and their fibres would be much stronger, and consequently they would draw more nourishment, and flower better, than in the common way. The common method of planting these roots renders them liable to be destroyed by either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> of a wet or a dry season. In the first case, they immediately rot by the abundant moisture they receive; and, in the second, they become dry as a stick and mouldy, so that they are infallibly rotted by the first <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> that falls afterwards. The directions necessary to the success of the bulbs planted in water are these. When the leaden false bottoms are fixed down tight within two or three inches of the bottom of the vessel (which is only designed to hold the sticks steady which are to support the leaves and stalks), then lay on the lead upon which the bulbs are to rest, placing the notched part opposite to that in the false bottom, as near as the sticks, when placed, will suffer it; then place the bulbs one in each hole, and fill up with water to the upper lead. The bottom of the bulb will then touch the water; and as the water diminishes in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>, keep it supplied with more up to the same height for a month or six weeks; in which time the bulbs will have shot strong fibres. Then fill up the water about half an inch above the surface of the lead; and, by degrees, as the fibres strengthen, and the plume floats from the head, keep the water higher and higher, till at length the whole bulb is covered. The water is to be kept at this standard till the season for drying them returns.—At the time of planting the bulbs, they must be carefully cleaned from any foulnesses at the bottom, by scraping them with the point of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a> till the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> part of the bulb appears; clear them likewise from any loose skins, and even take off their brown skin till they appear white; otherwise this brown skin will tinge the water, and the growth will not succeed so well. The notches in the side of each lead are intended to give easy passage to the water, that, if there should be any foulness or sediment in it, on shaking it a little it may all run through, and fresh water be put in its place. But this shifting the water need not be done more than once or twice in a winter, as there may be occasion from the foulness; and when this is done, the sides of the vessel should be cleaned with a painter's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRUSH">brush</a>, and rinsed out again, and the bulbs themselves washed, by pouring water on them at a little distance. At any time when the outer skins of the bulbs dry, they are to be peeled off, that they may not occasion foulness in the water; and if any dust or foul matter be at any time observed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> on the surface, the method is to fill up the pot or vessel to the rim, and let it run over: this will carry off that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> foulness, and the water may afterwards be poured away to the proper standard. Bulbs of equal sizes should be planted together in the the same pot, that they may all have the same benefit of the water. Narcissuses and hyacinths do well together; as also tulips and jonquils, and crocuses and snowdrops.

FLUDD

Pages 317-317

ROBERT, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and physician of some celebrity in his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>, was the son of Sir Thomas Fludd, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TREASURER">treasurer</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WAR">war</a> to <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a>; and was born at Milgate in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, in the year 1574. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> at St John's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, and afterwards spent six years in travelling through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EUROPE">Europe</a>. He acquired a strong <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTACHMENT">attachment</a> to the Rosicrucian <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, which chiefly consisted of mysticism and jargon, and such as were admitted among them had certain secrets analogous to those of free masonry. On his return home, he took the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of M.D., settled in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, and was chosen a fellow of the college of physicians. His piety was of an enthusiastic <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>, and the seeming depth of his knowledge procured him much admiration, and gave him a temporary fame. It is said that he employed a kind of unintelligible cant when speaking to his patients, which sometimes contributed to their <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RECOVERY">recovery</a>, as it operated on their <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FAITH">faith</a>. He is chiefly known as a sectary in philosophy, and not as a physician. He bleeded the incomprehensible reveries of the Cabalists and Paracelsians, forming a new physical system replete with mystery and absurdity. He believed in two universal principles, the northern <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> condemning, and the southern or rarefying power. Innumerable geniuses he conceived to preside over these, and committed the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a> of diseases to legions of spirits collected from the four winds of heaven. In his estimation, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> subsisted between the macrocosm and the microcosm, or the world of nature and of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a>. All his fancies and whims it is impossible to enumerate, yet they attracted the notice of the philosophers of that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, being supported by mysterious gravity and the shadow of erudition. Even Kepler himself thought his extravagant jargon worthy of refutation, and Gassendi for this purpose wrote his Examen Philosophiae Fluddiana. One of Fludd's performances, entitled Nexus utrinque <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONI">Coni</a>, is illustrated by some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINTS">prints</a> of a very singular and extraordinary nature.

FLUENT

Pages 317-317
