or FLOWING QUANTITY, in the doctrine of fluxions, is the variable quantity which is considered as increasing and decreasing; or the fluent of a given fluxion, is that quantity whose fluxion being taken, according to the rules of that doctrine, shall be the same with the given fluxion. See Fluxions.

FLUID

Pages 317-318

an appellation given to all bodies whose particles easily yield to the least partial pressure, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> force impressed. For the Laws and Properties of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">Fluids</a>, see <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYDROSTATICS">Hydrostatics</a>. There are various kinds of animalcules to be discerned in different fluids by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MICROSCOPE">microscope</a>. Of many remarkable kinds of these, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> is given under the article Animalcule. All of these little creatures are easily destroyed by separating them from their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> element. Naturalists have even fallen upon shorter methods. A <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol16.html#article-NEEDLE">needle</a> point, dipped in spirit of vitriol, and then immersed into a drop of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, readily kills all the animalcules; which, though before frisking about with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> liveliness and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>, no sooner come within the influence of the acid particles, than they spread themselves, and tumble <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> to all appearance dead. The like may be done by a solution of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; only with this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a>, that, by the latter application, they seem to grow vertiginous, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> round and round till they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> down. Tincture of tartar, used in the same manner, kills them still more readily; yet not so, but there <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be apparent marks of their first being sick and convulsed. Inks destroy them as fast as spirit of vitriol, and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> blood produces the same effect. Urine, lack, and <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, all destroy them, though not so fast; besides, that there is some diversity in their figures and appearances, as they receive their deaths from this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> or that. The point of a <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PIN">pin</a> dipped in spittle, presently killed all the kinds of animalcules in puddle water, as Mr Harris supposes it will other animalcules of this kind. All who are acquainted with microscopic observations, know very well, that in water, in which the best glasses can discover no particle of animated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, after a few grains of pepper, or a fragment of a plant of almost any kind, has been some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> in it, animals full of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> are produced; and those in such numbers, as to equal the fluid itself in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>.—When we see a numerous brood of young fishes in a pond, we make no doubt of their having owed their origin to the spawn, that is, to the eggs of the parents of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>. What are we then to think of these? <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> we will consider the progress of <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> in the insect tribes in general, and especially in such of them as are most analogous to these, we shall find it less difficult to give an account of their origin than might have been imagined. A small quantity of water taken from any ditch in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a> months, is found to be full of little <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, seeming in nothing so much as in size to differ from the microscopic animalcules. Nay, water, without these, exposed in open vessels to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>, will be always found to abound with multitudes of them, visible to the naked eye, and full of life and motion. These we know, by their future changes, are the fly worms of the different species of gnats, and multitudes of other fly species; and we can easily determine, that they have owed their origin only to the eggs of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a> fly there deposited. Nay, a closer observation will at any time give ocular <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this; as the flies may be seen laying their eggs there, and the eggs may be followed through all their changes to the fly again. Why then are we to doubt but that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> abounds with other flies and animalcules as minute as the worms in those fluids; and that these last are only the fly worms of the former, which after a proper time spent in that state, will suffer changes like those of the larger kinds, and become flies like those to whose eggs they owed their origin? Vid. Reaumur, Hist. Insect., vol. iv. p. 431. The differently medicated liquors made by infusions of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>, afford a proper matter for the worms of different species of these small flies: and there is no reason to doubt, but that among these some are viviparous, others oviparous; and to this may be, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> owing the different time taken up for the production of these insects in different fluids. Those which are a proper matter for the worms of the viviparous fly, may be soonest found full of them; as, probably the liquor is no sooner in a state to afford them. them proper nourishment, than their parents <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> them there; whereas those produced from the eggs of the little oviparous flies, must, after the liquor is in a proper state, and they are deposited in it in the form of eggs, have a proper time to be hatched, before they can appear alive. It is easy to prove, that the animals we find in these vegetable infusions were brought thither from elsewhere. It is not less easy to prove, that they could not be in the matter infused any more than in the water in which it is infused. Notwithstanding the fabulous accounts of salamanders, it is now well known, that no animal, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> or small, can bear the force of fire for any considerable time; and, by parity of reason, we are not to believe, that any insect, or embryo insect, in any state, can bear the heat of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> water for many minutes. To proceed to inquiries on this foundation: If several tubes filled with water, with a small quantity of vegetable matter, such as pepper, oak bark, truffles, &c., in which, after a time, insects will be discovered by the microscope; and other like tubes be filled with simple water boiled, with water and pepper boiled together, and with water with the two other ingredients all separately boiled in it; when all these liquors come to a proper time for the observation of the microscope, all, as well those which have been boiled as those which have not, will be found equally to abound with insects, and those of the same kind, in infusions of the same kind, whether boiled or not boiled. Those in the infusions which had sustained a heat capable of destroying animal life, must therefore not have subsisted either in the water or in the matters put into it, but must have been brought thither after the boiling; and it seems by no way so probably, as by means of some little winged inhabitants of the air depositing their eggs or worms in these fluids. On this it is natural to ask, how it comes to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a>, that while we see myriads of the progeny of these winged insects in water, we never see themselves? The answer is equally easy, viz. because we can always place a drop of this water immediately before the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FOCUS">focus</a> of the microscope, and keep it there while we are at leisure to examine its contents; but that is not the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> with regard to the air inhabited by the parent flies of these worms, which is an immense <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> in proportion to the water proper for nourishing these worms; and consequently, while the latter are clustered together in heaps, the former may be dispersed and scattered. Nor do we want instances of this, even in insects of a larger kind. In many of our gardens, we frequently find vessels of water filled with worms of the gnat kind, as plentifully, in proportion to their size, as those of other fluids are with animalcules. Every cubic inch of water in these vessels contains many <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-HUNDREDS">hundreds</a> of animals; yet we see many cubic inches of air in the garden not affording one of the parent flies. But neither are we positively to declare that the parent flies of these animalcules are in all states wholly invisible to us; if not singly to be seen, there are some strong reasons to imagine that they may in great clusters. Every one has seen in a clear <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, when looking steadfastly at the sky, that the air is in many places disturbed by motions and convolutions in certain spots. These cannot be the effects of imagination, or of faults in our eyes, because they appear the same to all; and if we consider what would be the case to an eye formed in such a manner as to see nothing smaller than an ox, on viewing the air on a marsh fully peopled with gnats, we must be sensible that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOUDS">clouds</a> of these insects, though to us distinctly enough visible, would appear to such an eye merely as the moving parcels of air in the former instance do to us; and surely it is hence no rash conclusion to infer, that the case may be the same, and that myriads of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> insects, too small to be singly the objects of our view, yet are to us what the clouds of gnats would be in the former case. Nervous Fluid. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">Elastic</a> Fluids. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index.

FLUIDITY

Pages 318-320

is by Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton defined to be, that <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of bodies by which they yield to any force impressed, and which have their parts very easily moved among one another. To this <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a> some have added, that the parts of a fluid are in a continual <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>. This <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> is supported by the solution of salts, and the formation of tinctures. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">If</a> a small bit of saffron is thrown into a phial full of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">yellow</a> tincture <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> soon be communicated to the water to a considerable height, though the phial is allowed to remain at rest; which indicates a motion in those parts of the fluid which touch the saffron, by which its colouring <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> is carried up. With regard to water, this can scarce be denied; the constant exhalations from its surface show, that there must be a perpetual motion in its parts from the ascent of the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STEAM">steam</a> through it. In <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, where sensible <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a> does not take <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, it might be doubted; and accordingly the Newtonian philosophers in general have been of opinion, that there are some substances essentially fluid, from the spherical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a> of their constituent particles. The congelation of mercury, however, by an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTREME">extreme</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, demonstrates that fluidity is not essentially inherent in mercury more than in other bodies. That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> have vacuities in their substance is evident, because they may be made to dissolve certain bodies without sensibly increasing their bulk. For example, water will dissolve a certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>; after which it will receive a little <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>, and after that a little <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-ALUM">alum</a>, without increasing its first dimensions. Here we can scarcely suppose anything else than that the saline particles were interposed between those of the fluid; and as, by the mixture of salt and water, a considerable degree of cold is produced, we may thence easily see why the fluid receives these substances without any increase of bulk. All substances are expanded by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and reduced into less dimensions by cold; therefore, if any substance is added to a fluid, which tends to make it cold, the expansion by the bulk of the substance added will not be so much perceived as if this effect had not happened; and if the quantity added be small, the fluid will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> as much, perhaps more, from the cold produced by the mixture, than it will be expanded from the bulk of the salt. This also may let us know with what these interfaces between the particles of the fluid were filled up; namely, the element of fire <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> heat. The saline particles, up Fluor Worm. See Fasciola, <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-HELMINTHOLOGY">Helminthology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fluke of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCHOR">Anchor</a>, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it which fattens in the ground. See Anchor. Flummery, a wholesome sort of jelly made of oatmeal. The manner of preparing it is as follows. Put three <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> handfuls of finely ground oatmeal to steep, for 24 hours, in two quarts of fair water; then pour off the clear water, and put two quarts of fresh water to it; strain it through a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> sieve, putting in two spoonfuls of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-ORANGE">orange</a> flower water, and a spoonful of sugar; boil it till it is as thick as a halcy pudding, stirring it continually while it is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a>, that it may be very smooth. Fluor, in Physics, a fluid; or, more properly, the state of a body that was before hard or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a>, but is now reduced by fusion or fire into a state of fluidity. Fluor Acid. See Fluoric Acid, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHEMISTRY">Chemistry</a> Index. Fluor Albus, a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLUX">flux</a> incident to women, <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of whiter. See Medicine Index. Fluor <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAR">Spar</a>, or Blue John, called also fluxing spars, vitreous or glass spars, are minerals composed of calcareous <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> united with fluoric acid. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol15.html#article-MINERALOGY">Mineralogy</a> Index. Flushing, a handsome, strong, and considerable town of the United Provinces, in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZEALAND">Zealand</a>, and in the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-WALCHEREN">Walcheren</a>, with a very good harbour, and a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> foreign trade. It was put into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUEEN">Queen</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> for a pledge of their fidelity, and as a security for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> she advanced. It is one of the three places which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> V. advised <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILIP">Philip</a> II. to prefer to with care. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 3. 32° N. Lat. 51° 26'. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUTE">Flute</a>, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> of music, the simplest of all those of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> kind. It is played on by blowing it with the mouth; and the tones or notes are changed by stopping and opening the holes disposed for that purpose along its side. This is a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> instrument. It was at first called the flute à bec, from bec an old Gaulish word signifying the beak of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a> or fowl, but more especially of a cock; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> flute à bec must therefore signify the beaked flute; which appears very proper, on comparing it with the traverso or German flute. The word flute is derived from fluita, the Latin for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAMPREY">lamprey</a> or small eel taken in the Sicilian seas, having <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SEVEN">seven</a> holes immediately below the gills on each side, the precise <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of those in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRONT">front</a> of the flute. By Merlemus this instrument is called the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISTULA">fistula</a> dulcis, seu Anglicus; the lowest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NOTE">note</a>, according to him, for the treble flute, is C fa ut, and the compass of the instrument 15 notes. There is, however, a flute known by the name of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONCERT">concert</a> flute, the lowest note of which is F. Indeed, ever since the introduction of the flute into concerts, the lowest note of the instrument, of what size ever it is, has been called F; when in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> its pitch is determinable only by its correspondence in respect of acuteness or gravity with one or other of the chords in the scala maxima or great system. Besides the true concert flute, others of a less size were soon introduced into concerts of violins; in which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> the method was to write the flute part in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> correspondent. correspondent to its pitch. This practice was introduced in 1710 by one Woodcock, a celebrated performer on this instrument, and William Babell organist of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a> of All-hallows, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">Bread</a> Street, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>. They failed, however, in procuring for the flute a reception into concerts of various instruments; for which reason, one Thomas Stanely, a very curious maker of flutes and other instruments of the like kind, about the year 1732, adverting to the <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SCALE">scale</a> of Mercennius, in which the lowest note was C, invented what he called the new system; in which, by making the flute of such a size as to be a fifth above concert pitch, the lowest note became C, sol, fa ut. By this contrivance the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> of transposing the flute part was taken away; for a flute of this size, adjusted to the system above mentioned, became an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OCTAVE">octave</a> to the violin. To further this <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVENTION">invention</a> of Stanely's, one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEWIS">Lewis</a> Merci, an excellent performer on the flute, published, about the year 1735, six folios for this instrument, three of which are said to be accommodated to Mr. Stanely's new system; but the German flute was now become a favourite instrument, and Stanely's ingenuity failed of its effect. One great objection indeed lies against this instrument, which, however, equally affects all perforated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a>; namely, that they are never perfectly in tune, or cannot be made to play all their notes with equal exactness. The utmost that the makers of them can do is to tune them to some one key; as the hautboy to C, the German flute to D, and the English flute to F; and to effect this truly, is a matter of no small difficulty. The English flutes made by the younger Stanely came nearest of any to perfection; but those of <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRESLAU">Breslau</a>, though excellent in their tone, are all too flat in the upper octave. For these reasons some are induced to think, that the utmost degree of proficiency on any of those instruments is not worth the labour of attaining it. German Flute, is an instrument entirely different from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> flute. It is not, like that, put into the mouth to be played; but the end is flopped with a stopper or plug, and the lower lip is applied to a hole about two inches and a half or three inches distant from the end. This instrument is usually about a foot and a half long; rather bigger at the upper end than the lower; and perforated with holes, besides that for the mouth, the lowest of which is stopped and opened by the little finger's pressing on a <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a> or sometimes a silver key, like those in hautboys, bassoons, &c. Its <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOUND">sound</a> is exceeding sweet and agreeable; and serves as a treble in a concert. Flute, or Flutti, is a kind of long vessel, with flat ribs or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOOR">floor</a> timbers, round behind, and swollen in the middle; serving chiefly for the carrying of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVISIONS">provisions</a> in fleets or squadrons of ships; though it is often used in merchandise. The word flute taken for a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> or vessel, is derived, according to Borel, from the ancient flotte, a little boat. In the verbal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MIRACLES">miracles</a> of St. Catharine of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWEDEN">Sweden</a>, in the 12th century, we read Unus equum suum una cum mercibus magni ponderis introduxit super infrumentum de lignis fabricatum, vulgariter dictum flotta. Upon which the Bollandists observe, that in some copies it is read flotta, an instrument called by the Latins ratis; and that the word flutta or flotta arose from flotten or flotten, "to float." Flutes, or Flutings, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">Architecture</a>, are perpendicular channels or cavities cut along the shaft of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLUMN">column</a> or pilaster. They are supposed to have been first introduced in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a> of the plaiting of women's robes; and are therefore called by the Latins fringes and rugae. The French call them cannelures, as being excavations; and we, flutes or flutings, as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEARING">bearing</a> some resemblance to the musical instrument so called. They are chiefly affected in the Ionic order, in which they had their first rise; though they are also used in all the richer orders, as the Corinthian and Composite; but rarely in the Doric, and scarcely ever in the Tuscan.

FLUX

Pages 320-321

in <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METALLURGY">Metallurgy</a>, is sometimes used synonymously with fufion. For instance, an ore, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, is said to be in a liquid flux, when it is completely fused. But the word flux is generally used to signify certain saline matters, which facilitate the fusion of ores, and other matters which are difficultly fusible in effays and reductions of ores; such are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ALKALIES">alkalies</a>, nitre, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BORAX">borax</a>, tartar, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>. But the word flux is more particularly applied to mixtures of different proportions of only nitre and tartar; and these fluxes are called by particular names, according to the proportions of these ingredients, as in the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">White</a> Flux, is made with equal parts of nitre and of tartar detonated together, by which they are alkalinized. The residuum of this detonation is an alkali composed of the alkalies of the nitre and of the tartar, both which are absolutely of the same <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a>. As the proportion of nitre in this mixture is more than is sufficient to consume entirely all the inflammable matter of the tartar, the alkali remaining after the detonation is perfectly white, and is therefore called white flux; and as this alkali is made very quickly, it is also called extemporaneous alkali. When a small <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> only of white flux is made, as a few ounces for instance, some nitre always remains undecomposed, and a little of the inflammable principle of the tartar, which gives a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> or even a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> to some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the flux; but this does not happen when a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantity of white flux is made; because then the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> is much greater. This small quantity of undecomposed nitre and tartar which remains in white flux is not hurtful in most of the metallic fusions in which this flux is employed; but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the flux be required perfectly pure, it might easily be disengaged from those extraneous matters by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and strong calcination, without fusion. Crude Flux. By crude flux is meant the mixture of nitre and tartar in any proportions, without detonation. Thus the mixture of equal parts of the two salts used in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of the white flux, or the mixture of one part of nitre and two parts of tartar for the preparation of the black flux, are each of them a crude flux before detonation. It has also been called white flux, from its colour; but this might occasion it to be confounded with the white flux above described. The name, therefore, of crude flux is more convenient. Crude flux is detonated and alkalinized during the reductions and fusions in which it is employed; and is then changed into white or black flux, according to the proportions of which it is composed. This detonation produces good effects in these fusions and reductions, if the swelling and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRAVASATION">extravasation</a> of the detonating matters be guarded against. Accordingly, crude flux may be employed successfully in many operations; as, for instance, in the ordinary operation for procuring the regulus of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>. Black Flux. Black flux is produced from the mixture of two parts of tartar and one part of nitre detonated together. As the quantity of nitre which enters into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a> of this flux is not sufficient to consume all the inflammable matters of the tartar, the alkali which remains after the detonation contains much black matter, of the nature of coal, and is therefore called black flux.

FLUXIONS

Pages 399-400

Inverse Method Let us suppose we know that when \( x = a \), then \( y = b \); assume \( x = a + t \), and \( y = b + u \), then it is manifest, that, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the value of \( u \) be found by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERIES">series</a> involving \( t \), all the terms of the series ought to vanish when \( t = 0 \). From the assumed values of \( x \) and \( y \) the equation \[ \dot{y} + \dot{x} - m \dot{x}^2 = 0 \] becomes \[ \dot{u} + (b + u) \dot{t} - m(a + t)\ddot{t} = 0. \] Assume now \[ u = A t^n + B t^{n+1} + C t^{n+2} + \ldots \] then, proceeding as before, we find \[ A t^n + (a + 1) B t^{n+1} + (a + 2) C t^{n+2} + \ldots \] \[ + b - m a^n - m a^{n-1} t - m \frac{n(n-1)}{1 \cdot 2} a^{n-2} t^2 + \ldots = 0. \] It is necessary, in this equation, to assume \( a = 1 = 0 \), <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> \( x = 1 \), and hence we find \[ A = m a^n - b, \quad B = \frac{m a^{n-1} - r a^n + b}{2}, \] \[ C = \frac{m n(n-1) a^{n-2} - m a^{n-1} + m a^n - b}{2 \cdot 3}, \] \&c. If we now substitute \( x = a \), and \( y = b \) for \( t \) and \( u \) respectively, the result <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> have all the generality that belongs to a primitive equation, expressing the relation between \( x \) and \( y \). Of Fluxional Equations of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> or higher orders. 194. Whatever difficulties occur in finding the primitive equation of a fluxional equation of the first order, it will easily be conceived, that these difficulties must be greater and more numerous when we have to consider fluxional equations of the second and higher orders. One of the most simple <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of an equation of the second order is this \[ \dot{y} - X \dot{x}^2 = 0, \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} = X, \] where \( X \) denotes a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FUNCTION">function</a> of \( x \), the variable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> whose fluxion is supposed to be constant; in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, because \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} = X \dot{x} \), we have \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x} = \int X \dot{x} \). Let \( P \) denote that function of which \( X \dot{x} \) is the fluxion, and \( c \), as usual, an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDETERMINATE">indeterminate</a> constant quantity, then \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x} = P + c \), and \( \dot{y} = P \dot{x} + c \dot{x} \), and taking the fluents a second <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> \[ \dot{y} = \int P \dot{x} + c \dot{x} + c' \] where \( c' \) denotes a second indeterminate constant quantity. As \( \int P \dot{x} = P x - \int \dot{P} x = x \int X \dot{x} - \int X x \dot{x} \) we have also \[ y = x \int X \dot{x} - \int X x \dot{x} + c x + c'. \] Suppose, for example, that the equation is \( y = ax^3 = 0 \), so that \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x^3} = ax^2 \); here \( X = ax \), and therefore \[ y = x \int ax^2 - \int ax^3 + c x + c' \] \[ = \frac{1}{2} ax^3 - \frac{1}{3} ax^3 + c x + c' \] \[ = \frac{1}{6} ax^3 + c x + c'. \] In the very same manner we may deduce from the equation of the third order \[ \dot{y} - X \dot{x}^3 = 0, \quad \text{or} \quad \frac{\dot{y}}{x^3} = X \] its primitive equation; thus we have \[ \frac{\dot{y}}{x^3} = X \dot{x}, \quad \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} = \int X \dot{x} = P + c, \] where \( P \) denotes such a function of \( x \), that its fluxion is \( X \dot{x} \), and \( c \) represents a constant quantity. Again \[ \frac{\dot{y}}{x} = P \dot{x} + c \dot{x}, \] \[ \frac{\dot{y}}{x} = \int P \dot{x} + c \dot{x} + c' = Q + c x + c'; \] here \( Q \) is put for \( \int P \dot{x} \), and \( c' \) for a second constant quantity. In like manner we have \[ \dot{y} = Q \dot{x} + c x + c' \dot{x}, \] and \( \dot{y} = \int Q \dot{x} + c x + c' \dot{x} + c'' \); and as \( P \) and \( Q \) are functions of \( x \), the fluents of \( P \dot{x} \) and \( Q \dot{x} \) may be found by the methods formerly explained. 195. Let us next consider such equations as involve only \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} \) and constant quantities. In order to abridge let us put \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} = p \), then such an equation may be generally expressed thus \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} = P \), where \( P \) denotes some known known function of \( p \); now as \( \frac{y}{x} = p \), by taking the fluxions, and observing that \( x \) is constant, we have \[ \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} = \frac{\dot{p}}{x}, \quad \text{hence} \quad \frac{\dot{p}}{x} = P, \quad \text{and} \quad \dot{x} = \frac{\dot{p}}{P}, \quad \text{and} \quad x = \int \frac{\dot{p}}{P}; \] let the value of \( \dot{x} \) be substituted instead of it in the equation \( y = p \dot{x} \), and it becomes \( \dot{y} = \frac{\dot{p}}{P} \) and hence \[ y = \int \frac{\dot{p}}{P}; \] thus it appears that if we can find the fluents \( \int \frac{\dot{p}}{P} \) and \( \int \frac{\dot{p}}{P} \), we shall have the primitive equation when we eliminate \( p \) by means of these two equations \[ x = c + \int \frac{\dot{p}}{P}, \quad y = c' + \int \frac{\dot{p}}{P}, \] where \( c \) and \( c' \) denote the two indeterminate constant quantities that ought to enter into the primitive equation. Suppose for example that the equation is \[ \frac{(x^2 + y^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{x} = a, \] which, by putting \( p \) for \( \frac{y}{x} \), and \( \frac{\dot{p}}{x} \) for \( \frac{\dot{y}}{x^2} \) becomes transformed to \[ \frac{(1 + p^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{p} = a; \] hence we have \[ \dot{x} = -\frac{a p}{(1 + p^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}, \quad \dot{y} = p \dot{x} = \frac{-a p \dot{p}}{(1 + p^2)^{\frac{3}{2}}}, \] \[ x = c - \frac{a p}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}, \quad y = c' + \frac{a}{\sqrt{(1 + p^2)}}; \]

fluxions of geometrical plane magnitudes: And first let it be required to find the expression for the fluxion of BDPC the area bounded fig. 1. by CP, a curve line, and by CB, PD, the ordinates at its extremities, and BD, the portion of AE, the line of the abscissas, which lies between those ordinates. Let the numerical measures of AD and PD, the co-ordinates at the point P, be denoted by \( x \) and \( y \), and the numerical measure of the area BDPC by \( s \); then then \( y \) and \( x \) may both be considered as functions of the abscissa \( x \). Let \( x \), or \( AD \), be supposed to change its value, and to become \( AD' \), and let \( DP' \) and \( BD'PC \) be the corresponding new values of \( y \) and \( s \); then \( DD' \) and \( DD'P'P \) will be the geometrical expressions for the simultaneous increments of the abscissa and area. But, as one of these quantities is a line, and the other a space, they cannot be compared in respect of their ratio. Therefore, let us consider \( a \) as denoting a line whose numerical value is unity, and then the numerical values of the increments of the abscissa and area may be considered as analogous to the geometrical quantities \( DD' \times a \), and the area \( DD'P'P \) respectively, which quantities being homogeneous may now be compared with each other. We are now to investigate the limit of \[ \frac{\text{area } DD'P'P}{a \times DD'} \] the general expression for the ratio of the increments of \( s \) and \( x \). Draw \( PM \) and \( PN \) parallel to \( AE \), meeting the ordinates in \( M \) and \( N \). The curvilinear area \( DD'P'P \) is greater than the rectangle \( DD'MP \), that is greater than \( PD \times DD' \); but less than the rectangle \( DD'PN \), that is, less than \( PD' \times DD' \), therefore \[ \frac{\text{area } DD'P'P}{a \times DD'} > \frac{PD \times DD'}{a \times DD'} > \frac{PD'}{a} \] and \[ \frac{\text{area } DD'P'P}{a \times DD'} < \frac{PD' \times DD'}{a \times DD'} < \frac{PD'}{a} \] But the increments being supposed to be continually diminished, \( \frac{PD}{a} \) is the limit of \( \frac{PD'}{a} \), therefore \( \frac{PD}{a} \) is also the limit of \( \frac{\text{area } DD'P'P}{a \times DD'} \), and hence (§ 21.) \[ \frac{s}{x} = \frac{PD}{a} = \frac{y}{1} = y, \quad \text{and} \quad \dot{s} = \dot{y} \dot{x}. \] That is, the fluxion of a curvilinear area is equal to the product of the ordinate, and the fluxion of the abscissa. 62. Before we proceed to investigate the expression for the fluxion of an arch of a curve, it is necessary that we should inquire what is the limiting ratio of an arch of a curve to its chord. Let \( APB \) be any curve line, all the parts of which are concave towards its chord \( AP \). Let \( AQ, QP \) be tangents at the extremities of the arch, and let \( aq \rho \) be a triangle similar to \( APQ \), but having its base \( ap \) of a given magnitude, then \[ AQ + QP : AP :: aq + q \rho : ap. \] Suppose now the point \( P \) to approach to \( A \), then the angles at \( A \) and \( P \), and consequently the angles at \( a \) and \( \rho \), which are equal to them, will decrease, and may become less than any assignable angles; therefore, the limit of the ratio of \( aq + q \rho \) to \( ap \) is evidently a ratio of equality; hence also the limit of the ratio of \( AQ + QP \) to \( AP \) is the ratio of equality; and since the arch \( AP \) is less than \( AQ + QP \), but greater than its chord \( AP \), the limit of the arch \( AP \) to its chord \( AP \) must also be the ratio of equality. 63. We proceed now to find the fluxion of an arch of a curve. Let \( APP' \) be a curve line of any kind, and \( AB, BP \) any two co-ordinates at a point \( P \) in the curve. Put \( x \) for \( AB \), the abscissa, \( y \) for \( BP \), the ordinate, and \( z \) for the curve line \( AP \), then \( z \) and \( y \) may be considered as each a function of \( x \). Draw \( P'B' \) another ordinate, and draw \( PM \) parallel to \( AB \), meeting \( P'B' \) in \( M \); and draw the chord \( PP' \); then \( PM, MP' \) and the arch \( PP' \) are the simultaneous increments of \( x, y, \) and \( z \) respectively. Now we have \[ \frac{\text{arch } PP'}{PM} = \frac{\text{arch } PP'}{\text{chord } PP'} \times \frac{\text{chord } PP'}{PM}. \] But chord \( PP' = \sqrt{(PM^2 + MP'^2)} = PM \sqrt{(1 + \frac{MP'^2}{PM^2})} \); therefore, \[ \frac{\text{arch } PP'}{PM} = \frac{\text{arch } PP'}{\text{chord } PP'} \times \sqrt{(1 + \frac{MP'^2}{PM^2})}. \] Suppose now the increments to be continually diminished, then, as \( \frac{z}{x} = \text{limit of } \frac{\text{arch } PP'}{PM} \), and \( \frac{y^2}{x^2} = \text{limit of } \frac{\text{chord } PP'}{\text{chord } PP'} \) (inf. §) we have \[ \frac{z}{x} = \sqrt{(1 + \frac{y^2}{x^2})}, \quad \text{and} \quad \dot{z} = \sqrt{(\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)}. \] Hence it appears that the square of the fluxion of a curve line of any kind is equal to the sum of the squares of the

fluxions may be applied to deduce from some one of those properties rules for finding that centre in any proposed case. The property of centres of gravity which we shall employ as the foundation of the application of the method of fluxions to its determination may be enunciated shortly thus. Let \( C \) be the centre of gravity of a mass of matter denoted by \( M \), and \( c \) the centre of gravity of another mass \( m \), and \( D \) the centre of gravity of the two masses \( M \) and \( m \), from these points let perpendiculars \( CA, c a, DE \) be drawn to any straight line \( PQ \), then \[ M \times CA + m \times c a = (M + m) \times DE. \] 167. Let us now suppose that \( AP \) is any curve line having weight, of which the centre of gravity is required, and that \( PB, PD \) are co-ordinates drawn from any point in the curve perpendicular to \( AB, AD \) two axes at right angles to each other; let the arch \( AP \) receive any increment \( Pp \), let \( C \) be the centre of gravity of \( AP \), \( G \) the centre of gravity of \( Pp \), and \( C' \) the centre of gravity of \( APp \). From \( C \) and \( G \) draw \( CE, CF, GH, GK \) perpendicular to the axes \( AB, AD \). Put \( PD = x, PB = y, CF = X, CE = Y, AP = z \), also let the arch \( APp = z' \), and let the distances of \( C' \) its centre of gravity from the axes \( AD, AB \) be denoted by \( X', Y' \) respectively; then, observing that the arch \( Pp = z' - z \), by the proposition in last §, \[ X + (z' - z) \times GK = z' X' \] \[ \frac{z' X'}{z' - z} = z X = GK; \] If we now suppose the arch \( Pp \) to be continually diminished, and observe that \( z' X' - z X \), and \( z' - z \) are the simultaneous increments of \( z X \) and \( z \), it will appear (\$ 23.) that \[ \frac{\text{flux. of } (z X)}{z} = \text{limit of } GK. \] By the very same way of reasoning we find \[ \frac{\text{flux. of } (z Y)}{z} = \text{limit of } GH, \] but the point \( p \) approaching to \( P \), it is manifest that the point \( G \) will also approach to \( P \), so that the limit of \( GK \) is \( PD \) or \( x \), and the limit of \( GH \) is \( PB \) or \( y \), hence \[ \frac{\text{flux. } (z X)}{z} = x, \quad \frac{\text{flux. } (z Y)}{z} = y, \] \[ \text{flux. } (z X) = x \dot{z} \text{ flux. } (z Y) = y \dot{z}. \] Taking now the fluents of each side of these equations, and dividing by \( z \), \[ X = \int \frac{x \dot{z}}{z}, \quad Y = \int \frac{y \dot{z}}{z}; \] It is evident that by these two equations the position of \( C \) the centre of gravity is determined. 168. Let us next suppose that it is required to find \( C \) Fig. 37., the centre of gravity of the plane area \( APB \). As the arch \( AP \) was in last § supposed to receive the increment \( Pp \), so let the area \( APB \) now receive the increment \( BPp \), and let \( C, C' \) and \( G \) (which in the former case were supposed to be the centres of gravity of the arches \( AP, APp, \) and \( Pp \) respectively) now be supposed to be the centres of gravity of the areas \( APB, A_p b, \) and \( BPPp \); put the area \( APB = r \), the area \( A_p b = r' \), and let \( X, Y, X', Y' \) denote as before. Then, reasoning exactly as in last case, we have (by § 166.), \[ s X + (z' - z) \times GK = z' X', \] \[ s Y + (z' - z) \times GH = z' Y' \] hence... 169. Let it next be required to find the centre of gravity of the surface of a solid generated by the revolution of the curve AP about AB as an axis. Let the surface of the solid be conceived to receive an increment generated by Pp an arch of the curve. In this case it is evident that the centres of gravity of the surface generated by the curve AP, the surface generated by the curve APp, and the surface generated by the arch PP, will each be in AB, the axis of the solid; suppose them to be at E, E' and H respectively. Put AE = X, AE' = X', also put s for the surface generated by AP, and s' for the surface generated by APp, then as before (from § 166.) we have \[ sX + (s'-s)AH = s'X', \] hence \[ \frac{s'X' - sX}{s-s} = AH, \] and \[ \text{flux.}(sX) = \lim. AH. \] but the point p approaching to P, the limit of AH is manifestly AB or x, therefore \[ \text{flux.}(sX) = x, \quad \text{and } X = \int \frac{x}{s}, \] or since \( s = 2\pi y^2 \) (\$ 65.), then \[ X = \frac{2\pi \int xy}{\int y^2}. \] 170. If instead of the centre of gravity of the surface generated by AP, the centre of gravity of the solid generated by the revolution of the plane figure APB about AB as an axis be required, the reasoning will be the very same as in last §, substituting the solid generated by the plane figure instead of the surface generated by the curve line; so that putting s for the content of the solid, and X for AE the distance of its centre of gravity from the vertex, we have also \[ X = \int \frac{x}{s}, \] but in this case \( s = \pi y^2 \) (\$ 64.), therefore \[ X = \frac{\pi \int y^2 x}{\int y^2}. \] 171. We shall now apply these formulas to some examples. Example 1. Let it be required to find the centre of gravity of AP an arch of a circle. Suppose AB to be a part of the diameter, and in addition to the notation of § 167. put a for the radius of the circle, then from the nature of the curve, \( y^2 = 2ax - x^2 \), hence (proceeding as in § 165. Ex. 1.) we have \( \dot{x} = \frac{a}{y} \) and therefore \( \dot{y} = a \dot{x} \), and \( \ddot{x} = \frac{a \dot{x}}{y} \), but from the equation \( y^2 = 2ax - x^2 \), by taking the fluxions we get \( \dot{y} = a \dot{x} - x \dot{x} \), and hence \( \frac{\dot{x}}{y} = \frac{a \dot{x}}{y} - \dot{y} = \dot{x} - \dot{y} \), therefore \( \dot{x} = a(\dot{x} - \dot{y}) \); substituting now the values of \( \dot{x} \) and \( \dot{y} \) in the formula of § 167 we have \[ X = \int \frac{x \dot{x}}{z} - \frac{a}{z} \int (\dot{x} - \dot{y}) \] \[ = \frac{a}{z} (x - y + c) \] \[ Y = \int \frac{y \dot{x}}{z} = \frac{a}{z} \int \dot{x} \] \[ = \frac{a}{z} (x + c). \] To discover the values of the constant quantities c, c', we have from the equations in which they occur, \[ ac = X - ax + ay, \quad ac' = Y - ax; \] but when \( x = 0 \), then \( x, y, X \) and \( Y \) are each = 0, therefore \( c = 0 \), and \( c' = 0 \), thus we have simply \[ X = \frac{a(x-y)}{z}, \quad Y = \frac{ax}{z}. \]

FLY

Pages 402-408

in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-ZOOLOGY">Zoology</a>, a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> order of insects, the distinguishing characteristic of which is, that their wings are transparent. By this they are distinguished from beetles, butterflies, grasshoppers, &c. Flies are subdivided into those which have four, and those which have two wings. Of those with four wings there are several genera <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> kinds; as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANT">ant</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEE">bee</a>, the ichneumon, &c. Of those with two wings, there are likewise several kinds, as the gad-fly, gnat, <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>-fly, &c. For their classification and <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURAL_HISTORY"><a class="xref"</a> href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, see Entomology. House Fly. See <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSCA">Musca</a>. Petiflent Fly. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABYSSINIA">Abyssinia</a>. Fly, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CROSS">cross</a> with leaden weights at its ends; or rather, a heavy wheel at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> to the axis of a windlass, jack, or the like; by means of which, the force of the power, whatever it is, is not only preserved, but equally distributed in all parts of the revolution of the machine. See Mechanics. Flies for <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">Fishing</a>. See Fishing Fly. Vegetable Fly, a curious natural production chiefly found in the West Indies. "Excepting that it has no wings, it resembles the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRONE">drone</a> both in size and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a> more than any other British insect. In the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of May it buries itself in the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a>, and begins to vegetate. By the latter end of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a>, the tree is arrived at its full growth, and resembles a coral branch; and is about three inches <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>, and bears several little pods, which dropping off become <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WORMS">worms</a>, and from thence flies, like the British caterpillar." Such was the account originally given of this extraordinary production. But several boxes of these flies having been sent to Dr Hill for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a>, his report was this: "There is in Martinique a fungus of the clavaria kind, different in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> from those hitherto known. It produces sboles from its sides; I call it therefore clavaria lobolifera. It grows on putrid animal bodies, as our fungus ex pede equino from the dead <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>'s hoof. The cicada is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> in Martinique; and in its nymphal state, in which the old authors call it tettigometra, it buries itself under dead leaves to wait its change; and when the season is unfavourable, many perish. The seeds of the clavaria find a proper <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BED">bed</a> on this dead insect, and grow. The tettigometra is among the cicadas in the British <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MUSEUM">museum</a>; the clavaria is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> now known. This is the fact, and all the fact; though the untaught inhabitants suppose a fly to vegetate, and though there is a Spanish <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of the plant's growing into a trifoliate tree, and it has been figured with the creature <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLYING">flying</a> with this tree upon its back." See Edwards' Gleanings of Natural History. Fly-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">Boat</a>, or Flight, a large flat-bottomed Dutch vessel, whose burden is generally from 600 to 1200 tons. It is distinguished by a very high stern, resembling a Gothic turret, and by very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROAD">broad</a> buttocks below. Fly-Catcher, in Zoology. See Muscicapa. Venus's Fly-Trap, a kind of sensitive plant. See Dionaea Muscipula, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Fly-Tree, in Natural History, a name given by the common people of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMERICA">America</a> to a tree, whose leaves, they say, at a certain <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the year produce flies. On examining these leaves about the middle of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>, the time at which the flies used to be produced, there are found on them a sort of bags of a tough <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>, of about the size of a filbert, and of a dusky greenish colour. On opening one of these bags with a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-KNIFE">knife</a>, there is usually found a single full grown fly, of the gnat kind, and a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of small worms, which in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> or two more have wings and fly away in the form of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARENT">parent</a>. The tree is of the mulberry kind, and its leaves are usually very largely stocked with these insect bags; and the generality of them are found to contain the insects in their worm state; when they become winged, they soon make their way out. The bags begin to appear when the leaves are young, and afterwards grow with them; but they never rumple the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> or injure its shape. They are of the kind of leaf-<a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-GALLS">galls</a>, and partake in all respects, except size, of a species we have frequent on the large maple, or, as it is called, the ficamore. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLYERS">Flyers</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCHITECTURE">architecture</a>, such stairs as go straight, and do not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WIND">wind</a> round, or have the steps made tapering; but the fore and back <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of each stair and the ends respectively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARALLEL">parallel</a> to one another: So that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> one flight do not carry you to your designed height, there is a broad half space; and then you fly again, with steps everywhere of the same breadth and length as before. Flyers, the performers in a celebrated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> among the Mexicans, which was made on certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> festivals, and is thus described by Clavigero in his History of that people. "They fought in the woods for an extremely lofty tree, which, after stripping it of its branches and bark, they brought to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a>, and fixed in the centre of some large <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a>. They called the point of the tree in a wooden <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CYLINDER">cylinder</a>, which, on account of some resemblance in its shape, the Spaniards called a <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-MORTAR">mortar</a>. From this cylinder hung four strong <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROPES">ropes</a>, which served to support a square frame. In the space between the cylinder and the frame, they fixed four other thick ropes, which they twisted as many times round the tree as there were revolutions to be made by the flyers. These ropes were drawn through four holes, made in the middle of the four planks of which the frame consisted. The four <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> flyers, disguised like <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EAGLES">eagles</a>, herons, and other birds, mounted the tree with great agility, by means of a rope which was laced about it from the ground up to the frame; from the frame they mounted one at a time successively upon the cylinder, and after having danced there a little, they tied themselves round with the ends of the ropes, which were drawn through the holes of the frame, and launching with a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a> from it, began their flight with their wings expanded. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a> of their bodies put the frame and the cylinder in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a>; the frame by its revolutions gradually untwisted the cords by which the flyers swung; so that as the ropes lengthened, they made so much the greater circles in their flight. Whilst these four were flying, a fifth danced upon the cylinder, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> a little drum, or waving a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FLAG">flag</a>, without the smallest <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a> of the danger he was in of being precipitated from such a height. The others who were upon the frame (10 or 12 persons generally mounted), as soon as they <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> the flyers in their last revolution, precipitated themselves by the same ropes, in order to reach the ground at the same time amidst the acclamations of the populace. Those who precipitated themselves in this manner by the ropes, that they might make a still greater display of their agility, Flying agility, frequently passed from one rope to another, at that part where, on account of the little distance between them, it was possible for them to do so. The most essential point of this performance consisted in proportioning to justify the height of the tree with the length of the ropes, that the flyers should reach the ground with 13 revolutions, to represent by such number their century of 52 years, composed in the manner we have already mentioned. This celebrated diversion is still in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>; but no particular <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> is paid to the number of the revolutions of the flyers; as the frame is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> hexagonal or octagonal, and the flyers six or eight in number. In some places they put a rail round the frame, to prevent accidents, which were frequent after the conquest; as the Indians became much given to drinking, and used to mount the tree when intoxicated with wine or brandy, and were unable to keep their station on so great a height, which was usually 60 feet.

FLYING

Pages 408-409

the progressive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BIRD">bird</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other winged animal, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>. The parts of birds chiefly concerned in flying are the wings and tail; by the first, the bird sustains and wafts himself along; and by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, he is assisted, in ascending and descending, to keep his body poised and upright, and to obviate the vacillations thereof. It is by the size and strength of the pectoral muscles, that birds are so well disposed for quick, strong, and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> flying. These muscles, which in men are scarcely a 70th <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the muscles of the body, in birds exceed and outweigh all the other muscles taken together; upon which Mr Willoughby makes this reflection, that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it be possible for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> to fly, his wings must be so contrived and adapted, that he may make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of his legs, and not his arms, in managing them. The tail, Messrs Willoughby, Ray, and many others, imagine to be principally employed in steering and <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TURNING">turning</a> the body in the air, as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUDDER">rudder</a>; but Borelli has put it beyond all doubt, that this is the least use of it, which is chiefly to assist the bird in its ascent and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCENT">descent</a> in the air, and to obviate the vacillations of the body and wings; for, as to turning to this or that side, it is performed by the wings and inclination of the body, and but very little by the help of the tail. The flying of a bird, in effect, is quite a different thing from the rowing of a vessel. Birds do not vibrate their wings towards the tail, as oars are struck towards the stern, but waft them downwards; nor does the tail of the bird cut the air at <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANGLES">angles</a> as the rudder does the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; but is disposed horizontally, and preserves the same situation whatever way the bird turns. In effect, as a vessel is turned about on its centre of gravity to the right, by a brisk application of the oars to the left; so a bird, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEATING">beating</a> the air with its right wing alone, towards the tail, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> turn its fore part to the left. Thus pigeons changing their course to the left, would labour it with their right wing, keeping the other almost at rest. Birds of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> neck alter their course by the inclination of their head and neck; which altering the course of gravity, the bird will proceed in a new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>. The manner of Flying is thus. The bird first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BENDS">bends</a> his legs, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a> with a violent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAP">leap</a> from the ground; then opens and expands the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JOINTS">joints</a> of his wings, so as to make a right line perpendicular to the sides of his body: thus the wings, with all the feathers therein, constitute one continued lamina. Being now raised a little above the horizon, and vibrating the wings with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> force and velocity perpendicularly against the subject air, that fluid resists those succussions, both from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> inactivity and elasticity, by means of which the whole body of the bird is protruded. The resistance the air makes to the withdrawing of the wings, and consequently the progress of the bird, will be so much the greater, as the waft or stroke of the fan of the wing is longer: but as the force of the wing is continually diminished by this resistance, when the two forces continue to be in equilibrium, the bird will remain suspended in the same <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>; for the bird only ascends so long as the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARCH">arch</a> of air the wing describes makes a resistance equal to the excess of the specific gravity of the bird above the air. If the air, therefore, be so rare as to give way with the same velocity as it is struck withal, there will be no resistance, and consequently the bird can never mount. Birds never fly upwards in a perpendicular line, but always in a parabola. In a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a> ascent, the natural and <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a> tendency would oppose and destroy each other, so that the progress would be very slow. In a direct descent they would aid one another, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> would be too precipitate. Artificial Flying, that attempted by men, by the affluence of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">mechanics</a>. The art of flying has been attempted by several persons in all ages. The Leucadians, out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>, are reported to have had a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of precipitating a man from a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> cliff into the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, first fixing feathers, variously expanded, round his body, in order to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> the fall. Friar <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-BACON">Bacon</a>, who lived near 500 years ago, not only affirms the art of flying possible, but affords us, that he himself knew how to make an engine wherein a man fitting might be able to convey himself through the air like a bird; and further adds, that there was then one who had tried it with success. The secret consisted in a couple of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> thin hollow <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a> globes, exhausted of air; which being much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than air, would sustain a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> whereon a person might sit. Father Francisco Lana, in his Prodromo, proposes the same thing, as his own thought. He computes, that a round vessel of plate <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BRASS">brass</a>, 14 feet in diameter, weighing three ounces the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> foot, will only weigh 1848 ounces; whereas a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of air of the same bulk will weigh 2155½ ounces; so that the globe will not only be sustained in the air, but will carry with it a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> of 373½ ounces; and by increasing the bulk of the globe, without increasing the thickness of the metal, he adds, a vessel might be made to carry a much greater weight.—But the fallacy is obvious: a globe of the dimensions he describes, Dr Hook shows, would not sustain the prelure of the air, but be crushed inwards. Besides, in whatever ratio the bulk of the globe were increased, in the same must the thickness of the metal, and consequently the weight be increased: so that there would be no advantage in such augmentation. See Aerostation. The same author describes an engine for flying, invented by the Sieur Belnier, a smith of Sablé, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAINE">Maine</a>. Vid. Philosoph. Collect. No. 1. The philosophers of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">King</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARLES">Charles</a> the second's reign were mightily busied about this art. The famous Bishop Wilkins was so confident of success in it, that he says, he does not question but in future ages it will be as usual to hear a man call for his wings, when he is going a journey, as it is now to call for his boots. Flying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDGE">Bridge</a>. See Bridge. Flying Fish, a name given to several <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of fish, which, by means of long fins, can keep themselves out of the water for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>. See Exocoetus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ICHTHYOLOGY">Ichthyology</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Flying <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PINION">Pinion</a>, is part of a clock, having a fly or fan whereby to gather air, and to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BRIDLE">bridle</a> the rapidity of the clock's motion, when the weight descends in the striking part.

FO

Pages 409-409
or Foe; an idol of the Chinese. He was originally worshipped in the Indies, and transported from thence into China, together with the fables with which the Indian books were filled. He is said to have performed most wonderful things, which the Chinese have described in several volumes, and represented by cuts. See of Fo. See China, No 104. Fo-Kien. See Foreign.

FOCUS

Pages 409-409

in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GEOMETRY">Geometry</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONIC_SECTIONS">Conic Sections</a>, is applied to certain <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POINTS">points</a> in the parabola, ellipse, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HYPERBOLA">hyperbola</a>, where the rays reflected from all parts of these curves concur and meet. See Conic Sections. Focus, in <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPTICS">Optics</a>, a point in which any <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of rays, after being reflected <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> refracted, meet.

FODDER

Pages 409-409

any kind of meat for horses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> other cattle. In some places, hay and straw, mingled together, is peculiarly denominated fodder. Fodder, in the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is used for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREROGATIVE">prerogative</a> that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> has, to be provided with corn and other meats for his horses, by the subjects, in his warlike expeditions. Fodder, among miners, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> containing 22 hundred and a half <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a> the fodder is only 20 hundred weight. FODDERING a ship. See Fothering. FOENUGREEK. See Trigonella, <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. FOENUS nauticum. Where <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONEY">money</a> was <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LENT">lent</a> to a merchant, to be employed in a beneficial trade, with condition to be repaid with extraordinary <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> such voyage was safely performed. The agreement was sometimes called foenus nauticum, sometimes usura maritima. But as this gave an opening for furious and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> contracts, 19 Geo. II. c. 37. enacts, that all money lent on <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTTOMRY">bottomry</a>, or at respondentia, on vessels bound to or from the East Indies, shall be expressly lent only upon the ship or merchandise; the lender to have the benefit of salvage, &c. Blackst. Com. ii. 459. Mol. de Jur. Mar. 361.

FOETOR

Pages 409-409

in Medicine, fetid effluvia arising from the body <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> thereof.

FOETUS

Pages 409-409

the young of all viviparous animals whilst in the womb, and of oviparous animals before being hatched: the name is transferred by botanists to the embryos of vegetables. Strictly, the name is applied to the young after it is perfectly formed; previous to which it is usually called Embryo. See Anatomy <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. In the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> fetus are several peculiarities not to be found in the adult; some of them are as follow: 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTERIES">arteries</a> of the navel string, which are continuations of the hypogastrics, are, after the birth, shrivelled up, and form the ligamenta umbilici, inter. 2. The veins of the navel string are formed by the union of all the venous branches in the placenta, and, finding into the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABDOMEN">abdomen</a> become the falciform ligament of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>. 3. The lungs, before being inflated with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a> and heavy, but after one <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSPIRATION">inspiration</a> they become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a>, and as it were spongy; and it may be noted here, that the notion of the lungs sinking in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> before the child breathes, and of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SWIMMING">swimming</a> after the reception of air, are no certain proofs that the child had <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> had not breathed, much less that it was murdered; for the uninflated lungs become specifically <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-LIGHTER">lighter</a> than water as soon as any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a> takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in them; and this soon happens after the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of the child; besides, where the utmost care hath been taken to preserve the child, it hath breathed once or twice, and then died. 4. The thymus gland is very <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> in the fetus, but dwindles away in proportion as years advance. 5. The foramen ovale in the heart of a fetus, is generally closed in an adult.

FOG

Pages 409-409
or Mist, a meteor, consisting of gross vapours, floating near the surface of the earth. Mists, according to Lord Bacon, are imperfect condensations of the air, consisting of a large proportion of the air, and a small one of the aqueous vapour; and these happen in the winter, about the change of the weather from frost to thaw, or from thaw to frost; but in the summer, and in the spring, from the expansion of the dew. If the vapours, which are raised plentifully from the earth and waters, either by the solar or subterraneous heat, do at their first entrance into the atmosphere meet with cold enough to condense them to a considerable degree, their specific gravity is by that means increased, and so they will be stopped from ascending; and either return back in form of dew or of drizzling rain, or remain suspended some time in the form of a fog. Vapours may be seen on the high grounds as well as the low, but more especially about marshy places. They are easily diffused by the wind, as also by the heat of the sun. They continue longest in the lowest grounds, because these places contain most moisture, and are least exposed to the action of the wind. Hence we may easily conceive, that fogs are only low clouds, or clouds in the lowest region of the air; as clouds are no other than fogs raised on high. See Cloud. When fogs sink, then the vapours are mixed with sulphurous exhalations, which smell so. Objects viewed through fogs appear larger and more remote than through the common air. Mr Boyle observes, that upon the coast of Coromandel, and most maritime parts of the East Indies, there are, notwithstanding the heat of the climate, annual fogs so thick, as to occasion people of other nations who reside there, and even the more tender sort of the natives, to keep their houses close shut up. Fogs are commonly strongly electrified, as appears

FOGAGE

Pages 409-410

in the forest <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, is <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RANK">rank</a> grass not eaten up in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>.

FOIBLE

Pages 410-410

a French <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a>, frequently used also in our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>. It literally signifies weak; and in that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> is applied to the body of animals and the parts thereof, as foible reins, foible sight, &c., being derived from the Italian foibole, of the Latin flebilis, to be "lamented, pitied." But it is chiefly used with us substantively, to denote a defect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> flaw in a person or thing. Thus we say, Every person has his foible; and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> secret consists in hiding it artfully: Princes are gained by flattery, that is their foible. The foible of young people is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a>; the foible of old men is avarice; the foible of the great and learned is vanity; the foible of women and girls, coquetry, or an affection of having gallants: You should know the forte and the foible of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> before you employ him: We should not let people perceive that we know their foible.

FOIL

Pages 410-410

among jewellers, a thin <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of metal placed under a precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a>, in order to make it transparent, and give it an agreeable different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, either deep <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALE">pale</a>: thus, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you want a stone to be of a pale colour, put a foil of that colour under it; or if you would have it deep, lay a dark one under it. These foils are made either of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COPPER">copper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GOLD">gold</a>, or gold and silver together. The copper foils are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> known by the name of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUREMBERG">Nuremberg</a> or German foils; and are prepared as follows: Procure the thinnest copper plates you can get: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAT">beat</a> these plates gently upon a well-polished anvil, with a polished hammer, as thin as possible; and placing them between two <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a> plates as thin as <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> them in the fire; then boil the foil in a pipkin, with equal quantities of tartar and <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a>, constantly stirring them till by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> they become <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a>; after which, taking them out and drying them, give them another hammering, till they are made fit for your purpose: however, care must be taken not to give the foils too much heat, for fear of melting; nor must they be too <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> boiled, for fear of attracting too much salt.
