The manner of polishing these foils is as follows: Take a plate of the best copper, one foot long and about five or six inches wide, polished to the greatest perfection; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEND">bend</a> this to a long convex, fasten it upon a half roll, and fix it to a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BENCH">bench</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>; then take some chalk, washed as clean as possible, and filtered through a fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> cloth, till it be as fine as you can make it; and having laid some thereof on the roll, and wetted the copper all over, lay your foils on it, and with a polishing stone and the chalk polish your foils till they are as bright as a looking-glass; after which they must be dried, and laid up secure from dust.

FOKIEN

Pages 410-410

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASIA">Asia</a>, commodiously situated for <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NAVIGATION">navigation</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMERCE">commerce</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of it bordering on the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a>, in which they catch <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> quantities of fish, which they send salted to other parts of the empire. Its shores are very uneven, by reason of the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> and variety of its bays; and there are many forts built thereon to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is hot, but pure and wholesome. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a> are almost everywhere disposed into a kind of amphitheatres, by the labour of the inhabitants, with terraces placed one above another. The fields are watered with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIVERS">rivers</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>, which issue out of the mountains, and which the husbandmen conduct in such a manner as to overflow the fields of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RICE">rice</a> when they please, because it thrives best in watery ground. They make <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PIPES">pipes</a> of bamboo for this purpose. They have all commodities in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> with the rest of China; but more particularly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MUSK">musk</a>, precious <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a>, quicksilver, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SILK">silk</a>, hempen cloth, calico, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IRON">iron</a>, and all sorts of utensils wrought to the greatest perfection. From other countries they have cloves, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CINNAMON">cinnamon</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEPPER">pepper</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SANDAL">sandal</a> wood, <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AMBER">amber</a>, coral, and many other things. The <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> is Fou-tcheou Fou; <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a>, as others would have it written, Fuchefou. But as for Fokien, which most geographers make the capital, Grosier informs us there is no such <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>.

FOLARD

Pages 410-411
Charles, an eminent Frenchman, famous for his skill and knowledge in the military art, was born at Avignon in 1669, of a noble family, but not a rich one. He discovered an early turn for the sciences, and a strong passion for arms; which last was so inflamed by reading Caesar's Commentaries, that he enlisted at 16 years of age. His father got him off, and shut him in a monastery; but he made his escape in about two years after, and entered himself a second time in quality of cadet. His inclination for military affairs, and the great pains he took to accomplish himself in that way, recommended him to notice; and he was admitted into the friendship of the first rate officers. M. de Vendome, who commanded in Italy in 1720, made him his aide-de-camp, having conceived the highest regard for him; and soon after sent him with part of his forces into Lombardy. He was entirely trusted by the commander of that army; and no measures were concerted, or steps taken, without consulting him. By pursuing his plans, many places were taken, and advantages gained; and such, in short, were his services, that he had a pension of 400 livres settled upon him, and was honoured with the crois of St Louis. He distinguished himself greatly, August 15, 1705, at the battle of Caffano; where he received a wound upon his left hand, which deprived him of the use of it ever after. It was at this battle that he conceived the first idea of that system of columns, which he afterwards prefixed to his Commentaries upon Polybius. The duke of Orleans sending De Vendome again into Italy in 1706, Folard had orders to throw himself into Modena to defend it against Eugene: where, though he acquitted himself with his usual skill, he was very near being assassinated. The description which he has given of the conduct and character of the governor of this town, may be found in his Treatise of the Defence of Places, and deserves to be read. He received a dangerous wound on the thigh at the battle of Malplaquet, and was some time after made prisoner by Prince Eugene. Being exchanged in 1711, he was made Folc-lands, made governor of Bourbourg. In 1714, he went to Folcmote, Malta, to assist in defending that island against the Turks. Upon his return to France, he embarked for Sweden, having a passionate desire to see Charles XII. He acquired the esteem and confidence of that famous general, who sent him to France to negotiate the re-establishment of James II. upon the throne of England; but that project being dropped, he returned to Sweden, followed Charles XII. in his expedition to Norway, and served under him at the siege of Fredrikshall, where that prince was killed, Dec. 11, 1718. Polard then returned to France; and made his last campaign in 1719, under the duke of Berwick, in quality of colonel. From that time he applied himself intensely to the study of the military art as far as it could be studied at home; and built his theories upon the foundation of his experience and observations on facts. He contracted an intimacy with Count Saxe, who, as he then declared, would one day prove a very great general. He was chosen a fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1749; and, in 1751, made a journey to Avignon, where he died in 1752, aged 83 years. He was the author of several works, the principal of which are: 1. Commentaries upon Polybius, in five volumes, 4to. 2. A Book of New Discoveries in War. 3. A Treatise concerning the Defence of Places, &c., in French. Those who would know more of this eminent soldier, may consult a French piece, entitled, Memoires pour servir à l'Histoire de M. le Chevalier de Polard. Ratibone, 1753, 12mo.

FOLC-LANDS

Pages 411-411

(Sax.) copyhold lands so called in the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> of the Saxons, as <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol6.html#article-CHARTER">charter</a>-lands were called boc-lands, Kitch. 174. Folkland was terra vulgi <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> popularis; the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> of the vulgar people, who had no certain estate therein, but held the same, under the rent and services accustomed or agreed, at the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> only of their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THANE">thane</a>; and it was therefore not put in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a>, but accounted praedium rusticum et ignobile. Spelm. of Feuds, c. 5.

FOLCMOTE

Pages 411-411
or FOLKMOTE, (Sax. Folgemote, i.e., convenitus populi), is compounded of folk, populus, and mote, or genitiv, convenire; and signified originally, as Somner in his Saxon Dictionary informs us, a general assembly of the people, to confer of and order matters of the commonwealth. And Sir Henry Spelman says, the folcmote was a fort of annual parliament or convention of the bishops, thanes, aldermen, and freemen, upon every May-day yearly; where the laymen were sworn to defend one another and the king, and to preserve the laws of the kingdom; and then consulted of the common safety. But Dr Brady infers from the laws of the Saxon kings of England, that it was an inferior court, held before the king's reeve or steward, every month, to do folk right, or compose smaller differences, from whence there lay appeal to the superior courts; Gloff. p. 48. Squire seems to think the folcmote not distinct from the fibremote, or common general meeting of the county. See his Angl. Sax. Gov. 155, n. Manwood mentions folcmote as a court holden in London, wherein all the folk and people of the city did complain of the mayor and aldermen, for misgovern- ment within the said city; and this word is still in use among the Londoners, and denotes celebrem ex tota ci- vitate convenium. Slow's Survey. According to Ken- net, the folcmote was a common council of all the inhabitants of a city, town, or borough, convened often by sound of bell, to the Mote Hall, or House; or it was applied to a larger congress of all the freemen within a county, called the fibremote, where formerly all knights and military tenants did fealty to the king, and elected the annual sheriff on the 1st of October; till this popular election, to avoid tumults and riots, devolved to the king's nomination, anno 1315, 3 Edw. I. After which the city folcmote was swallowed up in a select committee or common council, and the country folcmote in the sheriff's tourn and affizes. The word folcmote was also used for any kind of popular or public meeting; as of all the tenants at the court lect, or court baron, in which signification it was of a less extent. Paroch. Antiq. 120.

FOLENGIO

Pages 411-411

Theophilus, an Italian poet, was a native of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MANTUA">Mantua</a>. He was known also by the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Merlin Cocceye, a name which he gave to a poem, and which has been adopted ever since for all trifling performances of the same <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a>, consisting of buffoonery, puns, anagrams, <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> without <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WISDOM">wisdom</a>, and humour without good <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a>. His poem was called The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MACARONI">Macaroni</a>, from an Italian cake of the same name, which is sweet to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, but has not the least alimentary virtue, on the contrary, pulls the appetite and clogs the stomach. These idle poems, however, became the reigning taste in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a> and in France; they gave birth to macaroni <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACADEMIES">academies</a>; and, reaching England, to macaroni clubs; till, in the end, every thing insipid, contemptible, and ridiculous, in the character, dress, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> behaviour, of both men and women, is now summed up in the defpicable appellation of a macaroni. Folengio died in 1544.

FOLIA

Pages 411-411

among botanists, particularly signify the leaves of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; those of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a> being expressed by the word petals. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a>.

FOLIAGE

Pages 411-412

a cluster <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> assemblage of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLOWERS">flowers</a>, leaves, branches, &c. Foliage, is particularly used for the representations of such flowers, leaves, branches, rinds, &c. whether <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> or <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARTIFICIAL">artificial</a>, as are used for enrichments on capitals, friezes, pediments, &c. FOLIATING of Looking-glasses, the spreading the plates over, after they are polished, with quicksilver, &c. in order to reflect the image. It is performed thus: A thin blotting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> is spread on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, and sprinkled with fine chalk; and then a fine lamina or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAF">leaf</a> of tin, called foil, is laid over the paper; upon this is poured <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MERCURY">mercury</a>, which is to be distributed equally over the leaf with a hare's foot or cotton; over this is laid a clean paper, and over that the glass plate, which is pressed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, and the paper gently drawn out with the left: this being done, the plate is covered with a thicker paper, and loaded with a greater <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, that the superfluous mercury may be driven out and the tin adhere more closely to the glass. When it is dried, the weight is removed, and the looking-glass is complete. Some add an ounce of marcasite, melted by the fire; and, left the mercury should evaporate in <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SMOKE">smoke</a>, they pour it into <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; and when cooled, squeeze through a cloth, or through <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEATHER">leather</a>. Some add a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTER">quarter</a> of an ounce of tin and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEAD">lead</a> to the marcasite, that the glass may dry the sooner. Foliating of Globe looking-glasses, is done as follows: Take five ounces of quicksilver and one ounce of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISMUTH">bismuth</a>; of lead and tin, half an ounce each: first put the lead and tin into fusion, then put in the bismuth; and when you perceive that in fusion too, let it stand till it is almost cold, and pour the quicksilver into it: after this, take the glass globe, which must be very clean, and the inside free from dust: make a paper funnel, which put into the hole of the globe, as near the glass as you can, so that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMALGAM">amalgam</a>, when you pour it in, may not splash, and cause the glass to be full of spots; pour it in gently, and move it about, so that the amalgam may touch everywhere: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> you find the amalgam begin to be curdly and fixed, then hold it over a gentle fire, and it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> easily flow again; and if you find the amalgam too thin, add a little more lead, tin, and bismuth to it. The finer and clearer your globe is, the better will the looking glass be. Dr Shaw observes, that this operation has considerable advantages, as being performable in the cold; and that it is not attended with the danger of poisonous fumes from arsenic, or other unwholesome matters, usually employed for this purpose: besides, how far it is applicable to the more commodious foliating of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> looking glasses, and other speculums, he thinks, may deserve to be considered.

FOLIO

Pages 412-412

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> books, denotes a page, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather both the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> and left <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAGES">pages</a>, these being expressed by the same <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FIGURE">figure</a>, and corresponding to each other. See <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol4.html#article-BOOK_KEEPING">BOOK-KEEPING</a>. Folio, among printers and bookellers, the largest form of books, when each sheet is so printed that it may be bound up in two leaves only. FOLIS. See FOLLIS.

FOLKES

Pages 412-412

MARTIN, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PHILOSOPHER">philosopher</a> and antiquarian of considerable eminence, was born in Welfminter in the year 1690. A Mr Cappel, once professor of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> at <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAUMUR">Saumur</a>, was his private <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TUTOR">tutor</a>. When 17 years of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, he was sent to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLARE">Clare</a>-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HALL">hall</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAMBRIDGE">Cambridge</a>, where he successfully applied himself to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a> and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol1.html#article-MATHEMATICS">mathematics</a>; and when only twenty-three years of age he was chosen a fellow of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOCIETY">Society</a>. His ingenious communications acquired him so much applause, that he was frequently chosen into its <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COUNCIL">council</a>. He was in habits of friendship with the illustrious Newton, at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, and by his influence was elected one of the vice-presidents in the year 1723. Mr Folkes became a candidate for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAIR">chair</a> on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Sir <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISAAC">Isaac</a> Newton; but the superior <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of Sir Hans Sloane rendered his application ineffectual. In 1733, and the two subsequent years, his residence was for the most <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>, with the view of improving himself in the knowledge of classical antiquities. To ascertain the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> and value of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> coins, he carefully consulted the cabinets of the curious; and on his return home he presented to the Antiquarian Society, of which he was a member, a dissertation on this subject. He read before the same learned body, a dissertation on the measurement of Trajan's and Antonine's pillars, together with other remains of antiquity. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> of his observations he presented to the Royal Society; and, in particular, "Remarks on the standard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a> preserved in the Capitol of Rome," and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODEL">model</a> of an ancient globe in the Farnesian <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>. He visited <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a> in 1739, where he was received with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> respect, and honoured with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> of the most eminent literary <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> in that <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-METROPOLIS">metropolis</a>. This respect indeed he was entitled to by his unwearied application to many branches of knowledge which were both curious and useful. His valuable <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>, entitled "A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> of English silver coins, from the Norman Conquest to the present time, with their weights, intrinsic values, and some remarks upon the several pieces," was printed in the year 1745. Among the many honours conferred upon Mr Folkes, he was created <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a> of laws by both <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-UNIVERSITIES">universities</a>, and chosen president of the Antiquarian Society. He <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> to furnish the Philosophical Transactions with many learned papers, till his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAREER">career</a> was stopped by a paralytic stroke, which terminated his useful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> in the year 1754. He was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of very extensive knowledge and great accuracy; but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> benefit to science which resulted from his labours, was his treatise on the intricate subject of coins, weights, and <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-MEASURES">measures</a>. His cabinet and library were <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> and valuable, and exposed to public <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALE">sale</a> after his death. His private character was distinguished for <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol18.html#article-POLITENESS">politeness</a>, generosity, and friendship.

FOLKESTONE

Pages 412-412

a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, between <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-HYTHE">Hythe</a>, 72 miles from <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>, appears to have been a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, from the Roman coins and British bricks often found in it. Stillington and Tanner take it for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAPIS">Lapis</a> Tituli of Nennius. It was burnt by <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARL">Earl</a> Godwin, and by the French in the reign of Edward III. It had five churches, now reduced to one. It is a member of the town and port of Dover: and has a weekly market and an annual fair. It is chiefly noted for the multitude of <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FISHING">fishing</a>-boats that belong to its harbour, which are employed in the season in catching mackerel for London; to which they are carried by the mackerel boats of London and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARKING">Barking</a>. About Michaelmas, the Folkestone barks, with others for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUSSEX">Sussex</a>, go away to the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUFFOLK">Suffolk</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORFOLK">Norfolk</a> coasts, to catch herrings for the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MERCHANTS">merchants</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YARMOUTH">Yarmouth</a> and Leedestoff.—Folkestone gives the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of Viscount to William Henry Bouvierie, whose grandfather, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-JACOB">Jacob</a>, was so created in 1747. It has been observed of some hills in this neighbourhood, that they have visibly sunk and grown lower within <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMORY">memory</a>.

FOLLICULUS

Pages 412-412

(from follis, "a bag.") a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of seed-vessel first mentioned by Linnaeus in his Delineatio Plantarum, generally consisting of one <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>, which opens from bottom to top on one side, and has no future for fattening <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> attaching the seeds within it. FOLLICULI are likewise defined by the same author to be small glandular vessels distended with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a>, which appear on the surface of some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a>; as at the root of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-milfoil, and on the leaves of aldrovanda. In the former, the vessels in question are roundish, and furnished with an appearance like two horns; in the latter, pot-shaped, and semicircular.

FOLLIS

Pages 412-413
or FOLLIS, anciently signified a little bag or purse; whence it came to be used for a sum of money, and very different sums were called by that name: thus the scholiast on the Baffites mentions a follis of copper which was worth but the 24th part of the millarenfis; the glotte nomiae, quoted by Gronovius and others, one of 125 millarenfes, and another of 250 denarii, which was the ancient felttertum; and three different sums of eight, four, and two pound of gold, were each each called follis. According to the account of the scholiast, the ounce of silver, which contained five milliaries of 60 in the pound, was worth 120 folles of copper. The gloflographer, describing a follis of 250 denarii, says it was equal to 312 pounds 6 ounces of copper, and as the denarius of that age was the 8th part of an ounce, an ounce of silver must have been worth 120 ounces of copper; and therefore the scholiast's follis was an ounce of copper, and equal to the gloflographer's nummus. But as Constantine's copper money weighed a quarter of a Roman ounce, the scholiast's follis and the gloflographer's nummus contained four of them, as the ancient nummus contained four asses.

FOLLY

Pages 413-413

according to Mr Locke, consists in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> of false conclusions from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a> principles; by which it is distinguished from madness, which draws just conclusions from false principles. But this seems too confined a <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-DEFINITION">definition</a>; folly, in its most general acceptation, denoting a weakness of intellect <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, or some partial absurdity in sentiment or conduct.

FOMAHAUT

Pages 413-413

in <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ASTRONOMY">Astronomy</a>, a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STAR">star</a> of the first magnitude in the constellation <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-AQUARIUS">AQUARIUS</a>.

FOMENTATION

Pages 413-413

in Medicine, is a fluid externally applied, usually as warm as the patient can bear it, and in the following manner. Two <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> cloths are dipped into the heated liquor, one of which is wrung as dry as the necessary speed <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> admit, then immediately applied to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> affected; it lies on until the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a> begins to go off; and the other is in readiness to apply at the instant in which the first is removed; thus these flannels are alternately applied, so as to keep the affected part constantly supplied with them warm. This is <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> 15 <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> 20 minutes, and repeated two or three times a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>. Every intention of relaxing and soothing by fomentations may be answered as well by warm <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> alone as when the whole tribe of emollients are boiled in it; but when disfectants or antifebrics are required, such ingredients must be called in as are adapted to that end. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of heat should never exceed that of producing a pleasing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a>; <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> heat produces effects very opposite to that intended by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of fomentations.

FONG-YANG

Pages 413-413

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CITY">city</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHINA">China</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Kiang-Nan. It is situated on a mountain, which hangs over the <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol21.html#article-YELLOW_RIVER"><a class="xr</a>ef" href="vol20.html#article-YELLOW">Yellow</a> river, and encloses with its walls several fertile little hills. Its jurisdiction is very extensive: for it comprehends 18 cities; five of which are of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a>, and 13 of the third class. As this was the birth-<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-EMPEROR">emperor</a> Hong-vou, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of the preceding dynasty, this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCE">prince</a> formed a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESIGN">design</a> of rendering it a famous and magnificent city, in order to make it the seat of empire. After having expelled the Western Tartars, who had taken possession of China, he transferred his <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> hither, and named the city Fong-yang; that is to say, "The Place of the Eagle's Splendour." His intention, as we have said, was to beautify and enlarge it; but the inequality of the ground, the scarcity of fresh <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>, and above all the vicinity of his father's <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TOMB">tomb</a>, made him change his design. By the unanimous advice of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> officers, this prince established his court at Nan-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>, a more beautiful and commodious place. When he had formed this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RESOLUTION">resolution</a>, a stop was put to the intended works: the imperial <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a> which was to have been enclosed by a triple wall, the Fontaine, walls of the city to which a circumference of <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> leagues were assigned, and the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CANALS">canals</a> that were begun, all were abandoned; and nothing was finished, but three monuments that still remain. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> and magnificence of these sufficiently show what the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a> of this city would have been, had the emperor pursued his original design. The first is the tomb of the father of Hong-vou, to decorate which no expense was spared; it is called Hoan-lin, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">Royal</a> Tomb. The second is a tower built in the middle of the city, which is of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OBLONG">oblong</a> form, and 100 feet <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a>. The third is a magnificent temple erected to the god Fo. At first it was only a pagod, to which Hong-vou retired after having lost his parents, and where he was admitted as an inferior <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a>; but, having soon become weary of this kind of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he enlisted with the chief of a band of banditti, who had revolted from the Tartars. As he was bold and enterprising, the general made choice of him for his son-in-<a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; soon after, he was declared his successor by the unanimous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a> of the troops. The new chief, seeing himself at the head of a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> party, had the presumption to carry his views to the throne. The Tartars, informed of the progress of his arms, sent a numerous <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a> into the field; but he surprized and attacked them with so much impetuosity, that they were obliged to fly; and, though they several times returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>, they were still defeated, and at length driven entirely out of China. As soon as he mounted the throne, he caused the superb temple which we have mentioned to be raised out of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GRATITUDE">gratitude</a> to the Bonzes, who had received him in his distress, and assigned them a revenue sufficient for the maintenance of 300 persons, under a chief of their own feet, whom he constituted a mandarin, with power of governing them, independent of the officers of the city. This pagod was supported as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as the preceding dynasty lasted; but that of the Eastern Tartars, which succeeded, suffered it to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> to ruin. Fong-Choui, the name of a ridiculous <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a> among the Chinese. See CHINA, No 105.

FONTAINBLEAU

Pages 414-414

a town in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ISLE">Isle</a> of France, and in the Gatinois, remarkable for its fine <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PALACE">palace</a>, which has been the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where the kings of France used to lodge when they went a hunting. It was first embellished by Francis I. and every succeeding <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a> has added something to it; so that it may now be called the finest <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a> in the world. It stands in the midst of a forest, consisting of 26,424 arpents of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a>, each containing 100 <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">square</a> perches, and each perch 18 feet. E. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. 2. 33. N. Lat. 40. 22.

FONTAINE

Pages 413-414

JOHN, the celebrated French poet, and one of the first-rate geniuses of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, was born at Chateau-Thierry in Champagne, the 8th of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JULY">July</a> 1621, of a good family. At the age of 19 he entered amongst the Oratorians, but quitted that order 18 months after. He was 22 years of age before he knew his own talents for <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>; but hearing an ode of Malherbe read, upon the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AFFIRMATION">affirmation</a> of Henry IV., he was so taken with admiration of it, that the poetical fire, which had before lain dormant within him, seemed to be enkindled from that of the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> poet. He applied himself to read, to meditate, to repeat, in fine to imitate, the works of Malherbe. The first essays of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PEN">pen</a> he confined to one of his relations who made him read the best Latin authors, Horace, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VIRGIL">Virgil</a>, Terence, Quintilian, &c. and then the best best compositions in French and Italian. He applied himself likewise to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of the Greek authors, particularly <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLATO">Plato</a> and Plutarch. Some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> afterwards his parents made him marry a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAUGHTER">daughter</a> of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIEUTENANT">lieutenant</a>-general, a relation of the great Racine. This young lady, besides her very great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BEAUTY">beauty</a>, was remarkable for the delicacy of her <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a>, and Fontaine never composed any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> without consulting her. But as her temper was none of the best, to avoid <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a>, he separated himself from her <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> as often as he well could. The famous duchess of Bouillon, niece to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CARDINAL">Cardinal</a> Mazarine, being exiled to Chateau-Thierry, took particular notice of Fontaine. Upon her recall, he followed her to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>; where by the <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INTEREST">interest</a> of one of his relations, he got a pension settled upon him. He met with great friends and protectors amongst the most distinguished persons of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>, but Madame de la Sablière was the most particular. She took him to live at her <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and it was then that Fontaine, divested of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> concerns, led a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a> conformable to his disposition, and cultivated an acquaintance with all the great men of the age. It was his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a>, after he was fixed at Paris, to go every year, during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONTH">month</a> of September, to his native <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> of Chateau-Thierry, and pay a visit to his wife, carrying with him Racine, Defreux, Chapelle, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> some other celebrated writers. When he has sometimes gone thither alone by himself, he has come away without remembering even to call upon her; but seldom omitted telling some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of his lands, by which means he squandered away a considerable fortune. After the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of Madame de la Sablière, he was invited into England, particularly by Madame Mazarine, and by St Evremont, who promised him all the sweets and comforts of life; but the difficulty of learning the English <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, and the liberality of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, prevented his voyage. About the end of the year 1692 he fell dangerously ill; and, as is customary upon these occasions in the Roman <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHURCH">church</a>, he made a general confession of his whole life to P. Poguet, an Oratorian; and, before he received the sacrament, he sent for the gentlemen of the French Academy, and in their presence declared his sincere compunction for having composed his Tales; a work he could not reflect upon without the greatest <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-REPENTANCE">repentance</a> and detestation; promising that <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> it should please God to restore his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, he would employ his talents only in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> upon matters of morality or piety. He survived this illness two years, living in the most exemplary and edifying manner, and died the 13th of <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARCH">March</a> 1695, being 74 years of age. When they stripped his body, they found next his skin a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAIR">hair</a> shirt; which gave room for the following <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> of the younger Racine: Et l'Auteur de Jaconde est orné d'un Cilice. Fontaine's character is remarkable for a simplicity, candour, and probity, seldom to be met with. He was of an obliging disposition; cultivating a real friendship with his <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol5.html#article-BROTHER">brother</a> poets and authors; and what is very rare, beloved and esteemed by them all. His conversation was neither gay nor brilliant, especially when he was not amongst his intimate friends. One <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> being invited to a dinner at a <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARMER">farmer</a> general's, he ate a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEAL">deal</a>, but did not speak. Rising up from <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a> very early, under <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRETEXT">pretext</a> of going to the academy, one of Fontaine's company represented to him that it was not yet a proper time: "Well (says he), if it is not, I <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> stay a little longer." He had one son by his wife in the year 1660. At the age of 14, he put him into the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> of M. de Harley, the first <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a>, recommending to him his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> and fortune. It is said, that having been a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> time without seeing him, he happened to meet him one day visiting, without recollecting him again, and mentioned to the company that he thought that young <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> had a good deal of wit and understanding. When they told him it was his own son, he answered in the most tranquil manner, "Ha! truly I am glad on't." An indifference, or rather an absence of mind, influenced his whole conduct, and rendered him often insensible to the inclemency of the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a>. Madame de Bouillon going one morning to Verfaillies, <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SAW">saw</a> him, abstracted in thought, sitting in an arbour; returning at night, she found him in the same place, and in the same attitude, although it was very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>, and had rained almost the whole day. He carried this simplicity so far, that he was scarcely sensible of the bad effects some of his writings might occasion, particularly his Tales. In a great sickness, his confessors exhorted him to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRAYER">prayer</a> and alms deeds: "As for alms deeds (replied Fontaine), I am not able, having nothing to give; but they are about publishing a new edition of my Tales, and the bookeller owes me a hundred copies; you shall have them to sell, and distribute their amount amongst the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a>." Another time P. Poguet exhorting him to repent of his faults, "If he has committed any (cried the nurse), I am sure it is more from <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IGNORANCE">ignorance</a> than malice, for he has as much simplicity as an infant." One time having composed a tale, wherein he made a profane application of those words of the Gospel, "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a>, five talents thou didst deliver to me," he dedicated it, by a most ingenious prologue, to the celebrated Arnauld, telling him, it was to show how to povertify the great esteem he had for the learned <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOCTOR">doctor</a>. He was not sensible of the indecency of the dedication, and the profane application of the text, till Boileau and Racine represented it to him. He addressed another, by a dedication in the same manner, to the archbishop of Paris. His Fables are an immortal work, exceeding everything in that kind, both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> of the learned. People of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, the oftener they read them, will find continually new beauties and charms, not to be met with elsewhere. The descendants of this great poet are exempted in France from all taxes and impositions; a privilege which the intendants of <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOISSONS">Soissons</a> to this day think it an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> to confirm to them.

FONTAINES

Pages 414-415
Peter Francis, a French critic, was born of a good family at Rouen in 1685. At 15, he entered into the society of the Jesuits; and at 30, quitted Fontaines quitted it, for the sake of returning to the world. He was a priest, and had a cure in Normandy; but left it, Fontarabia, and was, as a man of wit and letters, some time with the cardinal d'Auvergne. Having excited some attention at Paris by certain critical productions, the Abbé Bignon in 1724 committed to him the Journal des Savans. He acquitted himself well in this department, and was peaceably enjoying the applause of the public, when his enemies, whom by critical strictures in his Journal he had made such, formed an accusation against him of a most abominable crime, and procured him to be imprisoned. By the credit of powerful friends, he was set at liberty in 15 days: the magistrate of the police took upon himself the trouble of justifying him in a letter to the Abbé Bignon; and this letter having been read amidst his fellow labourers in the Journal, he was unanimously re-established in his former credit. This happened in 1725. But with whatever repute he might acquit himself in this Journal, frequent difficulties made him frequently abandon it. He laboured meanwhile in some new periodical works, from which he derived his greatest fame. In 1731, he began one under the title of Nouvelliste du Parnasse, ou Réflexions sur les Ouvrages nouveaux: but only proceeded to two volumes; the work having been suppressed by authority, from the incessant complaints of authors ridiculed therein. About three years after, in 1735, he obtained a new privilege for a periodical production, entitled, Observations sur les Écrits Modernes; which, after continuing to 33 volumes, was suppressed again in 1743. Yet the year following, 1744, he published another weekly paper, called, Juges sur les Ouvrages nouveaux, and proceeded to 11 volumes: the two last being done by other hands. In 1745, he was attacked with a disorder in the breast, which ended in a dropy that proved fatal in five weeks. "He was (says M. Freron) born a sentimental person; a philosopher in conduct as well as in principle; exempt from ambition; and of a noble firm spirit, which would not submit to sue for preferments or titles. In common conversation he appeared only a common man; but when subjects of literature, or any thing out of the ordinary way, were agitated, he discovered great force of imagination and wit." Besides the periodical works mentioned above, he was the author of many others: his biographer gives us no less than 17 articles; many of them critical, some historical, and some translations from English writers, chiefly from Pope, Swift, Fielding, &c. The Abbé de la Porte, published, in 1757, L'Esprit de l'Abbé des Fontaines, in 4 vols. 12mo; prefixed to which is the Life of Fontaines, a catalogue of his works, and another catalogue of writings against him.

FONTANELLA

FONTANELLE

Pages 415-422

Bernard le Bovier de, was a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of letters, born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROUEN">Rouen</a> in 1657, the most universal genius of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LOUIS">Louis</a> XIV. in the estimation of Voltaire. He received his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a> of Jesuits at Rouen, where the quickness of his parts became conspicuous at a very early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PERIOD">period</a>. He was capable of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WRITING">writing</a> Latin verses when only 13, which were deemed worthy of being published. He studied the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> at the desire of his father; but as he lost the very first cause in which he was employed as an advocate, he became disgusted with his profession, and devoted himself entirely to literature and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>. He composed a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the operas of Pyche and Bellerophon, which were printed under the name of his uncle Thomas Corneille. He wrote a tragedy called Alpar, but as it did not succeed, he consigned the manuscript to the flames, and never afterwards attempted that <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>. His Dialogues of the dead were published in the year 1683, which were well received, as a specimen of elegant composition, combining morality with the charms of literature. His "Lettres du Chevalier d'Her," published in 1685 without his name, discovered much <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-WIT">wit</a> and ingenuity, but at the same <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> no small share of affectation. His "Entretiens sur la Pluralité des Mondes" has been regarded as one of his ablest performances, combining science and philosophy with vivacity and humour, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TALENT">talent</a> which may be said to belong almost exclusively to the French. It was perused by all, and translated into several foreign languages. In his "<a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">History</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ORACLES">Oracles</a>," he supported the <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-OPINION">opinion</a> that oracles were forgeries, in opposition to those who contended that they were supernatural operations of evil spirits, put to silence by the appearing of Christ, and of <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> he exposed himself to clerical animadversion. His "Pastoral Poems" appeared in the year 1688, with a discourse on the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the eclogue, which were very much admired for their delicacy of sentiment, as was also his <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OPERA">opera</a> of "Theis and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PELEUS">Peleus</a>;" but his "Aeneas and Lavinia" was not so successful. In the year 1699, Fontanelle was chosen secretary of the Academy of Sciences, which office he held during the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> period of 42 years. He published a volume annually of the history of that learned body, filled with analyses of <a class="xref" href="vol13.html#article-MEMOIRS">memoirs</a>, and eulogiums on deceased members. As a poet, he did not rise above elegance and ingenuity; as a man of science, he rather excelled in throwing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the inventions of others, than in discovering any new <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TRUTH">truth</a> himself, and as a general writer, he united <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">solid</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> with the delicacy and refinement of a man of wit. He studied his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAPPINESS">happiness</a> as much as most men, but he never sacrificed to the promotion of it, the duties of a man of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONOUR">honour</a> and virtue. He had many friends, and towards the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CLOSE">close</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, scarcely a single enemy. He was never married, and for a man of letters he acquired considerable affluence. Although of a delicate <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSTITUTION">constitution</a>, he reached the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> age of 90 without any complaint but dullness of hearing. He died on the 9th of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol12.html#article-JANUARY">January</a> 1757, being almost a hundred years of age. When asked by a certain person FOOD Fontenoy, a town <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> village of the Austrian <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NETHERLANDS">Netherlands</a>, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROVINCE">province</a> of Hannault, and on the borders of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANDERS">Flanders</a>; remarkable for a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BATTLE">battle</a> fought between the allies and the French on the first of May 1745. The French were commanded by Marshal Saxe, and the allies by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">Duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-CUMBERLAND">Cumberland</a>. On account of the superior numbers of the French <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>, and the superior generalship of their commander, the allies were defeated with great slaughter. The British troops behaved with great intrepidity, as their enemies themselves acknowledged. It has been said, that the battle was lost through the cowardice of the Dutch, who failed in their attack on the village of Fontenoy, on which the event of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a> depended. E. Long. 2. 25. N. Lat. 50. 35. Fontenoy, a village of France, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUCHY">duchy</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BURGUNDY">Burgundy</a>, remarkable for a bloody battle fought there in 841, between the Germans and the French, in which were killed above 100,000 men; and the Germans were defeated. E. Long. 3. 48. N. Lat. 47. 28. Fontevraud, or Frontevaux, Order of, in <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ECCLESIASTICAL">ecclesiastical</a> history, a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGIOUS">religious</a> order instituted about the latter end of the 11th century, and taken under the protection of the holy see by Pope Paschal II. in 1116, confirmed by a bull in 1113, and invested by his successors with very extraordinary privileges. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHIEF">chief</a> of this order is a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FEMALE">female</a>, who is appointed to inspect both the monks and nuns. The order was divided into four provinces, which were those of France, Aquitaine, Auvergne, and Bretagne, in each of which they had formerly several priories. Fonticulus, or Fontanella, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, an inflame, feton, or small ulcer, made in various parts of the body, in order to excite irritation, or to produce the discharge of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a>. Fontinalia, or Fontanalia, in antiquity, a religious feast held among the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROMANS">Romans</a> in honour of the deities who presided over fountains or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPRINGS">springs</a>. Varro observes, that it was the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> to visit the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WELLS">wells</a> on those days, and to <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAST">cast</a> crowns into fountains. Scaliger, in his conjectures on Varro, takes this not to be a feast of fountains in general, as Feltus intimates, but of the fountain which had a temple at Rome, near the Porta Capena, called also Porta Fontinalis: he adds, that it is of this fountain Cicero speaks in his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> book De Legibus. The fontinalia were held on the 13th of October. Fontinalis, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>-moss, a genus of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLANTS">plants</a> belonging to the cryptogamia class, and to the order of mucil. See <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BOTANY">Botany</a> <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Food, in the most extensive signification of the word, implies whatever aliments are taken into the body, whether solid or fluid; but in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>, it is generally used to signify only the solid part of our aliment. We are told, that in the first ages men lived upon acorns, berries, and such <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> as the <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EARTH">earth</a> spontaneously produces; then they proceeded to eat the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLESH">flesh</a> of wild animals taken in hunting; But their numbers decreasing and mankind multiplying, <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NECESSITY">necessity</a> taught them the art of cultivating the ground, to sow corn, &c. By and by they began to affix to each other, by general consent, portions of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> to produce them their supply of vegetables; after this, reason suggested the expedient of domesticating certain animals, both to assist them in their labours and supply them with food. Hogs were the first animals of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> kind that appeared upon their tables; they held it to be ungrateful to devour the beasts that afflicted them in their labours.—When they began to make a free <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of domestic animals, they roasted them only: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOILING">boiling</a> was a refinement in cookery which for ages they were strangers to; and fish living in an element men were unused to, were not eaten till they grew somewhat civilized. Menelaus complains, in the Odyssey, that they had been constrained to feed upon them. The most remarkable distinction of foods, in a medical view, is into those which are already assimilated into the animal nature, and such as are not. Of the first kind are animal substances in general; which <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> not entirely similar, are nearly so, to our nature. The second comprehends vegetables, which are much more difficultly assimilated. But as the nourishment of all animals, even those which live on other animals, can be traced originally to the vegetable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KINGDOM">kingdom</a>, it is plain, that the principle of all nourishment is in vegetables. Though there is perhaps no vegetable which does not afford nourishment to some species of animals or other; yet, with regard to mankind, a very considerable distinction is to be made. Those vegetables which are of a mild, bland, agreeable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a>, are proper nourishment; while those of an acrid, bitter, and nauseous nature, are improper. We use, indeed, several acid substances as food; but the mild, the bland, and agreeable, are in the largest proportion in almost every vegetable. Such as are very acrid, and at the same time of an aromatic nature, are not used as food, but as spices or condiments, which answer the purposes of medicines rather than any thing else. Sometimes, indeed, acrid and bitter vegetables seem to be admitted as food. Thus celeri and endive are used in common food, though both are substances of considerable acrimony; but it must be observed, that, when we use them, they are previously blanched, which almost totally destroys their acrimony. Or if we employ other acrid substances, we generally, in a great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, deprive them of their acrimony by boiling. In different countries, the same plants grow with different degrees of acrimony. Thus, garlic here seldom enters our food; but in the southern countries, where the plants grow more mild, they are frequently used for that purpose. The plant which furnishes <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAYENNE">cayenne</a>, being very acrimonious, and even poisonous, in its recent state, affords an instance of the necessity of preparing acid substances even in the hot countries; and there are other plants, such as arum root, which are so exceedingly acrimonious in their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> state, that they cannot be swallowed with safety; yet, when deprived of that acrimony, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> afford good nourishment. The most remarkable properties of different vegetable substances as food, are taken notice of under their different names: here we shall only compare vegetable foods in general with those of the animal kind. I. In the Stomach, they differ remarkably, in that the vegetables always have a tendency to acidity, while animal animal food of all kinds rather tends to alkalescence and <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PUTREFACTION">putrefaction</a>. Some animal foods, indeed, turn manifestly acid before they putrefy; and it has been asserted, that some <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEGREE">degree</a> of acclency takes <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> in every kind of animal food before digestion. This acclency of animal food, however, never comes to any morbid degree, but the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> is always on the side of putrefaction. The acclency of vegetables is more frequent, and ought to be more attended to, than the alkalescence of animal food; which last, even in weak stomachs, is seldom felt; while acclency greatly affects both the stomach and system. With regard to their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> of solution:—Heaviness, as it is called, is seldom felt from vegetables, except from tough farinaceous pastes, or the most viscous substances; while the heaviness of animal food is more frequently noticed, especially when in any great <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a>. Difficulty of solution does not depend so much on firmness of texture (as a man, from fills of all kinds, is more oppressed than from firmer substances) as on viscosity; and hence it is more frequent in animal food, especially in the younger animals. With regard to mixture:—There is no influence of difficult mixture in vegetables, except in vegetable oils; while animal foods, from both viscosity and oiliness, especially the fatter meats, are refractory in this respect. Perhaps the difference of animal and vegetable foods might be referred to this head of mixture. For vegetable food continues long in the stomach, giving little stimulus: Now the system is affected in proportion to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTENT">extent</a> of this stimulus, which is incomparably greater from the animal viscous oily food, than from the vegetable, firmer, and more aqueous. However, there are certain applications to the stomach, which have a tendency to bring on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a> fit of fever, independent of stimulus, merely by their refrigeration: and this often arises from vegetables; as we see, in those hot countries where intermittents prevail, they are often induced from a surfeit of vegetable than of animal food. A <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> of this is, that when one is recovering of an intermittent, there is nothing more apt to cause a relapse than cold food, especially if taken on those days when the fit should return, and particularly acclent, fermentable vegetables, as salads, melons, cucumbers, &c., acido-dulces, &c., which, according to Dr <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULLEN">Cullen</a>, are the most frequent causes of epidemics; therefore, when an intermittent is to be avoided, we shun vegetable diet, and give animal foods, although their stimulus be greater. II. In the Intestines. When the putrefaction of animal food has gone too far, it produces an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVE">active</a> stimulus, causing diarrhoea, dysentery, &c. But these effects are but rare; whereas from vegetable food and its acid, which, united with the bile, proves a pretty strong stimulus, they more frequently occur; but, luckily, are of less consequence, if the refrigeration is not very great. In the autumnal season, when there is a tendency to dysentery, if it is observed that eating of fruits brings it on, it is rather to be ascribed to their cooling than stimulating the intestines. As to stool:—Wherever neither putrefaction nor acidity has gone a great length, animal food keeps the belly more regular. Vegetable food gives a greater proportion of succulent matter, and, when excreted by the stomach and intestines, is more apt to stagnate, and produce slow belly and costiveness, than animal stimulating food; which, before it comes to the great guts, where stoppage is made, has obtained a putrefactive tendency, and gives a proper stimulus: and thus those who are colicive from the use of vegetables; when they have recourse to animal food are in this respect better. III. In the blood-vessels. They both give a blood of the same kind, but of different <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUALITY">quality</a>. Animal food gives it in greater quantity, being in great part, as the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> is, convertible in succum et sanguinem, and of easy digestion; whereas vegetable is more watery, and contains a portion of unconquerable saline matter, which causes it to be thrown out of the body by some excretion. Animal food affords a more dense stimulating <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-ELASTIC">elastic</a> blood than vegetable; stretching and causing a great resistance in the solids, and again exciting their stronger <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTION">action</a>. It has been supposed that acclency of vegetable food is carried into the blood-vessels, and there exerts its effects; but the tendency of animal <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLUIDS">fluids</a> is so strong to alkalescence, that the existence of an acid acrimony in the blood seems very improbable. Animal food alone will soon produce an alkalescent acrimony; and if a person who lives entirely on vegetables were to take no food for a few days, his acrimony would be alkalescent. IV. We are next to take notice of the quantity of nutriment these different foods afford. Nutriment is of two kinds: the first repairs the waste of the solid fibres; the other supplies certain fluids, the chief of which is <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OIL">oil</a>. Now, as animal food is easier converted, and also longer retained in the system, and as it contains a greater proportion of oil, it will afford both kinds of nutriment more copiously than vegetables. V. Lastly, As to the different degrees of perspirability of these foods. This is not yet properly determined. Sanctius constantly speaks of mutton as the most perspirable of all food, and of vegetables as checking perspiration. This is a consequence of the different stimulus these foods give to the stomach, so that persons who live on vegetables have not their perspiration so suddenly excited. In time of digestion, perspiration is stopped from whatever food, much more so from cooling vegetables. Another reason why vegetables are less perspirable is, because their aqueo-saline juices determine them to go off by urine, while the more perfectly mixed animal food is more equally diffused over the system, and so goes off by perspiration. Hence Sanctius's accounts may be understood; for vegetable aliment is not longer retained in the body, but mostly takes the course of the kidneys. Both are equally perspirable in this respect, viz., that a person living on either returns once a day to his usual <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>; and if we consider the little nourishment of vegetables, and the great tendency of animal food to corpulency, we must allow that vegetable is more quickly perspired than animal food. As to the question, Whether man was originally designed for animal or vegetable food, see the article CARNIVOROUS. With regard to the effects of these foods on men, it must be observed, that there are no persons who live entirely on vegetables. The Pythagoreans themselves ate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MILK">milk</a>; and those who do so mostly, as the Pythagoreans, are weakly, sickly, and meagre, labouring ing under a constant diarrhoea and several other difficul- ties. None of the hardy, robust, live on these; but chiefly such as <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> a livelihood by the exertion of their mental faculties, as (in the East Indies) factors and brokers; and this method of life is now confined to the hot climates, where vegetable diet, without incon- venience, may be carried to great excess. Though it be granted, therefore, that man is intended to live on these different foods promiscuously, yet the vegetable should be in very great proportion. Thus the Lap- landers are said to live entirely on animal food: but this is contradicted by the best accounts; for Linnaeus says, that besides milk, which they take four, to ob- viate the bad effects of animal food, they use also cala- menyanthes, and many other plants, copiously. So there is no instance of any <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATION">nation</a> living entirely either on vegetable or animal food, though there are indeed some who live particularly on one or other in the greatest proportion. In the cold countries, e.g. the inhabi- tants live chiefly on animal food, on account of the rigour of the season, their smaller perspiration, and little tendency to putrefaction. Of more importance, however, is the following than the former question, viz. In what proportion animal and vegetable food ought to be mixed? 1. Animal food certainly gives most strength to the system. It is a known aphorism of Sanctorius, that *pondus addit robur*; which may be explained from the impletion of the blood-vessels, and giving a proper degree of tension for the performance of strong oscil- lations. Now animal food not only goes a greater way in supplying fluid, but also gives the fluid more dense and elastic. The art of giving the utmost strength to the system is best understood by those who breed fighting cocks. These people raise the cocks to a cer- <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TAIN">tain</a> weight, which must bear a certain proportion to the other parts of the system, and which at the same time is so nicely proportioned, as that, on losing a few ounces of it, their strength is very considerably im- paired. Dr Robinson of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUBLIN">Dublin</a> has observed, that the force and weight of the system ought to be deter- mined by the largeness of the heart, and its proportion to the system: for a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> heart will give large blood- vessels, while at the same time the vasa are less, par- ticularly the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIVER">liver</a>; which last being increased in size, a greater quantity of fluid is determined into the cel- lular texture, and less into the sanguineous system. Hence we see how animal food gives strength, by fill- ing the sanguiferous vessels. What pains we now be- low on cocks, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENTS">ancients</a> did on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ATHLETE">athlete</a>, by proper nourishment bringing them to a great degree of strength and agility. It is said that men were at first fed on figs, a proof of which we have from their nu- tritious quality; however, in this respect they were soon found to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> far short of animal food; and thus we see, that men, in some measure, will <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> in pro- portion to the quality of their food. The English la- bour more than the Scots; and wherever men are ex- posed to hard labour, their food should be animal.— Animal food, although it gives strength, yet loads the body; and <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HIPPOCRATES">Hippocrates</a> long ago observed, that the athletic <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a>, by a small increase, was exposed to the greatest hazards. Hence it is only proper for bodily labours, and entirely improper for mental exercises; for whoever would keep his mind acute and penetrat- ing, will exceed rather on the side of vegetable food. Even the body is oppressed with animal food; a full <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAL">meal</a> always produces dulness, laziness, and yawning; and hence the feeding of gamesters, whose mind must be ready to take advantage, is always performed by avoiding a large quantity of animal food. Farther, With regard to the strength of the body, animal food, in the first stage of life, is hardly necessary to give strength: in manhood, when we are exposed to active licences, it is more allowable; and even in the decline of life, some proportion of it is necessary to keep the body in vigour. There are some diseases which come on in the decay of life, at least are aggravated by it; among these the most remarkable is the gout. This, when it is in the system, and does not appear with in- flammation in the extremities, has pernicious effects there, attacking the lungs, stomach, head, &c. Now to determine this to the extremities, a large proportion of animal food is necessary, especially as the person is <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> incapable of much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXERCISE">exercise</a>. Animal food, although it gives strength, is yet of many hazards to the system, as it produces plethora and all its consequences. As a stimulus to the stomach and to the whole system, it excites fever, urges the circula- tion, and promotes the perspiration. The system, however, by the repetition of these stimuli, is soon worn out; and a man who has early used the athletic diet, is either early carried off by inflammatory diseases, or, if he takes exercise sufficient to render that diet salutary, such an accumulation is made of putrefactive fluids, as in his after life lays a foundation for the most inveterate chronic distempers. Therefore it is to be questioned, whether we should desire this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HIGH">high</a> degree of bodily strength, with all the inconveniences and dangers at- tending it. Those who are chiefly employed in mental researches, and not exposed to too much bodily labour, should always avoid an excess of animal food. There is a disease which seems to require animal food, viz. the hysterical, or hypochondriac; and which appears to be very much akin to the gout, affecting the alimentary canal. All people affected with this disease are much disposed to acephaly; which sometimes goes so far, that no other vegetable but <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> can be taken in, without occasioning the worst consequences. Here then we are obliged to prefer the animal diet, even to those of very weak organs; for it generally obviates the symptoms. However, several instances of fever in ex- cess have been produced by a long <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> use of this diet, which it is always unlucky to be obliged to pre- scribe; and when it is absolutely necessary to prescribe, it should be joined with as much of the vegetable as possible, and when a cure is performed we should gradu- ally recur to that again. 2. Next, let us consider the vegetable diet. The chief inconvenience of this is difficulty of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ASSIMILATION">assimilation</a>; which, however, in the vigorous and exercised, will not be li- able to occur. In warm climates, the assimilation of vegetable aliment is more easy, so that there it may be more used, and when joined to exercise gives a pretty tolerable degree of strength and vigour; and though the general rule be in favour of animal diet, for giving strength, yet there are many instances of its being remarkably produced from vegetable. Vegetable diet has this advantage, that it whets the appetite, and that we can hardly suffer from a full meal of it. Besides. the disorders it is liable to produce in the prime via, and its falling short to give strength, there seem to be no bad consequences it can produce in the blood vessels; for there is no influence where its peculiar acrimony was ever carried there, and it is certainly less putrefactive than animal food; nor, without the utmost indolence, and a sharp appetite, does it give plethora, or any of its consequences: so that we cannot here but conclude, that a large proportion of vegetable food is useful for the generality of mankind. There is no <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ERROR">error</a> in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a> more dangerous, or more common, than the neglect of bread; for it is the safest of vegetable aliments, and the best corrector of animal food; and, by a large proportion of this alone, its bad consequences, when used in a hypochondriac state, have been obviated. The French apparently have as much animal food on their tables as the British; and yet, by a greater use of bread and the dried acid fruits, its bad effects are prevented; and therefore bread should be particularly used by the English, as they are so voracious of animal food. Vegetable food is not only necessary to secure <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a>, but long life: and, as we have said, in infancy and youth we should be confined to it mostly; in manhood, and decay of life, use animal food; and, near the end, vegetable again. There is another question much agitated, viz. What are the effects of variety in food? Is it necessary and allowable, or universally hurtful?
