Variety of a certain kind seems necessary; as vegetable and animal foods have their mutual advantages, tending to correct each other. Another variety, which is very proper, is that of liquid and solid food, which should be so managed as to temper each other; and liquid food, especially of the vegetable kind, is too ready to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PASS">pass</a> off before it is properly assimilated, while solid food makes a long stay. But this does not properly belong to the question, whether variety of the same kind is necessary or proper, as in animal foods, beef, fish, fowl, &c. It doth not appear that there is any inconvenience arising from this mixture or difficulty of assimilation, provided a moderate quantity be taken. When an inconvenience does arise, it probably proceeds from this, that one of the particular substances in the mixture, when taken by itself would produce the same effects; and, indeed, it would appear, that this effect is not heightened by the mixture, but properly obviated by it. There are few exceptions to this, if any, e.g. taking a large proportion of acidulent substances with milk. The coldness, &c. acidity, flatulence, &c. may appear; and it is possible that the coagulum, from the aceticity of the vegetables, being somewhat stronger induced, may give occasion to too long retention in the stomach, and to acidity in too great degree. Again, the mixture of fish and milk often occasions inconveniences. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEORY">theory</a> of this is difficult, though, from universal consent, it must certainly be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUST">just</a>. Can we suppose that fish gives occasion to such a coagulum as runnet? If it does so, it may produce bad effects. Besides, fishes approach somewhat to vegetables, in giving little stimulus; and are accused of the same bad effects as these, viz. bringing on the cold fit of fever. Thus much may be said for variety. But it also has its disadvantages, provoking to gluttony; this, and the art of cookery, making men take in more than they properly can digest: and hence, perhaps very justly, physicians have universally almost preferred simplicity of diet; for, in spite of rules, man's eating will only be measured by his appetite, and satiety is sooner produced by one than by many substances. But this is so far from being an argument against variety, that it is one for it, as the only way of avoiding a full meal of animal food, and its bad effects, is by presenting a quantity of vegetables. Another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEAN">mean</a> of preventing the bad effects of animal food, is to take a large proportion of liquid; and hence the bad effects of animal food are less felt in Scotland, on account of their drinking much with it, and using broths, which are at once excellent correctors of animal food and preventives of gluttony. With regard to the difference between animal foods, properly so called, the first regards their solubility, depending on a lax or firm texture of their different kinds. I. Solubility of animal food seems to deserve less <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a> than is commonly imagined; for there are many instances of persons of a weak stomach incapable of breaking <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> the texture of vegetables, or even of dissolving a light pudding, to whom hung beef, or a piece of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAM">ham</a>, was very grateful and easily digested. None of the theories given for the solution of animal food in the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> stomach seem to have explained the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PROCESS">process</a> sufficiently. Long ago has been discarded the supposition of an active corrosive menstruum there; and also the doctrine of trituration, for which, indeed, there seems no mechanism in the human body; and, till lately, physicians commonly agreed with Boerhaave in supposing nothing more to be necessary than a watery menstruum, moderate <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEAT">heat</a>, and frequent agitation. This will account for solution in some <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a>, but not entirely. Let us try to imitate it out of the body with the same circumstances, and in ten times the time in which the food is dissolved in the stomach we shall not be able to bring about the same changes. Take the coagulated <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> of an <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EGG">egg</a>, which almost every body can easily digest, and yet no artifice shall be able to dissolve it. Hence, then, we are led to seek another cause for solution, viz. <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FERMENTATION">fermentation</a>; a notion, indeed, formerly embraced, but on the introduction of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">mechanical</a> philosophy, industriously banished, with every other supposition of that process taking place at all in the animal economy. Many of the ancients imagined this fermentation to be putrefactive. But this we deny, as an acid is produced; though hence the fermentation might be reckoned the venous, which, however, seems always to be morbid. Neither, indeed, is the fermentation purely <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACETOUS">acetous</a>, but modified by putrefaction; for Pringle has observed, that animal matters raise and even expedite the acetous process. The fermentation, then, in the stomach is of a mixed nature, between the acetous and putrefactive, mutually modifying each other; though, indeed, in the intestines, somewhat of the putrefactive seems to take place, as may be observed from the state of the feces broke down, and from the little disposition of such substances to be so, which are not liable to the putrefactive process, as the firmer parts of vegetables, &c. Upon this view solution seems to be extremely easy, and those substances to be most easily broken down which FOO which are most subject to putrefaction. See ANATOMY, and GASTRIC JUICE. But solution also depends on other circumstances, and hence requires a more particular regard. 1. There is a difference of solubility with respect to the manducation of animal food, for which bread is extremely necessary, in order to keep the more slippery parts in the mouth till they be properly comminuted. From want of proper manducation persons are subject to eruptions; and this more frequently from the firm vegetable foods, as apples, almonds, &c., than from the animal, though, indeed, even from animal food, very tendinous, or swallowed in unbroken masses, such sometimes occur. Manducation is so much connected with solution, that some, from imperfectly performing that, are obliged to belch up their food, remanducate it, and swallow it again before the stomach can dissolve it, or proper nourishment be extracted. Another proof of our regard to solubility, is our rejecting the firmer parts of animal food, as bull beef, and generally carnivorous animals. 2. Its effects with regard to solubility seem also to be the foundation of our choice between fat and lean, young and old meats. In the lean although perhaps a single <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FIBRE">fibre</a> might be sufficiently tender, yet these, when collected in fasciculi, are very firm and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPACT">compact</a>, and of difficult solution; whereas in the fat there is a greater <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of vessels, a greater quantity of juice, more interposition of cellular substance, and consequently more solubility. Again, in young animals, there is probably the same number of fibres as in the older, but these more connected: whereas, in the older, the growth depending on the separation of these, and the increase of vessels and cellular substance, the texture is less firm and more soluble; which qualities, with regard to the stomach, are at that time too increased, by the increased alkalinity of the animal. To this also may be referred our choice of castrated animals, viz. on account of their disposition to fatten after the operation. 3. It is with a view to the solubility, that we make a choice between meats recently killed, and those which have been kept for some time. As soon as meat is killed, the putrefactive process begins; which commonly we allow to proceed for a little, as that process is the most effectual breaker down of animal matters, and a great afflatus to solution. The length of time during which meat ought to be kept, is proportioned to the meat's tendency to undergo the putrid fermentation, and the degree of those circumstances which favour it: Thus, in the torrid zone, where meat cannot be kept above four or five hours, it is used much more recent than in these northern climates. 4. Boiled or roasted meats create a difference of solution. By boiling we extract the juices interposed between the fibres, approximate them more to each other, and render them of more difficult solubility; which is increased too by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRACTION">extraction</a> of the juices, which are much more alkaline than the fibres: but when we want to avoid the stimulus of alkaline food, and the quick solution, as in some cases of disease, the roasted is not to be chosen. Of roasted meat it may be asked, which are more proper, those which are moist or least roasted? That which is least done is certainly the most soluble: even raw meats are more soluble than dressed, as Dr Cullen was informed by a person who from necessity was obliged, for some time, to eat such. But at the same time that meats little done are very soluble, they are very alkaline; so that, wherever we want to avoid alkalinity in the prime use, the most roasted meats should be chosen. Those who throw away the broths of boiled meat do very improperly; for, besides their supplying a fluid, from their greater alkalinity they increase the solubility of the meat. Here we shall observe, that pure blood has been thought insoluble. Undoubtedly it is very nutritious; and though out of the body, like the white of eggs, it seems very insoluble, yet, like that too, in the body it is commonly easily digested. Moses very properly forbade it the Israelites, as in warm countries it is highly alkaline; and even here, when it was used in great quantity, the scurvy was more frequent: but to a moderate use of it, in these climates, no such objection takes place. 5. Solubility is varied from another source, viz. viscosity of the juice of aliment. Young animals, then, appear more soluble than old, not only on account of the compaction and firmness of texture in the latter, but also their greater viscosity of juice. And nothing is more common, than to be longer oppressed from a full meal of veal, than from the same quantity of beef, &c. Upon account, too, of their greater viscosity of juice, are the tendinous and ligamentous parts of animals longer retained than the purely muscular, as well as on account of their firmness of texture. Even fishes, whose muscular parts are exceedingly tender, are, on account of their gluey viscosity, longer of solution in the stomach. And eggs, too, which are exceedingly nourishing, have the same effect, and cannot be taken in great quantity: For the stomach is peculiarly sensitive to gelatinous substances; and by this means has nature perhaps taught us, as it were by a sort of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTINCT">instinct</a>, to limit ourselves in the quantity of such nutritive substances. 6. With regard to solution, we must take in the oils of animal food; which, when tolerably pure, are the least putrefactive part of it, and, by diminishing the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COHESION">cohesion</a> of the fibres, render them more soluble. On this last account is the lean of fat meat more easily dissolved than other lean. But when the meat is exposed to much heat, this oil is separated, leaving the solid parts less easily soluble, and becoming itself empyreumatic, rancid, and of difficult mixture in the stomach. Fried meats, from the reasons now given, and baked meats, for the same, as well as for the tenacity of the paste, are preparations which diminish the solubility of the food. From what has been said, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREPARATION">preparation</a> of food by fattening it, and keeping it for some time after being killed, although it may administer to gluttony, will yet, it must be confessed, increase the solution of the food. II. The second difference of animal food is with regard to ALKALINEGENCY. Of this we have taken a little notice already under the head of Solubility. 1. From their too great alkalinity we commonly avoid the carnivorous animals, and the feræ; and choose rather the granivorous. Some birds, indeed, which live on insects, are admitted into our food; but no man, without nausea, can live upon these alone for any length of time. Fishes, too, are an exception to this rule, living almost universally on each other. But in these the alkaline deficiency does not proceed so far; whether from the viscosity of their juice, their want of heat, or some peculiarity in their economy, is not easy to determine. 2. Alkaline deficiency is determined by difference of age. The older animals are always more alkaline than the young, from their continual progress to putrefaction. <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOMBERG">Homberg</a> always found, in his endeavors to extract an acid from human blood, that more was obtained from the young than from the old animals. 3. A third circumstance which varies the alkaline deficiency of the food, is the wildness or tameness of the animal; and this again seems to depend on its exercise. Dr Cullen knew a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GENTLEMAN">gentleman</a> who was fond of cats for food; but he always used to feed them on vegetable food, and kept them from exercise; and in the same manner did the Romans rear up their rats, when intended for food. In the same way the flesh of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARTRIDGE">partridge</a> and the hen seems to be much the same; only, from its being more on the wing, the one is more alkaline than the other. Again, Tame animals are commonly used without their blood; whereas the wild are commonly killed in their blood, and upon that account, as well as their greater exercise, are more alkaline. 4. The alkaline deficiency of food may be determined from the quantity of volatile <a class="xref" href="vol18.html#article-SALT">salt</a> it affords. The older the meat is, it is found to give the greater proportion of volatile salt. 5. The alkaline deficiency of aliment may also, in some measure, be determined from its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>, the younger animals being whiter and less alkaline. We also take a mark from the colour of the gravy poured out, according to the redness of the juices judging of the animal's alkaline deficiency. 6. The relish of food is found to depend much on its alkaline deficiency, as does also the stimulus it gives and the fever it produces in the system. These effects are also complicated with the viscosity of the food, by which means it is longer detained in the stomach, and the want of alkaline deficiency supplied. Having mentioned animal food as differing in solubility and alkaline deficiency, which often go together in the same subject, we come to the third difference, viz. III. Quantity of Nutrient. Which is either <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ABSOLUTE">absolute</a> or relative; absolute with respect to the quantity it really contains, sufficient powers being given to extract it; relative, with respect to the assimilatory powers of those who use it. The absolute nutrient is of some consequence; but the relative, in the robust and healthy, and except in cases of extraordinary weakness, may, without much inconvenience, be disregarded. In another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is the quantity of nourishment relative, viz. with regard to its perspiration; for if the food is soon carried off by the excretions, it is the same thing as if it contained a less proportion of nourishment. For, giving more fluid, that which is longer retained affords most; and, for the repair of the solids, that retention also is of advantage. Now, gelatinous substances are long retained; and besides, are themselves animal substances dissolved: so that, both absolutely and relatively, such substances are nutritious. Of this kind are eggs, shell fish, &c. In adults, though it is disputed whether their solids need any repair, yet at any rate, at this period, fluid is more required; for this purpose the alkaline foods are most proper, being most easily dissolved. They are, at the same time, the most perishable; on one <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a> that alkaline deficiency leading to disease, while on the other their perishability obviates it. Adults, therefore, as writers justly observe, are better nourished on the alkaline; the young and growing, on gelatinous foods. All this leads to a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPARISON">comparison</a> of young and old meats; the first being more gelatinous, and the last more alkaline. This, however, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPERIENCE">experience</a>, is not yet properly ascertained. Mr Geoffroy is the only person who has been taken up with the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALYSIS">analysis</a> of foods. See Memoires de l'Academie, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAN">Pan</a>. 1731 & 1732. His attempt was certainly laudable, and in some respects usefully performed; but, in general, his experiments were not sufficiently repeated, nor are indeed sufficiently accurate. He has not been on his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GUARD">guard</a> against the various circumstances which affect meats; the cow-kind liking a moist succulent herbage, which is not to be got in warm climates; while the sheep are fond of dry food, and thrive best there. Again, Some of his experiments seem contradictory. He says, that veal gives more solution than beef, while lamb gives less than mutton, which is much to be doubted. If both he and Sanctorius had examined English beef, the result probably would have been very different as to its perspiration, &c. Besides, Mr Geoffroy has only analyzed beef and veal when raw; has made no proper circumstantial comparisons between <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a> and birds; and has examined these last along with their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BONES">bones</a>, and not their muscles, &c. by themselves, as he ought to have done, &c. If a set of experiments of this kind were properly and accurately performed, they might be of great use; but at present, for the purpose of determining our present subject, we must have recourse to our alkaline, solubility, &c. IV. The fourth difference of animal food is, The Nature of the Fluids they afford. The whole of this will be understood from what has been said on alkaline deficiency; the fluid produced being more or less dense and stimulating, in proportion as that prevails. V. The fifth difference of animal foods is with respect to their Perspiration. The sum of what can be said on this matter is this, that such foods as promote an accumulation of fluid in our vessels and dispose to plethora, are the least perishable, and commonly give most strength; that the more alkaline foods are the most perishable, though the viscid and less alkaline may attain the same <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> by long retention in the system. The authors on perspiration have determined the perspiration of foods as imperfectly as Mr Geoffroy has done the solubility, and in a few cases only. We must not lay hold on what Sanctorius has said on the perspiration of mutton, because he has not examined in the same way other meats in their perfect state; far less on what Keil says of oysters, as he himself was a valetudinarian, and consequently an unfit subject for such experiments, and probably of a peculiar <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERAMENT">temperament</a>. As to the effects of Food on the Mind, we have already hinted at them above. It is plain, that deli- cacy of feeling, liveliness of imagination, quickness of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-APPREHENSION">apprehension</a>, and acuteness of judgment, more frequently accompany a weak state of the body. True it is indeed, that the same state is liable to timidity, fluctuation and doubt; while the strong have that steadiness of judgment, and firmness of purpose, which are proper for the higher and more active scenes of life. The most valuable state of the mind, however, appears to reside in somewhat less firmness and vigour of body. Vegetable aliment, as never over-stimulating the vessels or loading the system, never interrupts the stronger motions of the mind; while the heat, fulness, and weight, of animal food, are an enemy to its vigorous efforts. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEMPERANCE">Temperance</a>, then, does not so much consist in the quantity, for that always will be regulated by our appetite, as in the quality, viz., a large proportion of vegetable aliment. A considerable change has now taken place in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> made use of as food by the ancients, by substituting, instead of what were then used, particularly of the vegetable kind, a number of more bland, agreeable, and nutritive juices. The acorns and nuts of the primitive times have given way to a variety of sweeter farinaceous seeds and roots. To the malvaceous tribe of plants so much used by the Greeks and Romans, hath succeeded the more grateful spinach; and to the bitter, the garden orach. The rough borage is supplanted by the excellent <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SORREL">sorrel</a>; and asparagus has banished a number of roots recorded by the Roman writers under the name of bulbis; but Linnaeus is of opinion, that the parsnip has undeservedly usurped the place of the skirret. The bean of the ancients, improperly so called, being the roots as well as other parts of the nymphaea melumbo, or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIAN">Indian</a> water-lily, is superseded by the kidney bean. The garden rocket, eaten with and as an antidote against the chilling qualities of the lettuce, is banished by the more agreeable cress and tarragon; the apium by the meliorated celery; the pompion, and others of the cucurbitaceous tribe, by the melon; and the fennel berries, by the fragrant <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUTMEG">nutmeg</a>. The filipium, or succus Cyrenaicus, which the Romans purchased from <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol3.html#article-PERSIA">Persia</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDIA">India</a> at a great price, and is thought by some to have been the affaecida of the present time, is no longer used in preference to the alliaceous tribe. To turn from the vegetable to some of the animal substitutes, we may mention the carp among fishes as having excluded a great number held in high estimation among the Romans; the change of oil for <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-BUTTER">butter</a>; of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HONEY">honey</a> for <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SUGAR">sugar</a>; of mulfa, or liquors made of wine, water, and honey, for the wines of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> times; and that of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> zythus for the present improved malt liquors; not to mention also the Callida of the Roman taverns, analogous to our <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">tea</a> and coffee. Food of Plants. See <a class="xref" href="vol1.html#article-AGRICULTURE">Agriculture</a> Index.

FONTARABIA

Pages 415-415

a <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">sea</a> port town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SPAIN">Spain</a>, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BISCAY">Biscay</a>, and in the territory of Guipúzcoa, seated on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PENINSULA">peninsula</a> on the sea shore, and on the river Bidafoa. It is small, but well fortified both by <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> and art; and has a good harbour, though dry at low <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>. It is built in the form of an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AMPHITHEATRE">amphitheatre</a>, on the declivity of a hill, and surrounded on the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LAND">land</a> side by the lofty Pyrenean <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOUNTAINS">mountains</a>. It is a very important <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, being accounted the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KEY">key</a> of Spain on that side. W. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">Long</a>. i. 43. N. Lat. 43. 23.

FOOSHT

Pages 422-422

an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ISLAND">island</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RED_SEA"><a clas</a>s="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">Red</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SEA">Sea</a>; situated, according to the observations of Mr Bruce, in N. Lat. 13° 59' 43". It is described by him as about five miles in length from <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NORTH">north</a> to south, though only <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NINE">nine</a> in circumference. It is low and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-SANDY">sandy</a> in the southern <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, but the north rises in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BLACK">black</a> hill of inconsiderable height. It is covered with a kind of bent grass, which never arises at any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> length by reason of want of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RAIN">rain</a> and the constant browsing of the goats. There are great appearances of the black hill having once been a volcano; and near the north <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPE">cape</a> the ground sounds hollow like the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol20.html#article-SOLFATARA">Solfatara</a> in <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-ITALY">Italy</a>. There are a vast <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of beautiful fish met with upon the coasts, but few fit for eating; and our traveller observed, that the most beautiful were the most noxious when eaten; none indeed, being salutary food excepting those which resembled the fish of the northern seas. There are many beautiful shell-fish, as the concha veneris, of several colours and sizes; sea urchins, &c. Sponges are likewise found all along the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COAST">coast</a>. There are also pearls, but neither <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LARGE">large</a> nor of a good-<a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a>; in <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of which they sell at no great price. They are produced by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> of bivalve shells. Several large shells, from the fish named biffer, are met with upon <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONES">stones</a> of ten <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> twelve tons <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a> along the coast. They are turned upon their faces and sunk into the stones, as into a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATE">pate</a>, the <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-STONE">stone</a> being raised all about them in such a manner as to cover the edge of the shell; "a <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROOF">proof</a> (says Mr Bruce) that this stone must some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> lately have been soft or liquefied: for had it been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> ago, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUN">sun</a> and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> would have worn the surface of the shell; but it seems perfectly entire, and is set in that hard <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BROWN">brown</a> rock as the stone of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RING">ring</a> is in a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOLDEN">golden</a> casing."—The water in this island is very good. The inhabitants of Fooht are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POOR">poor</a> fishermen of a swarthy <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLOUR">colour</a>; going naked, excepting only a rag about their waist. They have no <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREAD">bread</a> but what they procure in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXCHANGE">exchange</a> for the fish they catch. What they <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BARTER">barter</a> in this manner is called fejan. But besides this they catch another species, which is flat, with a long tail, and the skin made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHAGREEN">shagreen</a>, of which the handles of knives and swords are made. There is a small town on the island, consisting of about 30 huts, built with faggots of bent grass or spartum, supported by a few sticks, and thatched with grass of the same kind of which they are built.

FOOT

Pages 422-423

a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the body of most animals whereon they stand, walk, &c. See Anatomy. Foot, in the Latin and Greek <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-POETRY">poetry</a>, a metre <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MEASURE">measure</a>, composed of a certain <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> and short syllables. These feet are <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-COMMONLY">commonly</a> reckoned 28: of which some are simple, as consisting of two or three syllables, and therefore called difyllabic or trifyllabic feet; others are <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>, consisting of four syllables, and are therefore called tetrafyllabic feet. The difyllabic feet are four in number, viz., the pyrrhichius, spondeus, <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IAMBUS">iambus</a>, and trocheus. See Pyrrhichius, &c. The trifyllabic feet are eight in number, viz., the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol7.html#article-DACTYLUS">dactylus</a>, anaepetus, tribrachys, molossus, amphibrachys, amphimacer, bacchius, and antibacchius. See Dactyl, &c. The tetrafyllabic are in number 16, viz., the proceleufmaticus, dispondeus, choriambus, antipausus, diambus, dichoreus, ionicus a majore, ionicus a minore, epitritus primus, epitritus secundus, epitritus tertius, epitritus Foot is also a long measure consisting of 12 inches. Geometricians divide the foot into 10 digits, and the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol8.html#article-DIGIT">digit</a> into 10 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINES">lines</a>. Foot-Halt, the name of a disorder peculiar to sheep. It is occasioned by an insect, which, when it comes to a certain maturity, resembles a worm of two, three, or four inches in length. See Farriery <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Foot <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SQUARE">Square</a>, is the same measure both in breadth and length, containing 144 square or superficial inches. Cubic or <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SOLID">Solid</a> Foot, is the same measure in all the three dimensions, length, breadth, and depth or thickness, containing 1728 cubic inches. Foot of a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">Horse</a>, in the manege, the extremity of the leg, from the coronet to the lower part of the hoof. Foot <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">Level</a>, among artificers, an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> that serves as a foot rule, a square, and a level. See Level, Rule, and Square.

FOOTE

Pages 423-424

SAMUEL, Esq., the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODERN">modern</a> <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARISTOPHANES">Aristophanes</a>, was born at <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol21.html#article-TRURO">Truro</a>, in Cornwall; and was descended from a very <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANCIENT">ancient</a> family. His father was member of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> for Tiverton, in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVONSHIRE">Devonshire</a>, and enjoyed the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POST">post</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSIONER">commissioner</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRIZE">prize</a> office and fine-contrat. His mother was heiress of the Dinley and Goodere families. In <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONSEQUENCE">consequence</a> of a fatal misunderstanding between her two brothers, Sir John Dinley Goodere, Bart. and Samuel Goodere, Esq. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CAPTAIN">captain</a> of his majesty's ship the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RUBY">Ruby</a>, which ended in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEATH">death</a> of both, a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of the Goodere estate, which was better than 5000l. per annum, descended to Mr Foote. He was educated at <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORCESTER">Worcester</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLLEGE">college</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-OXFORD">Oxford</a>, which owed its foundation to Sir Thomas Cookes Winford, Bart. a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUSIN">cousin</a> of our author's. On leaving the university, he commenced student of <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a> in the Temple; but as the dryness of this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUIT">suit</a> the liveliness of his genius, he soon relinquished it. He married a young lady of a good family and some fortune; but their tempers not agreeing, a perfect <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HARMONY">harmony</a> did not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> subsist between them. He now launched into all the fashionable foibles of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAMING">gaming</a> not excepted, and in a few years spent his whole fortune. His necessities led him to the stage, and he made his first appearance in the character of Othello. He next performed Pendlewife with much more applause; and this, indeed, was ever after one of his <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CAPITAL">capital</a> parts. He attempted <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">Lord</a> Foppington likewise, but prudently gave it up. But as Mr Foote was never a capital <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTOR">actor</a> in the plays of others, his salary was very unequal to his gay and extravagant turn; and he contracted debts which forced him to take refuge within the verge of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a>. On this occasion, he relieved his necessities by the following stratagem. Sir Fr—s D—l—l had long been his intimate friend, and had dissipated his fortune by similar extravagance. Lady N—n—P—let, who was likewise an intimate acquaintance of Foote's, and who was exceedingly rich, was fortunately at that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> bent upon a matrimonial scheme. Foote strongly recommended to her to consult upon this momentous affair the conjurer in the Old Bailey, whom he represented as a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> of surprising skill and penetration. He employed an acquaintance of his own to perforate the conjurer; who depicted Sir Fr—s D—l—l at full length; described the time when, the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a> where, and the dress in which she would see him. The lady was so struck with the coincidence of every circumstance, that she married D—l—l in a few days. For this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVICE">service</a> Sir Francis settled an annuity upon Foote; and this enabled him once more to emerge from obscurity. In 1747 he opened the little <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-THEATRE">theatre</a> in the Haymarket, taking upon himself the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOUBLE">double</a> character of author and performer; and appeared in a dramatic piece of his own <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOSITION">composition</a>, called the Divertions of the Morning. This piece consisted of nothing more than the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of several <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARACTERS">characters</a> well known in real <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>; whose manner of conversation and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXPRESSION">expression</a> this author very happily <a class="xref" href="../1860/vol11.html#article-HIT">hit</a> off in the diction of his drama, and still more happily represented on the stage, by an exact and most amazing <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-IMITATION">imitation</a>, not only of the manner and tone of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-VOICE">voice</a>, but even of the very persons, of those whom he intended to take off. In this performance, a certain physician, Dr L—n, well known for the oddity and singularity of his appearance and conversation, and the celebrated Chevalier Taylor, who was at that time in the height of his popularity, were made objects of Foote's <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIDICULE">ridicule</a>; the latter, indeed, very deservedly; and, in the concluding part of his speech, under the character of a theatrical <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTOR">director</a>, Mr Foote took off, with <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GREAT">great</a> humour and accuracy, the several styles of acting of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> performer on the English stage. This performance at first met with some opposition from the civil magistrates of Westminster, under the sanction of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a> of parliament for limiting the <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of playhouses, as well as from the jealousy of one of the managers of Drury-lane <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol0.html#article-PLAYHOUSE">playhouse</a>; but the author being patronized by many of the principal <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NOBILITY">nobility</a>, and other persons of distinction, this opposition was overruled; and having altered the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of his performance, Mr Foote proceeded, without further molestation, to give <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TEA">Tea</a> in a Morning to his friends, and represented it through a run of 40 mornings to crowded and splendid audiences.—The ensuing season he produced another piece of the same kind, which he called An Auction of Pictures. In this performance he introduced several new and popular characters; particularly Sir Thomas de Veil, then the acting <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JUSTICE">justice</a> of peace for Westminster, Mr Cock the celebrated auctioneer, and the equally famous Orator Henley. This piece also had a very great run.—His Knights, which was the produce of the ensuing season, was a performance of somewhat more dramatic regularity: but still, although his plot and characters seemed less immediately personal, it was apparent that he kept some particular real persons strongly in his eye in the performance; and the town took upon themselves to fix them where the resemblance appeared to be the most striking. Thus Mr Foote <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-CONTINUED">continued</a> from time to time to select, for the entertainment of the public, such characters, as well general as individual, as seemed most likely to engage their <a class="xref" href="vol3.html#article-ATTENTION">attention</a>. His dramatic pieces, exclusive of the interlude called Piety in Patterns, are as follow: <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">Taste</a>, the Knights, The Author, The Englishman in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARIS">Paris</a>, The Englishman returned from Paris, The Mayor of Garrat, The Liar, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PATRON">Patron</a>, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MINOR">Minor</a>, The Orators, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMISSARY">Commissary</a>, Commissary, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DEVIL">Devil</a> upon Two Sticks, The Lame Lover, The Maid of Bath, The Nabob, The Cozeners, The Capuchin, The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BANKRUPT">Bankrupt</a>, and an unfinished <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMEDY">comedy</a> called The Slanderer. All these works are only to be ranked among the petticoat pieces of the theatre. In the execution they are somewhat loose, negligent, and unfinished; the plots are often <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IRREGULAR">irregular</a>, and the catastrophes not always conclusive: but, with all these deficiencies, they contain more strength of character, more strokes of keen satire, and more touches of temporary humour, than are to be found in the writings of any other modern dramatist. Even the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> spoken by his characters, incorrect as it may sometimes seem, <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> on a closer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXAMINATION">examination</a> be found entirely dramatical; as it abounds with those <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> minute of expression which frequently form the very basis of character, and which render it the truest mirror of the conversation of the times in which he wrote. In the year 1766, being on a party of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PLEASURE">pleasure</a> with the late <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DUKE">duke</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-YORK">York</a>, Lord Mexborough, and Sir Francis Delaval, Mr Foote had the misfortune to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAK">break</a> his leg, by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FALL">fall</a> from his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a>; in consequence of which, he was compelled to undergo an amputation. This accident so sensibly affected the duke, that he made a point of obtaining for Mr Foote a patent for life; whereby he was allowed to perform, at the little theatre in the Haymarket, from the 15th of May to the 15th of September every year. He now became a greater favourite of the town than ever: his very laughable pieces, with his more laughable performance, constantly filled his <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>; and his receipts were some seasons almost incredible. Parsimony was never a vice to be ascribed to Mr Foote; his hospitality and generosity were ever conspicuous; he was visited by the first nobility, and he was sometimes honoured even by <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> guests. The attack made upon his character by one of his domestics, whom he had dismissed for misbehaviour, is too well known to be particularized here. Suffice it to say, he was honourably acquitted of that <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CHARGE">charge</a>: but it is believed by some, that the shock which he received from it accelerated his death; others pretend, that his literary altercation with a certain then duchess, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> rather her agents, much affected him, and that from that time his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEALTH">health</a> declined. It is probable, however, that his natural volatility of spirits could scarcely fail to support him against all impressions from either of these <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUARTERS">quarters</a>. Mr Foote, finding his health decline, entered into an agreement with Mr Colman, for his patent of the theatre; according to which, he was to receive from Mr Colman, £600 per annum, besides a stipulated sum whenever he chose to perform. Mr Foote made his appearance two or three times in some of the most admired characters; but, being suddenly affected with a paralytic stroke one night whilst upon the stage, he was compelled to retire. He was advised to bathe; and accordingly repaired to Brighthelmstone, where he apparently recovered his former health and spirits, and was what is called the fiddle of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPANY">company</a> who resorted to that agreeable place of amusement. A few weeks before his death, he returned to <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-LONDON">London</a>; but, by the advice of his physicians, set out with an intention to spend the winter at Paris and in the south of France. He had got no farther than <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOVER">Dover</a>, when he was suddenly attacked by another stroke of the palsy, which in a few hours terminated his existence. He died on the 21st of October 1777, in the 56th year of his age, and was privately interred in the cloisters of Westminster <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol2.html#article-ABBEY">abbey</a>.

FORAMEN

Pages 424-424

in Anatomy, a name given to several apertures <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perforations in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIVERS">divers</a> parts of the body; as, 1. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTERNAL">external</a> and internal foramina of the cranium or skull. 2. The foramina in the upper and lower jaw. 3. Foramen lachrymale. 4. Foramen membranae tympani. Foramen Ovalis, an oval aperture or passage through the heart of a fetus, which closes up after birth. It arises from the coronal vein, near the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> auricle, and passes directly into the left auricle of the heart, serving for the circulation of the blood in the fetus, till such <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> as the infant breathes, and the lungs are open: in this the fetus differs from the adult; although almost all anatomists, Mr Chefelden excepted, assure us, that the foramen ovale has sometimes been found in adults. See FOETUS.

FORBES

Pages 424-424

DUNCAN, Esq., of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CULLODEN">Culloden</a>, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LORD">lord</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRESIDENT">president</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol6.html#article-COURT">court</a> of session in Scotland, was born in the year 1685. In his early <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, he was brought up in a family remarkable for hospitality; which, perhaps, led him afterwards to a freer <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INDULGENCE">indulgence</a> in social pleasures. His <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> disposition inclined him to the <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ARMY">army</a>; but, as he soon discovered a superior genius, by the advice of his friends he applied himself to letters. He directed his studies particularly to the civil <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>; in which he made a quick progress, and in 1709 was admitted an advocate. From 1722 to 1737, he represented in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PARLIAMENT">parliament</a> the boroughs of <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INVERNESS">Inverness</a>, Fortrose, Nairn, and Forres. In 1725, he was made <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KING">king</a>'s advocate; and lord president of the court of session in 1737. In the rebellions which broke out in Scotland in 1715 and 1745 he espoused the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol19.html#article-ROYAL">royal</a> cause; but with so much <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRUDENCE">prudence</a> and moderation did he conduct himself at this delicate conjuncture, that not a whisper was at any <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> heard to his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PREJUDICE">prejudice</a>. The <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GLORY">glory</a> he acquired in advancing the prosperity of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, and in contributing to re-establish peace and order, was the only reward of his services. He had even impaired, and almost ruined, his private fortune in the cause of the public: but <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GOVERNMENT">government</a> did not make him the smallest recompense. The minister, with a meanness for which it is difficult to account, desired to have a state of his disbursements. Shocked at the incivility and rudeness of this treatment, he left the minister without making any reply. Throughout the whole course of his life he had a lively <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSE">sense</a> of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RELIGION">religion</a>, without the least taint of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUPERSTITION">superstition</a>; and his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHARITY">charity</a> was extended to every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECT">sect</a> and denomination of religionists indiscriminately. He was well versed in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HEBREW">Hebrew</a> <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a>; and wrote in a flowing and oratorical style, concerning religion natural and revealed, some important discoveries in <a class="xref" href="../1797/vol18.html#article-THEOLOGY">theology</a> and <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">philosophy</a>, and concerning the sources of incredulity. He died in 1747, in the 62nd year of his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a>; and his works have since been published in two volumes octavo.

FORCE

Pages 424-425

in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol17.html#article-PHILOSOPHY">Philosophy</a>, denotes the cause of the change. change in the state of a body, when, being at rest, it begins to move, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MOTION">motion</a> which is either not uniform or not <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECT">direct</a>. While a body remains in the same state, either of rest or of uniform and rectilinear motion, the cause of its remaining in such a state is in the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of the body, and it cannot be said that any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXTRINSIC">extrinsic</a> force has acted on it. This internal cause or principle is called <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-INERTIA">inertia</a>. <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICAL">Mechanical</a> forces may be reduced to two sorts: one of a body at rest, the other of a body in motion. The force of a body at rest, is that which we conceive to be in a body lying still on a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TABLE">table</a>, or hanging by a rope, or supported by a <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPRING">spring</a>, &c. and this is called by the names of preflure, tension, force, or vis mortua, solicitatio, <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONATUS">conatus</a> movendi, conamen, &c. To this class also of forces we must refer centripetal and centrifugal forces, though they reside in a body in motion; because these forces are homogeneous to weights, preflures, or tensions of any kind. The force of a body in motion is a power residing in that body so <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> as it continues its motion; by means of which it is able to remove obstacles lying in its way; to lessen, destroy, or overcome the force of any other moving body which meets it in an opposite <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIRECTION">direction</a>; or to surmount any dead preflure or resistance, as tensity, gravity, friction, &c. for some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a>; but which <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be lessened or destroyed by such resistance as lessens or destroys the motion of the body. This is called moving force, vis motrix, and by some late writers vis viva, to distinguish it from the vis mortua spoken of before; and by these appellations, however different, the same thing is understood by all mathematicians; namely, that power of displacing, of withstanding opposite moving forces, or of overcoming any dead resistance, which resides in a moving body, and which, in whole or in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a>, continues to accompany it, so long as the body moves. See <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>. We have several curious as well as useful observations in Defaguliers's <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-EXPERIMENTAL_PHILOSOPHY">Experimental Philosophy</a>, concerning the comparative forces of men and horses, and the best way of applying them. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> draws with the greatest advantage when the line of direction is <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVEL">level</a> with his <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BREAST">breast</a>; in such a situation, he is able to draw 200lb. eight hours a-<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, walking about two miles and a half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a>. And <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> the same horse is made to draw 240lb., he can <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> but six hours a-day, and cannot go quite so fast. On a carriage, indeed where friction alone is to be overcome, a middling horse will draw 1000lb. But the best way to try a horse's force, is by making him draw up out of a well, over a single pulley or <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ROLLER">roller</a>; and, in such a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a>, one horse with another will draw 200lb. as already observed. Five men are found to be equal in strength to one horse, and can, with as much ease, push round the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HORIZONTAL">horizontal</a> beam of a mill, in a walk 40 feet wide; whereas three men will do it in a walk only 19 feet wide. The worst way of applying the force of a horse, is to make him carry or draw up hill: for if the hill be steep, three men will do more than a horse, each <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> climbing up faster with a burden of 100lb. <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEIGHT">weight</a>, than a horse that is loaded with 300lb.; a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> which is owing to the position of the parts of the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> body being better adapted to climb than those of a horse. On the other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HAND">hand</a>, the best way of applying the force of a horse, is in a horizontal direction, wherein a man can exert least force; thus a man weighing 140lb. and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BOAT">boat</a> along by means of a rope coming over his shoulders, cannot draw above 27lb. or exert above one seventh part of the force of a horse employed to the same purpose. The very best and most effectual posture in a man, is that of rowing, in which he not only acts with more muscles at once for overcoming the resistance, than in any other position; but as he pulls backward, the weight of his body assists by way of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LEVER">lever</a>. See Defaguliers, Exp. Phil. vol. i. p. 241, where we have several other observations relative to force acquired by certain positions of the body, from which that author accounts for most feats of strength and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACTIVITY">activity</a>. See also Memoire on this subject by M. de la Hire, in Mem. Roy. Acad. Sc. 1629; or in Defaguliers, Exp. &c. 267, &c. who has published a translation of part of it, with remarks. Citizen Regnier has invented an <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INSTRUMENT">instrument</a> for ascertaining the relative strength of men and animals, for an account of which, see Dynamometer; and for a fuller <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-APPARATUS">apparatus</a>, the reader may consult the original <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PAPER">paper</a> on the subject in Journal de l'Ecole Polytechn., vol. ii. or the translation in Phil. Mag. vol. i. Force, in <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">Law</a>, signifies any unlawful violence offered to things or persons, and is divided into simple and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMPOUND">compound</a>. Simple force is what is so committed, that it has no other crime attending it; as where a person by force enters another's possession, without committing any other unlawful <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Compound force, is where some other violence is committed, with such an act which of itself alone is criminal; as if one enters by force into another's <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUSE">house</a>, and there kills a person, or ravishes a woman. There is likewise a force implied in law, as in every trepans, rescue, or distress, and an actual force with weapons, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of persons, &c.—Any person may lawfully enter a tavern, inn, or victualling house; so may a landlord his tenant's house to view repairs, &c. But if, in these <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> the person that enters commits any violence or force, the law will intend that he entered for that purpose.

FORCEPS

Pages 425-425

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SURGERY">Surgery</a>, &c. a <a class="xref" href="../1778/vol0.html#article-PAIR">pair</a> of scissors for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUTTING">cutting</a> off, <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> dividing, the fleshy membranous parts of the body, as occasion requires. See Surgery.

FORCER

Pages 425-425

in <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MECHANICS">Mechanics</a>, is properly a piston without a <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VALVE">valve</a>. For, by <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DRAWING">drawing</a> up such a piston, the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AIR">air</a> is drawn up, and the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WATER">water</a> follows; then pushing the piston <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> again, the water, being prevented from descending by the lower valve, is forced up to any height above, by means of a side branch between the two.

FORCIBLE ENTRY

Pages 425-426

is a violent and actual entry into houses <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> lands; and a forcible detainee, is where one by violence withholds the possession of lands, &c. so that the person who has a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-RIGHT">right</a> of entry is barred, or hindered, therefrom. At <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LAW">law</a>, any person that had a right to enter into lands, &c. might retain possession of it by force. But this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIBERTY">liberty</a> being abused, to the <a class="xref" href="vol4.html#article-BREACH">breach</a> of the peace, it was therefore found necessary that the same should be restrained: Though, at this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DAY">day</a>, he who is wrongfully dispossessed of goods may by force retake them. By statute, no persons shall make an entry on any lands or tenements, except where it is given by law, and in a peaceable manner; even though they have <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TITLE">title</a> of entry, on pain of imprisonment: and where a forcible entry is committed, justices of peace are authorized to view the <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLACE">place</a>, and inquire of the force by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-JURY">jury</a>, summoned by the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHERIFF">sheriff</a> of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTY">county</a>; and they may cause the tenements, &c., to be restored, and imprison the offenders till they pay a fine. Likewise a writ of forcible entry lies, where a person seised of freehold, is by force put out thereof. **Forcible <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MARRIAGE">Marriage</a>**, of a woman of estate, is felony. For by the statute 3 H. VII. c. 2, it is enacted, "That <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> any persons shall take away any woman having lands or goods, or that is heir apparent to her ancestor, by force, and against her <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a>, and marry or defile her; the takers, procurers, abettors, and receivers, of the woman taken away against her will, and knowing the same, shall be deemed <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PRINCIPAL">principal</a> felons; but as to procurers and accessories before the fact, they are to be excluded the benefit of clergy, by 39 <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ELIZABETH">Elizabeth</a> c. 9. The <a class="xref" href="vol11.html#article-INDICTMENT">indictment</a> on the statute H. VII. is expressly set forth, that the woman taken away had lands or goods, or was heir apparent; and also that she was married or defiled, because no other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> is within the statute; and it ought to allege that the taking was for lucre. It is no excuse that the woman at first was taken away with her consent: for if she afterwards refuse to continue with the offender, and be forced against her will, she may from that <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> properly be said to be taken against her will; and it is not material whether a woman so taken away be at last married or defiled with her own consent or not, if she were under force at the time; the offender being in both <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> equally within the words of the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ACT">act</a>. Those persons who, after the fact, receive the offender, are but accessories after the offence, according to the rules of common law; and those that are only privy to the damage, but not parties to the forcible taking away, are not within the act, H. P. C. 119. A <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> may be indicted for taking away a woman by force in another <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>; for the continuing of the force in any country, amounts to a forcible taking there. Ibid. Taking away any woman-child under the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-AGE">age</a> of 16 years and unmarried, out of the custody and without the consent of the father or <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol11.html#article-GUARDIAN">guardian</a>, &c., the offender shall suffer fine and imprisonment; and if the woman agrees to any <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CONTRACT">contract</a> of matrimony with such person, she shall forfeit her estate during <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIFE">life</a>, to the next of kin, to whom the inheritance should descend, &c. Stat. 4 & 5, P. & M. c. 8. This is a force against the parents: and an information will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIE">lie</a> for forcing a young man or woman from their parents, against their consents, in order to marry them, &c. See Marriage. **Forcing**, in <a class="xref" href="vol9.html#article-GARDENING">Gardening</a>, a method of producing ripe <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FRUITS">fruits</a> from trees before their <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-NATURAL">natural</a> season. See Gardening <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol0.html#article-INDEX">Index</a>. Forcing, in the wine trade, a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TERM">term</a> used by the wine coopers for the fining <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOWN">down</a> wines, and rendering them fit for immediate draught. The principal inconvenience of the common way of fining down the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WHITE">white</a> wines with isinglass, and the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RED">red</a> with whites of eggs, is the slowness of the operation; these ingredients not performing their office in less than a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-WEEK">week</a>, or sometimes a fortnight, according as the <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WEATHER">weather</a> proves favourable, cloudy or clear, windy or calm: this appears to be <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MATTER">matter</a> of constant observation. But the wine merchant frequently requires a method that shall, with certainty, make the wines fit for taffing in a few hours. A method of this kind there is, but it is kept in a few <a class="xref" href="../1771/vol2.html#article-HANDS">hands</a> a valuable secret. Perhaps it depends upon a prudent <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-USE">use</a> of a tartarized spirit of wine, and the common forcing, as occasion is, along with gypsum, as the principal; all which are to be well stirred about in the wine, for half an <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HOUR">hour</a> before it is suffered to rest. **Fordoun**, John of, the father of Scottish <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-HISTORY">history</a>, flourished in the reign of Alexander III., towards the end of the 13th century. But of his life there is nothing known with certainty, though there was not a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MONASTERY">monastery</a> that possessed not copies of his <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a>. The first five books of the history which bears his name were written by him; the rest were fabricated from materials left by him, and from new collections by different persons. A manuscript in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-VELLUM">vellum</a> of this historian is in the library of the university of <a class="xref" href="vol7.html#article-EDINBURGH">Edinburgh</a>. **Fordwich**, a town of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-KENT">Kent</a>, called in Domesday Book "the little borough of Fordwich," is a member of the port of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SANDWICH">Sandwich</a>, and was anciently incorporated by the style of the barons of the town of Fordwich, but more lately by the name of the mayor, jurats, and <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMONALTY">commonalty</a>, who enjoy the same privileges as the cinque ports. This place is famous for excellent trouts in its river Stour.

OUR AUTHOR

Pages 290-290

r author expresses his surprise, that the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CUSTOM">custom</a> of wearing <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-FLANNEL">flannel</a> next the skin should not have prevailed more universally. He is confident it would prevent a <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of diseases; and he thinks there is no greater <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LUXURY">luxury</a> than the comfortable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SENSATION">sensation</a> which arises from wearing it, especially after one is a little accustomed to it. "It is a mistaken notion (says he), that it is too warm a clothing for <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SUMMER">summer</a>. I have worn it in the hottest climates, and at all seasons of the year; and never found the least inconvenience from it. It is the warm bath of perspiration confined by a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LINEN">linen</a> shirt, wet with sweat, which renders the summer heats of southern climates so unsupportable; but flannel promotes perspiration, and favours its <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EVAPORATION">evaporation</a>; and evaporation, as is well known, produces positive <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COLD">cold</a>. It has been observed that new flannel, after some <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> wearing, acquires the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of thinning in the dark, but loses it on being washed. Philosophical Transactions, No. 483, § 7.

POPE

Pages 23-31

The <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAGUE">plague</a> of boils that raged among the Egyptians (Exod. ix. 10.) affected both <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MAN">man</a> and beast. Similar instances are related both by sacred and profane historians. Almost the whole tribe of inflammations, even the gout (according to Van Swieten), are found to affect the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DOMESTIC">domestic</a> animals, are produced by the same causes, (A) It may be thought by some, that we have gone too far in accusing the farriers and grooms, &c. of having a fellow-feeling; but, when it is known, that "a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-PART">part</a> of every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SHILLING">shilling</a> paid to <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COMMON">common</a> farriers, is in some shape returned to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GROOM">groom</a>, as a fee <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-OR">or</a> perquisite;" that "the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SERVANT">servant</a> receives at least five per cent. from the <a class="xref" href="vol8.html#article-FARRIER">farrier</a> on every <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-BILL">bill</a> paid by his <a class="xref" href="vol12.html#article-MASTER">master</a>;" and that "<a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-IF">if</a> a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HORSE">horse</a> dies under the care of a farrier, he generally becomes the <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-PROPERTY">property</a> of the groom;" (See Veterinary Transactions, No. 1. Introduction); it <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WILL">will</a> be allowed that there is some ground for the surmise. Domestic animals are subject to eruptive diseases, both chronic, and such as are attended with fever; and both are very similar to those by which man is affected. It is pretty certain that the smallpox sometimes rages among sheep, as we shall see hereafter; and a complaint very like the measles often attacks swine. Some of them are transferable to man; and to this transference in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CASE">case</a> of the cowpox, a blessing which will render immortal the name of Jenner, we owe the probable annihilation of one of the most dreadful pests that ever afflicted the <a class="xref" href="vol10.html#article-HUMAN">human</a> <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-RACE">race</a>. Scrofula and consumption attack monkeys. Apoplexy, epilepsy, and many others of what are called nervous diseases, indigestion, and even mental derangement, are not uncommon among domestic animals; spasmodic affections are very frequent among them, and it is said, that for one case of tetanus or locked jaw among the human <a class="xref" href="vol19.html#article-SPECIES">species</a> in these climates, there are ten or twenty among horses. The <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ANALOGY">analogy</a> might be pursued much farther; but what has been stated is sufficient to show the advantages that medical men may derive from the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-STUDY">study</a> of veterinary medicine. Many obscure and dangerous diseases may thus in <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-TIME">time</a> be illustrated or mitigated; and the effect of doubtful remedies may be ascertained by experiments on the inferior animals. For, though there are a few instances of different effects following the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EXHIBITION">exhibition</a> of the same medicines in man and animals; yet, on the whole, the analogy is nearly as complete with respect to remedies as diseases (B). It will appear, from what has been said, that the reasoning, and much of the treatment, in the diseases of animals must be nearly the same as in man, and, of course, that the veterinary practitioner will <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-GAIN">gain</a> much by acquiring a knowledge of human medicine. Were the practitioners in farriery generally instructed in the principles of medicine, little more would be required, in a treatise on farriery, than to point out the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFERENCE">difference</a> in the structure and functions of domestic animals, to describe the diseases peculiar to them, and to mark the varieties that it is necessary to observe in the treatment of <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DISEASE">disease</a> and the administration of remedies. But, as many of these gentlemen have not the opportunity of attending medical lectures, and most of them have not received an <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-EDUCATION">education</a> that would enable them to understand the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LANGUAGE">language</a> in which medical writings are usually composed; it becomes necessary in a treatise of this kind to accommodate the language to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-TASTE">taste</a> and capacity of general readers, and to introduce much that will be found in other <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-ARTICLES">articles</a> on subjects connected with medicine. To prevent repetition, as much as possible, and to avoid swelling this article to a greater length than is necessary, we shall, however, where the similarity of the subject will admit of it, occasionally refer to some of the medical articles in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DICTIONARY">dictionary</a>. The successful practice of farriery, like that of medicine in general, requires that the practitioner should possess a considerable share of knowledge. It is not sufficient to have been <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LONG">long</a> in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-HABIT">habit</a> of managing the veterinary horses and cattle; this indeed, to a person of a strong mind, and attentive observation, will furnish a considerable <a class="xref" href="vol15.html#article-NUMBER">number</a> of facts, with respect to the symptoms and progress of the diseases to which domestic animals are subject. But, to mark the minute differences between such as resemble each other, to investigate their causes, and to contrive a rational <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-MODE">mode</a> of treatment, requires a much greater share of abilities, and much more extensive information, than we can expect to find among grooms and shepherds, or falls to the <a class="xref" href="../1842/vol13.html#article-LOT">lot</a> of most of those, who call themselves farriers and cattle-doctors. It must be obvious to every thinking mind, that no Anatomy practice either in medicine or farriery can be rational, but such as is founded on a comprehensive knowledge of the structure and functions of those animals, the treatment of whose diseases is the object of that practice. The first thing, therefore, necessary to the veterinary practitioner is, to acquire some idea of the anatomical structure of the domestic animals. We have already, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-SECOND">second</a> part of the article Anatomy, given a general account of the structure of <a class="xref" href="vol17.html#article-QUADRUPEDS">quadrupeds</a>; and in exemplifying this, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-CHAPTER">chapter</a> on the anatomy of a dog, we pointed out the most striking peculiarities that are to be found in this animal; as we have done with respect to ruminating animals, viz. the cow and sheep, in the succeeding chapter of that part. To that article we must refer our readers for the anatomical part of our subject, as far as relates to the ox, the sheep, and the dog. It will naturally be expected, that a <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DESCRIPTION">description</a> of the structure of the horse should be given in this article; but this description must, in general, be concise, as the <a class="xref" href="vol14.html#article-NATURE">nature</a> of our <a class="xref" href="vol16.html#article-PLAN">plan</a> prevents us from enlarging on the subject, excepting in those parts where a pretty minute knowledge appears to be necessary. Those who wish to study the anatomy of the horse minutely, may consult Vitet's Medicine Veterinaire, tom. i.; Blaine's Outlines, and Stubb's elegant <a class="xref" href="vol20.html#article-WORK">work</a> on the anatomy of the horse. The practitioner should take every opportunity of inspecting the bodies of those animals that die of diseases, which are very important, or which are not very well understood. Morbid affections often throw considerable <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-LIGHT">light</a> on the nature and treatment of diseases; and it fortunately happens, that with respect to domestic animals, these affections are very easy, and are not obstructed by those absurd prejudices, which, especially in this <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-COUNTRY">country</a>, are opposed to the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-DIFFUSION">diffusion</a> of human bodies. In treating of the diseases of domestic animals, in (B) One of the most remarkable <a class="xref" href="vol5.html#article-CASES">cases</a> of anomaly in the effect of remedies is that of arsenic, which, in the <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-QUANTITY">quantity</a> of a few grains will prove a deadly <a class="xref" href="vol0.html#article-POISON">poison</a> to man and most animals, but may be given with impunity to horses to the amount of two drams or more. The story of the different effects of <a class="xref" href="vol2.html#article-ANTIMONY">antimony</a>, on hogs and monkeys, is well known. See Antimony.
